children.title: Cycle Route Objects
children.top_down_role: Closed tour objects represented as cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Route Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic cycle routes in finite simple directed or undirected routing networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple undirected graph, or let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite simple directed graph. A cycle route is a finite sequence \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) such that \(v_k=v_0\), every \(e_i\) joins \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\) in the permitted direction, and \(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\) are pairwise distinct, where \(k\ge 3\) in the undirected case and \(k\ge 2\) in the directed case. Its incidence vector is \(x^R\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) or \(x^R\in\{0,1\}^{A}\), with \(x^R_e=1\) exactly when \(R\) uses edge or arc \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle route is a closed, direction-feasible route that repeats no vertex except its coincident start and end. In a simple graph it has at least three edges when undirected and at least two arcs when directed; its binary incidence vector identifies the edges or arcs it uses.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph or finite simple digraph.
In the directed case, every traversal respects arc orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is a simple closed route, and \(x^R\) is its binary edge- or arc-incidence vector.

children.title: Path Route Objects
children.top_down_role: Open route objects represented as paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Route Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple graph-theoretic routes with specified, possibly distinct endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, or let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph. For vertices \(s,t\in V\), a path route from \(s\) to \(t\) is a finite sequence \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) such that \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), every \(e_i\) joins \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\) in the permitted direction, and \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\) are pairwise distinct. The zero-edge route is permitted exactly when \(s=t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path route is a direction-feasible, vertex-simple route between specified endpoints, including the zero-edge route when both endpoints coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph.
\(s,t\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is a simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) route.

children.title: Route Collections
children.top_down_role: Solutions represented by sets or multisets of routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Route Collections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite indexed families of feasible route objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a specified class of feasible path or cycle routes in a routing graph. A route collection is a finite indexed family \(\mathbf R=(R_i)_{i\in I}\in\mathcal R^I\), where \(I\) is a finite index set. Repeated routes are allowed unless distinctness is imposed separately. Its aggregate traversal vector is \(x(\mathbf R)=\sum_{i\in I}x^{R_i}\); hence \(x(\mathbf R)_e\) counts how many member routes traverse edge or arc \(e\). Coverage, disjointness, capacity, and fleet-size requirements are additional constraints on \(\mathbf R\), not part of the collection definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A route collection is a finite indexed family of feasible routes whose summed incidence vector records aggregate edge or arc usage.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is a class of feasible routes.
\(I\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf R\in\mathcal R^I\) and \(x(\mathbf R)=\sum_{i\in I}x^{R_i}\).

children.title: Cycle-to-Path Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences between closed-tour and open-route representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-to-Path Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depot splitting converts rooted cycles into fixed-terminal paths and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a digraph with distinguished vertex \(d\). Form \(G'\) by replacing \(d\) with vertices \(d^+\) and \(d^-\), redirecting every arc \((d,v)\) to \((d^+,v)\), every arc \((v,d)\) to \((v,d^-)\), and preserving all other arcs and their costs. Cutting a simple directed cycle through \(d\) at \(d\) yields a simple \(d^+\)-to-\(d^-\) path in \(G'\). Identifying \(d^+\) and \(d^-\) reverses this operation. These maps are mutually inverse and preserve the used-arc multiset and total additive cost under the redirection correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting a depot into departure and arrival copies bijectively converts depot-containing cycles into paths while preserving additive route cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite digraph with depot \(d\).
Route cost is additive over arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{simple cycles through }d\}\leftrightarrow\{\text{simple }d^+\text{-to-}d^-\text{ paths in }G'\}\) cost-preservingly.

notation.meaning: departure and arrival copies of the depot

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The depot-splitting correspondence is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as a representation, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the asserted bijection and cost preservation.

children.title: Depot-Rooted Routes
children.top_down_role: Routes anchored at a designated depot.

knowledge_statements.title: Depot-Rooted Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routes anchored at a designated depot, without requiring return unless stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) or \(G=(V,A)\) be a routing graph with a designated depot \(d\in V\). A depot-rooted route is a feasible route \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) whose initial vertex is \(v_0=d\). It is returning when \(v_k=d\) and nonreturning when \(v_k\ne d\). Thus depot-rootedness specifies the origin only; closure, terminal choice, customer coverage, and resource feasibility are separate properties unless included in the ambient feasible-route class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depot-rooted route begins at a designated depot; it may return to that depot or terminate elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite routing graph.
\(d\in V\) is the designated depot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is depot-rooted exactly when \(v_0=d\).

children.title: Open Routes
children.top_down_role: Routes whose terminal endpoint need not return to the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Open Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint regime for routes whose terminal differs from their origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a routing graph and let \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) be a feasible route with \(k\ge 1\). The route \(R\) is open if \(v_k\ne v_0\). Consequently, its two endpoint occurrences represent distinct vertices, although either endpoint may be prescribed, selected from an admissible terminal set, or left free by a surrounding optimization model. Openness concerns only endpoint equality and does not by itself require vertex simplicity or prohibit repeated internal vertices or edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open route has different initial and terminal vertices; endpoint eligibility and internal repetition are governed by separate constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite routing graph.
\(R\) is a feasible route with at least one edge or arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is open if and only if \(v_k\ne v_0\).

children.title: Closed Routes
children.top_down_role: Routes that return to their prescribed origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint regime for routes returning to their initial vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a routing graph and let \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) be a feasible route with \(k\ge 1\). The route \(R\) is closed if \(v_k=v_0\). Closedness imposes equality of the initial and terminal vertices but does not alone imply that \(R\) is a simple cycle: internal vertices or edges may repeat unless the ambient route class forbids repetition. If \(v_0\) is a designated depot, \(R\) is also a returning depot-rooted route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed route ends where it begins, but it need not be a simple cycle unless repetition is separately prohibited.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite routing graph.
\(R\) is a feasible route with at least one edge or arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is closed if and only if \(v_k=v_0\).

children.title: Distinct-Terminal Routes
children.top_down_role: Routes with separately prescribed start and terminal locations.

knowledge_statements.title: Distinct-Terminal Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routes constrained to start and finish at two prescribed distinct terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) or \(G=(V,A)\) be a routing graph, and fix terminals \(s,t\in V\) with \(s\ne t\). A distinct-terminal route is a feasible route \(R=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) satisfying \(v_0=s\) and \(v_k=t\). In a directed graph, each arc is traversed in its orientation. The terminal distinction makes every such route open, while simplicity, permitted intermediate terminals, and resource restrictions remain properties of the ambient feasible-route class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distinct-terminal route runs from one prescribed terminal to another prescribed, different terminal and is therefore open.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite routing graph.
\(s,t\in V\) and \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), and hence \(v_k\ne v_0\).

children.title: Single-Route Objects
children.top_down_role: Solutions represented by one route.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Route Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing solutions represented by exactly one feasible route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the feasible-route class of a routing instance. A single-route object is a route collection \(\mathbf R=(R_i)_{i\in I}\) with \(I=\{1\}\) and \(R_1\in\mathcal R\). Equivalently, it may be identified with the sole route \(R_1\). Any required customers, edges, demands, or services must therefore be covered by that one route, subject to the instance's endpoint, capacity, duration, and other feasibility constraints. The aggregate traversal vector equals \(x(\mathbf R)=x^{R_1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-route object is a feasible route collection containing exactly one route, which alone must satisfy all imposed service requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is the feasible-route class of the instance.

children.title: Multiple-Route Objects
children.top_down_role: Solutions represented by several coordinated routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Route Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing solutions represented by two or more feasible routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the feasible-route class of a routing instance. A multiple-route object is a finite route collection \(\mathbf R=(R_i)_{i\in I}\in\mathcal R^I\) with \(|I|\ge 2\). Its aggregate traversal vector is \(x(\mathbf R)=\sum_{i\in I}x^{R_i}\). Customer or edge coverage is evaluated across the collection, while routewise requirements are imposed on every \(R_i\). The definition does not assign routes to physical vehicles and does not require the member routes to be mutually distinct or disjoint unless the model states such constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-route object contains at least two feasible routes, with coverage assessed collectively and routewise constraints assessed separately.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is the feasible-route class of the instance.
\(I\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf R\in\mathcal R^I\), \(|I|\ge 2\), and \(x(\mathbf R)=\sum_{i\in I}x^{R_i}\).

children.title: Fleet Route Objects
children.top_down_role: Route collections coupled to vehicle assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Fleet Route Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vehicle-indexed routes coupled to vehicle availability and compatibility data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set, let \(\mathcal R_k\) be the feasible-route class for vehicle \(k\), and let \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\) indicate its use. A fleet route object is a vehicle-indexed family \(\mathbf R=(R_k)_{k\in K}\) such that \(R_k\in\mathcal R_k\) whenever \(y_k=1\), while \(R_k=\varnothing\) whenever \(y_k=0\). Its active routes are \(\{R_k:k\in K,\ y_k=1\}\), and its size is \(\sum_{k\in K}y_k\). Fleet availability, vehicle-route compatibility, and any cross-route service constraints are imposed on this indexed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fleet route object assigns a feasible route or inactivity to each available vehicle, retaining vehicle identity and compatibility constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite vehicle set.
Each vehicle \(k\) has a specified feasible-route class \(\mathcal R_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_k=1\Rightarrow R_k\in\mathcal R_k\) and \(y_k=0\Rightarrow R_k=\varnothing\) for every \(k\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vehicle-indexed route-and-inactivity representation fits the fleet-route leaf, but no source or locator supports the chosen formalization, including the empty-route convention and use indicators.

children.title: Homogeneous Fleet Objects
children.top_down_role: Fleet representations with interchangeable vehicle types.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Fleet Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fleet route objects whose vehicles share common routing attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set. A homogeneous fleet object is a fleet route object for which all vehicles share one feasible-route class \(\mathcal R\) and the same route-dependent parameter data. Formally, \(\mathcal R_k=\mathcal R\) for every \(k\in K\), and every parameter entering route feasibility or route cost is invariant under replacing one vehicle index by another. Consequently, any route feasible for one vehicle is feasible for every vehicle, and permuting vehicle labels in a feasible fleet assignment preserves feasibility and objective value. Vehicle availability indicators may still differ without changing route capabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous fleet has interchangeable vehicle capabilities: relabeling vehicles preserves route feasibility and route-dependent cost.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite vehicle set.
Vehicle-specific fixed availability may be modeled separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_k=\mathcal R\) for all \(k\in K\), and vehicle-label permutations preserve feasibility and route-dependent objective value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim strengthens common route-capability homogeneity into invariance of every route-dependent parameter and objective value under all vehicle-label permutations. No cited source supports that exact formulation or its availability qualification.

children.title: Heterogeneous Fleet Objects
children.top_down_role: Fleet representations with differentiated vehicle types.

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Fleet Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fleet whose vehicle capabilities or operating data vary by type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set and \(T\) a finite type set. A heterogeneous fleet object is a tuple \(\mathcal F=(K,T,\tau,(Q_t,c^t,A_t)_{t\in T})\), where \(\tau:K\to T\) assigns each vehicle a type, \(Q_t\) is its capacity, \(c^t\) its route-cost function, and \(A_t\) its admissible-service set. The fleet is heterogeneous when two used types differ in at least one of these data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heterogeneous fleet contains typed vehicles whose capacities, costs, or service permissions are not all identical.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) and \(T\) are finite and nonempty.
\(\tau(k)\) is defined for every \(k\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists t,u\in\tau(K): (Q_t,c^t,A_t)\ne(Q_u,c^u,A_u)\).

notation.meaning: type-dependent capacity, cost, and admissible services

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the fleet-taxonomy leaf and is mathematically plausible, but the type-dependent tuple is unsupported by any cited routing source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Mandatory Service
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes requiring service for every designated item.

knowledge_statements.title: Mandatory Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the all-targets-required service-obligation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite set of service targets and let \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether target \(s\) is served by the selected routes. A mandatory-service regime requires every target to be served, so feasibility includes \(y_s=1\) for every \(s\in S\). Equivalently, the served set must equal \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every designated service target must be served by the routing solution.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is the designated finite target set.
\(y_s=1\) exactly when target \(s\) receives its prescribed service.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_s=1\quad\forall s\in S\).

notation.meaning: binary service indicator for target s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mandatory-service definition is precise and fits the terminal container, but no source reference is supplied.

children.title: Optional Service
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes permitting selection among service candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines service targets whose selection is determined by the optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite target set and \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate service of \(s\). Service is optional when feasibility does not impose \(y_s=1\) for every \(s\); instead, each \(y_s\) may be selected by the optimizer, commonly through a reward \(p_s y_s\) or rejection penalty \(p_s(1-y_s)\) in the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimizer may accept or reject each target, usually trading service rewards or rejection penalties against routing cost.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
\(y_s=1\) exactly when target \(s\) is served.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall s\in S\), with no universal constraint \(y_s=1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard optional-service or prize-collecting convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optional-service definition and reward/penalty interpretation fit the leaf, but they lack a cited authoritative source and specific locator.

children.title: Quota Service
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes governed by an aggregate service threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines service selection subject to a minimum aggregate coverage requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite target set, let \(w_s\ge 0\) be the credited service weight of target \(s\in S\), let \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether \(s\) is served, and let \(Q\) satisfy \(0<Q\le\sum_{s\in S}w_s\). A quota-service regime requires \(\sum_{s\in S}w_s y_s\ge Q\). This aggregate constraint does not impose \(y_s=1\) separately for every \(s\), although particular data may make full service necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected routes must attain a prescribed total service weight. The quota is aggregate rather than a separate requirement for every target, though some data may still force all targets to be served.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
\(w_s\ge0\) for every \(s\in S\).
\(0<Q\le\sum_{s\in S}w_s\).
\(y_s=1\) exactly when target \(s\) is served.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{s\in S}w_s y_s\ge Q\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative service weight of target s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quota-service constraint with aggregate rather than per-target obligation

children.title: Mixed-Obligation Service
children.top_down_role: Instances combining compulsory items with selectable items.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Obligation Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines one instance containing at least two service-obligation regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the finite target set be partitioned as \(S=S_M\mathbin{\dot\cup}S_O\mathbin{\dot\cup}S_Q\), with at least two parts nonempty, and let \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate service. Targets in \(S_M\) satisfy \(y_s=1\); targets in \(S_O\) are individually optional; and quota targets satisfy \(\sum_{s\in S_Q}w_s y_s\ge Q\), where \(w_s\ge0\). If \(S_Q=\varnothing\), set \(Q=0\); otherwise require \(0<Q\le\sum_{s\in S_Q}w_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One routing instance combines at least two of mandatory, optional, and quota-governed service classes; an absent quota class contributes no quota constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(S_M,S_O,S_Q\) are finite and pairwise disjoint, and their union is \(S\).
At least two of \(S_M,S_O,S_Q\) are nonempty.
\(w_s\ge0\) for every \(s\in S_Q\).
If \(S_Q=\varnothing\), then \(Q=0\); otherwise \(0<Q\le\sum_{s\in S_Q}w_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_s=1\ \forall s\in S_M,\qquad \sum_{s\in S_Q}w_s y_s\ge Q\).

notation.meaning: mandatory, optional, and quota target classes
nonnegative weight of quota target s
quota threshold, zero when the quota class is empty

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combination of mandatory, optional, and quota service regimes with explicit empty-class convention

children.title: Service-Target Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Arc-service models are represented only as an interface to the separate arc-routing chapter.

children.title: Node Service
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around service at individual vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Node Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines service whose target is a vertex of the routing graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed routing graph, let \(S\subseteq V\) be the service-vertex set, let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set, and let \(R_k\) be the vertex sequence of vehicle \(k\in K\). For \(v\in S\), let \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\) indicate service. Then \(v\) is served exactly when some vehicle route visits \(v\) and that vehicle is assigned to execute the prescribed service at \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A service target is a graph vertex, and it is served when an assigned vehicle route visits the vertex and performs its prescribed service.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(S\subseteq V\).
\(K\) is a finite vehicle set.
\(R_k\) is the vertex sequence of vehicle \(k\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_v=1\iff\exists k\in K:\ v\in R_k\text{ and }v\text{ is assigned for service to }k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard node-routing service target with explicit vehicle domain

children.title: Cluster Service
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around service choices within vertex groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines service of a target represented by a set of eligible vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a routing graph and \(\mathcal C\subseteq2^V\) a finite family of nonempty clusters. For visit indicators \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\), a cluster \(C\in\mathcal C\) is served when at least one eligible vertex in \(C\) is visited and serviced. Its indicator therefore satisfies \(y_C=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{v\in C}x_v\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cluster is served when a route services at least one eligible vertex belonging to that cluster.
assumptions_latex: Every \(C\in\mathcal C\) is a nonempty subset of \(V\).
\(x_v=1\) exactly when vertex \(v\) is visited and serviced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_C=1\iff\sum_{v\in C}x_v\ge1\quad\forall C\in\mathcal C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cluster-service definition is internally consistent and fits the service-target taxonomy, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Transportation-Request Service
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around origin-destination service requests.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation-Request Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines direct transportation-request service in which one vehicle carries a request from its origin to its destination without transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed routing graph and \(K\) a finite vehicle set. A transportation request is a tuple \(r=(o_r,d_r,q_r)\), where \(o_r,d_r\in V\), \(o_r\ne d_r\), and \(q_r>0\). Under direct service, request \(r\) is served by vehicle \(k\in K\) when the route of \(k\) visits \(o_r\) before \(d_r\), picks up \(q_r\) at \(o_r\), carries it without transfer, and delivers it at \(d_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under direct transportation-request service, one vehicle picks up the request quantity at its origin and later delivers it at its destination without transferring it to another vehicle.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed routing graph.
\(K\) is a finite vehicle set.
\(o_r,d_r\in V\), \(o_r\ne d_r\), and \(q_r>0\).
Each vehicle route has a position map \(\operatorname{pos}_k\) on its visited vertices.
Transfers between vehicles are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_r=1\iff\exists k\in K:\operatorname{pos}_k(o_r)<\operatorname{pos}_k(d_r)\text{ and }k\text{ transports }q_r\text{ from }o_r\text{ to }d_r\).

notation.meaning: origin-destination transportation request and its quantity
position of visited vertex v on vehicle k's route

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct pickup-and-delivery request semantics with explicit domains

children.title: Arc-Service Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary linking customer-routing models to the separate arc-routing chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Service Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the linkage between route traversal and service of an arc target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed routing graph, let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set, and let \(S_A\subseteq A\) be the service-arc set. For \(a\in A\) and \(k\in K\), let \(x_a^k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) count traversals of \(a\) by vehicle \(k\), and for \(a\in S_A\), let \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\) indicate service. The arc-service interface requires \(y_a\le\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\); if every traversal of a service arc performs service, then \(y_a\) equals the indicator that the total traversal count is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A service arc can be declared served only if some vehicle traverses it. Models may distinguish traversal from service; when every traversal performs service, the service indicator equals the positive-traversal indicator.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(K\) is a finite vehicle set.
\(S_A\subseteq A\).
\(x_a^k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_a\le\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\quad\forall a\in S_A\).

notation.meaning: number of traversals of arc a by vehicle k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard arc-routing traversal-service linkage with explicit variable domains

children.title: Single-Visit Service
children.top_down_role: Service regimes restricted to one visit per service object.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Visit Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines mandatory service completed in exactly one complete service occurrence per target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite mandatory-target set, let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set, and let \(z_{sk}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that vehicle \(k\in K\) performs the complete prescribed service of target \(s\in S\). A single-visit service regime permits neither division nor repetition of that service and requires \(\sum_{k\in K}z_{sk}=1\) for every \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each mandatory target's complete service is performed once by exactly one vehicle.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(K\) are finite.
Every \(s\in S\) is mandatory.
\(z_{sk}=1\) denotes complete, not partial, service.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}z_{sk}=1\quad\forall s\in S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard unsplit single-service convention with repaired LaTeX

children.title: Split Service
children.top_down_role: Service regimes permitting an obligation to be divided across visits.

knowledge_statements.title: Split Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a regime in which a target's required quantity may be divided among multiple service occurrences or vehicles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite service-target set and \(K\) a finite vehicle set. For each \(s\in S\), let \(q_s>0\) be its required quantity and let \(d_{sk}\ge0\) be the quantity served at \(s\) by vehicle \(k\in K\). A split-service regime requires \(\sum_{k\in K}d_{sk}=q_s\) for every \(s\in S\) and permits more than one vehicle or service occurrence to contribute a positive amount, subject to vehicle and route feasibility. A feasible solution is actually split at \(s\) only when at least two distinct contributions are positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target's required quantity may be partitioned among multiple feasible service contributions that sum to the full requirement; a particular solution is split only when it uses at least two positive contributions.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(K\) are finite.
\(q_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\).
\(d_{sk}\ge0\) for every \(s\in S\) and \(k\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}d_{sk}=q_s\quad\forall s\in S\), with multiple positive contributions permitted.

notation.meaning: quantity served at s by vehicle k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: split-service convention distinguishing permission from an actually split solution

children.title: Repeated Service
children.top_down_role: Service regimes requiring or permitting recurring visits.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Service
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact-frequency repeated service over a finite planning horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite target set, \(K\) a finite vehicle set, and \(H\) a finite period set. For each \(s\in S\), let \(m_s\ge2\) be an integer prescribed service frequency, and let \(z_{skt}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate a service occurrence for target \(s\) by vehicle \(k\in K\) in period \(t\in H\). An exact-frequency repeated-service regime requires \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{t\in H}z_{skt}=m_s\) for every \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each target receives exactly its prescribed number of distinct service occurrences over the planning horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(S\), \(K\), and \(H\) are finite.
\(m_s\in\mathbb Z\) and \(m_s\ge2\) for every \(s\in S\).
\(z_{skt}\in\{0,1\}\) records one service occurrence for the indexed vehicle and period.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{t\in H}z_{skt}=m_s\quad\forall s\in S\).

notation.meaning: exact required service frequency of target s
service-occurrence indicator for target s, vehicle k, and period t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact-frequency repeated-service routing convention with explicit index domains

children.title: Visit-Multiplicity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model boundaries created by changing visit-count or service-divisibility restrictions.

assumptions_latex: A finite customer set \(V\), vehicle set \(K\), and feasible route family \(\mathcal R\) are given.
Each customer \(i\in V\) has prescribed visit bounds \(0\le \ell_i\le u_i\), with \(u_i\in\mathbb Z_+\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A routing solution satisfies the visit-multiplicity boundaries exactly when \(\ell_i\le m_i\le u_i\) for every \(i\in V\).

notation.meaning: number of service occurrences at customer i across all selected vehicle routes
lower and upper permitted visit multiplicities for customer i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers single, split, and repeated service through customer-specific integer visit bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each customer \(i\in V\), let \(m_i\) be the total number of service occurrences across the selected routes. Given bounds \(\ell_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) and \(u_i\in\mathbb Z_+\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(\ell_i\le u_i\), the visit-multiplicity condition is \[\ell_i\le m_i\le u_i\qquad(i\in V).\] The choices \(\ell_i=u_i=1\), \(1\le m_i<+\infty\), and \(0\le m_i<+\infty\) respectively encode mandatory single visits, mandatory service allowing repeated visits, and optional service allowing repeated visits. Additional delivered-quantity constraints determine whether multiple visits constitute split service.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Customer-specific integer lower and upper bounds on total service occurrences distinguish mandatory single visits, repeated visits, optional visits, and, with quantity constraints, split service.
knowledge_statements.title: Visit-Multiplicity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the Visit-Multiplicity Boundaries leaf, but the record supplies no citation with an inspectable locator. A routing-specific source is required to support the claimed classification of single, repeated, optional, and split service regimes.

children.title: Routing-Cost Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on aggregate travel or operating cost.

assumptions_latex: A finite directed graph \(G=(N,A)\) and vehicle set \(K\) are given.
Each arc \((i,j)\in A\) has vehicle-dependent traversal cost \(c_{ij}^k\), and \(\mathcal X\) is the feasible routing set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum-routing-cost solution is any \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X} C(x)\).

notation.meaning: binary indicator that vehicle k traverses arc (i,j)
cost of vehicle k traversing arc (i,j)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines additive monetary or generalized traversal cost over feasible fleet routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible routing vector \(x\in\mathcal X\), define its additive routing cost by \[C(x)=\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}^k x_{ij}^k.\] A routing-cost objective minimizes \(C(x)\) over \(\mathcal X\). Fixed vehicle-use costs \(f_k\) may be included by introducing usage indicators \(y_k\) and replacing the objective by \(C(x,y)=\sum_{k\in K}f_k y_k+\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}^k x_{ij}^k\). Thus an optimizer belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in\mathcal X}C(x,y)\), with the first form obtained when fixed costs vanish or are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Routing-cost objectives minimize the sum of traversal costs, optionally augmented by fixed costs for vehicles used, over all feasible fleet routes.
knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Cost Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive objective is standard and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the routing formulation or its fixed-vehicle-cost extension. The listed local network-flow sources are not attached to the record and do not by themselves establish this vehicle-routing statement.

children.title: Route-Duration Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on elapsed route or schedule duration.

assumptions_latex: A finite vehicle set \(K\) is given.
Travel times \(t_{ij}^k\ge 0\) and service times \(s_i^k\ge 0\) are specified.
The ordered route \(r_k\) of every used vehicle \(k\in K\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Route-duration objectives minimize a specified nondecreasing aggregate \(\Phi((T_k)_{k\in K})\), such as total duration or makespan, over feasible route collections.

notation.meaning: ordered route assigned to vehicle k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes sum-of-durations and longest-route-duration objectives; waiting is included only under an elapsed-time duration convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set. If route \(r_k=(v_0^k,v_1^k,\ldots,v_{q_k}^k)\) is assigned to vehicle \(k\in K\), define its active travel-and-service duration by \[T_k=\sum_{h=0}^{q_k-1}t_{v_h^k v_{h+1}^k}^k+\sum_{h=1}^{q_k-1}s_{v_h^k}^k.\] A route-duration objective minimizes a specified nondecreasing aggregate \(\Phi((T_k)_{k\in K})\) over feasible route collections. Two standard choices are total duration, \(\Phi((T_k)_{k\in K})=\sum_{k\in K}T_k\), and makespan, \(\Phi((T_k)_{k\in K})=\max_{k\in K}T_k\). Waiting time is included in \(T_k\) only when the adopted duration convention counts elapsed schedule time rather than active travel-and-service time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route-duration objectives minimize a specified nondecreasing aggregate of vehicle route times, such as total duration or the longest route duration; the duration convention determines whether waiting is counted.
knowledge_statements.title: Route-Duration Objectives

children.title: Route-Balance Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on disparities across routes or vehicles.

assumptions_latex: A finite vehicle set \(K\) is given, with route workload \(w_k\in\mathbb R\) for each vehicle.
A reference workload \(\bar w\) or a pairwise dispersion measure is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route-balance optimizer minimizes a nonnegative dispersion functional that vanishes exactly under the selected equality convention.

notation.meaning: mean workload across the vehicles included in balancing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance may concern distance, duration, demand, stops, or another explicitly chosen route workload.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_k\) denote the workload of vehicle \(k\in K\), and let \(\bar w=|K|^{-1}\sum_{k\in K}w_k\). A route-balance objective minimizes a dispersion functional \(B(w)\) over feasible route collections. Standard examples are \[B_{\mathrm{range}}(w)=\max_{k\in K}w_k-\min_{k\in K}w_k,\qquad B_1(w)=\sum_{k\in K}|w_k-\bar w|,\] and \(B_2(w)=\sum_{k\in K}(w_k-\bar w)^2\). Each is nonnegative and equals zero when all workloads included in the comparison are equal. Whether unused vehicles belong to \(K\) must be fixed before evaluating balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route-balance objectives minimize a stated dispersion of vehicle workloads, with the workload measure and treatment of unused vehicles fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Route-Balance Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dispersion objectives are internally consistent and the definition content kind fits the leaf. No source with a specific routing locator is cited, however, so the choice and interpretation of balance measures remain unsupported candidate knowledge.

children.title: Cost-Duration Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes exposing tradeoffs between monetary cost and elapsed time.

assumptions_latex: The feasible routing set \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty.
Every \(x\in\mathcal X\) has finite routing cost \(C(x)\) and duration measure \(T(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Supported tradeoffs minimize \(\lambda C+(1-\lambda)T\); constrained formulations recover all Pareto-efficient points under suitable thresholds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses weighted-sum and epsilon-constraint representations of bicriteria cost-duration routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(C(x)\) be routing cost and \(T(x)\) a duration criterion. A weighted cost-duration tradeoff solves \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\ \lambda C(x)+(1-\lambda)T(x),\qquad 0\le\lambda\le1.\] An epsilon-constraint representation instead solves \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}C(x)\) subject to \(T(x)\le\tau\), or symmetrically minimizes \(T(x)\) subject to \(C(x)\le\kappa\). A feasible solution \(x^*\) is Pareto efficient when no \(x\in\mathcal X\) satisfies \(C(x)\le C(x^*)\) and \(T(x)\le T(x^*)\) with at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-duration tradeoffs use weighted sums or criterion bounds; Pareto efficiency excludes any feasible route plan that improves one criterion without worsening the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Duration Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-sum, epsilon-constraint, and Pareto-efficiency formulations are coherent and representation is the correct content kind. No source is cited for these multiobjective claims, including the conclusion's recovery claim for constrained formulations.

children.title: Reward Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on collected value from served items.

assumptions_latex: A finite customer set \(V\) has rewards \(p_i\ge 0\).
The binary variable \(z_i\) records whether customer \(i\) receives qualifying service.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reward-optimal routing solution maximizes \(R(z)=\sum_{i\in V}p_i z_i\) over the feasible service-route set.

notation.meaning: reward obtained by qualifying service at customer i
indicator of qualifying service at customer i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines additive value collected from customers whose prescribed service condition is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each customer \(i\in V\), let \(p_i\ge0\) be its reward and let \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that the routing solution provides the service required to earn that reward. The additive reward is \[R(z)=\sum_{i\in V}p_i z_i.\] A reward objective maximizes \(R(z)\) over all jointly feasible routing and service-selection decisions. If reward depends on delivered quantity \(q_i\), the separable extension is \(R(q)=\sum_{i\in V}r_i(q_i)\), where each function \(r_i\) and its admissible quantity domain must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reward objective maximizes the total value earned from customers receiving qualifying service, with optional quantity-dependent reward functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Reward Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive reward formulation is precise and definition is appropriate for the leaf, but neither the binary-reward model nor its quantity-dependent extension has a cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Profit Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on service value net of routing cost.

assumptions_latex: Each customer \(i\in V\) has earned revenue \(p_i z_i\).
A feasible routing decision \(x\) incurs finite operating cost \(C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A profit-optimal solution maximizes \(P(x,z)=\sum_{i\in V}p_i z_i-C(x)\).

notation.meaning: indicator that customer i earns its revenue
operating cost of routing decision x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Net profit equals collected service revenue minus route-dependent and fixed operating costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that customer \(i\in V\) receives revenue-earning service, let \(p_i\ge0\) be that revenue, and let \(C(x)\) be the total operating cost of feasible routing decision \(x\). The profit objective is \[\max_{(x,z)\in\mathcal X}\ P(x,z),\qquad P(x,z)=\sum_{i\in V}p_i z_i-C(x).\] The feasible set \(\mathcal X\) must link each \(z_i\) to the corresponding service decision. Equivalently, profit maximization minimizes \(C(x)-\sum_{i\in V}p_i z_i\) over the same feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Profit objectives maximize collected customer revenue minus route operating cost, with service indicators linked to the routes that earn revenue.
knowledge_statements.title: Profit Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net-revenue-minus-cost formulation is mathematically coherent and fits a definition of profit objectives. It lacks a routing-specific citation supporting the formulation and the required service-route linkage.

children.title: Penalty Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on costs associated with omitted or delayed service.

assumptions_latex: Each customer \(i\in V\) has nonservice penalty \(\pi_i\ge0\).
The binary variable \(z_i\) equals one precisely when customer \(i\) receives qualifying service.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A penalty objective minimizes \(P(z)=\sum_{i\in V}\pi_i(1-z_i)\), possibly together with routing cost.

notation.meaning: penalty for failing to serve customer i
indicator of qualifying service at customer i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers penalties for omitted service; lateness or shortage penalties require corresponding violation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every customer \(i\in V\), let \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate qualifying service and let \(\pi_i\ge0\) be the penalty for omission. The additive nonservice penalty is \[P(z)=\sum_{i\in V}\pi_i(1-z_i).\] A penalty objective minimizes \(P(z)\) over feasible routing and selection decisions, or minimizes \(C(x)+P(z)\) when routing cost is also charged. More general soft constraints use nonnegative violation variables \(v_i\) and specified penalty functions \(g_i\), giving \(P(v)=\sum_{i\in V}g_i(v_i)\); feasibility constraints must define each violation quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty objectives minimize charges for omitted service or quantified constraint violations, either alone or added to routing cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The omission-penalty model and soft-violation extension fit the leaf and are stated consistently, but no authoritative routing source with a specific locator is attached.

children.title: Coverage Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives centered on the extent or quality of service coverage.

assumptions_latex: A finite demand set \(D\) has nonnegative weights \(w_j\).
A finite service-location set \(V\) is linked to demand by coverage indicators \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\).
Each activation variable \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) is linked by the routing constraints to actual service at location \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A maximum-coverage routing solution maximizes \(\sum_{j\in D}w_jy_j\) subject to exact coverage links and routing feasibility.

notation.meaning: indicator that demand point j is covered
indicator that service at i covers demand point j
indicator that service location i is visited or activated

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage is induced by routed service locations through a specified binary incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a finite set of demand points, let \(V\) be a finite set of candidate service locations, let \(w_j\ge0\) be the weight of each \(j\in D\), and let \(a_{ij}=1\) exactly when service at \(i\in V\) covers \(j\in D\). With activation variables \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\), exact binary coverage indicators \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) satisfy \[y_j\le\sum_{i\in V}a_{ij}z_i\qquad(j\in D)\] and \[y_j\ge a_{ij}z_i\qquad(i\in V,\ j\in D).\] A coverage objective maximizes \(\sum_{j\in D}w_jy_j\) over these constraints and the routing constraints linking each \(z_i\) to actual service at \(i\). For unit weights, the objective maximizes the number of covered demand points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage objectives maximize the weighted demand covered by visited service locations, using exact incidence constraints that make a demand indicator equal to one precisely when at least one activated location covers it.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Objectives

children.title: Service-Selection Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relations among collected value, omission cost, and route expenditure.

assumptions_latex: The jointly feasible route-selection set \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty.
Each feasible pair \((x,z)\) has routing cost \(C(x)\) and selected-service value \(R(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Service selection is governed by a value-cost scalarization, a budget constraint, or Pareto efficiency in \((C,-R)\).

notation.meaning: relative weight assigned to routing cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the conflict between serving valuable customers and consuming routing resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x,z)\in\mathcal X\) couple feasible routes \(x\) with selected services \(z\), let \(C(x)\) be routing cost, and let \(R(z)\) be service value. A scalarized service-selection tradeoff solves \[\max_{(x,z)\in\mathcal X}\ R(z)-\lambda C(x),\qquad \lambda\ge0.\] A budgeted representation maximizes \(R(z)\) subject to \(C(x)\le B\). A feasible pair \((x^*,z^*)\) is Pareto efficient when no feasible \((x,z)\) has \(C(x)\le C(x^*)\) and \(R(z)\ge R(z^*)\), with at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Service-selection tradeoffs balance collected value against routing cost through scalarization, a cost budget, or Pareto efficiency.
knowledge_statements.title: Service-Selection Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalarized, budgeted, and Pareto representations are coherent, and representation is the correct content kind for this tradeoff leaf. No source with a specific locator supports the service-selection formulation.

children.title: Capacity Resources
children.top_down_role: Load or carrying resources that constrain route feasibility.

assumptions_latex: A finite vehicle set \(K\) is given, and every vehicle \(k\in K\) has scalar capacity \(Q_k\ge0\).
Each service action on vehicle \(k\) changes its load by a specified signed amount, and route order is fixed by the routing decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route is capacity feasible exactly when an initial load and a load trajectory exist that satisfy load propagation and remain within the vehicle's bounds at every route position.

notation.meaning: load after service at position h on vehicle k's route
signed load change at route position h
number of service positions on vehicle k's route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States routewise feasibility for a single scalar load resource with pickups or deliveries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite vehicle set. For each vehicle \(k\in K\) with capacity \(Q_k\), let \(L_h^k\) be its load immediately after service at position \(h\), let \(\Delta_h^k\) be the signed load change there, and let \(q_k\) be the number of service positions on its route. Capacity feasibility requires an initial load \(L_0^k\) and subsequent loads satisfying \[L_h^k=L_{h-1}^k+\Delta_h^k,\qquad 0\le L_h^k\le Q_k\qquad(h=1,\ldots,q_k).\] For pure deliveries with customer demands \(d_i\ge0\) and a single depot loading, this reduces to \(\sum_{i\in r_k}d_i\le Q_k\). With multiple commodities, capacity bounds must be imposed componentwise or through a specified shared-capacity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity feasibility requires an initial load and a route load trajectory whose service-induced changes keep vehicle load between zero and capacity at every position.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Resources

children.title: Time Resources
children.top_down_role: Temporal budgets, horizons, or service availability regimes.

assumptions_latex: Each traversed arc has travel time \(t_{ij}\ge0\), and each serviced vertex has service time \(s_i\ge0\).
Every serviced vertex \(i\) has an allowed start-time window \([a_i,b_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route is time feasible exactly when arrival and service-start variables satisfy propagation and all applicable time-window bounds.

notation.meaning: travel time from i to j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models travel, service, waiting, and time-window consumption along an ordered route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an ordered route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_q)\). Let \(u_{v_h}\) be service-start time, \(s_{v_h}\ge0\) service duration, and \(t_{v_hv_{h+1}}\ge0\) travel time. The route is time feasible when service-start times exist satisfying \[u_{v_{h+1}}\ge u_{v_h}+s_{v_h}+t_{v_hv_{h+1}}\qquad(h=0,\ldots,q-1)\] and \(a_{v_h}\le u_{v_h}\le b_{v_h}\) at every vertex having window \([a_{v_h},b_{v_h}]\). Strict inequality in propagation represents waiting. A route-duration limit \(H\) additionally requires completion time minus departure time to be at most \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time feasibility requires service starts to respect travel-and-service propagation, customer time windows, and any route-duration limit, while permitting waiting.
knowledge_statements.title: Time Resources

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-propagation and time-window condition is coherent, all mathematical commands in the statement are delimited, and condition is the correct content kind. No vehicle-routing or scheduling source with an inspectable locator is supplied for the formulation or route-duration extension.

children.title: Energy Resources
children.top_down_role: Propulsion or battery resources coupled to route execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic additive energy consumption with optional charging and finite battery capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a route traverse arcs \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). Let \(b_0\in[0,B]\), and let \(r_i\ge 0\) be energy restored after arc \(a_i\), with \(r_i=0\) when charging is unavailable. Define the charge recursively by \(b_i=\min\{B,b_{i-1}-e_{a_i}+r_i\}\). The route satisfies the energy-resource regime if \(b_{i-1}\ge e_{a_i}\) and \(0\le b_i\le B\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), together with any prescribed bounds on charging amounts or charging locations. Thus feasibility is determined by a resource state propagated along the ordered route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Energy-feasible routes propagate battery charge along traversed arcs, never consume more charge than currently available, never exceed battery capacity, and recharge only where and by amounts permitted.
assumptions_latex: A routing instance is defined on a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with a specified depot set and feasible routes.
Each arc \(a\in A\) has energy consumption \(e_a\ge 0\); designated charging vertices may restore energy.
Each vehicle has energy capacity \(B>0\) and begins with a specified initial charge not exceeding \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route is energy-feasible precisely when its state of charge remains in \([0,B]\) after every traversal and charging event.

notation.meaning: routing graph with arc set A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resource-extension definition for energy-constrained routing

children.title: Workload Resources
children.top_down_role: Labor or duty resources allocated across routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Workload Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive route workload with per-route lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a route \(R\), define its workload by \(W(R)=\sum_{i\text{ serviced by }R}s_i+\sum_{a\text{ traversed by }R}t_a\), omitting either sum when that contribution is not modeled. A solution \((R_1,\ldots,R_k)\) satisfies its workload-resource regime when \(L_r\le W(R_r)\le U_r\) for every used vehicle \(r\). An upper bound models a maximum duty, distance, duration, or service burden; a positive lower bound may enforce minimum utilization. Workload feasibility is routewise unless additional balancing constraints couple different routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A route's workload is the sum of modeled service and traversal burdens. Every used vehicle route must satisfy its prescribed minimum and maximum workload.
assumptions_latex: A feasible routing solution consists of finitely many vehicle routes \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\).
Each serviced customer \(i\) contributes nonnegative workload \(s_i\), and each traversed arc \(a\) contributes nonnegative workload \(t_a\).
Route-specific workload bounds \(L_r\le U_r\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A routing solution is workload-feasible exactly when \(L_r\le W(R_r)\le U_r\) for every used route \(R_r\).

notation.meaning: lower and upper workload bounds for route r

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive route-resource definition for workload-constrained routing

children.title: Coupled Resource Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings where multiple resource dimensions interact.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Resource Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint feasibility for multiple route resources whose transitions or bounds interact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a route traverse \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) from initial state \(z_0\in\mathcal F\). Generate states recursively by \(z_i=F_{a_i}(z_{i-1})\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). The route satisfies a coupled resource regime if \(z_i\in\mathcal F\) at every step. Coupling is present when some component update depends on another component, or when \(\mathcal F\neq\mathcal F_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal F_p\). Consequently, checking each resource against independent scalar bounds is generally insufficient; feasibility must be tested using the joint state and its joint transition rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled resource routing propagates a vector state. Feasibility requires every joint state to satisfy constraints that may link capacity, time, energy, workload, or other resources.
assumptions_latex: Each partial route has a resource state \(z\in\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^p\).
Traversing arc \(a\) applies a specified update map \(F_a:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R^p\).
Feasible states form a specified set \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal Z\), which need not be a Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route is feasible precisely when every recursively generated state belongs to \(\mathcal F\), so nonproduct constraints encode coupling among resources.

notation.meaning: resource update associated with arc a

children.title: Single-Criterion Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around one primary objective.

assumptions_latex: The feasible routing-solution set \(X\) is nonempty.
A scalar objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is specified and is to be minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal solution set is \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar optimization definition specialized to routing
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar minimization over an otherwise arbitrary feasible routing family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-criterion routing problem is the optimization problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\), where \(X\) contains exactly the routing solutions satisfying all structural and resource constraints and \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\) assigns one scalar value to each solution. A feasible solution \(x^*\in X\) is optimal if \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Multiple operational quantities may appear inside \(f\), but the regime remains single-criterion only when their aggregation into the scalar objective is fixed before optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-criterion routing minimizes one fixed scalar objective over all feasible routing solutions; a solution is optimal when no feasible solution has a smaller value.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Criterion Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar-optimization definition is mathematically precise and fits Single-Criterion Routing, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Lexicographic Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around strictly prioritized objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact priority ordering of finitely many minimization criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u,v\in\mathbb R^p\), write \(u\prec_{\mathrm{lex}}v\) if, at the smallest index \(j\) with \(u_j\ne v_j\), one has \(u_j<v_j\). A routing solution \(x^*\in X\) is lexicographically optimal when no \(x\in X\) satisfies \(f(x)\prec_{\mathrm{lex}}f(x^*)\). Equivalently, first minimize \(f_1\) over \(X\); then minimize \(f_2\) over the resulting minimizers; continue through \(f_p\). Lower-priority improvement never compensates for deterioration in any higher-priority criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic routing minimizes criteria in strict priority order. A lower-priority gain cannot compensate for any loss in the first higher-priority criterion where two solutions differ.
assumptions_latex: The feasible routing-solution set \(X\) is nonempty.
Each solution has criterion vector \(f(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_p(x))\in\mathbb R^p\), with every component minimized.
The priority order is \(f_1,\ldots,f_p\), from highest to lowest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lexicographic optimum is any \(x^*\in X\) whose criterion vector is least under the lexicographic order.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: lexicographic vector-optimization definition specialized to routing

children.title: Multicriteria Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing organized around simultaneous evaluation of several criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicriteria Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued routing objectives before selection of a particular scalarization or efficiency concept.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multicriteria routing problem is specified by \((X,f)\), where \(X\) is the feasible routing set and \(f:X\to\mathbb R^p\) has \(p\ge 2\) components representing distinct criteria. Because the componentwise order on \(\mathbb R^p\) is partial, the data \((X,f)\) alone need not select one optimum. A complete formulation therefore specifies a solution concept or preference rule, such as Pareto efficiency, lexicographic priority, or a scalarization \(\min_{x\in X}\phi(f(x))\). Different rules may select different routing solutions from the same attainable set \(f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multicriteria routing assigns each feasible solution several objective values. A preference rule, efficiency concept, or scalarization is required to select among generally incomparable criterion vectors.
assumptions_latex: The feasible routing-solution set \(X\) is nonempty.
Each solution has a vector \(f(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_p(x))\in\mathbb R^p\) of at least two criteria to be minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem seeks solutions according to a specified preference relation or solution concept on the attainable set \(f(X)\), rather than an intrinsically scalar order.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: vector-optimization definition specialized to routing
specific preference model intentionally left local to each multicriteria formulation

children.title: Pareto Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings organized around nondominated objective tradeoffs.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Pareto efficiency for finitely many minimization criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in X\), say that \(y\) dominates \(x\) when \(f_i(y)\le f_i(x)\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(f_j(y)<f_j(x)\) for at least one index \(j\). A routing solution \(x^*\in X\) is Pareto efficient if no feasible solution dominates it. Hence the Pareto set is \(P=\{x\in X:\nexists y\in X\text{ that dominates }x\}\), and its image \(f(P)\) is the Pareto front. Distinct members of \(P\) may remain incomparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A routing solution is Pareto efficient when no feasible alternative is at least as good in every criterion and strictly better in at least one.
assumptions_latex: The feasible routing-solution set \(X\) is nonempty.
The criterion map \(f:X\to\mathbb R^p\) has components to be minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pareto set consists of feasible solutions not dominated componentwise by another feasible solution.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto-efficiency definition specialized to routing

children.title: Undirected Routing Networks
children.top_down_role: Routing settings with bidirectional edge representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Routing Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected network orientation with direction-invariant edge data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected routing network is a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) whose edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) permits traversal in either direction. A route is a walk \((v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_m,v_m)\) with \(e_i=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\in E\) for every \(i\). Under the undirected routing convention, edge data are direction-invariant: traversing \(e\) from \(u\) to \(v\) or from \(v\) to \(u\) incurs the same cost \(c_e\) and the same modeled resource increment. Direction-dependent restrictions instead require a directed or mixed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected routing network permits every edge to be traversed in either direction with the same edge-associated cost and resource data.
assumptions_latex: The routing network is a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\).
Every edge \(e=\{u,v\}\in E\) may be traversed from \(u\) to \(v\) or from \(v\) to \(u\).
Any traversal cost or resource increment assigned to \(e\) is independent of traversal direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Routes are walks in \(G\), and reversing an edge traversal preserves its edge-associated cost and resource increment.

notation.meaning: unordered edge joining u and v

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Computing a minimum cut of an undirected graph p. 219

review_flags: malformed walk and edge notation repaired

children.title: Directed Routing Networks
children.top_down_role: Routing settings with orientation-specific arc representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Routing Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed network orientation with arc-specific feasibility and data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed routing network is a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\). A route is a directed walk \((v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_m,v_m)\) satisfying \(a_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)\in A\) for every \(i\). The presence of \((u,v)\) does not require the reverse arc \((v,u)\), and when both exist their costs, resource increments, or admissibility conditions may differ. Consequently, reversing a feasible route need not produce a feasible route and need not preserve its objective value or resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed routing network permits traversal only along arc directions. Reverse arcs may be absent or may have different costs, resources, and restrictions.
assumptions_latex: The routing network is a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\).
Each arc \(a=(u,v)\in A\) permits traversal only from its tail \(u\) to its head \(v\).
Costs and resource increments are attached to arcs and may differ between opposite arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Routes are directed walks in \(D\), and \((u,v)\in A\) does not imply \((v,u)\in A\) or equality of their data.

notation.meaning: arc directed from u to v

source_refs.locator: 7.4 Sparse certificates for directed graphs and hypergraphs p. 240

source_witnesses.locator: 7.4 Sparse certificates for directed graphs and hypergraphs p. 240

children.title: Mixed Routing Networks
children.top_down_role: Routing settings containing both edges and arcs.

assumptions_latex: The routing network is a finite mixed graph \(M=(V,E,A)\).
Each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\) permits both traversal directions.
Each directed arc \((u,v)\in A\) permits only traversal from \(u\) to \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible routes are mixed walks respecting arc orientation while allowing either direction on undirected edges.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mixed-graph walk definition specialized to routing
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Networks containing both bidirectional edges and one-way arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed routing network is a finite triple \(M=(V,E,A)\), where \(E\) contains unordered edges and \(A\) contains ordered arcs. A mixed walk alternates vertices with members of \(E\cup A\); an edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\) may connect consecutive vertices in either order, whereas an arc \((u,v)\in A\) may connect them only in the order \(u,v\). Costs and resource increments are attached to the traversed edge or arc. Thus mixed routing simultaneously models bidirectional links and one-way links without replacing every bidirectional link by two necessarily identical arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed routing network contains both bidirectional edges and one-way arcs. Routes may traverse edges either way but must respect every arc's orientation.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Routing Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed-walk definition is precise, agrees with the plain statement, and fits the leaf, but it has no inspectable source citation.

children.title: Orientation-Asymmetry Effects
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of direction-dependent reachability or travel cost.

assumptions_latex: A routing instance is represented by a digraph \(D=(V,A)\).
Each arc \((u,v)\in A\) has cost \(c_{uv}\) and possibly direction-dependent resource data.
Route feasibility is defined by directed walks and the stated side constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orientation asymmetry can change reachability, route-reversal feasibility, route cost, and resource consumption; these effects vanish only under explicit reverse-arc symmetry.

notation.meaning: cost of the arc from u to v
reversal of a directed walk R

review_flags: locator supports directed structures but routing-specific reversal consequence remains provisional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of missing or unequal reverse arcs in directed routing.

source_refs.locator: 8.2 Directed splitting p. 258

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=(v_0,ldots,v_m)\) be a feasible directed route. Its reversal \(R^{\mathrm{rev}}=(v_m,ldots,v_0)\) is a directed walk only if \((v_i,v_{i-1})\in A\) for every \(i\). Even then, its cost is \(\sum_{i=1}^m c_{v_i v_{i-1}}\), which need not equal \(\sum_{i=1}^m c_{v_{i-1}v_i}\), and its resource profile may differ. If every used reverse arc exists and has identical cost and resource data, reversal preserves those quantities; otherwise orientation creates genuine asymmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In directed routing, reversing a route may be impossible or may change its cost and resources. Reversal invariance requires explicit symmetry of reverse arcs and their data.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Asymmetry Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 8.2 Directed splitting p. 258
