children.title: Metric Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings governed by metric travel costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric finite metric routing; asymmetric directed metrics are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric routing regime is defined on a finite metric space \((V,d)\): for all \(u,v,w\in V\), \(d(u,v)\ge 0\), \(d(u,v)=0\) if and only if \(u=v\), \(d(u,v)=d(v,u)\), and \(d(u,w)\le d(u,v)+d(v,w)\). The travel cost of a route \(R=(v_0,\ldots,v_m)\) is \(c(R)=\sum_{i=1}^m d(v_{i-1},v_i)\). The triangle inequality ensures that replacing two consecutive legs through an optional intermediate vertex by the direct leg cannot increase travel cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric routing uses symmetric nonnegative distances satisfying identity and the triangle inequality. A route's travel cost is the sum of distances between consecutive locations.
assumptions_latex: The routing vertex set \(V\) is finite.
Travel costs are given by \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\).
The cost function is symmetric and separates distinct vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is metric when \(d\) is a metric; route costs are sums of metric leg lengths.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite metric-space definition specialized to routing

children.title: Nonmetric Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings without metric cost structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmetric Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies routing models that do not require their ordered travel costs to form a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing model is in a nonmetric regime when its travel costs \(c_{ij}=c(i,j)\) are not required to define a metric on \(V\). Accordingly, one or more of symmetry \(c_{ij}=c_{ji}\), identity of indiscernibles \(c_{ij}=0\Leftrightarrow i=j\), finiteness and nonnegativity \(0\le c_{ij}<+\infty\), and the triangle inequality \(c_{ij}\le c_{ik}+c_{kj}\) may fail. Route feasibility and cost are evaluated using the original ordered-arc costs unless a separate transformation is justified. A particular instance admitted by this regime may nevertheless happen to satisfy all metric axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmetric routing regime does not impose all metric axioms on travel costs, although a particular admitted instance may still happen to be metric.
assumptions_latex: A finite routing model has vertex set \(V\) and directed travel-cost function \(c:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime permits, but does not require, realized travel costs that violate one or more metric axioms.

notation.meaning: Travel cost from vertex i to vertex j

children.title: Geometric Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings induced by an ambient geometric space.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a finite-dimensional norm-induced geometric routing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing instance is in the norm-induced geometric regime when each vertex \(i\in V\) has a specified location \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and its travel costs satisfy \(c_{ij}=\lVert p_i-p_j\rVert\) for every \(i,j\in V\), where \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) is a fixed norm on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). These costs are finite, nonnegative, symmetric, and satisfy \(c_{ij}\le c_{ik}+c_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-induced geometric routing instance embeds every routing vertex in finite-dimensional space and uses distances under one fixed norm as its pairwise travel costs.
assumptions_latex: The routing vertex set \(V\) is finite.
A location map \(p:V\to\mathbb{R}^d\) and a fixed norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Route costs are determined by the norm geometry of the embedded locations.

notation.meaning: Location assigned to routing vertex i
Fixed norm inducing the travel costs

children.title: Graph-Metric Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing settings induced by shortest-path distances in a graph.

assumptions_latex: A finite graph \(G=(W,E)\) has nonnegative edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
Every pair of routing vertices is connected in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced routing costs form the shortest-path metric restricted to the routing vertices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected nonnegative-length graph-metric convention.

source_refs.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing instance is in a graph-metric regime when its routing vertices satisfy \(V\subseteq W\) for an undirected graph \(G=(W,E)\) with nonnegative edge lengths \(\ell\), and \(c_{ij}=d_G(i,j)\) for all \(i,j\in V\), where \(d_G(i,j)\) is the minimum total length of an \(i\)-to-\(j\) path. Connectivity on \(V\) makes every \(c_{ij}\) finite, and shortest-path distances satisfy symmetry and the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-metric routing instance uses shortest-path distances in a connected, nonnegatively weighted undirected graph as its pairwise travel costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Metric Routing Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

children.title: Metric-Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Changes in routing structure caused by metric completion or its absence.

assumptions_latex: A finite directed graph has arc costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
Every relevant ordered vertex pair admits a finite-cost directed walk, and no reachable negative-cost directed cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric closure preserves optimal routing value exactly only under compatible feasibility and realizability conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when shortest-path closure is and is not an exact routing reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the directed metric closure by \(d_{ij}=\inf\{\sum_{a\in P}c_a:P\text{ is a directed }i\text{-to-}j\text{ walk}\}\). Then \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\). Replacing \(c\) by \(d\) is value-preserving only when every closure arc used by a feasible route can be expanded into its realizing walk without violating constraints, and every original feasible route remains admissible after shortcutting. Exactness can fail when expansion changes capacities, visit multiplicities, time feasibility, resource consumption, or forbidden-vertex conditions; it is undefined or unbounded when relevant pairs are unreachable or reachable negative cycles exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortest-path closure is exact only when shortcutting and path expansion preserve every routing constraint; resource, timing, visitation, or reachability restrictions can break equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Closure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-preservation boundary depends on the precise routing constraints and on formal mappings between original and closure solutions. No source supports the asserted necessary conditions or failure list. Moreover, an asymmetric directed shortest-path closure is generally a directed semimetric rather than a metric in the symmetric sense.

children.title: Static Routing Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings with fixed data available before planning.

assumptions_latex: The complete routing instance and all exogenous data are known before route construction begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A static routing decision is a single plan chosen from the initially revealed data.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible complete route plans under I_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes information timing from deterministic versus uncertain data values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing problem has static information when a complete data object \(I_0\), including all customers, travel data, demands, service requirements, and vehicle data used by the model, is revealed before any routing decision is implemented and does not change during execution. A solution is therefore a complete plan \(x\in\mathcal{X}(I_0)\) selected as a function of \(I_0\), with no later observations permitted to alter the plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static routing reveals all model data before execution and chooses one complete route plan that is not revised using later observations.
knowledge_statements.title: Static Routing Information

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and distinguishes information timing from uncertainty, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Time-Dependent Routing Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings whose travel data varies with execution time.

assumptions_latex: Travel time on each arc is a known function of its departure time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible arrival times are generated recursively from departure-time-dependent arc travel times.

notation.meaning: Travel time on arc (i,j) when departing at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Known time-dependent data, distinct from information revealed dynamically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing problem has time-dependent information when its travel or service data are known functions of clock time. For a route arc \((i,j)\), if service begins at \(i\) at time \(t_i\) and lasts \(s_i\), then the induced arrival time at \(j\) is \(a_j=t_i+s_i+\tau_{ij}(t_i+s_i)\). Thus the cost or feasibility of a fixed vertex sequence may depend on its departure schedule even though every function \(\tau_{ij}:\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is known initially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time-dependent routing uses initially known travel or service functions whose realized values depend on when a vehicle departs or receives service.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Routing Information

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The known time-dependent travel-time formulation and arrival recursion are internally consistent, but the record lacks an inspectable time-dependent-routing source.

children.title: Dynamic Routing Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings where relevant data arrives during operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Routing Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines dynamic routing information through progressively revealed data and nonanticipative decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing problem has dynamic information when some decision-relevant data become known only during route execution. Let \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge0}\) represent the information revealed by time \(t\). An admissible routing policy \(\pi\) chooses each action \(u_t=\pi_t(\mathcal{F}_t)\) so that \(u_t\) is \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable; equivalently, histories indistinguishable at time \(t\) induce the same action at that time. Subsequent observations may revise unimplemented decisions but not actions already executed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic routing reveals decision-relevant data during execution and requires each action to depend only on information available when that action is chosen.
assumptions_latex: Routing data are revealed through a filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge0}\).
Decisions implemented by time \(t\) cannot be revoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissible dynamic routing policies are nonanticipative with respect to the revealed information.

notation.meaning: Routing action selected at time t

children.title: Rolling-Horizon Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings organized around successive planning windows.

assumptions_latex: Decision epochs satisfy \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots\).
At each epoch, current state and a finite forecast window are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rolling-horizon control repeatedly optimizes a truncated future and commits only the prescribed leading decisions.

notation.meaning: Routing state observed at epoch k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-look-ahead reoptimization with partial commitment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given decision epochs \(t_k\), initialize with observed state \(s_0\). At epoch \(t_k\), incorporate all information then available, construct the routing subproblem over \([t_k,t_k+H_k]\), and compute a feasible plan \(x^{(k)}\). Implement only the designated prefix of \(x^{(k)}\), typically until \(t_{k+1}\); observe the resulting state \(s_{k+1}\), update forecasts and requests, and repeat. Stop when no unserved required request remains, and output the concatenation of all committed prefixes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rolling-horizon routing repeatedly solves a finite-look-ahead problem, executes only its leading portion, updates information, and reoptimizes until service is complete.
knowledge_statements.title: Rolling-Horizon Information

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role appropriately captures the rolling-horizon procedure, and the variables and stopping rule are explicit. No inspectable rolling-horizon routing source is supplied.

children.title: Deterministic Routing Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings using fixed input values.

assumptions_latex: All data defining feasibility and objective value are fixed known quantities at the decision time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each feasible route plan has a uniquely determined feasibility status and objective value.

notation.meaning: Cost of plan x under xi_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic uncertainty regime; information may still be time-dependent if known exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing model has deterministic information when every decision-relevant parameter is represented by one known data realization \(\xi_0\), rather than by multiple scenarios, a probability law, or an uncertainty set. Its optimization problem has the form \(\min\{C(x,\xi_0):x\in\mathcal{X}(\xi_0)\}\). Consequently, for every candidate plan \(x\), both membership in \(\mathcal{X}(\xi_0)\) and the value \(C(x,\xi_0)\) are determined without probabilistic or worst-case evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic routing uses one known data realization, so every route plan has a fixed feasibility status and cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Routing Information

children.title: Robust Routing Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings using uncertainty sets or protected scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Routing Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static robust counterpart without probability distributions or adjustable recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing model has robust information when uncertain data \(\xi\) are known only to lie in a nonempty set \(\mathcal{U}\). Under the static robust convention, a route plan must satisfy \(x\in\bigcap_{\xi\in\mathcal{U}}\mathcal{X}(\xi)\), and its worst-case objective is \(\sup_{\xi\in\mathcal{U}}C(x,\xi)\). The robust routing problem is therefore \(\min_x\{\sup_{\xi\in\mathcal{U}}C(x,\xi):x\in\bigcap_{\xi\in\mathcal{U}}\mathcal{X}(\xi)\}\), with no probability law required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static robust routing requires one plan to remain feasible for every realization in an uncertainty set and minimizes its worst-case cost.
assumptions_latex: Uncertain routing data range over a specified nonempty uncertainty set \(\mathcal{U}\).
No probability law is required for optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust feasibility and cost are assessed against every realization in \(\mathcal{U}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible routing plans under realization xi
Routing cost of plan x under realization xi

children.title: Distributionally Robust Information
children.top_down_role: Routing settings using ambiguity families for uncertain distributions.

assumptions_latex: The unknown routing-data law belongs to a specified nonempty ambiguity set \(\mathcal{P}\) of probability measures.
Plans or policies satisfy the stated information constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distributionally robust evaluation takes the worst probabilistic value over all laws in \(\mathcal{P}\).

notation.meaning: Routing cost under data realization xi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case expected-cost form of distributionally robust routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing model has distributionally robust information when the probability law of uncertain data \(\xi\) is not fixed but is known to belong to a nonempty ambiguity set \(\mathcal{P}\). For admissible decisions or policies \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), the worst-case expected-cost formulation is \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{P}[C(x,\xi)]\). Feasibility requirements must likewise state whether they hold for every \(P\in\mathcal{P}\), almost surely under every such law, or through a worst-case chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust routing optimizes against the worst probability law in an ambiguity set, with feasibility interpreted uniformly over that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Information

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the complete undirected graph \(K_V\) and edge costs \(c:E(K_V)\to\mathbb{R}\), the symmetric traveling-salesman problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{\{i,j\}\in H}c_{ij}: H\subseteq E(K_V)\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle}\right\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A metric TSP instance consists of a finite set \(V\) and a symmetric nonnegative cost function \(c:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) satisfying \(c_{ii}=0\) and the triangle inequality \(c_{ij}\le c_{ik}+c_{kj}\). Its feasible solutions are Hamiltonian cycles \(H\) in \(K_V\), and its optimum is
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(V,c)=\min_H\sum_{\{i,j\}\in H}c_{ij}.
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted connected-graph version, allowing repeated edges in the spanning walk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The graphic TSP value of \(G\) is
\[
\tau(G)=\min\{\lvert W\rvert:W\text{ is a closed walk in }G\text{ visiting every vertex}\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\tau(G)=\min\left\{\sum_{\{u,v\}\in H}d_G(u,v):H\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle of }K_V\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic TSP seeks a shortest closed walk visiting every graph vertex, equivalently a TSP tour in the graph's shortest-path metric.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected unweighted graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Metric Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-weight undirected completion; zero weights would yield only a pseudometric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u,v\in V\), define
\[
d_G(u,v)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in P}w(e):P\text{ is a }u\text{-}v\text{ path in }G\right\}.
\]
The shortest-path metric completion of \((G,w)\) is the complete graph \(K_V\) whose edge \(\{u,v\}\) has cost \(d_G(u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each missing edge by the length of a shortest path between its endpoints, producing a complete metric instance.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, and undirected.
\(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The completion \((K_V,d_G)\) is a finite metric space agreeing with shortest-path distances in \(G\).

children.title: Nonmetric TSP
children.top_down_role: TSP instances lacking metric cost structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmetric TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric complete-graph nonmetric regime; feasibility remains Hamiltonian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonmetric TSP instance is a symmetric TSP instance \((K_V,c)\) for which \(c\) is not a metric on \(V\). With \(c_{ii}=0\) and symmetry imposed, this means either there are distinct \(i,j\in V\) with \(c_{ij}\le 0\), or there are \(i,j,k\in V\) such that
\[
c_{ij}>c_{ik}+c_{kj}.
\]
Feasible solutions remain Hamiltonian cycles of \(K_V\), and total edge cost is minimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonmetric TSP retains complete-graph Hamiltonian tours but allows a failure of positive separation or the triangle inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite with \(|V|\ge 3\).
\(c:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and symmetric, with \(c_{ii}=0\) for every \(i\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is nonmetric precisely when positive separation or the triangle inequality fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Forbidden-Link TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard link prohibitions, not finite penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The forbidden-link TSP is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{e\in H}c_e:H\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle of }K_V,\ H\cap F=\varnothing\right\}.
\]
It is equivalent to incomplete-graph TSP on \(G=(V,E(K_V)\setminus F)\). Replacing forbidden edges by finite penalties does not preserve the hard-feasibility semantics, although separately justified bounds can sometimes preserve the identity of an optimal allowed tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a cheapest Hamiltonian cycle avoiding every prohibited edge; deleting those edges gives the equivalent incomplete-graph instance.

\(F\subseteq E(K_V)\) is the set of forbidden edges.
\(c:E(K_V)\setminus F\to\mathbb{R}\) gives allowed-edge costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible tour is a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) satisfying \(H\cap F=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set of distinct points in real Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Euclidean TSP on \(P\) assigns cost \(c_{ij}=\lVert p_i-p_j\rVert_2\) and minimizes
\[
\min_{\pi}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lVert p_{\pi(k)}-p_{\pi(k+1)}\rVert_2,
\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1),
\]
where \(\pi\) ranges over permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean TSP finds the shortest cyclic ordering of finitely many distinct points using ordinary Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) has \(|P|=n\ge 3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the shortest Hamiltonian cycle under Euclidean distances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean and nice Euclidean TSP instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the geometric input model and the normalized subclass used by the approximation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Euclidean TSP instance consists of points $(x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^2$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, with travel costs $c_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$; the input specifies the points rather than the pairwise distances. For a fixed constant $\epsilon>0$, the instance is nice if the minimum nonzero distance between its points is at least $4$ and all coordinates $x_i,y_i$ are integers in $[0,O(n)]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean TSP instance is specified by planar city coordinates, with travel costs equal to Euclidean distances rather than an input distance matrix. For fixed positive epsilon, it is nice when the minimum nonzero interpoint distance is at least 4 and all coordinates are integers in a range bounded by O(n).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Norm TSP

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be a full-dimensional convex polytope satisfying \(P=-P\) and \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). Given a finite point set \(V=\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), polyhedral-norm TSP asks for a cyclic permutation \(\pi\) minimizing \[L_P(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|p_{\pi(i+1)}-p_{\pi(i)}\|_P,\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\] The representation of \(P\), such as its facets or vertices, is part of the specified geometric model.

children.title: Norm-Sensitivity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative sensitivity of optimal tour length under replacement of the ambient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be finite, and let \(\|\cdot\|_a\) and \(\|\cdot\|_b\) be norms satisfying \(\alpha\|z\|_a\le \|z\|_b\le\beta\|z\|_a\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty\). Every tour \(T\) then satisfies \(\alpha L_a(T)\le L_b(T)\le\beta L_a(T)\). children.title: High-Dimension TSP

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary explicit-coordinate upper bounds exposing dependence on dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), assume evaluation of the specified norm distance between two explicit points uses \(O(d)\) arithmetic operations. Computing all pairwise distances uses \(O(n^2d)\) operations and \(O(n^2)\) stored distances. Enumerating every cyclic ordering and evaluating each tour directly yields an exact algorithm using \(O(n!\,nd)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(nd)\) coordinate storage. If the distance matrix is precomputed, enumeration instead uses \(O(n!\,n+n^2d)\) operations and \(O(n^2+nd)\) storage. These bounds are computational baselines, not tractability claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit coordinates impose dimensional costs: pairwise distances take quadratic-times-dimension work, while brute-force exact tour enumeration remains factorial.

children.title: Dimensionality Transition Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Dimensionality Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for algorithm families whose exponent grows linearly with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an algorithm family with running time \(n^{c d}\operatorname{poly}(n,d)\) for a constant \(c>0\). When \(d=O(1)\), this expression is polynomial in \(n\). When \(d=\Theta(\log n)\), it equals \(\exp(\Theta((\log n)^2))\) up to polynomial factors and is generally quasipolynomial rather than polynomial. When \(d=\Theta(n)\), it becomes \(\exp(\Theta(n\log n))\). Consequently, a guarantee stated only for each fixed \(d\) does not imply a uniform polynomial-time guarantee when dimension belongs to the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An n-to-the-order-d algorithm is polynomial only for bounded dimension, quasipolynomial near logarithmic dimension, and exponential near linear dimension.

children.title: Bounded-Growth TSP

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Growth TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: TSP on finite metrics satisfying a uniform polynomial ball-covering condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,\rho)\) be a finite metric space. It has covering growth bounded by parameters \((C,k)\) if, for every \(x\in V\) and \(0<r\le R\), the ball \(B(x,R)\) can be covered by at most \(C(R/r)^k\) balls of radius \(r\) whose centers lie in \(V\). A bounded-growth TSP instance is the metric TSP on such a space, with \(C\) and \(k\) fixed or explicitly parameterized, and objective \[\min_{\pi\in S_{|V|}}\sum_{i=1}^{|V|}\rho\bigl(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(|V|+1)=\pi(1).\]

knowledge_statements.title: Doubling-Metric TSP

knowledge_statements.title: Growth-to-Doubling Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between doubling and polynomial multiscale covering growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,\rho)\) have doubling constant at most \(\lambda\). Iterating the half-radius cover shows that, for every \(x\in V\) and \(0<r<R\), \[N(B(x,R),r)\le \lambda^{\lceil\log_2(R/r)\rceil}\le \lambda(R/r)^{\log_2\lambda}.\] Conversely, if every ball \(B(x,R)\) can be covered by at most \(C(R/r)^k\) balls of radius \(r\), then setting \(r=R/2\) gives doubling constant at most \(C2^k\). Hence uniform polynomial covering growth and finite doubling dimension are equivalent up to their quantitative constants.

children.title: Unbounded-Growth Failure Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Growth Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniform packing and covering bounds when doubling dimension is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\ge2\), let \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(\rho(i,j)=1\) whenever \(i\ne j\). The ball \(B(i,1)\) is all of \(V_n\), whereas every ball of radius \(1/2\) is a singleton. Thus its least doubling constant is \(\lambda_*(V_n)=n\) and \(\operatorname{ddim}(V_n)=\log_2 n\). Consequently, no covering or packing bound depending on a dimension constant independent of \(n\) applies to this family. Algorithms whose state count or running time contains a factor exponential in doubling dimension therefore lose a uniform constant-dimensional guarantee on these instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equilateral n-point metrics have doubling constant n, so dimension-independent packing bounds and algorithms exponential in doubling dimension lose uniform guarantees.

children.title: Planar TSP

knowledge_statements.title: Planar TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-metric TSP induced by a connected edge-weighted planar graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected planar graph with positive edge lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\), and let \(d_G\) be its shortest-path metric. Planar graph-metric TSP asks for a cyclic ordering \(\pi\) of \(V\) minimizing \[\sum_{i=1}^{|V|}d_G\bigl(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(|V|+1)=\pi(1).\] Equivalently, it asks for a minimum-length closed walk in \(G\) visiting every vertex, where edges may be traversed repeatedly. Here planarity constrains the underlying graph generating the metric, not the complete metric closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar graph-metric TSP finds a shortest closed walk visiting every vertex of a positively weighted planar graph, allowing repeated edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Planarity-Parameter Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Planarity-Based Guarantee Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes planarity of a sparse support graph from planarity of its metric completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_5\) be the unweighted five-vertex cycle and let \(d(u,v)\) be its shortest-path distance. The support graph \(C_5\) is planar, but the metric TSP instance containing an edge of cost \(d(u,v)\) for every distinct pair \(u,v\) has underlying graph \(K_5\), which is nonplanar. Consequently, a guarantee whose hypothesis requires the TSP optimization graph itself to be planar cannot be transferred merely from planarity of a graph generating the distances. The applicable planarity notion—support graph, required-edge graph, or completed metric graph—must therefore be stated explicitly.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Treewidth TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact weighted Hamiltonian-cycle optimization with a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(n=\lvert V\rvert\), edge weights \(c:E\to\mathbb{Q}\), and a supplied tree decomposition of width \(w\). A dynamic program over a nice tree decomposition may record, for each bag vertex, degree \(0,1,\) or \(2\), together with the pairing or partition data describing partial-path connectivity. It returns a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle, or reports that none exists, using \(2^{O(w\log w)}n^{O(1)}\) time and \(2^{O(w\log w)}n^{O(1)}\) space. Thus exact TSP is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to treewidth when a decomposition is available.

knowledge_statements.title: Special Distance-Matrix TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kalmanson inequalities as a canonical exactly solvable distance-matrix regime.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-tour minimization of the largest selected edge cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite complete graph \(G=(V,E)\) with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(\mathcal H(G)\) denote its Hamiltonian cycles. The bottleneck value of a tour \(T\in\mathcal H(G)\) is \(b(T):=\max_{e\in T}c_e\). The bottleneck traveling-salesman problem is \[\operatorname{BTSP}(G,c):=\min_{T\in\mathcal H(G)}\max_{e\in T}c_e.\] Thus the objective aggregates the costs of the selected tour edges by their maximum rather than by their sum.

children.title: Min–Max TSP

knowledge_statements.title: Min–Max TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust single-tour TSP with finitely many additive cost scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph, let \(\mathcal H(G)\) be its Hamiltonian cycles, and let \(c^s:E\to\mathbb{R}\) be the edge-cost vector under each scenario \(s\) in a finite nonempty set \(\mathcal S\). The discrete-scenario min–max TSP is \[\min_{T\in\mathcal H(G)}\ \max_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{e\in T}c_e^s.\] A feasible solution is one tour selected before the scenario is known; its objective value is its largest total tour cost across the scenarios. This differs from bottleneck TSP, whose maximum ranges over edges of one cost vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Min–max TSP selects one tour minimizing its worst total cost across a finite set of cost scenarios.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has at least one Hamiltonian cycle.
\(\mathcal S\) is finite and nonempty.
Every scenario specifies a real cost for each edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MMTSP}(G,\{c^s\})=\min_{T\in\mathcal H(G)}\max_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{e\in T}c_e^s\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold characterization and verifiable certificate for a bottleneck bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph having at least one Hamiltonian cycle, let \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). Define \(\mathcal H(G)\) to be the set of Hamiltonian cycles of \(G\), \(\operatorname{BTSP}(G,c):=\min_{T\in\mathcal H(G)}\max_{e\in T}c_e\), and \(G_\lambda=(V,\{e\in E:c_e\le\lambda\})\). A Hamiltonian cycle \(T\) certifies that the bottleneck optimum is at most \(\lambda\) exactly when every edge of \(T\) belongs to \(G_\lambda\). Equivalently, \[\operatorname{BTSP}(G,c)\le\lambda\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_\lambda\text{ contains a Hamiltonian cycle}.\] The certificate is checked by verifying that \(T\) visits every vertex once, closes into a cycle, and satisfies \(c_e\le\lambda\) for every \(e\in T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph having a Hamiltonian cycle, a bottleneck bound lambda is feasible exactly when the subgraph of edges costing at most lambda contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Bottleneck Criteria

children.title: Tour-Balance Min–Max Criteria
children.top_down_role: Worst-tour objective regimes for multiple-tour solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour-Balance Min–Max Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fleet routing objective minimizing the longest of several depot tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite customer set, let \(r\notin V\) be a depot, and let \(c_{ij}\) be travel costs on \(V\cup\{r\}\). A feasible \(m\)-tour fleet solution is a tuple \((T_1,\ldots,T_m)\) of depot-rooted cycles whose customer sets are pairwise disjoint and have union \(V\). With \(L(T_q):=\sum_{e\in T_q}c_e\), the tour-balance min–max criterion is \[\min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)}\max_{1\le q\le m}L(T_q).\] Empty depot tours may be allowed or forbidden by convention; that convention is part of the feasible-set specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tour-balance criterion partitions customers among depot tours while minimizing the length of the longest tour.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(m\ge1\).
Each nonempty route starts and ends at the common depot \(r\).
Every customer is assigned to exactly one route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BAL}_m=\min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)}\max_{1\le q\le m}L(T_q)\).

notation.meaning: route assigned to fleet member q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The makespan-style fleet objective fits the leaf, but the graph orientation, route model, and empty-route convention are not fixed. A source is needed to determine the intended local variant before revising those conventions.

children.title: Edge-Incidence Formulations
children.top_down_role: TSP formulations using variables indexed by undirected edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Incidence Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected binary edge-incidence formulation with subtour-elimination inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the complete undirected graph \(K_n=(V,E)\), associate \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\) with each edge. The symmetric TSP is represented by \[\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\quad\text{subject to}\quad x(\delta(v))=2\ \ (v\in V),\qquad x(\delta(S))\ge2\ \ (\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\qquad x_e\in\{0,1\}.\] The degree equations make the selected subgraph two-regular, while the cut inequalities exclude disconnected unions of cycles. Hence the binary feasible vectors are exactly the edge-incidence vectors of Hamiltonian cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary edge variables, degree-two equations, and subtour cuts represent exactly the undirected Hamiltonian tours.
assumptions_latex: \(K_n=(V,E)\) is complete and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x=\chi^T\text{ for some Hamiltonian cycle }T\text{ of }K_n\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S
sum of x_e over edges in F

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard symmetric TSP subtour-elimination representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary degree equations and cut inequalities correctly characterize undirected Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vectors, and representation is the correct content kind. The formulation nevertheless lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Arc-Incidence Formulations
children.top_down_role: TSP formulations using variables indexed by directed arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Incidence Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed binary arc-incidence formulation with directed subtour cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the complete digraph \(D=(V,A)\), associate \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) with each arc \((i,j)\). The asymmetric TSP is represented by \[\min\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}y_{ij}\] subject to \[\sum_{j
e i}y_{ij}=1,\qquad \sum_{j
e i}y_{ji}=1\quad(i\in V),\qquad y(\delta^+(S))\ge1\quad(\varnothing
e S\subsetneq V).\] The in-degree and out-degree equations produce a directed cycle cover, and the cut inequalities force that cover to consist of one directed Hamiltonian cycle. Thus the binary feasible vectors are precisely directed-tour incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-in, one-out arc constraints plus directed subtour cuts represent exactly the directed Hamiltonian tours.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a complete loopless digraph.
\(\lvert V\rvert\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\text{ is feasible}\iff y=\chi^T\text{ for some directed Hamiltonian cycle }T\text{ of }D\).

notation.meaning: sum of y_ij over arcs in F
arc-incidence vector of directed tour T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard asymmetric TSP subtour-elimination representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-in, one-out equations with directed cut inequalities correctly characterize directed Hamiltonian tours, and representation fits the leaf. No inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Incidence-Representation Translations
children.top_down_role: Correspondences between edge-based and arc-based tour representations.

assumptions_latex: Every undirected edge is replaced by both possible directed arcs.
Arc costs satisfy \(c_{ij}=c_{ji}=c_{\{i,j\}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{\{i,j\}}=y_{ij}+y_{ji}\), and each undirected tour has exactly two cost-preserving directed lifts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between undirected edge incidence and oriented arc incidence for symmetric tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_n\) be the complete undirected graph on \(n\ge3\) vertices, and replace each edge \(\{i,j\}\) by the two arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\). For any directed Hamiltonian-tour incidence vector \(y\), define \[x_{\{i,j\}}:=y_{ij}+y_{ji}.\] Then \(x\) is the incidence vector of the underlying undirected Hamiltonian cycle. Conversely, every undirected Hamiltonian-cycle vector \(x\) admits exactly two directed-tour lifts, corresponding to its two cyclic orientations. If arc costs are symmetric, \(c_{ij}=c_{ji}=c_{\{i,j\}}\), each lift preserves objective value: \[\sum_{\{i,j\}}c_{\{i,j\}}x_{\{i,j\}}=\sum_{i\ne j}c_{ij}y_{ij}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For symmetric costs and at least three vertices, forgetting orientation maps a directed tour to an undirected tour, and each undirected tour has two cost-preserving orientations.
knowledge_statements.title: Incidence-Representation Translations

children.title: Assignment Formulations
children.top_down_role: Compact TSP representations based on assignment structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-matrix assignment model and its cycle-cover interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a complete loopless digraph with vertex set \(V\), let \(z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate assignment of successor \(j\) to vertex \(i\). The assignment formulation is \[\min\sum_{i
e j}c_{ij}z_{ij}\quad	ext{subject to}\quad \sum_{j
e i}z_{ij}=1\ \ (i\in V),\qquad \sum_{i
e j}z_{ij}=1\ \ (j\in V).\] Every binary feasible matrix is a permutation matrix with forbidden diagonal and therefore represents a vertex-disjoint directed cycle cover. It represents a traveling-salesman tour exactly when the induced permutation consists of one cycle containing all vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The assignment equations produce a minimum-cost directed cycle cover; it is a TSP tour only when the permutation has one cycle.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is complete and has no loops.
\(\lvert V\rvert\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\text{ is an assignment solution}\iff z\text{ is a loopless permutation matrix};\quad z\text{ is a tour}\iff z\text{ has one cycle}.\)

notation.meaning: cost of assigning j as successor of i

children.title: Cycle-Cover Formulations
children.top_down_role: Compact TSP representations whose base solutions are cycle covers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Cover Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed assignment representation of cycle covers on a complete digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be the complete loopless digraph and let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selection of arc \((i,j)\). The system \[\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}}x_{ij}=1,\qquad \sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}}x_{ji}=1\qquad(i\in V)\] represents precisely the spanning directed cycle covers of \(V\): every feasible integral vector is the incidence vector of vertex-disjoint directed cycles whose vertex sets partition \(V\), and every such cover satisfies the system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary assignment vectors with one incoming and one outgoing arc at every vertex are exactly spanning collections of vertex-disjoint directed cycles.
assumptions_latex:
\(A=\{(i,j):i,j\in V,
 i\ne j\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\text{ represents a spanning directed cycle cover}\).

notation.meaning: indicator of selected directed arc from i to j

children.title: Assignment-to-Tour Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Structural restrictions separating tour representations from general assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-to-Tour Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed subtour-elimination restrictions converting an assignment cycle cover into one tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the directed assignment system on \(V\), impose for every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) with \(2\le |S|\le |V|-1\) the restriction \[\sum_{i\in S}\sum_{j\in V\setminus S}x_{ij}\ge 1.\] An integral assignment vector satisfies all these restrictions if and only if its cycle cover has one component; equivalently, its selected arcs form a directed Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring every proper vertex subset to have a selected outgoing arc eliminates all proper cycles and leaves exactly Hamiltonian tours.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is an integral directed assignment vector
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ satisfies every directed cut restriction}\iff x\text{ is a Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vector}\).

notation.meaning: proper vertex subset tested for a subtour

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed cut restrictions and condition role are appropriate, but no citation supports the exact equivalence with Hamiltonian tours.

children.title: Cycle-Cover Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundaries created by disconnected cycle-cover solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Cover Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded nonmetric gap between minimum cycle covers and Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be partitioned into \(m\ge 2\) pairs. Assign cost \(0\) to both arcs joining the two vertices within each pair and cost \(M>0\) to every other arc. The assignment relaxation has a cycle cover of cost \(0\), consisting of \(m\) directed 2-cycles. Every Hamiltonian cycle uses at least \(m\) interpair arcs and therefore costs at least \(mM\). Thus without metric assumptions the cycle-cover bound has an unbounded additive gap and no finite multiplicative approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without metric costs, disjoint zero-cost 2-cycles can coexist with arbitrarily expensive tours, so the cycle-cover relaxation has no bounded gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{CC}}=0\) and \(z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\ge mM\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample family fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the unbounded-gap conclusion has no cited source. A source should also clarify the convention behind a multiplicative gap when the cycle-cover optimum is zero.

children.title: Ordering Formulations
children.top_down_role: TSP formulations using variables that encode visit order.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-order representation excluding cycles that avoid a distinguished depot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a depot \(r\in V\). An ordering formulation augments directed assignment variables with potentials \(u_i\) for \(i\in V\setminus\{r\}\) and valid bounds \(L_i\le u_i\le U_i\). For every distinct nondepot pair \(i,j\), it imposes a big-\(M\) implication \[u_j\ge u_i+1-M_{ij}(1-x_{ij}).\] Hence every selected arc between nondepot vertices strictly increases the potential, making a selected directed cycle contained in \(V\setminus\{r\}\) impossible. Together with integral degree equations, this yields one Hamiltonian cycle through \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order variables must increase along selected nondepot arcs; this prevents depot-free subtours and turns an integral assignment into a tour.
assumptions_latex: \(M_{ij}\ge U_i+1-L_j\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{ij}=1\Rightarrow u_j\ge u_i+1\), so no selected cycle avoids \(r\).

notation.meaning: order potential of nondepot vertex i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic potential-order representation is coherent and correctly excludes depot-free integral cycles, but the formulation and big-M condition lack a supporting locator.

children.title: Miller–Tucker–Zemlin Formulations
children.top_down_role: The MTZ family of compact ordering-based TSP representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Miller–Tucker–Zemlin Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard directed MTZ formulation with one distinguished depot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with depot \(1\), and impose the directed assignment equations on binary variables \(x\). Introduce \(u_i\) for \(i=2,\ldots,n\) and require \[1\le u_i\le n-1,\qquad u_i-u_j+n x_{ij}\le n-1\quad(i\ne j;\ i,j\ne1).\] If a selected cycle avoided vertex \(1\), summing its MTZ inequalities would give \(0\le-|C|\). Consequently, feasible integral \(x\)-vectors are exactly directed Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard MTZ order inequalities exclude every nondepot subtour; with binary assignment variables they represent directed Hamiltonian cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies the directed assignment equations
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ extends to an MTZ-feasible }u\iff x\text{ represents a directed Hamiltonian cycle}\).

notation.meaning: MTZ order variable for nondepot vertex i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed standard MTZ system is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but it has no citation and includes a proof-style summation argument that should be removed from knowledge-fill text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Miller–Tucker–Zemlin formulation of the asymmetric TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the compact MTZ formulation's integer correctness and its weaker continuous-relaxation bound. The omitted first displayed condition is represented as the binary arc-variable domain indicated by the surrounding text.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$, let $n=|V|$, and fix $v_0\in V$. For $x\in\{0,1\}^A$ and $z\in\mathbb R^V$, impose $x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v))=1$ for every $v\in V$ and $z_u-z_v+n x_{uv}\le n-1$ for every $(u,v)\in A$ with $u,v\ne v_0$. The feasible $x$-vectors are exactly the incidence vectors of Hamiltonian circuits in $D$. The formulation has polynomial size, but its linear-programming relaxation generally yields a weaker bound than the directed subtour-elimination relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The compact MTZ formulation uses binary arc variables, one-in and one-out equations, and continuous ordering variables. Its ordering inequalities exclude directed subtours disjoint from a fixed vertex, and its feasible integer arc vectors are exactly Hamiltonian circuits. Its LP relaxation is generally weaker than the exponential directed subtour relaxation.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a directed graph}
n=|V|
v_0\in V\text{ is fixed}
z\in\mathbb R^V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x\left\{(x,z):x\in\{0,1\}^A,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v))=1\ \forall v,\ z_u-z_v+n x_{uv}\le n-1\ \forall (u,v)\in A,\ u,v\ne v_0\right\}=\{\chi^C:C\text{ is a Hamiltonian circuit of }D\}.

children.title: Lifted MTZ Variants
children.top_down_role: Strengthened variants within the MTZ formulation family.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted MTZ Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard pairwise lifting of directed MTZ inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(i,j\in V\setminus\{1\}\), the lifted inequality \[u_i-u_j+(n-1)x_{ij}+(n-3)x_{ji}\le n-2\] is valid for every directed Hamiltonian tour with its natural nondepot ordering. It implies \(u_j\ge u_i+1\) when \(x_{ij}=1\), implies the reverse order when \(x_{ji}=1\), and strengthens the corresponding unlifted MTZ restriction when neither reverse arc is fixed. Replacing the pairwise MTZ inequalities by these valid lifted inequalities preserves every integral tour while tightening the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-arc lifting strengthens each MTZ order inequality while retaining all Hamiltonian tours and their natural orders.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le u_i\le n-1\) for nondepot vertices
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{lifted\ MTZ}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{MTZ}}\) after projection to the common variables.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient pattern and resulting projection comparison require a variant-specific source. Moreover, the single displayed inequality with x_{ji}=1 yields u_i-u_j<=1, not the asserted strict reverse order; that order follows only from the counterpart inequality with indices reversed.

children.title: Ordering-Strength Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-strength limitations across ordering-based formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Strength Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation boundary between compact MTZ ordering and subtour-elimination formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{\mathrm{MTZ}}\) denote the projection onto \(x\) of the continuous standard MTZ system, and let \(P_{\mathrm{SEC}}\) denote the continuous assignment system augmented by every directed subtour-elimination inequality. The ordering relaxation does not generally recover the subtour-elimination relaxation: for sufficiently large complete digraphs, \[P_{\mathrm{SEC}}\subsetneq P_{\mathrm{MTZ}}.\] Thus MTZ is exact for integral assignment vectors but may admit fractional points excluded by directed cut inequalities; lifting selected order inequalities can tighten, but does not automatically close, this boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MTZ is exact for binary assignments but its linear relaxation is generally strictly weaker than the full directed subtour-elimination relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Both relaxations use the same directed assignment equations
Arc variables are relaxed to \(0\le x_{ij}\le1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{SEC}}\subsetneq P_{\mathrm{MTZ}}\) in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is suitable, but strict containment of the projected MTZ relaxation over the SEC relaxation requires a theorem locator or explicit sourced witness.

children.title: Single-Commodity-Flow Formulations
children.top_down_role: TSP formulations using one auxiliary flow commodity.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Commodity-Flow Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-commodity directed flow formulation rooted at the depot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with depot \(1\), and let binary \(x\) satisfy the directed assignment equations. Introduce nonnegative flow \(f_{ij}\) and impose \[\sum_j f_{1j}-\sum_j f_{j1}=n-1,\qquad \sum_j f_{ji}-\sum_j f_{ij}=1\quad(i\ne1),\qquad 0\le f_{ij}\le(n-1)x_{ij}.\] The depot sends one unit to every other vertex. Any proper selected cycle avoiding the depot has positive net demand but no entering selected arc, so integral feasible solutions are exactly directed Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single depot flow delivers one unit to each other vertex; capacity linking prevents any selected subtour disconnected from the depot.
assumptions_latex: All sums range over existing loopless directed arcs
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,f)\text{ is integral-feasible}\Rightarrow x\text{ is a directed Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vector}\).

children.title: Multicommodity-Flow Formulations
children.top_down_role: TSP formulations using destination-specific or source-specific commodities.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicommodity-Flow Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One depot-to-destination commodity for each nondepot vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let binary \(x\) satisfy the directed assignment equations on \(V\), with depot \(1\). For each destination \(k\ne1\), introduce \(f^k_{ij}\ge0\) satisfying \[\sum_j f^k_{1j}-\sum_j f^k_{j1}=1,\qquad \sum_j f^k_{jk}-\sum_j f^k_{kj}=1,\] with zero balance at every other vertex, and impose \(0\le f^k_{ij}\le x_{ij}\). Each commodity certifies a selected-arc path from \(1\) to its destination; hence no integral assignment component can avoid the depot, and \(x\) represents one directed Hamiltonian tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separate unit flow from the depot to every destination certifies reachability and eliminates all depot-free subtours.
assumptions_latex: Flow balance is imposed separately for every commodity
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,f)\text{ is integral-feasible}\Rightarrow x\text{ is a directed Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vector}\).

children.title: Flow-Formulation Strength Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparative relaxation structure across flow representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Formulation Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection comparison for standard directed flow and subtour-elimination relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relax integrality of the common arc variables and project away all flow variables. For the standard formulations with individual, unshared commodity capacities, the multicommodity projection equals the directed subtour-elimination relaxation, because unit flow to every destination exists exactly when every depot-separating directed cut has capacity at least one. The single-commodity balance system aggregates destination demands and is weaker. Consequently, \[P_{\mathrm{SEC}}=P_{\mathrm{MCF}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{SCF}},\] and the last inclusion is strict in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard multicommodity projection matches directed subtour elimination, while the smaller single-commodity relaxation is generally weaker.
assumptions_latex: All formulations use identical directed assignment equations
Each multicommodity flow has capacity \(f^k_{ij}\le x_{ij}\) independently
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{SEC}}=P_{\mathrm{MCF}}\subsetneq P_{\mathrm{SCF}}\) in general.

notation.meaning: arc-space projection of the multicommodity relaxation
arc-space projection of the single-commodity relaxation

children.title: Flow-Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between formulation size and relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic size versus relaxation-strength tradeoff for standard directed flow formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a complete digraph with \(n\) vertices, the single-commodity formulation adds one flow variable per arc and \(O(n^2)\) linking and balance constraints, so its extended formulation has \(O(n^2)\) variables and constraints. The destination-indexed multicommodity formulation adds \(n-1\) flow copies, giving \(O(n^3)\) flow variables and linking constraints. This cubic enlargement yields the stronger arc-space relaxation \(P_{\mathrm{MCF}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{SCF}}\), with strict containment possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-commodity flow has quadratic size; multicommodity flow has cubic size but generally provides a stronger linear relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The underlying digraph is complete and loopless
Formulations are written explicitly without constraint-generation compression
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}(\mathrm{SCF})=O(n^2)\), \(\operatorname{size}(\mathrm{MCF})=O(n^3)\), and \(P_{\mathrm{MCF}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{SCF}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic and cubic size counts follow the displayed formulation conventions, but the combined size-versus-strength property relies on the unsourced projection comparison and needs an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Tour Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull definition for undirected Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the complete undirected graph \(K_n=(V,E)\) with \(n\ge3\), let \(\chi^C\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) be the edge-incidence vector of a Hamiltonian cycle \(C\). The symmetric tour polytope is \[P_{\mathrm{STSP}}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:C\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle of }K_n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{E}.\] Every point in this polytope satisfies the affine degree equations \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=2\) for all \(v\in V\), as well as \(0\le x_e\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric tour polytope is the convex hull of edge-incidence vectors of all undirected Hamiltonian cycles in the complete graph.
assumptions_latex: \(K_n\) is undirected and loopless
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{STSP}}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C:C\text{ Hamiltonian in }K_n\}\).

notation.meaning: edge-incidence vector of Hamiltonian cycle C
set of edges incident to vertex v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-hull definition is standard, precise, and correctly classified as a definition, but no source with a specific definition, section, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric traveling-salesman polytope and its complexity boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tour polytope, gives its linear-optimization interpretation, and records the conditional obstruction to polynomially certifiable emptiness descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, define
$$P_{\mathrm{TSP}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C\in\mathbb R^E:C\text{ is a Hamiltonian circuit of }G\}.$$
Whenever this polytope is nonempty,
$$\min_{C\text{ Hamiltonian}} l(C)=\min_{x\in P_{\mathrm{TSP}}(G)}l^\top x.$$
Moreover, deciding whether $P_{\mathrm{TSP}}(G)$ is nonempty is NP-complete. Unless $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$, there is therefore no general polynomial-time-certifiable system of valid inequalities that certifies emptiness by having no common solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric TSP polytope is the convex hull of Hamiltonian-tour incidence vectors. Linear optimization over it is exactly symmetric TSP when a tour exists, and deciding whether the polytope is nonempty is NP-complete. Unless NP equals co-NP, emptiness cannot generally be certified by an inconsistent collection of valid inequalities whose validity is polynomial-time certifiable.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph}
P_{\mathrm{TSP}}(G)\neq\varnothing\text{ for the optimization equality}
\mathrm{NP}\neq\mathrm{coNP}\text{ for the certificate impossibility conclusion}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymmetric traveling-salesman polytope and directed subtour relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the asymmetric tour polytope, gives its degree-and-cut relaxation, and records both tractable linear optimization and failure of exactness. The malformed extracted facet-range claim is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph $D=(V,A)$, let $P_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(D)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C\in\mathbb R^A:C\text{ is a Hamiltonian circuit of }D\}$. Then $P_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(D)$ is contained in the polytope defined by $0\le x_a\le1$ for all $a\in A$, $x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v))=1$ for all $v\in V$, and $x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge1$ for every $\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V$. Linear optimization over this relaxation is strongly polynomial-time solvable. The inclusion need not be equality: there is a four-vertex example in which the vector assigning $\tfrac12$ to every arc satisfies the relaxation but does not belong to the tour polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymmetric TSP polytope is the convex hull of directed Hamiltonian-circuit incidence vectors. The directed subtour relaxation imposes arc bounds, one entering and one leaving arc at every vertex, and an entering-cut inequality for every nonempty proper vertex set. Linear objectives can be optimized over this relaxation in strongly polynomial time, but the relaxation can be strictly larger than the tour polytope, even on four vertices.

x\in\mathbb R^A
l\in\mathbb R^A\text{ for the linear-optimization claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(D)\subseteq\left\{x:0\le x\le1,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v))=1\ \forall v,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge1\ \forall\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V\right\},\quad\text{and this inclusion is strict for some four-vertex digraph.}

children.title: Degree Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Tour-polyhedral restrictions associated with vertex incidence.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph
\(x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) represents selected edges
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\delta(v))=2\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: edges having exactly one endpoint in S
sum of x_e over edges in F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected symmetric-tour degree system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each vertex \(v\in V\), the degree condition is
\[
x(\delta(v)):=\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=2.
\]
Equivalently, it is the pair of degree inequalities \(x(\delta(v))\le 2\) and \(x(\delta(v))\ge 2\). For a binary vector \(x\), these conditions require the selected spanning subgraph to be a two-factor, although they do not by themselves ensure connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each vertex must have exactly two selected incident edges; binary solutions are two-factors but may contain several disjoint cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric degree condition is mathematically precise and appropriately classified, but it has no cited source.

children.title: Subtour-Elimination Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Tour-polyhedral restrictions excluding disconnected subtours.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is complete and undirected with \(|V|=n\ge 3\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\le |S|-1\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\).

notation.meaning: edges with both endpoints in S
sum of x_e over edges in F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Internal-edge form for the symmetric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The subtour-elimination system consists of
\[
x(E(S)):=\sum_{e\in E(S)}x_e\le |S|-1
\]
for every nonempty proper subset \(S\subsetneq V\). Under the degree equations, the cases \(|S|=1\) and \(|S|=n-1\) are redundant. For binary degree-feasible vectors, these inequalities exclude every cycle whose vertex set is a proper subset of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No proper vertex subset may contain as many selected internal edges as vertices, thereby excluding disconnected subtours.
knowledge_statements.title: Subtour-Elimination Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The internal-edge subtour system is correctly scoped, but the record provides no inspectable source for the formulation and redundancy claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper vertex set \(S\subsetneq V\), the symmetric connectivity-cut inequality is
\[
x(\delta(S)):=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge 2.
\]
The equivalent complementary cut \(\delta(V\setminus S)\) gives the same inequality. A binary degree-feasible vector satisfying all such cuts represents one connected two-regular spanning subgraph and hence one Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper vertex set must have at least two selected edges crossing its boundary; with binary degree-two constraints, this enforces one tour.

children.title: Degree-Connectivity Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural interaction between local incidence restrictions and global connectivity.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is undirected
\(x(\delta(v))=2\) for every \(v\in V\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\le |S|-1\iff x(\delta(S))\ge 2\).

notation.meaning: edges crossing from S to its complement
sum of x_e over edges in F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of internal-edge and cut forms under degree two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Summing the degree equations over any \(S\subseteq V\) counts internal edges twice and cut edges once, giving
\[
2x(E(S))+x(\delta(S))=2|S|.
\]
Consequently, for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\),
\[
x(E(S))\le |S|-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x(\delta(S))\ge 2.
\]
Thus the degree equations make the subtour-elimination and connectivity-cut descriptions interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree-two equations convert each internal subtour inequality exactly into its corresponding two-edge connectivity cut inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Connectivity Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated equivalence follows under the degree equations and fits the interaction leaf, but no source is cited.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is complete and undirected
\(H\subseteq V\), and \(T\subseteq\delta(H)\) is a matching of odd size at least three

source_refs.locator: Section 11.5. The Matching Polytope p. 297

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let every edge of \(T\) have exactly one endpoint in \(H\), and let no two edges of \(T\) share an endpoint. If \(|T|\ge 3\) is odd, every incidence vector \(x\) of a Hamiltonian cycle satisfies the two-matching inequality
\[
x(E(H))+x(T)\le |H|+\frac{|T|-1}{2}.
\]
This inequality strengthens the degree-and-subtour relaxation for suitable handles and tooth matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd matching crossing a handle limits the total selected handle edges and matching teeth in every Hamiltonian tour.

notation.meaning: an odd-cardinality subset of the cut

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity inequalities valid for incidence vectors of undirected two-factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), a two-factor crosses \(\delta(S)\) an even number of times. Hence, for every odd-cardinality set \(F\subseteq\delta(S)\), its incidence vector satisfies
\[
x(F)-x(\delta(S)\setminus F)\le |F|-1.
\]
Equivalently, a selected cut cannot agree with an odd cut pattern consisting exactly of \(F\). These parity inequalities are valid for the convex hull of spanning two-factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every two-factor crosses each cut evenly, odd cut patterns are excluded by standard parity inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Factor Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity inequality is valid for binary two-factors, but the exact family name and polyhedral placement require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom-Type Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-set blossom restriction for the undirected matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every odd set \(U\subseteq V\), each incidence vector \(y\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) of a matching in \(G\) satisfies
\[
y(E(U)):=\sum_{e\in E(U)}y_e\le \frac{|U|-1}{2}.
\]
Together with nonnegativity and the vertex inequalities \(y(\delta(v))\le 1\) for all \(v\in V\), these odd-set restrictions describe the matching polytope of an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within any odd vertex set, a matching contains at most one half of the set's cardinality rounded down in internal edges. These restrictions, vertex degree bounds, and nonnegativity describe the undirected matching polytope.

children.title: Matching-to-Factor Relations

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a cubic undirected graph
\(M\subseteq E\) is a perfect matching

notation.meaning: incidence vector of an edge set F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement relation between perfect matchings and two-factors in cubic graphs.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.5. The Matching Polytope p. 297

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Since every vertex of \(G\) has degree three and is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\), every vertex is incident with exactly two edges of \(E\setminus M\). Therefore \(E\setminus M\) is a spanning two-factor, and
\[
\chi^{E\setminus M}=\mathbf{1}-\chi^M.
\]
Conversely, the complement of any spanning two-factor in a cubic graph is a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a cubic graph, complementation gives a bijection between perfect matchings and spanning two-factors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-matching inequalities as edge-tooth specializations of comb inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=\{e_1,\ldots,e_t\}\) be an odd matching crossing \(H\), and define each tooth \(T_i\) as the two endpoints of \(e_i\). Then \(|T_i|=2\) and \(x(E(T_i))=x_{e_i}\). Substitution into the comb inequality gives
\[
x(E(H))+x(T)\le |H|+2t-\frac{3t+1}{2}=|H|+\frac{t-1}{2},
\]
which is precisely the two-matching inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every comb tooth is a single matching edge crossing the handle, the comb inequality reduces exactly to a two-matching inequality.

children.title: Comb-to-Clique-Tree Relations
children.top_down_role: Containment and specialization relations between the two families.

assumptions_latex: The graph is complete and undirected: \(G=(V,E)\).
The comb has an odd number \(t\ge 3\) of pairwise disjoint teeth, each meeting and leaving the handle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The comb inequality is the star-shaped specialization of the corresponding clique-tree inequality.

notation.meaning: Handle and teeth of the comb
Sum of edge variables across a cut

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard symmetric-TSP cut formulation and the star-shaped clique-tree convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H,T_1,\ldots,T_t\subset V\), where \(t\ge 3\) is odd, the teeth are pairwise disjoint, and \(H\cap T_i\ne\varnothing\ne T_i\setminus H\) for every \(i\). The associated comb inequality is
\[
x(\delta(H))+\sum_{i=1}^{t}x(\delta(T_i))\ge 3t+1.
\]
In the standard clique-tree construction, choose the support tree to be a star whose central clique represents \(H\) and whose leaf cliques represent the teeth. Substitution into the clique-tree template yields this comb inequality, so combs form a specialization of clique-tree inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comb inequality is obtained from the clique-tree template when its support tree is a star with the handle at the center and teeth at the leaves.
