children.title: Path Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Strong tour-polyhedral restrictions organized around path structures.

assumptions_latex: The inequality is considered on the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope of a complete graph.
Its nonzero edge coefficients induce a connected support graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed support predicate characterizes a path-supported inequality template; validity additionally requires \(\beta\le\min_{C}\sum_{e\in C}\alpha_e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the support predicate; the canonical coefficient normalization remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an inequality \(\sum_{e\in E}\alpha_e x_e\ge\beta\), define \(E_\alpha=\{e:\alpha_e\ne0\}\) and let \(G_\alpha\) be the graph induced by these edges after deleting isolated vertices. The inequality is path-supported when \(G_\alpha\) is connected, has exactly two vertices of degree one, and every other vertex has degree two; equivalently, \(G_\alpha\) is a simple path. Such a template is valid for the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope precisely when
\[
\beta\le \min_{C}\sum_{e\in C}\alpha_e,
\]
where the minimum ranges over Hamiltonian cycles \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-supported TSP inequality has nonzero coefficients arranged on a simple path; its right-hand side cannot exceed the minimum coefficient sum over Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.title: Path Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-over-tours condition is a tautological validity test for any coefficient vector and does not establish that simple-path coefficient support is the literature's Path Inequality family. A source specifying the canonical coefficients, right-hand side, and hypotheses is required.

children.title: Bridge Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Strong tour-polyhedral restrictions organized around bridge structures.

assumptions_latex: The inequality is considered on the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope.
Deleting one designated support edge separates the remaining coefficient support into two nonempty parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicate defines bridge support, while validity is equivalent to \(\beta\le\min_C\alpha^\top\chi^C\).

notation.meaning: Graph of edges with nonzero coefficients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Captures bridge support without selecting an unsupported literature-specific coefficient template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha^\top x\ge\beta\), let \(G_\alpha=(V_\alpha,E_\alpha)\) be its nonzero-coefficient support. A bridge-supported template consists of connected induced support subgraphs on disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(U\) and \(W\), together with a designated edge \(b=uw\), where \(u\in U\), \(w\in W\), such that \(G_\alpha-b\) has exactly the two components \(U\) and \(W\). Independently of the chosen coefficient normalization, the template defines a valid TSP inequality exactly when
\[
\beta\le\min_C \alpha^\top\chi^C,
\]
with \(C\) ranging over all Hamiltonian cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bridge-supported inequality joins two nonempty coefficient-support components by one designated edge; validity requires every Hamiltonian tour to satisfy its stated bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Bridge Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bridge-support predicate is coherent, but the minimum-over-tours condition applies to every inequality and does not identify the canonical Bridge Inequality family. Its coefficients, normalization, and validity theorem require an inspectable source.

children.title: Domino-Parity Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Strong tour-polyhedral restrictions organized around domino systems and parity.

assumptions_latex: Every base inequality used in the certificate is valid for the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope.
The multipliers are nonnegative and produce integral left-hand coefficients after summation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounded inequality \(a^\top x\ge\lceil\gamma\rceil\) is valid and supplies a parity-based certificate for the domino-supported inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the integer-rounding certificate underlying parity inequalities; exact domino incidence conventions remain unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a^{k\top}x\ge b_k\) be valid degree or cut inequalities, chosen according to a domino support system, and let \(\lambda_k\ge0\). Suppose
\[
a=\sum_k\lambda_k a^k\in\mathbb Z^E,
\qquad
\gamma=\sum_k\lambda_k b_k\notin\mathbb Z.
\]
Every tour incidence vector is integral, so aggregation and integer rounding give the valid inequality
\[
a^\top x\ge\lceil\gamma\rceil.
\]
When the selected cuts arise from paired domino shores and the fractional part of \(\gamma\) is forced by their odd parity, this rounded inequality is a domino-parity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domino-parity inequality is certified by nonnegative aggregation of valid cut or degree inequalities followed by integer rounding forced by odd parity.
knowledge_statements.title: Domino-Parity Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integer-rounding argument is mathematically standard, but neither a domino support system nor the paired shores and parity hypotheses are defined. Consequently, the statement does not yet specify a Domino-Parity Inequality or its exact certificate construction.

children.title: Support-Structure Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural relations among path, bridge, and domino supports.

assumptions_latex: Two coefficient templates are related by a vertex bijection preserving coefficients and right-hand sides.
The ambient complete graphs have corresponding vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Support-isomorphic templates have identical validity and violation behavior under the induced relabeling.

notation.meaning: Coefficient vectors before and after relabeling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers invariant relations among path, bridge, and domino-supported coefficient templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:V\to V'\) be a bijection and suppose \(\alpha'_{\varphi(u)\varphi(v)}=\alpha_{uv}\) for every edge \(uv\), with the same right-hand side \(\beta\). The map \(C\mapsto\varphi(C)\) is a bijection between Hamiltonian cycles, and therefore
\[
\alpha^\top\chi^C=\alpha'{}^\top\chi^{\varphi(C)}.
\]
Consequently, \(\alpha^\top x\ge \beta\) is valid if and only if \(\alpha'{}^\top x\ge \beta\) is valid. Moreover, corresponding tours have equal violation. Thus support structure is considered up to coefficient-preserving graph isomorphism when comparing path, bridge, and domino-parity templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-preserving isomorphisms of support graphs preserve TSP-inequality validity and map violating tours bijectively, allowing support families to be compared up to relabeling.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Structure Relations

assumptions_latex: The instance is a complete undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with finite edge costs.
At least three vertices are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum \(z_{\mathrm{HK}}\) of the displayed linear program satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{HK}}\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric Held–Karp relaxation in edge variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For costs \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), the symmetric Held–Karp subtour relaxation is
\[
z_{\mathrm{HK}}=\min\left\{c^\top x:
 x(\delta(v))=2\ \forall v\in V,
 x(\delta(S))\ge2\ \forall\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,
 x_e\ge0\ \forall e\in E\right\}.
\]
Every Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vector satisfies the degree equations, every proper-cut inequality, and nonnegativity. Hence the convex hull of tours is contained in the feasible region of this linear program, and minimization gives \(z_{\mathrm{HK}}\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Held–Karp relaxation imposes degree two at every vertex, at least two edges across every proper cut, and nonnegativity; its optimum lower-bounds the symmetric TSP.
knowledge_statements.title: Held–Karp Subtour Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric Held-Karp formulation and lower-bound direction are mathematically correct and the representation kind fits the topic, but the record supplies no citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-programming representation of the Held–Karp bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality between the optimized 1-tree Lagrangian bound and the stated subtour-elimination relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every TSP instance \((K_n,c)\) with \(V(K_n)=\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[HK(K_n,c)=\min\left\{c^\top x:\begin{array}{l}0\le x_e\le1\quad(e\in E(K_n)),\\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=2\quad(v\in V(K_n)),\\ \sum_{e\in E(K_n[I])}x_e\le |I|-1\quad(\varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{2,\ldots,n\})\end{array}\right\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-tree Lagrangian lower bound for TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines one-trees, their incidence-vector hull, and the concave multiplier-dependent lower bound stated before the extract's truncated Held–Karp theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a vertex $1\in V$. A one-tree is an edge set $F\subseteq E$ such that $|F\cap\delta(1)|=2$ and $F\setminus\delta(1)$ is a spanning tree on $V\setminus\{1\}$. A shortest one-tree consists of a shortest spanning tree of $G-1$ together with the two shortest edges incident with $1$. Its incidence-vector hull is described by
$$0\le x_e\le1,\quad x(\delta(1))=2,\quad x(E[U])\le |U|-1\ \ (\varnothing\neq U\subseteq V\setminus\{1\}),\quad x(E)=|V|.$$
Adding the degree equations $x(\delta(v))=2$ for all $v\in V$ yields the subtour-elimination relaxation. For $y\in\mathbb R^V$, set $l_y(uv)=l(uv)-y_u-y_v$ and
$$f(y)=2y(V)+\min_{F\text{ one-tree}}l_y(F).$$
Then $f$ is concave, is computable through a minimum-one-tree calculation, and satisfies
$$f(y)\le \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}$$
for every $y\in\mathbb R^V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-tree is a spanning tree on all vertices except a fixed root, plus two edges incident with that root. Its polytope becomes the subtour relaxation after all degree-two equations are imposed. Vertex multipliers define an efficiently computable concave one-tree value that lower-bounds the length of every optimal Hamiltonian tour.

1\in V
y\in\mathbb R^V
l_y(uv)=l(uv)-y_u-y_v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y\in\mathbb R^V:\quad f(y)=2y(V)+\min_{F\text{ one-tree}}l_y(F)\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian 1-tree lower bound and its computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-multiplier lower bound for a complete-graph TSP instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a TSP instance \((K_n,c)\), with \(V(K_n)=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(\lambda=(\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n)\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\), define
\[LR(K_n,c,\lambda)=\min_{T\text{ a 1-tree}}\left\{c(E(T))+\sum_{i=2}^n\bigl(|\delta_T(i)|-2\bigr)\lambda_i\right\}.\]
Then \(LR(K_n,c,\lambda)\) is a lower bound on the length of an optimum tour and can be computed in the time needed to solve a minimum spanning tree problem on \(n-1\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any real degree multipliers on vertices 2 through n, minimizing the penalized cost over 1-trees gives a lower bound on the optimum TSP tour length. It can be computed in the time needed for a minimum spanning tree problem on n-1 vertices.
assumptions_latex: (K_n,c)\text{ is a TSP instance}
V(K_n)=\{1,\ldots,n\}
\lambda\in\mathbb R^{n-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: LR(K_n,c,\lambda)\le \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(K_n,c),\qquad LR(K_n,c,\lambda)\text{ is computable in the time needed for an MST problem on }n-1\text{ vertices}.

children.title: One-Tree Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds based on undirected one-tree structures.

assumptions_latex: The TSP instance is a complete undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with finite edge costs \(c\in\mathbb R^E\).
The vertex set satisfies \(|V|\ge 3\), and a root vertex \(r\in V\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum one-tree cost \(L_r\) satisfies \(L_r\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cost of a root-based one-tree

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected minimum one-tree lower bound with a fixed root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be complete and undirected, let \(|V|\ge 3\), let \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), and fix \(r\in V\). A one-tree rooted at \(r\) is the union of a spanning tree on \(V\setminus\{r\}\) and exactly two distinct edges incident with \(r\). Define
\[
L_r=\min\{c(T):T\text{ is a one-tree rooted at }r\}.
\]
Deleting \(r\) and its two incident tour edges from any Hamiltonian cycle leaves a spanning path, and hence a spanning tree, on \(V\setminus\{r\}\). Thus every Hamiltonian cycle is a feasible rooted one-tree, so
\[
L_r\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}.
\]
Moreover, \(L_r\) is obtained by a minimum-spanning-tree computation on \(V\setminus\{r\}\) together with the two cheapest distinct edges incident with \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete undirected TSP with at least three vertices, a minimum spanning tree away from a fixed root plus the two cheapest distinct root edges is a minimum rooted one-tree, and its cost lower-bounds every Hamiltonian tour.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Tree Bounds

children.title: Directed One-Tree Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds based on orientation-sensitive one-tree analogues.

assumptions_latex: The instance is a complete directed graph \(D=(V,A)\) with finite arc costs \(c\in\mathbb R^A\).
The vertex set satisfies \(|V|\ge 2\), and a distinguished vertex \(r\in V\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated out-arborescence convention, the minimum directed one-tree value \(L_r^{\rightarrow}\) satisfies \(L_r^{\rightarrow}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).

notation.meaning: Root of the out-arborescence on the remaining vertices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an out-arborescence convention; alternative directed one-tree definitions exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be complete and directed, let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), and fix \(r\in V\). Under the out-arborescence convention, a directed one-tree is the union of an out-arborescence on \(V\setminus\{r\}\), rooted at some \(q\in V\setminus\{r\}\), one arc from \(r\) to \(q\), and one arc entering \(r\). Let \(L_r^{\rightarrow}\) be the minimum cost over these objects. Removing \(r\) and its incident tour arcs from any directed Hamiltonian cycle leaves a directed Hamiltonian path, which is an out-arborescence rooted at its first vertex. Reattaching the removed arcs produces a feasible directed one-tree, and therefore
\[
L_r^{\rightarrow}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated out-arborescence convention, every directed Hamiltonian tour is a directed one-tree, so the minimum directed one-tree cost is an ATSP lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed One-Tree Bounds

children.title: Root-Choice Effects
children.top_down_role: Bound behavior associated with the distinguished root.

assumptions_latex: For every root \(r\), \(L_r\) is the minimum cost among one-trees rooted at \(r\).
The underlying undirected TSP instance is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Root-specific values may differ, while \(\max_{r\in V}L_r\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).

notation.meaning: One-tree lower bound for root r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates root-dependent computational values from root-independent validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(r\in V\), every Hamiltonian cycle is a one-tree rooted at \(r\), so \(L_r\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\). The minimizing spanning tree and the two selected root edges depend on \(r\); consequently, unequal edge costs can yield \(L_r\ne L_s\) for distinct roots \(r,s\). Nevertheless, taking the strongest root-specific bound preserves validity:
\[
L_*:=\max_{r\in V}L_r\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}.
\]
Thus root choice affects bound strength and computation but not the lower-bound guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different roots can produce different minimum one-tree costs. Every root gives a valid lower bound, and the maximum over roots is therefore the strongest such bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Root-Choice Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The root-dependent values and maximum-over-roots inequality are correct under the preceding undirected one-tree definition, and property is the appropriate content kind. No inspectable source is supplied for the claim.

children.title: Orientation-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring one-tree bounds between undirected and directed regimes.

assumptions_latex: Arc costs may be asymmetric.
An undirected surrogate assigns each edge the average of its two opposing arc costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Averaging opposite arc costs does not generally preserve the directed one-tree lower-bound property.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that orientation cannot be discarded by cost averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{1,2,3\}\). Assign cost zero to arcs \((1,2),(2,3),(3,1)\) and cost \(100\) to the three reverse arcs. The directed Hamiltonian cycle \(1\to2\to3\to1\) has cost \(0\), so \(z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=0\). If orientation is discarded by setting
\[
\bar c_{ij}=\frac{c_{ij}+c_{ji}}2,
\]
then every undirected edge has cost \(50\), and the unique undirected three-vertex tour has cost \(150\). Hence a one-tree bound computed from these averaged costs can exceed the directed optimum and is not a valid ATSP lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging opposite directed costs can make an undirected one-tree value exceed the ATSP optimum, so orientation-insensitive transfer is invalid without additional symmetry assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitivity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-vertex counterexample is internally correct and fits the failure-boundary container: the directed optimum is zero while every averaged undirected edge costs 50 and the rooted one-tree costs 150. The record nevertheless lacks source evidence beyond standard-field rationale.

children.title: Assignment Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds derived from assignment relaxations.

assumptions_latex: The directed TSP instance is complete on a finite vertex set \(V\), has finite arc costs \(c_{ij}\), and excludes self-arcs.
The vertex set satisfies \(|V|\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment optimum \(z_{\mathrm{AP}}\) satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{AP}}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite vertex set with \(|V|\ge 2\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) be the cost of arc \((i,j)\) for distinct \(i,j\in V\). The assignment relaxation of the asymmetric TSP is
\[
z_{\mathrm{AP}}=
\min\left\{
\sum_{\substack{i,j\in V\\i\ne j}}c_{ij}x_{ij}:
\sum_{\substack{j\in V\\j\ne i}}x_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in V,
\sum_{\substack{i\in V\\i\ne j}}x_{ij}=1\ \forall j\in V,
 x_{ij}\ge0\ \forall i,j\in V\text{ with }i\ne j
\right\}.
\]
Its feasible solutions need not be connected. Every directed Hamiltonian-cycle incidence vector satisfies one outgoing and one incoming assignment equation at every vertex. Therefore the ATSP feasible set is contained in the assignment feasible set, and minimization yields \(z_{\mathrm{AP}}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping the ATSP connectivity constraints leaves the assignment problem. Because every directed Hamiltonian tour is a feasible assignment, the assignment optimum is a lower bound on the directed tour cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Bounds

children.title: Cycle-Cover Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds derived from cycle-cover relaxations.

assumptions_latex: The directed graph is complete and self-arcs are excluded.
A cycle cover consists of vertex-disjoint directed cycles covering every vertex exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum cycle-cover value equals \(z_{\mathrm{AP}}\) and satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{CC}}=z_{\mathrm{AP}}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cost of a directed cycle cover

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial interpretation of integral solutions to the directed assignment relaxation.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.1. The Assignment Problem p. 278

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every integral feasible assignment selects exactly one outgoing and one incoming arc at each vertex. Its selected subgraph is therefore a disjoint union of directed cycles covering \(V\); conversely, every directed cycle cover defines such an assignment. Since the bipartite assignment polytope is integral, the linear assignment optimum equals the minimum cycle-cover cost:
\[
z_{\mathrm{CC}}=z_{\mathrm{AP}}.
\]
A directed Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle cover with exactly one component, so allowing multiple components enlarges the feasible family and gives
\[
z_{\mathrm{CC}}=z_{\mathrm{AP}}\le z_{\mathrm{ATSP}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral assignments are exactly directed cycle covers. Allowing several cycles instead of one Hamiltonian cycle yields the same assignment optimum and a valid ATSP lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-spanning-tree lower bound for a feasible symmetric TSP instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph containing at least one Hamiltonian cycle, with edge costs \(c_e\ge 0\). Let \(T\) be a minimum-cost spanning tree. For every Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) in \(G\) and every \(f\in H\), the graph \(H\setminus\{f\}\) is a spanning tree and \[c(T)\le c(H\setminus\{f\})=c(H)-c_f\le c(H).\] Consequently, \(c(T)\le \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a graph containing a Hamiltonian cycle, the minimum spanning-tree cost is no greater than the cost of any tour and therefore is a lower bound on the optimal tour cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected, undirected, and contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
\(c_e\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Dominance Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation among minimization relaxations and their lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq Q_1\subseteq Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty feasible regions and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Define \(z(P)=\inf\{c^\top x:x\in P\}\) and analogously define \(z(Q_1)\) and \(z(Q_2)\). Then \[z(Q_2)\le z(Q_1)\le z(P).\] Thus, for a minimization TSP, the relaxation with the smaller feasible region dominates the larger relaxation: it supplies a lower bound at least as large, although equality may occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, inclusion of relaxation regions reverses the ordering of optimal values; the tighter region provides the stronger lower bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian one-tree upper bound and degree-deficit subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight TSP specialization of Lagrangian one-tree bounding and subgradient multiplier search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix w\in V(G) and let \mathcal P_w(G) be the w\text{-tree polytope}. For \pi\in\mathbb R^{V(G)} with \pi_w=0 and \sum_{v\in V(G)}\pi_v=0, define
f(\pi)=\max_{x\in\mathcal P_w(G)}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}(c_{ij}-\pi_i-\pi_j)x_{ij}.
If \widetilde S is an optimizing w\text{-tree}, then \widetilde h_v=2-|\widetilde S\cap\delta_G(v)| is a subgradient of f relative to the admissible multiplier subspace. For every Hamiltonian tour H, its adjusted objective equals its original weight, so the maximum Hamiltonian-tour value z satisfies z\le f(\pi). Thus subgradient optimization can be used to seek \min f(\pi) over the stated multiplier subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the root multiplier fixed to zero and all multipliers summing to zero, endpoint penalties produce a maximum adjusted one-tree value that upper-bounds the maximum Hamiltonian-tour weight. For an optimizing one-tree, the degree deficits—two minus each vertex degree—form a subgradient relative to the permitted multiplier subspace, enabling subgradient search for a tighter upper bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian lower bounds obtained by dualizing coupling constraints in a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(z^*=\inf\{c^\top x:x\in X,\ h(x)=0\}\), where \(X\) retains the constraints that remain explicitly enforced. For \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p\), define \[\theta(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c^\top x+\lambda^\top h(x)\bigr).\] Every feasible \(x\) has \(h(x)=0\), hence \(\theta(\lambda)\le z^*\) for every multiplier. The Lagrangian dual value \(z_L=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p}\theta(\lambda)\) is therefore the strongest lower bound obtainable from this relaxation and satisfies \(z_L\le z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing equality constraints gives a lower bound for every multiplier; maximizing the dual function gives the strongest bound in that Lagrangian family.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(h:X\to\mathbb{R}^p\), and the primal feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(\lambda)\le z_L\le z^*\) for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Held–Karp bound as a Lagrangian dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of the TSP 1-tree Lagrangian lower bound over unrestricted equality-constraint multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because the relaxed degree conditions \(|\delta_T(i)|=2\), \(i=2,\ldots,n\), are equalities, their multipliers are unrestricted in sign. The Held–Karp bound is
\[HK(K_n,c):=\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^{n-1}}LR(K_n,c,\lambda).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed degree constraints are equalities, so their Lagrange multipliers may be arbitrary real numbers. Maximizing the resulting 1-tree lower bound over those multipliers defines the Held–Karp bound.
assumptions_latex: (K_n,c)\text{ is a TSP instance}
LR(K_n,c,\lambda)\text{ is the associated 1-tree Lagrangian lower bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: HK(K_n,c)=\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^{n-1}}LR(K_n,c,\lambda),\qquad \lambda_i\in\mathbb R\text{ for }i=2,\ldots,n.

children.title: Subgradient Multiplier Optimization
children.top_down_role: Multiplier-search techniques used to improve Lagrangian lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Multiplier Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected supergradient ascent for maximizing a concave Lagrangian dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a closed convex multiplier set \(\Lambda\), choose \(\lambda^0\in\Lambda\) and positive step sizes \(\alpha_k\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(x^k\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\{c^\top x+(\lambda^k)^\top h(x)\}\), set \(g^k=h(x^k)\), and update \[\lambda^{k+1}=\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda^k+\alpha_k g^k).\] Here \(g^k\) is a supergradient of the concave dual function at \(\lambda^k\). Stop under a prescribed iteration, step-size, or bound-improvement rule, and return the largest observed value \(\max_{0\le j\le k}\theta(\lambda^j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the relaxed problem, move multipliers along a dual supergradient, project if necessary, and retain the best lower bound encountered.
assumptions_latex: Each relaxed subproblem has an attained minimizer \(x^k\).
\(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(\max_{0\le j\le k}\theta(\lambda^j)\), a valid primal lower bound.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the multiplier set
a dual supergradient at iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected supergradient-ascent algorithm and best-bound return rule are mathematically consistent, but the record has no citation supporting the algorithmic specification.

children.title: Lagrangian Bound Quality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions affecting bound strength, stability, or practical usefulness.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Bound Quality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of the Lagrangian gap for finite discrete equality-constrained models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be finite and consider \(z^*=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X,\ Ax=b\}\). If the convexified problem is feasible, linear-programming duality gives \[\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p}\min_{x\in X}\bigl(c^\top x+\lambda^\top(Ax-b)\bigr)=\min\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{conv}(X),\ Ax=b\}.\] Hence the Lagrangian bound is exact precisely when the convexified constrained optimum equals \(z^*\); otherwise their difference is the Lagrangian duality gap. Multiplier optimization cannot remove a gap caused by this convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimized Lagrangian bound equals the convexified constrained optimum; it is exact exactly when convexification introduces no objective gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is finite.
\(\{x\in\operatorname{conv}(X):Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_L=\min\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{conv}(X),\ Ax=b\}\le z^*\).

notation.meaning: the convex hull of the retained discrete feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact convexification identity requires an authoritative theorem locator. The assumptions should also state that the discrete constrained feasible set is nonempty if the finite value \(z^*\) and an objective duality gap are intended.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the same TSP instance, the subtour lower bound and the optimal Held–Karp lower bound have equal values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-cut separation of the DFJ subtour constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the subtour relaxation, its integer-point characterization, and polynomial-time separation; approximation, facet, and exactness-recognition results remain cross-indexed specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, consider
$$0\le x_e\le1\quad(e\in E),\qquad x(\delta(v))=2\quad(v\in V),$$
$$x(\delta(U))\ge2\quad(\varnothing\neq U\subsetneq V).$$
The integer solutions are precisely the incidence vectors of Hamiltonian circuits. Under the degree equations, the cut inequalities are equivalent to
$$x(E[U])\le |U|-1\quad(\varnothing\neq U\subsetneq V).$$
After checking the bounds and degree equations, separation of the subtour inequalities reduces to finding a nontrivial minimum-capacity cut with capacities $x_e$: a violated inequality exists exactly when such a cut has capacity less than $2$. Consequently, the relaxation admits polynomial-time separation and polynomial-time linear optimization through the separation-optimization equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The DFJ relaxation uses edge bounds, degree-two equations, and a cut of capacity at least two across every proper nonempty vertex set. Its integer points are exactly tours. Violated subtour inequalities can be found by a minimum-cut computation, giving polynomial-time separation and hence polynomial-time linear optimization over the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph}
x(\delta(v))=2\quad\forall v\in V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\varnothing\neq U\subsetneq V:\ x(\delta(U))<2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{the nontrivial minimum }x\text{-capacity cut has value }<2

knowledge_statements.title: Subtour Separation via Cut Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation of undirected subtour-elimination inequalities by a global minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge 2\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\). Assign capacity \(x_e\) to every \(e\in E\) and compute a global minimum nontrivial cut \(\delta(S)\), where \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). If \[x(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e<2,\] return the violated inequality \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2\). Otherwise certify that \(x(\delta(U))\ge 2\) for every \(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite undirected graph with at least two vertices, a global minimum cut separates the subtour cut inequalities: capacity below two gives a violation, while minimum capacity at least two certifies the whole family.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge 2\).
\(x_e\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated subtour cut exists if and only if \(\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}x(\delta(S))<2\).

notation.meaning: edges having exactly one endpoint in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation of TSP subtour constraints by minimum cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation for the degree-and-bound relaxation of the undirected TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ satisfy $x^*(\delta(v))=2$ for every $v\in V$ and $0\le x_e^*\le1$ for every $e\in E$. Give each edge capacity $u_e=x_e^*$. Then a subtour constraint $x^*(\delta(S))\ge2$ is violated for some $\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V$ if and only if the capacitated graph has a cut of capacity less than $2$. Consequently, a global minimum-cut computation either returns a violated subtour constraint or certifies that none exists. If the positive-support graph is disconnected, the vertex set of each connected component gives a violated constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vector satisfying the TSP degree equations and edge bounds, subtour separation is a global minimum-cut problem with capacities equal to the vector entries. A cut below two is a violation, whereas a minimum cut of at least two certifies all subtour constraints. Disconnected positive support immediately supplies violated constraints.
assumptions_latex: $G=(V,E)$ is an undirected graph.
$x^*(\delta(v))=2$ for every $v\in V$.
$0\le x_e^*\le1$ for every $e\in E$.
Subtour constraints are $x^*(\delta(S))\ge2$ for every $\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V:\ x^*(\delta(S))<2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}u(\delta(S))<2.

children.title: Exact Strong-Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Complete separation procedures for selected strong TSP cut classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Strong-Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact oracle specification for a fixed family of valid TSP inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be the TSP feasible set and let \(\mathcal F=\{(a^i)^\top x\ge b_i:i\in I\}\), where \(a^i\in\mathbb{R}^m\), be a specified family of inequalities valid for every \(x\in K\). Given \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^m\), suppose the maximum \[v^*=\max_{i\in I}\{b_i-(a^i)^\top\bar x\}\] is attained at \(i^*\). An exact separation oracle returns \((a^{i^*})^\top x\ge b_{i^*}\) when \(v^*>0\); when \(v^*\le 0\), it certifies \((a^i)^\top\bar x\ge b_i\) for every \(i\in I\). Exactness concerns the entire declared family and does not assert polynomial-time solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified valid TSP inequality family, exact separation returns a maximally violated member or certifies that the given point violates no member of the family.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is the TSP feasible set.
Each member of \(\mathcal F\) is valid for every \(x\in K\).
The maximum violation over \(I\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns a violated member of \(\mathcal F\) if one exists and otherwise certifies that none exists.

children.title: Heuristic Strong-Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Incomplete procedures emphasizing rapid discovery of violated strong cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Strong-Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incomplete separation over a searched subset of a strong valid-inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a fractional point \(\bar x\), a valid-inequality family \(\mathcal F=\{a^i{}^\top x\ge b_i:i\in I\}\), and a search rule producing \(J(\bar x)\subseteq I\), evaluate violations only for indices in \(J(\bar x)\). Return any selected inequality with \(b_i-a^i{}^\top\bar x>0\), commonly one maximizing violation within \(J(\bar x)\). If none is found, return “no cut found,” not a certificate that \(\bar x\) satisfies every member of \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heuristic searches only selected strong cuts and may return a valid violated cut, but failure to find one is not a separation certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every inequality indexed by \(J(\bar x)\) belongs to the valid family \(\mathcal F\).
\(J(\bar x)\subseteq I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any returned cut is valid and violated, but an empty return does not imply feasibility for \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: the subset searched by the heuristic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-validity versus negative-incompleteness distinction is correct, but no source identifies or supports the strong-cut family and heuristic-search specification.

children.title: Strong-Cut Separation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Coverage, computational effort, cut strength, and reliability across separation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Cut Separation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity, completeness, strength, and computational cost in strong-cut separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid inequality family \(\mathcal F\), exact separation provides the implication “no cut returned” \(\Rightarrow\bar x\) satisfies all members of \(\mathcal F\), but may require substantially more computation than restricted search. Heuristic separation preserves correctness only positively: every returned member of \(\mathcal F\) may safely be added when violated, whereas no conclusion follows from finding none. Thus cut strength and search completeness must be assessed jointly with separation time and the resulting LP size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact separation certifies absence of violations but can be costly; heuristic separation is cheaper yet provides no certificate when it finds no cut.
assumptions_latex: All returned inequalities are valid for the integer feasible set.
Exact and heuristic procedures address the same declared family \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact failure certifies \(\mathcal F\)-feasibility; heuristic failure does not.

notation.meaning: a declared family of strong valid inequalities

children.title: Cut-Pool Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, filtering, activation, aging, and reuse of generated TSP cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Pool Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite active-set policy for retaining, activating, and retiring valid cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an active set \(A_k\) and an inactive pool \(P_k\) of previously generated valid inequalities. At iteration \(k\), add newly separated violated cuts, reactivate pooled cuts whose violation at \(x^k\) exceeds \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}>0\), and move an active cut to the pool only after its slack exceeds \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\) for at least \(r\) consecutive solves. Enforce \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\ge\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\) to provide hysteresis. Reoptimize over \(A_{k+1}\); retiring a cut changes only the relaxation, never the validity of retained cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pool activates sufficiently violated cuts and retires persistently slack cuts, using hysteresis to limit oscillation while retaining only valid inequalities.
assumptions_latex: Every stored inequality is valid for the integer feasible set.
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\ge\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}>0\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every active relaxation remains valid, though retiring cuts may weaken its lower bound.

notation.meaning: inactive stored cuts at iteration k
required consecutive slack solves before retirement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is one particular hysteretic cut-pool policy rather than a canonical definition, and no source supports its thresholds or retirement rule. The stated policy also imposes no explicit pool or active-set size limit despite the scope note calling it finite.

children.title: Cut-Pricing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Selection of candidate cuts for admission into the active relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Pricing Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle contract connecting an LP solution to violated-cut generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inequalities \(a^i{}^\top x\ge b_i\) indexed by \(i\in I\), a cut-pricing interface receives the current point \(\bar x\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and returns a finite set \(J\subseteq I\) satisfying \[b_i-a^i{}^\top\bar x>\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }i\in J.\] Each returned row must include its coefficients, right-hand side, family identifier, and measured violation. If the interface claims exact separation, \(J=\varnothing\) must additionally imply \(b_i-a^i{}^\top\bar x\le\varepsilon\) for every \(i\in I\); a heuristic interface makes no such claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface returns explicitly represented cuts violated beyond tolerance; only an exact interface may certify that an empty return means no violation exists.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{a^i{}^\top x\ge b_i:i\in I\}\) is a valid inequality family.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Returned rows are \(\varepsilon\)-violated; exact emptiness certifies \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility for \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: indices of cuts returned to the LP solver

children.title: LP Reoptimization
children.top_down_role: Repeated relaxation solves after changes to the active cut system.

knowledge_statements.title: LP Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-started reoptimization after valid inequalities are added to an LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an LP relaxation has an optimal basis \(B_k\) and new valid rows are appended. Extend the former primal solution with slack variables for the new rows and reuse \(B_k\) as a warm start. If the added rows are violated, apply dual-simplex pivots: repeatedly choose a primal-infeasible basic row and an eligible entering variable that preserves dual feasibility, until primal feasibility is restored or infeasibility is certified. The resulting feasible, dual-feasible basis is optimal for the augmented LP; its objective is a valid lower bound for the minimization integer problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After cuts are appended, dual simplex can reuse the old basis and pivot from dual feasibility to a new optimal relaxation solution.
assumptions_latex: The previous LP has an optimal basis \(B_k\).
Appended rows are valid for every integer-feasible solution.
Pivoting follows a finite anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with primal and dual feasibility yields an optimum of the augmented LP and a valid integer-program lower bound.

notation.meaning: the optimal basis before adding cuts

children.title: Stale-Cut Control
children.top_down_role: Performance risks caused by oversized, weak, redundant, or obsolete cut pools.

assumptions_latex: The current relaxation is \(P=\{x:Bx\le d\}\), and every pooled cut \(a_i^Tx\le\beta_i\) is globally valid for all feasible tours.
Parameters satisfy \(\tau\ge0\) and \(A\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned pool contains every cut that is active, sufficiently efficacious, or younger than \(A\); deleting the other globally valid cuts preserves all feasible tours, although it may weaken the relaxation.

notation.meaning: Efficacy score of pooled cut i at the current LP solution
Number of consecutive reoptimizations for which cut i has failed the retention test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A validity-preserving aging rule for a TSP LP cut pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current LP optimum \(x^*\), a pool of globally valid cuts \(a_i^Tx\le\beta_i\), an efficacy threshold \(\tau\), and an age limit \(A\), initialize a new cut with \(q_i=0\). After each reoptimization, retain cut \(i\) and reset \(q_i=0\) if it is active at \(x^*\) or \(e_i(x^*)\ge\tau\); otherwise set \(q_i\leftarrow q_i+1\). Remove it from the active relaxation only when \(q_i>A\), unless it is protected by the implementation. Stop after processing the pool and output the retained active set and the removed cuts kept for possible later reactivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Age cuts that remain inactive and ineffective, remove only over-age unprotected cuts, and retain removed cuts for possible reactivation; global validity guarantees that removal cannot exclude a tour.
knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Cut Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aging rule is mathematically coherent and algorithm is the correct kind, but the efficacy, protection, aging, and reactivation policy has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Tour Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence that a reported tour satisfies the applicable TSP visit and connectivity requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for an undirected Hamiltonian TSP tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tour-feasibility certificate is a sequence \(p=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\). The verifier accepts exactly when \(v_i\in V\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) are pairwise distinct, \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}=V\), and \(\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}\in E\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(v_{n+1}=v_1\). Acceptance establishes that the encoded closed walk visits every vertex exactly once and uses only edges of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex sequence certifies feasibility when it lists every vertex exactly once and every consecutive pair, including the closing pair, is an edge.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|=n\ge3\).
The claimed tour is encoded by a sequence \(p=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies that \(p\) describes a Hamiltonian cycle of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Vertex set of the claimed tour

children.title: Tour Cost Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence supporting the reported objective value of a feasible tour.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb Q\).
A tour-feasibility certificate \(p=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) has been accepted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies the exact objective value \(C=c(T)\) of the encoded tour.

notation.meaning: Edge set induced by the cyclic tour sequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational-cost certificate paired with an accepted tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tour-cost certificate consists of a rational number \(C\) paired with the accepted sequence \(p\). With \(v_{n+1}=v_1\), the verifier recomputes the sum \(\widehat C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(\{v_i,v_{i+1}\})\) using exact rational arithmetic and accepts exactly when \(C=\widehat C\). Equivalently, if the tour is represented by incidence variables \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\), it checks \(C=\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\) and that these variables encode the same cyclic edges as \(p\). Thus the certificate binds the reported objective value to the feasible tour rather than merely reporting an unsupported scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompute the exact sum of costs on the certified tour and accept the claimed cost only when it equals that sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Tour Cost Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact rational recomputation correctly binds the claimed value to an accepted tour, and certificate is the correct kind, but no source or locator supports the formulation.

children.title: Tour-Certificate Consistency Checks
children.top_down_role: Cross-checks linking the encoded instance, reported tour, and claimed cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour-Certificate Consistency Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-validation conditions for the two records in a tour certificate pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasibility record and a cost record are consistent exactly when both identify the same TSP instance \(I\), all referenced vertices and edges belong to \(I\), and the tour represented by the cost record has the canonical cyclic edge set \(T(p)\) derived from the feasibility sequence \(p\). The verifier recomputes \(\widehat C=\sum_{e\in T(p)}c_e\) from the instance data and requires \(C=\widehat C\). For an undirected TSP, cyclic rotations and reversal of \(p\) are equivalent because they induce the same edge set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The records are consistent when they reference the same instance and tour and the reported cost equals the cost recomputed from that tour.
assumptions_latex: A feasibility certificate encodes a tour \(p\), and a cost certificate reports \(C\).
Both records identify one fixed undirected TSP instance \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies that the feasibility and cost records describe the same tour of the same instance and that \(C\) is its exact cost.

notation.meaning: TSP instance identified by both records
Canonical undirected cyclic edge set induced by the tour sequence

children.title: Relaxation-Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Verifiable evidence for lower bounds produced by TSP relaxations.

assumptions_latex: The minimization relaxation is \(P=\{x\ge0:Ax\ge b,\ Ex=d\}\) and has objective \(c^Tx\).
The supplied multipliers satisfy \(y\ge0\), \(z\in\mathbb R^q\), and \(A^Ty+E^Tz\le c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(L=b^Ty+d^Tz\) is a certified lower bound on every feasible relaxation value and hence on every feasible TSP tour cost.

notation.meaning: Dual multipliers for inequality and equality rows

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality lower-bound certificate for a minimization TSP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relaxation-bound certificate supplies dual multipliers \((y,z)\) and the scalar \(L=b^Ty+d^Tz\). The verifier checks \(y\ge0\), \(A^Ty+E^Tz\le c\), and the displayed equality defining \(L\), all in exact arithmetic. For every \(x\in P\), these relations imply \(L\le c^Tx\). If every feasible tour incidence vector belongs to \(P\), then \(L\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), where both objectives are minimization values. Thus the verified dual data, together with the documented containment of tour vectors in \(P\), certifies the claimed lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible multiplier vector certifies its dual objective as a lower bound on the LP relaxation and therefore on the minimum tour cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Bound Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual-feasibility certificate for a rational TSP LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual-solution certificate is a pair \((y,z)\), with \(y\) indexed by the inequalities and \(z\) indexed by the equalities. The verifier checks that dimensions match the stated LP, that every component of \(y\) is nonnegative, and that the dual slack \(s=c-A^Ty-E^Tz\) is componentwise nonnegative; \(z\) is unrestricted in sign. It also recomputes the dual objective \(D=b^Ty+d^Tz\). Passing these finite rational checks certifies dual feasibility and makes \(D\) independently verifiable, but does not by itself certify dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verify dimensions, nonnegativity of inequality multipliers, and nonnegative dual slacks; the resulting feasible dual objective is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Certificates

children.title: Primal–Dual Gap Validation
children.top_down_role: Consistency checks between incumbent tour values and certified lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gap-validation conditions for a rational minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Primal–dual gap validation accepts after independently verifying primal feasibility of \(x\), dual feasibility of \((y,z)\), and the exact identities \(P=c^Tx\), \(D=b^Ty+d^Tz\), and \(g=P-D\). Weak duality gives \(D\le v^*\le P\), so \(g\ge0\), \(0\le P-v^*\le g\), and \(0\le v^*-D\le g\). Consequently, \(g=0\) certifies primal and dual optimality, while \(g\le\varepsilon\) certifies additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality for \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate primal and dual feasibility and recompute their objectives; their nonnegative difference bounds both suboptimalities, and a zero gap certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is primal feasible for \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ Ex=d,\ x\ge0\}\).
\((y,z)\) is dual feasible for \(\max\{b^Ty+d^Tz:A^Ty+E^Tz\le c,\ y\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated gap \(g=P-D\) is nonnegative and bounds both suboptimalities; if \(g=0\), both solutions are optimal.

children.title: Search-Exhaustion Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence that all relevant search regions were resolved or pruned.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Exhaustion Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-bound exhaustion certificate for exact TSP search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search-exhaustion certificate records a finite rooted search tree, every branching disjunction, a verified incumbent tour of cost \(U\), and a fathoming witness for every leaf \(v\). The verifier checks that the root covers every feasible tour and that the children of each internal node cover the feasible set represented by their parent. Each leaf must have either a valid infeasibility certificate or a certified lower bound \(L_v\ge U\); a leaf solved to proven optimality may use its verified optimum as \(L_v\). When all checks pass, every feasible tour lies in a fathomed leaf and no feasible tour has cost below \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite search tree certifies exhaustion when branching covers every case and each leaf is certified infeasible or has a valid lower bound no better than the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: A finite branch-and-bound tree represents a minimization TSP search, with the root covering every feasible tour.
Each internal node branches into children whose feasible sets cover its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every leaf is certified infeasible or has a valid lower bound at least \(U\), no tour improves the incumbent and the represented search is exhausted.

notation.meaning: Cost of the verified incumbent tour
Valid lower bound at search node v
Feasible set represented by node v

children.title: Absolute-Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence for the absolute difference between incumbent and bound values.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization TSP with verified incumbent value \(U\) and verified global lower bound \(L\).
The tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies \(0\le U-z^*\le U-L\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\), where \(z^*\) is the optimal tour cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive termination certificate for a minimization TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute-gap certificate consists of a feasible tour with exact cost \(U\), a valid global lower-bound certificate with value \(L\), and a tolerance \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). The verifier checks both component certificates, recomputes their values, and accepts exactly when \(L\le U\) and \(U-L\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). Since \(L\le z^*\le U\) for the optimal tour value \(z^*\), acceptance certifies \(0\le U-z^*\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). In particular, \(U=L\) certifies exact optimality, subject to exact arithmetic or explicitly validated outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible tour value and valid lower bound certify additive accuracy when their difference does not exceed the stated absolute tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Gap Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute-gap implication is correct for verified bounds and the certificate kind fits, but no source with an inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Relative-Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence for normalized optimality-gap claims.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization TSP with verified finite bounds \(L\le z^*\le U\).
The tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), and the normalization is fixed as \(\max\{1,|U|\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies \((U-z^*)/\max\{1,|U|\}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative termination certificate under an explicit incumbent-based normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relative-gap certificate supplies a feasible incumbent of cost \(U\), a valid global lower bound \(L\), and the declared normalization rule \(r(U,L)=(U-L)/\max\{1,|U|\}\). The verifier checks the two bound certificates, verifies \(L\le U\), recomputes \(r(U,L)\), and accepts exactly when \(r(U,L)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\). Because \(L\le z^*\le U\), acceptance implies \((U-z^*)/\max\{1,|U|\}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\). The normalization is part of the certificate because alternative solver conventions, especially near zero, need not be equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the declared normalization, a verified incumbent and lower bound certify relative accuracy when their normalized difference meets the tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Gap Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion follows under the explicitly declared normalization, but that noncanonical relative-gap convention and the certificate formulation require a cited source.

children.title: Termination-Claim Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks matching solver termination status to the strength of the claimed result.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination-Claim Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions binding a minimization-TSP termination status to its mathematical certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A termination claim is valid only after the incumbent tour and every bound or search-exhaustion component have been verified and the declared status \(s\) satisfies its associated predicate. Exact optimality requires verified search exhaustion or verified bounds with \(U=L\). Absolute-gap termination requires \(U-L\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). Relative-gap termination requires the declared normalized gap to be defined and at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\). Infeasibility requires certified exhaustive elimination of the root feasible set and cannot be inferred merely from the absence of an incumbent. All instance identifiers, objective conventions, arithmetic bounds, and tolerances must agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A termination status is valid only when all components are verified and its exact, absolute-gap, relative-gap, or infeasibility predicate holds.
assumptions_latex: A solver claims exact, absolute-gap, relative-gap, or infeasibility termination for a minimization TSP.
The validation data contain the components required by the declared status \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies precisely the optimality, gap, or infeasibility statement associated with \(s\); otherwise the termination claim is rejected.

children.title: Hamiltonicity Hardness
children.top_down_role: Complexity boundaries inherited from deciding the existence of Hamiltonian structures.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph with \(|V|=n\ge3\).
Construct the complete graph on \(V\) with cost \(c_{uv}=1\) for \(\{u,v\}\in E\) and \(c_{uv}=2\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed TSP instance has a tour of cost at most \(n\) if and only if \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle; consequently decision TSP is NP-complete and exact TSP optimization is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Edge cost in the constructed complete TSP instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected decision-TSP hardness via the standard \(1\)-\(2\) Hamiltonicity reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G\), form the complete undirected graph on \(V\) and assign cost \(1\) to each original edge and cost \(2\) to each added edge. Every tour contains exactly \(n\) edges, so its cost is at least \(n\). It has cost at most \(n\) exactly when all its edges have cost \(1\), which occurs exactly when those edges form a Hamiltonian cycle in \(G\). The transformation is polynomial, and a proposed tour and its cost are verifiable in polynomial time. Hence the decision problem asking whether a TSP tour of cost at most \(n\) exists is NP-complete, and computing an exact optimum is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign cost one to graph edges and two to nonedges; a tour costs at most the vertex count exactly when the original graph is Hamiltonian.
knowledge_statements.title: Hamiltonicity Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard 1–2 reduction correctly establishes decision-TSP NP-completeness and exact-optimization NP-hardness, and theorem is the correct kind, but no authoritative reduction source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Exact TSP Optimization Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Exact TSP Optimization Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization hardness for complete weighted undirected TSP via Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(n=|V|\ge 3\). On the complete graph over \(V\), assign \(c_{uv}=1\) when \(\{u,v\}\in E\) and \(c_{uv}=2\) otherwise. Every tour has cost at least \(n\), and its cost equals \(n\) exactly when \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle. Consequently, computing an optimal TSP tour or its optimal value is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard; the associated threshold decision problem is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard 1–2 edge-cost construction converts Hamiltonian cycle into exact TSP, proving that optimal TSP computation is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge 3\).
Edge costs are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact weighted TSP optimization is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard, and deciding whether \(\operatorname{OPT}\le n\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete.

knowledge_statements.title: Hamiltonicity-to-TSP Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-preserving threshold reduction from undirected Hamiltonian cycle to 1–2 TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\), construct the complete graph \(K_V\) and define \(c_{uv}=1\) if \(\{u,v\}\in E\), and \(c_{uv}=2\) otherwise. The construction is polynomial-time and satisfies
\[G\text{ has a Hamiltonian cycle}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{OPT}(K_V,c)=n.\]
Moreover, the costs obey \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\), so the same construction is a reduction to metric 1–2 TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace graph edges by cost one and nonedges by cost two. A tour of cost n exists exactly when the original graph is Hamiltonian.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, undirected, and has \(n\ge 3\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Hamiltonian cycle to the TSP threshold instance \((K_V,c,n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric TSP Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean TSP hardness in the fixed plane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb{Z}^{2}\) of points with binary-encoded coordinates and Euclidean costs \(c_{pq}=\|p-q\|_2\), the problem of finding a shortest Hamiltonian tour through \(P\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard. Thus restricting symmetric metric TSP to distances induced by points in the fixed-dimensional Euclidean plane does not make exact optimization polynomial-time unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding an exact shortest Euclidean tour through planar points is NP-hard, despite the strong geometric structure of the distances.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{Z}^{2}\) is finite.
Point coordinates are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact Euclidean TSP in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance between points p and q

children.title: Metric-to-Geometric Hardness Transfers
children.top_down_role: Relationships between metric hardness constructions and geometric restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-to-Geometric Hardness Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why arbitrary metric hardness does not automatically imply fixed-dimensional Euclidean hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_n\) be the \(n\)-point metric with \(d(x,y)=1\) for every distinct \(x,y\in X_n\). Any isometric embedding of \(X_n\) into Euclidean space requires dimension at least \(n-1\), because its image is an equilateral simplex. Therefore arbitrary finite metric TSP instances cannot generally be represented isometrically in any fixed \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\). A metric-TSP hardness reduction transfers to fixed-dimensional geometric TSP only after a separate polynomial construction preserving the relevant objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General metrics need unbounded Euclidean dimension, so metric TSP hardness alone does not establish hardness for fixed-dimensional geometric TSP.
assumptions_latex: The embedding is required to preserve every distance exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No fixed Euclidean dimension represents all finite metrics isometrically; geometric hardness requires a geometry-preserving reduction.

notation.meaning: metric on the source space or fixed Euclidean dimension, as indicated

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equilateral-metric obstruction correctly serves as a failure boundary, but no inspectable source is provided for the embedding claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmetric Inapproximability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded inapproximability for TSP without the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) be polynomial-time computable with \(\log \rho(n)\) polynomially bounded. For complete symmetric TSP with arbitrary positive binary-encoded costs, no polynomial-time algorithm can always return a tour of cost at most \(\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}\), unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Indeed, a Hamiltonicity reduction may assign cost \(1\) to graph edges and a sufficiently large cost \(M>\rho(n)n\) to nonedges, separating Hamiltonian from non-Hamiltonian instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the triangle inequality, arbitrary large penalties rule out every polynomially representable approximation ratio unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: Costs are positive, binary encoded, and need not satisfy the triangle inequality.
\(\rho\) is polynomial-time computable and \(\log\rho(n)\) is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial-time \(\rho(n)\)-approximation for nonmetric TSP would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: claimed approximation ratio on n-vertex instances

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric-TSP Approximation Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: APX-hardness of directed metric traveling-salesman optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For asymmetric TSP on a complete directed graph with nonnegative arc costs satisfying the directed triangle inequality \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\), there exists a constant \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that computing a tour of cost at most \((1+\varepsilon_0)\operatorname{OPT}\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard. Consequently metric ATSP is \(\mathrm{APX}\)-hard and admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed metric TSP is APX-hard: some fixed approximation factor above one is NP-hard to achieve, excluding a PTAS unless P equals NP.

knowledge_statements.title: Double-Tree Approximation Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical factor-two algorithm for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a complete undirected graph \(K_V\) with nonnegative symmetric metric costs. Compute a minimum spanning tree \(T\), duplicate every edge of \(T\), and find an Euler tour of the resulting connected even-degree multigraph. Traverse that Euler tour and shortcut every already visited vertex, retaining the initial vertex only as the final return. Output the resulting Hamiltonian cycle \(H\). Then
\[c(H)\le 2c(T)\le 2\operatorname{OPT}.\]
The construction and shortcutting run in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double a minimum spanning tree, take an Euler tour, and shortcut repeats. Triangle inequality yields a polynomial-time 2-approximation.
assumptions_latex: Costs are nonnegative, symmetric, and satisfy the triangle inequality.
The input graph is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output tour \(H\) satisfies \(c(H)\le 2\operatorname{OPT}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Christofides Approximation Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical three-halves approximation for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a complete undirected metric instance. Compute a minimum spanning tree \(T\), let \(O\) be its even-cardinality set of odd-degree vertices, and compute a minimum-cost perfect matching \(M\) on \(O\). Find an Euler tour of the connected even-degree multigraph \(T\cup M\), shortcut repeated vertices, and output the resulting Hamiltonian cycle \(H\). The algorithm is polynomial-time and satisfies
\[c(H)\le c(T)+c(M)\le \tfrac{3}{2}\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum spanning tree plus a minimum matching on its odd vertices, followed by shortcutting, gives a 3/2-approximation.
assumptions_latex: Costs are nonnegative, symmetric, and satisfy the triangle inequality.
The input graph is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output tour \(H\) satisfies \(c(H)\le \tfrac{3}{2}\operatorname{OPT}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Christofides' Algorithm and Approximation Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MST-and-matching construction and guarantee for Euclidean TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite Euclidean point set S, compute a minimum spanning tree T, compute a minimum-length perfect matching M on the odd-degree vertices of T, form an Euler tour of T\cup M, and shortcut repeated vertices. It returns a tour at most three halves as long as optimal, and this factor is tight for the algorithm. The cited Euclidean matching routine takes O(n^2.5 log^4 n) time.

n=|S|

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic-TSP Approximation Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time approximation bound for shortest-path metrics of unweighted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected unweighted graph, and let \(d_G(u,v)\) be its shortest-path metric. There exists a polynomial-time algorithm that returns a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) in the complete metric closure of \(G\) such that
\[d_G(H)\le \frac{7}{5}\operatorname{OPT}(V,d_G).\]
Equivalently, the algorithm produces a connected spanning Eulerian multigraph in \(G\) whose number of edges is at most \(7/5\) times the optimum graphic-TSP value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic TSP admits a polynomial-time 7/5-approximation in the shortest-path metric of any connected unweighted graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, and unweighted.
Distances are shortest-path lengths in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphic TSP has a polynomial-time approximation ratio of \(7/5\).

notation.meaning: returned Hamiltonian cycle in the metric closure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is suitable for this existence statement, but the nontrivial 7/5 graphic-TSP result and its equivalent formulation require an authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric-TSP Approximation Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of constant-factor approximation for directed metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There is a universal constant \(C<\infty\) and a polynomial-time algorithm such that, for every complete directed graph with nonnegative costs satisfying \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\), the algorithm returns a directed Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) with
\[c(H)\le C\operatorname{OPT}.\]
Thus metric asymmetric TSP belongs to the class of constant-factor approximable minimization problems, although the guarantee is not the symmetric \(3/2\) bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric asymmetric TSP has a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation, though its guarantee differs substantially from the symmetric Christofides bound.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is complete.
Arc costs are nonnegative and satisfy the directed triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric ATSP admits a polynomial-time \(C\)-approximation for some universal constant \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-factor approximability claim fits the family and may be recorded as a complexity bound, but it needs a cited algorithmic result and specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean-TSP Approximation-Scheme Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time approximation schemes for Euclidean TSP in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer dimension \(d\ge 2\) and an accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon>0\). For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\) with rational coordinates, a Euclidean-TSP approximation scheme returns a Hamiltonian tour \(H\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{len}(H)\le (1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(P).\]
For each fixed \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\), its running time is polynomial in \(|P|\) and the coordinate encoding length. Hence fixed-dimensional Euclidean TSP admits a \(\mathrm{PTAS}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed dimension and accuracy, Euclidean TSP has a polynomial-time algorithm returning a tour within factor one plus epsilon of optimal.
assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\ge 2\) is fixed.
The accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed.
Points have rational, finitely encoded coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-dimensional Euclidean TSP admits a \(\mathrm{PTAS}\) with approximation ratio \(1+\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean length of the returned tour
minimum Euclidean tour length through P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The PTAS complexity-bound formulation matches the leaf, but the rational-coordinate computational model and encoding-length runtime claim need an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar TSP Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-TSP PTAS for nonnegative edge-weighted planar graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected planar graph with nonnegative edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and let \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,\ell)\) be the minimum length of a closed walk visiting every vertex. For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a planar TSP approximation scheme returns a closed spanning walk \(W\) satisfying \[\ell(W)\le (1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G,\ell).\] Its running time is polynomial in \(|V|\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon\); the polynomial degree or multiplicative factor may depend on \(1/\varepsilon\).

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is connected and planar.
\(\ell(e)\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).
\(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Growth TSP Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS family on metrics of uniformly bounded doubling dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\in\mathbb{N}\). A bounded-growth TSP approximation scheme is a family of algorithms \(\{A_{d,\varepsilon}:\varepsilon>0\}\) for finite metrics \((X,\delta)\) such that every ball of radius \(r>0\) is coverable by at most \(2^d\) balls of radius \(r/2\). On input \((X,\delta)\), the algorithm outputs a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) with \[\delta(H)\le (1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(X,\delta),\] and, for fixed \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\), runs in time polynomial in \(|X|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-growth TSP scheme is a PTAS on finite metrics of fixed doubling dimension, with polynomial running time when dimension and accuracy are fixed.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\delta)\) is a finite metric space.
The doubling dimension is at most \(d\).
\(d\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed.

notation.meaning: approximation algorithm at dimension and accuracy parameters

children.title: Structural Decomposition Regimes
