knowledge_statements.title: Structural Decomposition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sufficient conditions for decomposition-based TSP approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a class of TSP instances. Suppose that, for every instance \(I\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), one can compute a decomposition \(D\) with a bounded interface set per piece such that some interface-respecting tour has length at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). If the minimum interface-respecting tour can be computed by dynamic programming over \(D\) in time \(f(	ext{interface size})|I|^{O(1)}\), then this decomposition and dynamic program form a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation scheme whenever the interface size is bounded solely by structural parameters and \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-optimal structure theorem plus bounded-interface dynamic programming yields a TSP approximation scheme when interface size depends only on structure and accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Every \(I\in\mathcal I\) has a computable bounded-interface decomposition.
A \((1+\varepsilon)\)-near-optimal interface-respecting tour exists.
The restricted optimum is computable by decomposition dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting algorithm has approximation ratio \(1+\varepsilon\) and runs in \(f(g(\varepsilon))|I|^{O(1)}\) time when the structural parameters are fixed.
review_flags: Abstract synthesis requires a source supporting the stated sufficient-condition formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract decomposition principle is plausible, but no cited theorem or framework supports these sufficient conditions or the claimed parameter dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Held–Karp Subset Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact directed TSP dynamic program with a fixed root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a complete directed graph on \(V=\{r\}\cup U\) with arc costs \(c_{ij}\), define \(D(S,j)\) for nonempty \(S\subseteq U\) and \(j\in S\) as the minimum cost of a path from \(r\) that visits exactly \(S\) and ends at \(j\). Initialize \(D(\{j\},j)=c_{rj}\), and update \[D(S,j)=\min_{i\in S\setminus\{j\}}\bigl(D(S\setminus\{j\},i)+c_{ij}\bigr).\] Output \(\min_{j\in U}(D(U,j)+c_{jr})\). The algorithm uses \(O(n2^n)\) states, \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time, and \(O(n2^n)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Held–Karp stores the cheapest rooted path for each visited subset and endpoint, then closes the cheapest full path into an optimal tour.
assumptions_latex: Every arc cost \(c_{ij}\) is finite or represented by \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output equals the minimum Hamiltonian-cycle cost and is computed in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time and \(O(n2^n)\) space.

notation.meaning: minimum rooted path cost for subset and endpoint

review_flags: Standard exact algorithm, but no supporting TSP-specific locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Held–Karp recurrence and standard time and space bounds are mathematically appropriate, but the record supplies no inspectable TSP-specific citation.

children.title: Inclusion–Exclusion TSP Methods
children.top_down_role: Exact TSP approaches organized around inclusion–exclusion transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion–Exclusion TSP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian-cycle counting by inclusion–exclusion over induced subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a loopless directed graph with \(|V|=n\), and let \(M_S\) be the adjacency matrix of the subgraph induced by \(S\subseteq V\). The number \(h(G)\) of directed Hamiltonian cycles, counted up to cyclic choice of starting vertex, satisfies \[h(G)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{S\subseteq V}(-1)^{n-|S|}\operatorname{tr}(M_S^n).\] Consequently, Hamiltonicity is decided by testing whether this integer is positive. Enumerating subsets and computing each trace without retaining all subset values gives an exponential-time, polynomial-space inclusion–exclusion method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inclusion–exclusion alternates counts of length-n closed walks in induced subgraphs; the resulting sum, divided by n, counts directed Hamiltonian cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite loopless directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a directed Hamiltonian cycle if and only if \(\sum_{S\subseteq V}(-1)^{n-|S|}\operatorname{tr}(M_S^n)>0\).

notation.meaning: adjacency matrix of the subgraph induced by S
number of directed Hamiltonian cycles up to rotation

review_flags: The inclusion–exclusion identity needs a supporting exact-algorithms locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion–exclusion trace identity is plausible and the representation role fits, but its normalization and counting convention require a specific exact-algorithms source.

children.title: Algebraic TSP Methods
children.top_down_role: Exact approaches using algebraic representations or computations beyond subset recurrence.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic TSP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian tours encoded as monomials of a generating polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), assign an indeterminate \(x_a\) to each arc and an integer cost \(c_a\ge 0\). Define the Hamiltonian-cycle polynomial \[P_G(z,\mathbf{x})=\sum_{H\in\mathcal H(G)}z^{\sum_{a\in H}c_a}\prod_{a\in H}x_a,\] where \(\mathcal H(G)\) is the set of directed Hamiltonian cycles counted once up to rotation. Then \(G\) is Hamiltonian exactly when \(P_G\ne0\), and the minimum TSP cost is the least exponent of \(z\) having a nonzero coefficient after setting every \(x_a=1\). Algebraic TSP methods compute, evaluate, or extract information from this polynomial without explicitly listing all tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generating polynomial encodes every Hamiltonian tour as a monomial; nonzeroness detects a tour, and its least cost exponent gives the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(c_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_G\ne0\) characterizes Hamiltonicity, and \(\min_{H\in\mathcal H(G)}\sum_{a\in H}c_a\) is the least nonzero exponent after \(x_a=1\).

notation.meaning: directed Hamiltonian cycles of G, counted up to rotation

review_flags: The chosen generating-polynomial formulation lacks a supplied algebraic-TSP source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generating-polynomial representation is internally coherent, but no algebraic-TSP source supports this particular formulation or its intended methodological significance.

children.title: Algebraic Space–Time Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational regimes distinguished by running time, memory use, or randomization.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Space–Time Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts subset storage with recomputed algebraic inclusion–exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For directed Hamiltonicity on an \(n\)-vertex graph, subset dynamic programming evaluates endpoint-indexed subset states in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time using \(O(n2^n)\) space. Alternatively, the inclusion–exclusion expression \(\sum_{S\subseteq V}(-1)^{n-|S|}\operatorname{tr}(M_S^n)\) can be evaluated one subset at a time. With polynomial-time matrix powering for each subset, this uses \(2^n n^{O(1)}\) arithmetic operations and polynomial space. Thus discarding subset tables preserves the exponential base in time while reducing storage from exponential to polynomial, at the cost of polynomial-factor recomputation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating inclusion–exclusion terms independently uses polynomial space and exponential time, whereas Held–Karp stores exponentially many states to reduce repeated computation.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic on intermediate integers is charged by arithmetic-operation count.
\(G\) has \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Directed Hamiltonicity is decidable in \(2^n n^{O(1)}\) arithmetic time and polynomial space by termwise inclusion–exclusion evaluation.

notation.meaning: adjacency matrix induced by vertex subset S

review_flags: Bit-complexity and arithmetic-model details require a supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source is required for the polynomial-space inclusion–exclusion bound and for the distinction between arithmetic-operation complexity and bit complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Decomposition Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph-TSP dynamic programming parameterized by treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative edge costs and a rooted nice tree decomposition of width \(k\). At each bag \(B\\,\), store, for every degree map \(d:B\to\{0,1,2\}\) and partition of the positive-degree boundary vertices, the minimum cost of a partial subgraph below the bag realizing those degrees and connectivity classes, while forbidding a closed component before the root state. Introduce, forget, and join transitions update these states. At the root, output the minimum state in which every vertex has degree two and all selected edges form one connected component. This yields an optimal Hamiltonian cycle in \(2^{O(k\log k)}|V|^{O(1)}\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm records boundary degrees and connectivity partitions in each tree-decomposition bag, combining them until one minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle remains.
assumptions_latex: A nice tree decomposition of width \(k\) is supplied.
Edge costs are nonnegative.
The sought tour is a Hamiltonian cycle in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal Hamiltonian cycle is computed in \(2^{O(k\log k)}|V|^{O(1)}\) time.
review_flags: The standard partition-DP bound needs a treewidth-algorithms source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition-DP approach and stated treewidth dependence require a source. The source should also clarify root acceptance states and the invariant preventing premature closed components.

children.title: TSP Branching Strategies
children.top_down_role: Search-space partitioning choices for exact TSP enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: TSP Branching Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary edge branching for exact branch-and-bound TSP search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node, let \(F\subseteq E\) be forced edges and \(X\subseteq E\) forbidden edges. Choose an undecided edge \(e\in E\setminus(F\cup X)\) and create two children \((F\cup\{e\},X)\) and \((F,X\cup\{e\})\). Reject a child immediately if some vertex is forced to degree above two, cannot still attain degree two, or if \(F\) contains a proper cycle. Otherwise compute a lower bound and continue branching until every vertex has forced degree two and \(F\) is one Hamiltonian cycle. Because the children partition all completions of the parent, exhaustive unpruned search is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on whether an undecided edge belongs to the tour, reject locally infeasible children, and continue until forced edges form a Hamiltonian cycle.
assumptions_latex: The instance is an undirected finite TSP graph.
Search nodes specify disjoint forced and forbidden edge sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two children partition all Hamiltonian completions compatible with \((F,X)\), so branching combined with sound pruning preserves an optimal tour.
review_flags: No TSP branch-and-bound source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary edge-branching strategy is plausible and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but no exact-TSP branch-and-bound source is cited.

children.title: TSP Bounding Procedures

knowledge_statements.title: TSP Bounding Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-based lower bounds at branch-and-bound nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization TSP search node \(N=(F,X)\), let \(\mathcal T(N)\) be its compatible tours and let \(R(N)\) be a relaxation satisfying \(\mathcal T(N)\subseteq R(N)\). Define \[L(N)=\min_{x\in R(N)}c^\top x.\] Then every compatible tour has cost at least \(L(N)\). Valid choices of \(R(N)\) include degree relaxations, assignment relaxations, and one-tree Lagrangian relaxations, provided forced and forbidden decisions are imposed. Any feasible compatible tour supplies an upper bound \(U\); the gap between \(L(N)\) and \(U\) guides node selection and pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing over a relaxation containing every compatible tour gives a valid node lower bound; any compatible tour gives an upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T(N)\subseteq R(N)\).
The relaxation objective agrees with tour cost.
The relaxation minimum exists or is interpreted as an infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(N)\le c^\top x\) for every \(x\in\mathcal T(N)\).

notation.meaning: search node with forced and forbidden edges
relaxed feasible set at the node

review_flags: Standard relaxation principle, but the supplied locators do not specifically support TSP bounding.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation lower-bound principle is correct in form, but the TSP-specific examples and their treatment of forced and forbidden decisions need an inspectable citation.

children.title: TSP Node-Pruning Criteria
children.top_down_role: Conditions supporting removal of search regions without further exploration.

knowledge_statements.title: TSP Node-Pruning Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound fathoming conditions for exact TSP branch-and-bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a TSP search node, let \(L(N)\) be a valid lower bound on every tour compatible with \(N\), and let \(U\) be the cost of the best incumbent tour. The node may be pruned if its constraints are infeasible, or if \(L(N)\ge U\). It may also be fathomed after producing a compatible tour of cost \(L(N)\), because that tour is optimal within the node. With the convention that ties need not be enumerated, these criteria cannot remove any tour having cost strictly smaller than the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune an infeasible node or one whose valid lower bound meets the incumbent; fathom it when a compatible tour attains its lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(L(N)\) is a valid lower bound.
\(U\) is the cost of a feasible incumbent.
Only one optimal tour is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(N\) is infeasible or \(L(N)\ge U\), pruning \(N\) cannot discard a tour of cost less than \(U\).

children.title: One-Tree-Based Search
children.top_down_role: Exact search organized around one-tree lower bounds or relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Tree-Based Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Held–Karp Lagrangian one-tree bounds inside exact search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a root \(r\) in an undirected TSP instance with edge costs \(c_e\). For vertex multipliers \(\pi\), assign modified costs \(c'_{uv}=c_{uv}+\pi_u+\pi_v\). At each search node, enforce its forced and forbidden edges and compute a minimum one-tree \(T_\pi\): a spanning tree on \(V\setminus\{r\}\) plus two edges incident to \(r\). Use \[L(\pi)=c'(T_\pi)-2\sum_{v\in V}\pi_v\] as a lower bound, update \(\pi\) by a subgradient proportional to \(\deg_{T_\pi}(v)-2\), and prune when the best obtained bound meets the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum one-tree under multiplier-adjusted costs gives a TSP lower bound; subgradient updates seek stronger bounds for branch-and-bound pruning.
assumptions_latex: The TSP graph is finite, undirected, and has edge costs.
Forced and forbidden decisions are imposed on the one-tree problem.
A feasible incumbent cost is maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every multiplier vector \(\pi\), \(L(\pi)\) is no greater than the cost of any tour compatible with the search node.

children.title: Assignment-Based Search
children.top_down_role: Exact search organized around assignment or cycle-cover bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Based Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact directed-TSP branch-and-bound using the cycle-cover assignment relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a directed complete graph with arc costs \(c_{ij}\), solve at each search node the assignment relaxation \[L=\min\left\{\sum_{i
e j}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j
e i}x_{ij}=1,\ \sum_{i
e j}x_{ij}=1,\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}ight\}.\] If its cycle cover is one Hamiltonian cycle, update the incumbent. Otherwise choose a proper subtour or one of its arcs and create finitely many children whose restrictions exclude the current cover while collectively retaining every feasible tour. Prune a child when its relaxation is infeasible or its lower bound is at least the incumbent value; output the incumbent after no live nodes remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve assignment relaxations, branch to eliminate non-Hamiltonian cycle covers, and prune by their lower bounds until the best remaining Hamiltonian tour is certified optimal.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is complete, with finite arc costs \(c_{ij}\).
The branching disjunction preserves every Hamiltonian tour not already excluded.
An initial incumbent is either available or assigned value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon exhaustion, the incumbent is an optimal Hamiltonian cycle, or infeasibility is certified if none exists.

children.title: Bound-Driven Node Ordering

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Driven Node Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-bound ordering within an exact relaxation-based TSP search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a set \(Q\) of live search nodes, an incumbent tour value \(U\), and a valid lower bound \(L(N)\) for every \(N\in Q\). Repeatedly select a node \(N\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in Q}L(M)\). Fathom \(N\) if it is infeasible or \(L(N)\ge U\); otherwise branch or separate cuts, insert every resulting unfathomed child into \(Q\), and update \(U\) whenever a cheaper feasible tour is found. Stop when \(Q=\varnothing\), or when \(U-\min_{N\in Q}L(N)\) meets a prescribed certified gap tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Always process a live node having the smallest valid lower bound; incumbent bounds then support safe pruning and a global optimality-gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every node bound \(L(N)\) is no greater than the cost of any feasible tour represented by \(N\).
Branching preserves all feasible tours represented by an expanded node.
The live-node minimum is computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For zero gap tolerance, exhaustion or \(U=\min_{N\in Q}L(N)\) certifies global optimality of the incumbent.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound for node N

children.title: Constraint-Programming TSP Search
children.top_down_role: Exact TSP search using constraint propagation and combinatorial domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Programming TSP Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain CP search using successor variables and a global circuit constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), introduce successor variables \(s_i\in V\setminus\{i\}\), impose \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), and impose a circuit constraint requiring the arcs \((i,s_i)\) to form one cycle. Minimize \(\sum_{i\in V}c_{i,s_i}\). Repeatedly propagate all constraints and an objective cutoff below the incumbent; fail a node whose domain becomes empty or whose valid objective lower bound reaches the incumbent. Otherwise branch on a non-singleton domain, creating children that partition its values. A singleton solution updates the incumbent; exhaustive failure of all remaining nodes terminates the search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model successors with all-different and single-circuit constraints, propagate domains and cost bounds, then branch exhaustively until the best feasible tour is certified.
assumptions_latex: The vertex set \(V\) and every successor domain are finite.
Propagation deletes only values having no completion satisfying the posted constraints.
Branch domains form a disjoint exhaustive partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive termination returns a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle, or certifies that none satisfies the posted constraints.

children.title: Decision-Diagram TSP Search

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Diagram TSP Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact search supported by layered decision diagrams over partial tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a layered acyclic diagram whose root-to-terminal paths encode vertex-successor decisions. An exact diagram represents precisely all tours compatible with the current search node. A relaxed diagram may merge states and represent a superset, so its shortest root-to-terminal path value \(L\) is a lower bound; a restricted diagram represents a subset, so any terminal path gives a feasible incumbent candidate. If the relaxed optimum is infeasible for the exact state semantics, branch on a distinguishing decision or refine a merged state. Prune when the relaxed diagram is empty or \(L\) reaches the incumbent, and continue until every live subproblem is fathomed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use relaxed diagrams for lower bounds, restricted diagrams for feasible tours, and refinement or branching to recover exactness and certify the optimum.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible tour has one corresponding path in the exact diagram.
Relaxation preserves all exact paths, while restriction introduces no inexact path.
Branching or refinement eventually separates every inexact relaxed optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After all live subproblems are fathomed, the incumbent is an optimal represented TSP tour.

notation.meaning: shortest-path value in a relaxed decision diagram

children.title: Hybrid CP–Diagram Search
children.top_down_role: Architectures combining constraint propagation with decision-diagram bounds or state representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid CP–Diagram Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional filtering between a CP model and a TSP decision diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain finite CP domains \(D_i\) for tour decisions and a layered decision diagram \(G\) whose paths encode a relaxation of assignments allowed by those domains. Iterate to a fixed point: delete from \(G\) arcs inconsistent with the current \(D_i\); remove from each \(D_i\) values unsupported by any root-to-terminal path in \(G\); apply CP propagation; and compute a shortest-path lower bound in \(G\). Fathom on domain failure, absence of a terminal path, or a bound reaching the incumbent. Otherwise branch on a domain value or diagram state, using exhaustive children, and update the incumbent from any path verified by the CP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate CP propagation with diagram filtering and shortest-path bounds, then branch exhaustively whenever their fixed point does not solve or prune the subproblem.
assumptions_latex: Diagram filtering retains every path corresponding to a feasible CP assignment.
CP propagation is sound, and each branching disjunction is exhaustive.
Every incumbent candidate is checked against the complete CP model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive termination returns an optimal feasible tour or certifies infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Root Cutting-Plane Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut generation at the root LP before TSP branching begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a root relaxation \(P_0\) containing the degree equations, variable bounds, and any initial valid inequalities for the TSP incidence vectors. At iteration \(k\), solve \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P_k\}\). If a separation routine finds valid inequalities \(a_r^{\mathsf T}x\le b_r\) violated by the optimizer, set \(P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\bigcap_r\{x:a_r^{\mathsf T}x\le b_r\}\) and reoptimize. Stop when no selected separator finds a violation, a resource limit is reached, or an integral tour is obtained; pass the resulting relaxation, bound, and cut pool to the search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the root LP, separate violated valid TSP inequalities, add selected cuts, and reoptimize before beginning branch-and-cut search.
assumptions_latex: Every generated inequality is valid for every feasible TSP incidence vector.
Each root linear program is solved to the accuracy required by the separation and pruning rules.

children.title: Branching-Rule Families

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Rule Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact disjunctive branching rules for TSP branch-and-cut nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional search node with feasible region \(R\), choose a branching object and replace \(R\) by finitely many children \(R_1,\ldots,R_q\) satisfying \[R\cap X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{q}R_i,\] where \(X\) is the set of TSP incidence vectors. Standard families include binary edge branching \(x_e=0\) versus \(x_e=1\), disjunctions on sums of selected edge variables, and structural disjunctions on successor or connection decisions. Candidate objects may be ranked by estimated bound improvement, infeasibility reduction, pseudocost, or limited strong-branching probes. Only the covering condition determines correctness; the ranking rule determines which valid disjunction is applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an exhaustive disjunction—on an edge, edge sum, or structural decision—and optionally score candidates by predicted bound or infeasibility improvement.
assumptions_latex: The parent region \(R\) is a valid relaxation of its represented tours.
Every feasible integral parent solution satisfies at least one child disjunct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching removes no feasible parent tour and permits exact enumeration when combined with valid fathoming.

children.title: Node-Selection Families

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Selection Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policies for choosing the next live TSP branch-and-cut node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be the live-node set. A node-selection policy repeatedly chooses one \(N\in Q\), processes it, and returns its unfathomed children to \(Q\). Best-bound chooses a node minimizing \(L(N)\); depth-first chooses a deepest node, commonly with a recency tie-break; breadth-first chooses a shallowest node; and hybrid policies switch or combine depth, bound, incumbent potential, and memory criteria. Regardless of policy, prune only by valid infeasibility or bound tests, and require that every node remaining live is eventually selected unless termination is justified by a global bound or prescribed gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select live nodes by best bound, depth, breadth, or a hybrid score while preserving fair processing and valid pruning conditions.

The policy cannot permanently starve a node needed for the requested exactness certificate.

children.title: Search-Tree Policy Interactions

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Policy Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness invariant and performance coupling among branching, node selection, cuts, and incumbents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two TSP search policies that differ only in branching choices, live-node order, cut scheduling, or primal-heuristic timing. If both use exhaustive branching, valid cuts, valid node lower bounds, sound infeasibility tests, and fair processing of all required live nodes, then both return the same optimal objective value upon exhaustive termination. Their intermediate trees need not coincide: an earlier incumbent can strengthen bound pruning, stronger cuts can alter branching scores, and node order can change pseudocost observations and incumbent discovery. Thus these components are performance-coupled even though correctness follows from the shared validity invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid exhaustive policies preserve the same optimum, but branching, cuts, node order, and incumbent timing can strongly alter one another and the resulting tree.
assumptions_latex: Both policies represent the same original TSP instance.
All cuts, bounds, branching disjunctions, and fathoming tests satisfy their stated validity conditions.
Live-node processing is fair whenever a global certificate has not already been reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Policy interactions may change search effort and tree shape, but not the certified optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Cut Separation Architecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation, selection, and management of strong valid inequalities in TSP branch-and-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an LP solution \(x^*\), run one or more exact or heuristic separators for valid TSP inequality families. Each separator returns inequalities \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) with positive violation \(a^{\mathsf T}x^*-b\). Discard invalid, duplicate, numerically unreliable, or weakly violated candidates; rank the remainder by violation, efficacy, orthogonality, predicted bound gain, or cost, add a selected batch, and reoptimize. Repeat until no accepted cut is found or a round or resource limit is reached. Cuts used for pruning must be valid globally or explicitly restricted to the subtree where their validity assumptions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate violated valid inequalities, filter and rank them, add a controlled batch, and reoptimize while respecting each cut’s domain of validity.

LP solutions and violations are evaluated with tolerances consistent with solver accuracy.

children.title: Primal Heuristics within TSP Exact Search

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Heuristics within TSP Exact Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Use of feasible-tour heuristics without weakening exact branch-and-cut guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At any search stage, a primal heuristic may map the current LP solution, partial assignment, or incumbent tour to a candidate Hamiltonian cycle \(H\). Accept \(H\) only after verifying all original TSP constraints, and update the incumbent value by \(U\leftarrow\min\{U,c(H)\}\). For every live node \(N\) with valid lower bound \(L(N)\), the updated incumbent permits fathoming when \(L(N)\ge U\). Failure of the heuristic proves nothing and cannot justify pruning; final optimality still requires exhaustive valid search or equality of the incumbent with a valid global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verified heuristic tours improve the incumbent and enable more pruning, but heuristic failure never certifies infeasibility or optimality.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted candidate is checked against all original tour constraints.
Every pruning bound \(L(N)\) is valid for its node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal heuristics can accelerate exact search while leaving its correctness certificate dependent on valid bounds and exhaustive fathoming.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Salesman-Count mTSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable fleet size with a per-salesman charge or an explicit admissible range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[\min_{m\in\{m_{\min},\ldots,m_{\max}\}}\ \min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\in\mathcal F_m}\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{m}c(T_k)+\lambda m\right\},\]
where each \(T_k\) is a depot-rooted tour and the tours partition \(V\). Empty tours are excluded unless explicitly included in \(\mathcal F_m\). An optimizer determines both the fleet size and its tours.

Every customer belongs to exactly one selected tour.
\(m\) is restricted to \(\{m_{\min},\ldots,m_{\max}\}\).

children.title: Salesman-Count Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in solution structure or objective behavior across fleet-cardinality choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Salesman-Count Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity for min-sum mTSP when unused salesmen are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each integer \(m\geq1\), let
\[z_m=\min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\in\mathcal F_m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}c(T_k).\]
Suppose \(\mathcal F_m\) permits empty depot tours and every feasible \(m\)-tour family remains feasible after appending one empty tour of cost zero. Then \(\mathcal F_m\subseteq\mathcal F_{m+1}\) under this embedding, and
\[z_{m+1}\leq z_m.\]
This monotonicity need not hold when every salesman must visit a customer, when fleet-dependent costs are included, or when the objective is not total tour cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing an additional unused salesman cannot increase optimal total travel cost; mandatory use or fleet charges can destroy this monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: An empty depot tour is feasible and has cost \(0\).
Appending an empty tour preserves all constraints.
The objective is the sum of tour costs only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{m+1}\leq z_m\) for every admissible \(m\).

children.title: Multiple-Depot mTSP

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Depot mTSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple-salesman tours based at one of several depots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V\cup D,E)\) have customers \(V\), depots \(D\), nonnegative edge costs, and salesmen \(K\). A feasible multiple-depot mTSP solution consists of an assignment \(a:K\to D\) and tours \((T_k)_{k\in K}\) such that \(T_k\) starts and ends at \(a(k)\), every customer belongs to exactly one tour, and no customer is repeated. knowledge_statements.title: Min-Sum mTSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-distance objective for a fixed feasible mTSP regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a nonempty feasible set \(\mathcal F_m\) of \(m\)-tour families and tour-cost function \(c\), the min-sum mTSP has objective
\[z_{\Sigma}=\min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\in\mathcal F_m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}c(T_k).\]
The feasibility set specifies the depot, endpoint, assignment, and tour-size regime. The objective charges every traveled edge with its multiplicity and seeks minimum aggregate travel; it does not directly constrain or minimize the longest individual tour.

children.title: Min–Max mTSP

knowledge_statements.title: Min–Max mTSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makespan objective for a fixed feasible mTSP regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a nonempty feasible set \(\mathcal F_m\) of \(m\)-tour families and tour-cost function \(c\), the min–max mTSP is
\[z_{\max}=\min_{(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\in\mathcal F_m}\max_{1\leq k\leq m}c(T_k).\]
Equivalently, introduce \(L\in\mathbb R\), minimize \(L\), and impose \(c(T_k)\leq L\) for every \(k\). Thus the objective minimizes the longest salesman tour, while aggregate travel cost is relevant only through feasibility or an additional tie-breaking criterion.

children.title: Balanced mTSP

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced mTSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: mTSP with an explicit dispersion penalty or balance constraint on route costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible tour family \(T=(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\), let \(\ell_k=c(T_k)\) and \(\bar\ell=m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\ell_k\). A balanced mTSP minimizes an aggregate routing objective together with a route-dispersion measure, for example
\[\min_{T\in\mathcal F_m}\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{m}\ell_k+\rho\max_{1\leq k\leq m}|\ell_k-\bar\ell|\right\},\]
where \(\rho\geq0\). A constraint form instead minimizes total cost subject to \(\max_k\ell_k-\min_k\ell_k\leq\Delta\). The selected balance measure and tolerance are part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize routing while penalizing or bounding disparities among individual tour costs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_m\neq\varnothing\) and \(m\geq2\).
Every tour cost \(\ell_k\) is finite.

children.title: mTSP Objective Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural tensions among aggregate efficiency, worst-route control, and workload equity.

knowledge_statements.title: mTSP Objective Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto relation between total travel and longest-tour cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible tour family \(T=(T_1,\ldots,T_m)\in\mathcal F_m\), define \(S(T)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}c(T_k)\) and \(M(T)=\max_k c(T_k)\). A solution \(T^*\) is Pareto efficient if no \(T\in\mathcal F_m\) satisfies \(S(T)\leq S(T^*)\) and \(M(T)\leq M(T^*)\), with at least one strict inequality. For every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), any minimizer of \(\lambda S(T)+(1-\lambda)M(T)\) is Pareto efficient. In a discrete nonconvex objective image, some Pareto-efficient solutions may not minimize any such weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total distance and longest-tour cost define a Pareto frontier; weighted sums recover supported, but not necessarily all, efficient solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_m\) is nonempty and finite.
Every feasible tour has finite cost.
The scalarization weight satisfies \(0<\lambda<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every weighted-sum minimizer is Pareto efficient for \((S,M)\), but unsupported efficient points may exist.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Endpoint TSP Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian path problem with both endpoints prescribed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), and let distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) be prescribed. A fixed-endpoint TSP path is a simple path
\[P=(v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|})\]
with \(v_1=s\), \(v_{|V|}=t\), \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|}\}=V\), and \(\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}\in E\) for every applicable \(i\). The optimization problem minimizes \(c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^{|V|-1}c_{\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}}\) over all such Hamiltonian \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost Hamiltonian path whose two endpoints are prescribed distinct vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
\(s,t\in V\) are distinct prescribed vertices.

children.title: Rooted TSP Paths

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted TSP Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian path problem with one prescribed endpoint and one free endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite edge-weighted graph and let \(r\in V\) be prescribed. A rooted TSP path is a Hamiltonian path
\[P=(r,v_2,\ldots,v_{|V|})\]
that visits every vertex exactly once; its terminal vertex \(v_{|V|}\in V\setminus\{r\}\) is chosen by the solution. The rooted TSP path problem minimizes
\[c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^{|V|-1}c_{\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}}\]
over all Hamiltonian paths having \(r\) as an endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost Hamiltonian path beginning at a prescribed root and ending at an optimally chosen vertex.

At least one Hamiltonian path having endpoint \(r\) exists.

children.title: Free-Endpoint TSP Paths

knowledge_statements.title: Free-Endpoint TSP Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian path problem with both endpoints selected by the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite edge-weighted graph. A free-endpoint TSP path is a simple path
\[P=(v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|})\]
whose vertex sequence contains every vertex of \(V\) exactly once; neither \(v_1\) nor \(v_{|V|}\) is prescribed. The free-endpoint TSP path problem minimizes
\[c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^{|V|-1}c_{\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}}\]
over all Hamiltonian paths in \(G\), jointly selecting the two distinct endpoints and their visiting order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost Hamiltonian path while allowing both endpoints to be chosen freely.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and edge weighted.
At least one Hamiltonian path exists.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: endpoint restrictions define nested feasible families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison among fixed-endpoint, rooted, and free-endpoint metric TSP paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For distinct vertices \(s,t\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_{s,t}\) be the minimum cost of a Hamiltonian path whose endpoints are exactly \(s\) and \(t\). For a root \(r\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_{r,*}\) impose only that \(r\) is an endpoint, and let \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}\) leave both endpoints unrestricted. Then
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}=\min_{s\ne t}\operatorname{OPT}_{s,t},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}_{r,*}=\min_{t\ne r}\operatorname{OPT}_{r,t}.
\]
Consequently, for every \(t\ne r\), \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}\le \operatorname{OPT}_{r,*}\le \operatorname{OPT}_{r,t}\).

children.title: Multi-Depot Multi-Trip Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings combining depot allocation with repeated vehicle reuse.

assumptions_latex: Vehicles are based at multiple depots.
A physical vehicle may perform multiple trips during the horizon.
Each customer is served exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every trip is linked to a depot and vehicle, while each vehicle's ordered trip sequence satisfies depot, capacity, compatibility, and horizon constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combined regime permits multiple depots and repeated trips per vehicle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined multi-depot and multi-trip operational regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given depots \(D\), depot-based fleets \(F_d\), customers, and a planning horizon, a multi-depot multi-trip regime selects customer trips and assigns each trip to a vehicle \(f\in F_d\) and its base depot \(d\). A vehicle may receive an ordered sequence \(\mathcal T_f\) containing several trips. Every trip starts and ends at its authorized depot, satisfies capacity and compatibility constraints, and the complete sequence respects turnaround and horizon limits. Across all trips, every customer is served exactly once, and total operating cost is minimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vehicles based at several depots may each run multiple feasible trips whose combined schedules cover all customers exactly once.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Depot Multi-Trip Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The combined multi-depot, multi-trip formulation fits the leaf, but no source establishes the precise base-depot, closed-trip, turnaround, and horizon conventions.

assumptions_latex: Each route starts at a designated depot.
Vehicles need not return to their starting depot after their final customer.
Each customer is served exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every route is a depot-rooted path rather than a depot-rooted cycle, with its terminal vertex unrestricted or restricted to an allowed terminal set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: open-route VRP removes the return-to-origin requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-route convention with depot departure and no required return to origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given depots \(D\), customers \(N\), vehicle resources, and travel costs, the open-route vehicle-routing problem seeks minimum-cost routes that each begin at an authorized depot, serve a sequence of customers, and do not have to return to that depot. A route therefore ends at its last customer or at an allowed terminal in \(T\), according to the model. Every customer is served exactly once, and each route satisfies capacity, duration, and compatibility constraints. Costs include only traversed arcs unless an explicit terminal or vehicle-repositioning charge is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct depot-originating customer paths that need not return to their starting depots, while retaining ordinary service and resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Route VRP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The no-return formulation fits Open-Route VRP, but terminal choices, endpoint conventions, and treatment of repositioning costs vary and need an inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: A complete directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) has depot \(0\), customers \(N=V\setminus\{0\}\), nonnegative demands \(d_i\), and vehicle capacity \(Q>0\).
Each vehicle route starts and ends at \(0\), and its total delivered quantity does not exceed \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution is a finite collection of vehicle routes together with quantities \(q_{ir}\ge 0\) delivered to customer \(i\) on route \(r\), such that \[\sum_r q_{ir}=d_i\quad(i\in N),\qquad q_{ir}>0\Longrightarrow i\text{ lies on }r,\qquad \sum_{i\in N}q_{ir}\le Q\quad(r).\] The split-delivery vehicle-routing problem minimizes the prescribed total route cost over these solutions. Unlike the classical capacitated VRP, it permits \(q_{ir}>0\) and \(q_{is}>0\) for distinct routes \(r\ne s\).

notation.meaning: quantity delivered to customer i by route r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the capacitated routing variant in which a customer's demand may be divided among multiple vehicle visits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible solution is a finite collection of vehicle routes together with quantities \(q_{ir}\ge 0\) delivered to customer \(i\) on route \(r\), such that \[\sum_r q_{ir}=d_i\quad(i\in N),\qquad q_{ir}>0\Longrightarrow i\text{ lies on }r,\qquad \sum_{i\in N}q_{ir}\le Q\quad(r).\] The split-delivery vehicle-routing problem minimizes the prescribed total route cost over these solutions. Unlike the classical capacitated VRP, it permits \(q_{ir}>0\) and \(q_{is}>0\) for distinct routes \(r\ne s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Customers may receive portions of their demand from several routes, provided all demand is met and every route respects vehicle capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Split-Delivery VRP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Split-Delivery VRP, but no inspectable authoritative citation supports the formulation.

children.title: VRP with Hard Time Windows
children.top_down_role: Vehicle-routing settings where time-window violations are prohibited.

assumptions_latex: Each customer \(i\) has service duration \(s_i\ge 0\) and a prescribed time window \([a_i,b_i]\).
Travel time from \(i\) to \(j\) is \(t_{ij}\ge 0\), and waiting before service is allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A routed schedule with service-start times \(T_i\) is feasible for the hard-time-window VRP exactly when every visited arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(T_j\ge T_i+s_i+t_{ij}\), subject to the usual route-order convention, and every customer satisfies \[a_i\le T_i\le b_i.\] Both bounds are feasibility constraints: a vehicle arriving before \(a_i\) may wait, whereas service beginning after \(b_i\) is forbidden. The optimization criterion, commonly routing cost or fleet size followed by routing cost, is minimized only over schedules satisfying these constraints.

notation.meaning: earliest and latest permitted service-start times

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses service-start windows, permitted early-arrival waiting, and strict prohibition of late service.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routed schedule with service-start times \(T_i\) is feasible for the hard-time-window VRP exactly when every visited arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(T_j\ge T_i+s_i+t_{ij}\), subject to the usual route-order convention, and every customer satisfies \[a_i\le T_i\le b_i.\] Both bounds are feasibility constraints: a vehicle arriving before \(a_i\) may wait, whereas service beginning after \(b_i\) is forbidden. The optimization criterion, commonly routing cost or fleet size followed by routing cost, is minimized only over schedules satisfying these constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every service must start inside its customer's time window; early vehicles may wait, but late starts make a route infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: VRP with Hard Time Windows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits hard time windows, but the record supplies no source for its timing convention, waiting rule, or stated optimization criteria.

children.title: VRP with Soft Time Windows
children.top_down_role: Vehicle-routing settings where time-window violations may incur penalties or service losses.

assumptions_latex: Each customer \(i\) has a preferred service-start interval \([a_i,b_i]\), service duration \(s_i\), and routed start time \(T_i\).
Nonnegative penalty functions \(p_i^-\) and \(p_i^+\) quantify earliness and lateness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In a soft-time-window VRP, violation of \([a_i,b_i]\) is permitted and charged rather than automatically declared infeasible. A standard objective is \[C(\mathcal R)+\sum_i\left[p_i^-\bigl((a_i-T_i)_+\bigr)+p_i^+\bigl((T_i-b_i)_+\bigr)\right],\qquad (x)_+=\max\{x,0\},\] minimized over routed schedules satisfying all remaining routing and timing constraints. The penalty functions may be linear, piecewise linear, or otherwise specified. A one-sided soft window is obtained by setting one violation penalty identically zero or retaining the corresponding bound as hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines soft windows through explicit earliness and lateness penalties; one-sided and mixed variants remain possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a soft-time-window VRP, violation of \([a_i,b_i]\) is permitted and charged rather than automatically declared infeasible. A standard objective is \[C(\mathcal R)+\sum_i\left[p_i^-\bigl((a_i-T_i)_+\bigr)+p_i^+\bigl((T_i-b_i)_+\bigr)\right],\qquad (x)_+=\max\{x,0\},\] minimized over routed schedules satisfying all remaining routing and timing constraints. The penalty functions may be linear, piecewise linear, or otherwise specified. A one-sided soft window is obtained by setting one violation penalty identically zero or retaining the corresponding bound as hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Service outside a preferred window remains feasible but incurs specified earliness or lateness penalties in the routing objective.
knowledge_statements.title: VRP with Soft Time Windows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and penalized-window formulation are plausible, but soft-window conventions vary and no citation supports this two-sided formulation or its one-sided variants.

children.title: Mixed Time-Window Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances containing customer classes with different time-window enforcement policies.

assumptions_latex: Customers are partitioned into hard-window customers \(H\), soft-window customers \(S\), and optionally unrestricted customers \(U\).
Each \(i\in H\cup S\) has an interval \([a_i,b_i]\) and service-start time \(T_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A mixed time-window regime combines distinct enforcement rules within one routing instance. Feasibility requires \[a_i\le T_i\le b_i\quad(i\in H),\] while customers \(i\in S\) may violate their intervals and contribute specified nonnegative penalties \(p_i^-(a_i-T_i)_++p_i^+(T_i-b_i)_+\) to the objective; customers in \(U\) have no window restriction. One-sided hard or soft bounds can be represented by omitting the opposite bound or penalty. Thus the regime is determined customer by customer, rather than by a single instance-wide window policy.

notation.meaning: hard, soft, and unrestricted customer subsets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers customer-level mixtures of hard, soft, one-sided, and absent service-time restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed time-window regime combines distinct enforcement rules within one routing instance. Feasibility requires \[a_i\le T_i\le b_i\quad(i\in H),\] while customers \(i\in S\) may violate their intervals and contribute specified nonnegative penalties \(p_i^-(a_i-T_i)_++p_i^+(T_i-b_i)_+\) to the objective; customers in \(U\) have no window restriction. One-sided hard or soft bounds can be represented by omitting the opposite bound or penalty. Thus the regime is determined customer by customer, rather than by a single instance-wide window policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different customers may have hard windows, penalized soft windows, one-sided restrictions, or no time window in the same routing instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Time-Window Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the proposed mixed-regime leaf, but no source establishes this customer-level taxonomy or the included one-sided and unrestricted cases.

children.title: Distance-Constrained VRP
children.top_down_role: Vehicle-routing settings limiting route length or traveled distance.

assumptions_latex: Each arc \((i,j)\) has nonnegative distance \(d_{ij}\), and each vehicle route begins and ends at its designated depot.
Route \(r\) has an allowed distance limit \(D_r>0\), possibly common to all vehicles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m,v_{m+1})\), its traveled distance is \[L(r)=\sum_{h=0}^{m}d_{v_hv_{h+1}}.\] A distance-constrained VRP admits only route collections satisfying \(L(r)\le D_r\) for every used vehicle route \(r\), in addition to customer coverage and any capacity constraints. The objective minimizes the prescribed fleet or routing cost over this feasible set. Distances need not equal travel times; consequently, this constraint limits spatial mileage even when congestion, waiting, or service durations determine schedule length separately.

notation.meaning: distance assigned to arc from i to j
total traveled distance of route r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates a route's accumulated spatial distance from elapsed duration and labor rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m,v_{m+1})\), its traveled distance is \[L(r)=\sum_{h=0}^{m}d_{v_hv_{h+1}}.\] A distance-constrained VRP admits only route collections satisfying \(L(r)\le D_r\) for every used vehicle route \(r\), in addition to customer coverage and any capacity constraints. The objective minimizes the prescribed fleet or routing cost over this feasible set. Distances need not equal travel times; consequently, this constraint limits spatial mileage even when congestion, waiting, or service durations determine schedule length separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every used route must have total traveled distance at most its specified mileage limit, independently of elapsed route time.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Constrained VRP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes route distance from elapsed time, but it has no inspectable VRP source supporting the exact variant.

children.title: Duration-Constrained VRP
children.top_down_role: Vehicle-routing settings limiting elapsed route or duty duration.

assumptions_latex: Each traversed arc \((i,j)\) has travel duration \(t_{ij}\ge 0\), and customer \(i\) has service duration \(s_i\ge 0\).
Any waiting time \(w_h\ge 0\) occurring along a route is included according to the stated duration convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m,v_{m+1})\), define elapsed route duration by \[T(r)=\sum_{h=0}^{m}t_{v_hv_{h+1}}+\sum_{h=1}^{m}s_{v_h}+\sum_h w_h.\] A duration-constrained VRP requires \(T(r)\le H_r\) for every used route \(r\), where \(H_r>0\) is its duration limit. Customer coverage, capacity, and other routing requirements remain in force. If the model excludes waiting or service from duration, the corresponding sum is omitted explicitly; the governing resource is elapsed time rather than distance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses elapsed route time including travel, service, and waiting under an explicit accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m,v_{m+1})\), define elapsed route duration by \[T(r)=\sum_{h=0}^{m}t_{v_hv_{h+1}}+\sum_{h=1}^{m}s_{v_h}+\sum_h w_h.\] A duration-constrained VRP requires \(T(r)\le H_r\) for every used route \(r\), where \(H_r>0\) is its duration limit. Customer coverage, capacity, and other routing requirements remain in force. If the model excludes waiting or service from duration, the corresponding sum is omitted explicitly; the governing resource is elapsed time rather than distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each route's elapsed travel, service, and included waiting time must not exceed its stated duration limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Duration-Constrained VRP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Duration-Constrained VRP, but inclusion of service and waiting time is convention-dependent and lacks a supporting citation.

children.title: Workday-Constrained VRP
children.top_down_role: Vehicle-routing settings governed by shift, break, overtime, or duty-horizon restrictions.

assumptions_latex: Vehicle \(k\) has a workday interval \([B_k,E_k]\), and its route is assigned departure time \(u_k\) and return time \(v_k\).
The labor rule specifies required breaks and a maximum compensated or active duty amount \(H_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A workday-constrained VRP admits a routed schedule only if each used vehicle \(k\) satisfies \[B_k\le u_k\le v_k\le E_k,\qquad W_k(u_k,v_k,\mathcal B_k)\le H_k,\] where \(\mathcal B_k\) is its scheduled break set and \(W_k\) is the model's explicitly defined duty-time functional, accounting for travel, service, waiting, and breaks as prescribed. Every mandatory break must also satisfy its placement and duration rule. Thus feasibility depends on a clock-based driver schedule, not merely on a bound for the physical route's travel duration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats shift bounds, duty accounting, and mandatory breaks as explicit route-schedule feasibility rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A workday-constrained VRP admits a routed schedule only if each used vehicle \(k\) satisfies \[B_k\le u_k\le v_k\le E_k,\qquad W_k(u_k,v_k,\mathcal B_k)\le H_k,\] where \(\mathcal B_k\) is its scheduled break set and \(W_k\) is the model's explicitly defined duty-time functional, accounting for travel, service, waiting, and breaks as prescribed. Every mandatory break must also satisfy its placement and duration rule. Thus feasibility depends on a clock-based driver schedule, not merely on a bound for the physical route's travel duration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Routes must fit driver workday bounds and satisfy the model's duty-time and mandatory-break rules, beyond ordinary route-duration limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Workday-Constrained VRP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the workday-constrained leaf, but the abstract duty functional and break rules are model- or jurisdiction-dependent and unsupported by a source.

children.title: Route-Resource Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where distance, elapsed time, and labor limits jointly shape route feasibility.

assumptions_latex: Each route \(r\) consumes a nonnegative resource vector \(g(r)=(g_1(r),\ldots,g_p(r))\).
The admissible resource set \(K_r\subseteq\mathbb R_+^p\) is specified for each route or vehicle type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route-resource interaction regime is defined by the joint feasibility condition \[g(r)\in K_r\qquad\text{for every used route }r.\] It is separable when \(K_r=\prod_{\ell=1}^p[0,H_{r\ell}]\), yielding independent limits \(g_\ell(r)\le H_{r\ell}\). It is coupled when membership in \(K_r\) cannot be expressed as such a Cartesian product, for example \(\alpha L(r)+\beta T(r)\le H_r\), or when one consumption changes another through time-dependent travel, load-dependent energy, breaks, or replenishment. Optimization is over routes satisfying the resulting joint resource constraints.

notation.meaning: distance and elapsed duration of a route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes independent route-resource bounds from constraints coupling distance, time, energy, load, or replenishment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A route-resource interaction regime is defined by the joint feasibility condition \[g(r)\in K_r\qquad\text{for every used route }r.\] It is separable when \(K_r=\prod_{\ell=1}^p[0,H_{r\ell}]\), yielding independent limits \(g_\ell(r)\le H_{r\ell}\). It is coupled when membership in \(K_r\) cannot be expressed as such a Cartesian product, for example \(\alpha L(r)+\beta T(r)\le H_r\), or when one consumption changes another through time-dependent travel, load-dependent energy, breaks, or replenishment. Optimization is over routes satisfying the resulting joint resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route resources are independent when bounded separately and interacting when feasibility depends on a joint, nonseparable consumption region.
knowledge_statements.title: Route-Resource Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is suitable, but the separable-versus-coupled resource taxonomy and examples require an authoritative source.

assumptions_latex: Planning periods form \(P=\{1,\ldots,H\}\), and customer \(i\) requires \(f_i\) visits during the horizon.
A finite set \(\mathcal S_i\subseteq 2^P\) specifies customer \(i\)'s admissible visit-day patterns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A periodic vehicle-routing solution chooses one pattern \(S_i\in\mathcal S_i\) for each customer \(i\), with \(|S_i|=f_i\), and constructs a feasible vehicle-route collection \(\mathcal R_p\) for every period \(p\in P\). Customer \(i\) is served in period \(p\) exactly when \(p\in S_i\), and each daily collection satisfies the applicable capacity, duration, depot, and fleet constraints. The periodic VRP minimizes an objective such as \(\sum_{p\in P}C_p(\mathcal R_p)\), possibly with fleet-consistency terms, jointly over visit-pattern selection and daily routing.

notation.meaning: admissible visit-day patterns for customer i
route collection operated in period p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-horizon problem jointly selecting customer visit patterns and feasible routes for each period.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A periodic vehicle-routing solution chooses one pattern \(S_i\in\mathcal S_i\) for each customer \(i\), with \(|S_i|=f_i\), and constructs a feasible vehicle-route collection \(\mathcal R_p\) for every period \(p\in P\). Customer \(i\) is served in period \(p\) exactly when \(p\in S_i\), and each daily collection satisfies the applicable capacity, duration, depot, and fleet constraints. The periodic VRP minimizes an objective such as \(\sum_{p\in P}C_p(\mathcal R_p)\), possibly with fleet-consistency terms, jointly over visit-pattern selection and daily routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over several periods, the model jointly chooses each customer's admissible visit days and feasible vehicle routes for every day.
knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Vehicle Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately captures joint visit-pattern selection and per-period routing, but no periodic-VRP citation is provided.

children.title: Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing settings where travel or service characteristics vary with time.

assumptions_latex: Traversing arc \((i,j)\) after departing \(i\) at time \(t\) requires travel time \(\tau_{ij}(t)\ge 0\).
A route schedule assigns service or departure times consistently with service durations and any waiting decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In time-dependent vehicle routing, temporal propagation along every used arc \((i,j)\) is governed by \[A_j\ge D_i+\tau_{ij}(D_i),\] where \(D_i\) is departure time from \(i\) and \(A_j\) is arrival time at \(j\). Consequently, the duration and cost of a fixed vertex sequence may depend on its departure schedule. A solution consists of routes and compatible times satisfying customer coverage, fleet, capacity, and any time-window constraints, and minimizes the prescribed schedule-dependent objective. Under the FIFO convention, \(t\mapsto t+\tau_{ij}(t)\) is nondecreasing for every arc.

notation.meaning: travel time on arc (i,j) when departure occurs at t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arc travel times as departure-time functions and states the commonly imposed FIFO convention separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In time-dependent vehicle routing, temporal propagation along every used arc \((i,j)\) is governed by \[A_j\ge D_i+\tau_{ij}(D_i),\] where \(D_i\) is departure time from \(i\) and \(A_j\) is arrival time at \(j\). Consequently, the duration and cost of a fixed vertex sequence may depend on its departure schedule. A solution consists of routes and compatible times satisfying customer coverage, fleet, capacity, and any time-window constraints, and minimizes the prescribed schedule-dependent objective. Under the FIFO convention, \(t\mapsto t+\tau_{ij}(t)\) is nondecreasing for every arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc travel time depends on departure time, so route feasibility and cost depend on both visit order and schedule.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits time-dependent routing and labels FIFO as a convention, but no source supports the propagation model or the role of FIFO.

children.title: Synchronized Vehicle Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing settings requiring coordinated timing across vehicles, visits, or services.

assumptions_latex: A set \(E\) of synchronization events is prescribed, and event \(e\) requires participation by vehicle-operation pairs in \(P_e\).
Each participating operation \((k,i)\) has event time \(T_{ki}\), and event \(e\) has tolerance \(\delta_e\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A synchronized vehicle-routing solution consists of vehicle routes and schedules satisfying ordinary routing constraints together with, for every event \(e\in E\), \[\max_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}-\min_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}\le\delta_e.\] The case \(\delta_e=0\) imposes exact simultaneous service or meeting. Precedence synchronization is represented instead by constraints such as \(T_{\ell j}\ge T_{ki}+s_{ki}+h_e\). Because a synchronization event links operations on distinct routes, the participating route schedules cannot generally be made feasible independently.

notation.meaning: participating vehicle-operation pairs for event e
scheduled time of vehicle k's operation at i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers simultaneous, tolerance-based, and precedence synchronization constraints linking operations on distinct vehicle routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A synchronized vehicle-routing solution consists of vehicle routes and schedules satisfying ordinary routing constraints together with, for every event \(e\in E\), \[\max_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}-\min_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}\le\delta_e.\] The case \(\delta_e=0\) imposes exact simultaneous service or meeting. Precedence synchronization is represented instead by constraints such as \(T_{\ell j}\ge T_{ki}+s_{ki}+h_e\). Because a synchronization event links operations on distinct routes, the participating route schedules cannot generally be made feasible independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Specified operations on different routes must occur simultaneously, within a tolerance, or in a prescribed temporal order.
knowledge_statements.title: Synchronized Vehicle Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits synchronized vehicle routing, but the unified coverage of tolerance-based simultaneity and precedence synchronization lacks authoritative support.

children.title: Time-Dependence Synchronization Interactions
children.top_down_role: Combined regimes where changing travel conditions affect coordinated service requirements.

assumptions_latex: Arc travel time is \(\tau_{ij}(t)\) for departure time \(t\), and synchronized event \(e\) links operation times indexed by \(P_e\).
All service, waiting, and departure times are decision variables consistent with route order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A time-dependence synchronization interaction regime requires both propagation constraints \[A_j\ge D_i+\tau_{ij}(D_i)\quad\text{on every used arc }(i,j)\] and synchronization constraints such as \[\max_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}-\min_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}\le\delta_e\quad(e\in E).\] These systems interact because changing a departure to meet one event changes downstream travel times and hence later event times. The regime is separable only when the time-dependent propagation on each route can be scheduled independently without altering satisfaction of any cross-route synchronization constraint; otherwise routes and schedules must be optimized jointly.

notation.meaning: participants and tolerance for synchronization event e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States joint feasibility when departure-time-dependent propagation and cross-route synchronization constrain the same schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-dependence synchronization interaction regime requires both propagation constraints \[A_j\ge D_i+\tau_{ij}(D_i)\quad\text{on every used arc }(i,j)\] and synchronization constraints such as \[\max_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}-\min_{(k,i)\in P_e}T_{ki}\le\delta_e\quad(e\in E).\] These systems interact because changing a departure to meet one event changes downstream travel times and hence later event times. The regime is separable only when the time-dependent propagation on each route can be scheduled independently without altering satisfaction of any cross-route synchronization constraint; otherwise routes and schedules must be optimized jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization changes departure times, which changes later travel durations; therefore cross-route event timing and time-dependent propagation generally require joint optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependence Synchronization Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind is appropriate for an interaction regime, but the claimed interaction and separability characterization is taxonomy-specific and has no supporting citation.
