children.title: Pseudopolynomial Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical or parameter restrictions supporting pseudopolynomial treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Running-time regime for integer-valued routing instances measured by numerical magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an integer-encoded vehicle-routing instance, let \(|I|\) denote its binary encoding length, and let \(M(I)=\max_j a_j(I)\) be its largest numerical value. An exact algorithm is pseudopolynomial if its running time is bounded by a polynomial in \(|I|\) and \(M(I)\), or in an explicitly specified sum of numerical values. Such a bound is polynomial when the values are unary encoded or polynomially bounded, but it need not be polynomial in their binary encoding length because \(M(I)\) may be exponential in \(|I|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudopolynomial routing algorithm is polynomial in instance length and numerical magnitude, but may be exponential in the binary length of those numbers.
assumptions_latex: All numerical data used by the running-time bound are nonnegative integers.
Arithmetic on values of polynomial bit length has polynomial cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time has the form \(\operatorname{poly}(|I|,M(I))\), without necessarily being \(\operatorname{poly}(|I|)\).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the instance.

source_refs.locator: Encoding and Time and Space Complexity, p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding and Time and Space Complexity, p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is precise and standard, but the cited encoding page is not sufficient evidence for the specific pseudopolynomial running-time definition.

children.title: Numerical-Encoding Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of complexity classifications on numerical encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Encoding Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which a magnitude-dependent running-time bound is polynomial in binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a routing instance, let \(L=|I|\) be its binary encoding length, let \(n(I)\le L\) measure its combinatorial size, and let \(M(I)\) be its largest nonnegative integer datum. Suppose an algorithm has running-time bound \(T(I)\le C(n(I)+M(I))^k\) for fixed constants \(C,k>0\). If an instance class satisfies \(M(I)\le L^c\) for some fixed \(c\), then this bound is polynomial in \(L\). Without a polynomial magnitude restriction, the bound alone need not be polynomial in \(L\), since a binary-encoded value can have magnitude \(2^{\Theta(L)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime polynomial in numerical magnitude is polynomial in binary input length when that magnitude is polynomially bounded in the input length. Without such a bound, the same runtime estimate may be exponential in the input length.
assumptions_latex: Numerical inputs are nonnegative integers represented in binary.
The constants \(C\), \(k\), and \(c\) do not depend on the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(M(I)\le |I|^c\), then \(T(I)=\operatorname{poly}(|I|)\); without such a restriction, the displayed magnitude-dependent bound does not imply polynomial time.

source_refs.locator: Encoding and Time and Space Complexity, p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding and Time and Space Complexity, p. 23

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Capacitated-VRP Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation ratio for metric capacitated vehicle routing with unsplittable demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric capacitated-VRP instance consists of a depot \(r\), clients \(V\), demands \(q_v\in(0,Q]\), vehicle capacity \(Q\), and a nonnegative metric \(d\) on \(V\cup\{r\}\). A feasible solution is a collection of depot-rooted tours that visits every client exactly once and assigns total demand at most \(Q\) to each tour. Its cost is the sum of traversed metric lengths. For \(\alpha\ge1\), an \(\alpha\)-approximation is a polynomial-time algorithm returning a feasible solution \(S\) satisfying \(c(S)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) on every feasible instance \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric CVRP approximation seeks polynomial-time depot tours obeying capacity whose total metric length is at most a fixed factor above optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality.
Each client demand is positive and does not exceed \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximation guarantee is \(c(S)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum feasible routing cost for instance I.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Capacity Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation regime in which vehicle capacity is not part of the growing input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed-capacity CVRP family is a sequence of metric capacitated-routing instances for which the capacity \(Q\) is a constant independent of the number \(n\) of clients; demands are integral and lie in \(\{1,\ldots,Q\}\). An approximation scheme for this family is a collection of algorithms \(\{A_{Q,\varepsilon}\}\) such that, for every fixed \(Q\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), algorithm \(A_{Q,\varepsilon}\) runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and returns a feasible solution of cost at most \((1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\). The polynomial degree may depend on \(Q\) and \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In fixed-capacity approximation, capacity is constant; a scheme may depend arbitrarily on that capacity while remaining polynomial in the client count.
assumptions_latex: Client demands and \(Q\) are positive integers.
The underlying routing costs and feasibility convention are fixed across the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(Q\) and \(\varepsilon\), \(c(A_{Q,\varepsilon}(I))\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) in time \(n^{O_{Q,\varepsilon}(1)}\).

notation.meaning: Algorithm specialized to fixed capacity and accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic VRP Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic approximation ratios for VRP families with unbounded positive optimal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a family of feasible minimization-VRP instances whose positive optimal costs are unbounded, and let algorithm \(A\) return a feasible solution for every \(I\in\mathcal{I}\). Its asymptotic approximation ratio is at most \(\alpha\ge1\) if \[\limsup_{B\to\infty}\ \sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}:\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)\ge B}\frac{c(A(I))}{\mathrm{OPT}(I)}\le\alpha.\] A sufficient finite-instance guarantee is \(c(A(I))\le\alpha\mathrm{OPT}(I)+\beta\) for every \(I\in\mathcal{I}\), where \(\beta\) is independent of \(I\). An asymptotic approximation scheme supplies, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a polynomial-time algorithm having asymptotic ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a VRP family with arbitrarily large positive optimum, an asymptotic ratio controls the algorithm's cost ratio as the optimum grows. An instance-independent additive loss is sufficient for the corresponding asymptotic guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The instance family \(\mathcal{I}\) contains instances with arbitrarily large \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)>0\).
Algorithm \(A\) returns a feasible solution on every \(I\in\mathcal{I}\).
Routing costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(c(A(I))\le\alpha\mathrm{OPT}(I)+\beta\) for all \(I\in\mathcal{I}\), with constant \(\beta\), then \(A\) has asymptotic approximation ratio at most \(\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-VRP Approximation-Scheme Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheme family for routing instances embedded in a fixed-dimensional geometric metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a dimension \(d\). A geometric-VRP approximation-scheme family is a collection \(\{A_{d,\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0}\) for instances whose depot and clients are points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with route cost induced by a specified norm. For every fixed \(d\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), \(A_{d,\varepsilon}\) must run in time polynomial in the number and encoding length of the points and return a feasible solution \(S\) satisfying \(c(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\). Each claimed family must separately state whether capacity is fixed or input-dependent and whether demands are unit, unsplittable, or splittable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric VRP scheme gives near-optimal routes in fixed dimension, with polynomial time for each accuracy, under explicitly stated capacity and demand conventions.
assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\) and norm are fixed.
Coordinates and demands have finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(d\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), \(c(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) in polynomial input time.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Window Approximation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation inheritance when unrestricted time windows include ordinary capacitated routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a metric capacitated VRP with service intervals \([a_v,b_v]\), travel times equal to route lengths, and waiting permitted. If the admissible time-window class contains the common unrestricted window \([0,+\infty)\) for every client, then ordinary metric CVRP is its restriction obtained by assigning that window to all clients. Hence any polynomial-time \(\alpha\)-approximation for the time-window class restricts to a polynomial-time \(\alpha\)-approximation for metric CVRP. Correspondingly, every approximation lower bound for metric CVRP transfers to this class; improved guarantees can only rely on additional window structure or a weaker feasibility model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because unrestricted windows recover ordinary CVRP, time-window algorithms inherit all base approximation barriers unless they exploit extra restrictions on the windows.
assumptions_latex: Waiting is allowed without changing route length.
The reduction preserves demands, capacity, metric costs, and objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\text{-approximation for CVRPTW}\Rightarrow\alpha\text{-approximation for CVRP}\).

notation.meaning: Permitted service-time interval for client v.

knowledge_statements.title: Pickup–Delivery Approximation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation inheritance from capacitated delivery to paired pickup–delivery routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a metric pickup–delivery routing problem with paired requests, precedence, and vehicle capacity \(Q\). Suppose its instance class permits every pickup to be placed at the depot with zero pickup-to-depot travel and associates one delivery client with each request. Then unsplittable capacitated delivery VRP is an objective-preserving restriction: a demand \(q_v\) becomes a depot pickup of size \(q_v\) paired with delivery at \(v\). Therefore a polynomial-time \(\alpha\)-approximation for the pickup–delivery class yields the same factor for that CVRP restriction, and all corresponding inapproximability bounds transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing depot pickups makes capacitated delivery a special case, so pickup–delivery routing cannot evade the base problem’s approximation barriers.
assumptions_latex: Loads are nonnegative and must respect capacity throughout each route.
The objective counts only route travel and is preserved by depot pickups.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\text{-approximation for pickup--delivery VRP}\Rightarrow\alpha\text{-approximation for capacitated delivery VRP}\).

children.title: Heterogeneous-Fleet Approximation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous-Fleet Approximation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound transfer through the identical-vehicle slice of a heterogeneous fleet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a heterogeneous-fleet routing class permit vehicle types \(t\in T\) with capacities \(Q_t\), travel costs \(c_t\), and available multiplicities \(m_t\). If the class includes instances having a single type, or instances in which every type has identical parameters, then homogeneous-fleet CVRP is an objective-preserving restriction. Consequently, any polynomial-time \(\alpha\)-approximation for the heterogeneous class induces an \(\alpha\)-approximation for homogeneous CVRP. Every hardness or inapproximability bound for the homogeneous restriction therefore applies to the heterogeneous class, irrespective of algorithms that exploit genuine type differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical vehicles form a special case of a heterogeneous fleet, so homogeneous-CVRP approximation lower bounds automatically transfer.
assumptions_latex: The heterogeneous model permits identical vehicle parameters.
Feasibility and route cost agree with homogeneous CVRP on that restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\text{-approximation for heterogeneous-fleet VRP}\Rightarrow\alpha\text{-approximation for homogeneous CVRP}\).

children.title: Multi-Attribute Approximation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Attribute Approximation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation barriers inherited by neutralizing all but one routing attribute.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{R}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) be a routing class with side-constraint attributes such as capacities, time windows, compatibility, precedence, or route-length limits. Suppose that for some attribute \(A_i\), neutral admissible values of every \(A_j\) with \(j\ne i\) remove those constraints without changing feasible solutions or costs. The single-attribute class \(\mathcal{R}(A_i)\) is then an objective-preserving restriction. Thus an \(\alpha\)-approximation for the multi-attribute class gives an \(\alpha\)-approximation for every such restriction, and its achievable factor cannot surpass a transferred lower bound from any constituent slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neutral settings expose each single-attribute problem inside the combined model, transferring every constituent approximation lower bound to the multi-attribute class.
assumptions_latex: Each nonselected attribute has a neutral admissible setting.
Neutralization preserves the objective and the remaining attribute’s feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{R}(A_i)\subseteq\mathcal{R}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) by an approximation-preserving embedding.

children.title: Heterogeneity–Attribute Coupling

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneity–Attribute Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction principle for approximation in models combining fleet types and side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{C}\) combine heterogeneous vehicle types with side-constraint attributes, and let \(\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{C}\) be the restriction obtained by neutralizing the attributes while retaining heterogeneity. Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}\) be the restriction obtained by making all vehicles identical while retaining the attributes. If both embeddings preserve feasible costs, then every \(\alpha\)-approximation for \(\mathcal{C}\) restricts to an \(\alpha\)-approximation for both \(\mathcal{H}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\). Hence the coupled class inherits the union of their approximation lower bounds; separate algorithms for the two slices do not themselves establish a guarantee for jointly active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled model inherits barriers from both heterogeneity-only and attribute-only slices, while separate slice algorithms do not automatically solve their interaction.
assumptions_latex: Neutral attribute values and identical-vehicle parameters are admissible.
Both restrictions preserve feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(\mathcal{C})\text{ achievable}\Rightarrow\alpha(\mathcal{H})\text{ and }\alpha(\mathcal{A})\text{ achievable}\).

children.title: Classical Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Single-route reward collection under a route-length or travel-budget limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Orienteering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted point-to-point, single-route orienteering with additive rewards and a hard travel budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with nonnegative edge lengths \(c_e\), vertex rewards \(p_v\ge 0\), terminals \(s,t\in V\), and budget \(B\ge 0\). Classical orienteering selects an \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk \(P\) satisfying \(c(P)=\sum_{e\in P}c_e\le B\) and maximizes \[p(P)=\sum_{v\in V(P)}p_v,\] where each visited vertex reward is counted once. When the edge lengths are metric, repeated vertices and cycles may be shortcut without increasing cost, so an optimal solution can be represented by a simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one route from the start to the finish whose travel cost respects a budget and whose distinct visited vertices yield maximum total reward.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(c_e,p_v\ge 0\).
\(s,t\in V\) and \(B\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{p(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-to-}t\text{ walk},\ c(P)\le B\}.\)

notation.meaning: Total travel length or cost of route P.
Sum of rewards of distinct vertices visited by P.

children.title: Budgeted Reward Maximization
children.top_down_role: Reward-maximization variants governed by explicit travel or resource budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Reward Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract reward-maximizing formulation over a budget-constrained family of feasible routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a finite family of feasible routes, let \(C:\mathcal R\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be a route-cost function, let \(F:\mathcal R\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be a reward function, and let \(B\ge0\). Budgeted reward maximization is the optimization problem \[\max\{F(R):R\in\mathcal R,\ C(R)\le B\}.\] For additive vertex rewards, \(F(R)=\sum_{v\in V(R)}p_v\), with each served vertex counted once. The route family may impose specified depots, endpoints, simplicity, or other routing restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among routes costing at most the prescribed budget, select one having maximum reward under the stated reward and routing conventions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{R\in\mathcal R}\{F(R):C(R)\le B\}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the container, but no inspectable source supports its identification as budgeted reward maximization in routing.

children.title: Orienteering–Budgeted-Reward Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between classical orienteering plus broader budgeted-reward models.

knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering–Budgeted-Reward Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identification under additive vertex rewards and identical endpoint and route-feasibility conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an orienteering instance \((G,c,p,s,t,B)\), set \(\mathcal R\) equal to its admissible \(s\)-to-\(t\) routes, define \(C(R)=\sum_{e\in R}c_e\), and define \(F(R)=\sum_{v\in V(R)}p_v\), counting each vertex once. Then \[\max\{F(R):R\in\mathcal R,\ C(R)\le B\}=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V(P)}p_v:P\text{ admissible},\ \sum_{e\in P}c_e\le B\right\}.\] Thus the feasible routes, objective values, and optimizers coincide. Conversely, an additive vertex-reward budgeted routing instance with fixed endpoints is an orienteering instance under the same conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the same routes, endpoints, travel budget, and additive vertex rewards, classical orienteering and budgeted reward maximization are identical optimization problems.
assumptions_latex: Rewards are additive over distinct visited vertices.
Both formulations use identical route and endpoint conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Opt}_{\mathrm{OR}}(G,c,p,s,t,B)=\operatorname{Opt}_{\mathrm{BR}}(\mathcal R,C,F,B).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence is valid under the stated matching conventions, but it has no cited source or locator. Its converse depends on the exact literature convention for orienteering and therefore requires authoritative support.

children.title: Selective TSP
children.top_down_role: Tour families permitting optional selection of profitable or desirable vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-minus-travel-cost version of selective traveling-salesperson routing with a designated depot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), nonnegative vertex profits \(p_v\), and depot \(r\in V\). A selective TSP solution is a closed tour \(T\) starting and ending at \(r\) and visiting an optional subset \(S(T)\subseteq V\). In the net-profit formulation, the problem is \[\max_T\left\{\sum_{v\in S(T)}p_v-\sum_{e\in T}c_e\right\}.\] Each selected vertex contributes its profit once, and unselected vertices incur neither service profit nor a mandatory visit requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose which vertices to visit and a depot tour through them so that collected profit minus travel cost is maximized.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(c_e,p_v\ge0\).
Every admissible tour begins and ends at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_T\left(\sum_{v\in S(T)}p_v-\sum_{e\in T}c_e\right).\)

notation.meaning: Set of vertices selected and visited by tour T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Selective TSP is used for differing objective formulations in the literature. No source establishes that this terminal denotes the stated profit-minus-cost formulation.

children.title: Quota TSP
children.top_down_role: Tour families requiring a prescribed reward or service quota.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost depot tour collecting at least a prescribed amount of vertex reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), vertex rewards \(p_v\ge0\), depot \(r\in V\), and quota \(Q\ge0\). Quota TSP seeks a closed tour \(T\) based at \(r\) that solves \[\min_T\left\{\sum_{e\in T}c_e:\sum_{v\in S(T)}p_v\ge Q\right\},\] where \(S(T)\) is the set of distinct visited vertices and every reward is counted once. The instance is feasible precisely when some admissible depot tour can collect reward at least \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost depot tour whose distinct visited vertices collectively supply at least the required reward quota.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(c_e,p_v,Q\ge0\).
Tours start and end at the designated depot \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}\{c(T):T\text{ is depot-based},\ p(S(T))\ge Q\}.\)

notation.meaning: Distinct vertices visited by tour T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quota formulation is precise and appropriate, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Selection–Quota Model Relations
children.top_down_role: Transformations plus structural distinctions between selection-based and quota-based tours.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Quota Model Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto-frontier relation between collected reward and minimum routing cost; not unconditional optimizer equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a common finite family \(\mathcal T\) of depot tours, define reward \(P(T)\), cost \(C(T)\), and the quota value function \[g(Q)=\min\{C(T):T\in\mathcal T,\ P(T)\ge Q\}.\] If \(T^*\) maximizes \(P(T)-\lambda C(T)\) for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(Q=P(T^*)\), then \(C(T^*)=g(Q)\); otherwise a cheaper tour meeting \(Q\) would improve the scalarized objective. Conversely, a quota-optimal tour need not maximize any weighted profit-minus-cost objective: only supported nondominated reward-cost points admit such a scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted selective-TSP optimum is quota-optimal at its achieved reward, but unsupported quota optima need not arise from any weighted objective.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a finite common feasible-tour family.
\(P(T),C(T)\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\arg\max_T(P(T)-\lambda C(T))\Rightarrow T^*\in\arg\min\{C(T):P(T)\ge P(T^*)\}.\)

notation.meaning: Minimum tour cost required to attain reward quota Q.
Positive cost weight in the scalarized objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-way scalarization implication and supported-point qualification are mathematically plausible and fit the relation container, but neither is supported by an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalty formulation balancing depot-tour travel cost against penalties for omitted vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), omission penalties \(\pi_v\ge0\), and depot \(r\in V\). Prize-collecting TSP selects a closed depot tour \(T\) and its visited set \(S(T)\) to solve \[\min_T\left\{\sum_{e\in T}c_e+\sum_{v\in V\setminus S(T)}\pi_v\right\}.\] A vertex may therefore be omitted by paying its penalty. Equivalently, because \(\sum_{v\in V}\pi_v\) is constant, the same tours maximize collected penalty value minus travel cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a depot tour while paying penalties for omitted vertices, minimizing travel cost plus the total omission penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(c_e,\pi_v\ge0\).
Admissible tours begin and end at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_T\left(\sum_{e\in T}c_e+\sum_{v\notin S(T)}\pi_v\right).\)

notation.meaning: Penalty paid when vertex v is omitted.
Set of vertices visited by tour T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The penalty formulation and constant-shift equivalence are standard and internally consistent, but the record supplies no source or locator.

children.title: Profitable Tour Problems
children.top_down_role: Single-tour objectives balancing collected profit against travel cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Profitable Tour Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-tour optional-service models maximizing collected revenue net of routing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\) be a finite family of admissible tours, let \(S(T)\) denote the customers served by \(T\), let \(p_i\ge0\) be customer profits, and let \(C(T)\ge0\) be routing cost. A profitable tour problem selects one tour according to \[\max_{T\in\mathcal T}\left\{\sum_{i\in S(T)}p_i-C(T)\right\}.\] Service is optional, each served customer contributes its profit once, and all route-feasibility restrictions are encoded in \(\mathcal T\). Variants may require a depot, prescribed endpoints, or resource constraints without changing the net-profit objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select one feasible tour and optional customers so that collected customer profit minus routing cost is maximized.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{T\in\mathcal T}\left(\sum_{i\in S(T)}p_i-C(T)\right).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net-profit single-tour model is coherent, but the scope of “profitable tour problems” varies across sources and no citation fixes the intended convention.

children.title: VRP with Profits
children.top_down_role: Multi-route vehicle-routing families with optional profitable service.

knowledge_statements.title: VRP with Profits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated multi-route optional-service model with fixed and variable fleet costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let customers \(V\) have demands \(d_i\ge0\) and profits \(p_i\ge0\), and let identical vehicles of capacity \(Q>0\) operate depot-based routes. For a feasible route family \(\mathcal R=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\), require each served customer to occur on exactly one route and \(\sum_{i\in S(R_k)}d_i\le Q\) for every \(k\). The VRP with profits solves \[\max_{m,\mathcal R}\left\{\sum_{i\in S(\mathcal R)}p_i-\sum_{k=1}^{m}C(R_k)-fm\right\},\] where \(f\ge0\) is an optional fixed vehicle cost and unserved customers are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose customers and capacity-feasible depot routes for a fleet, maximizing collected profit minus route and vehicle costs.
assumptions_latex: Customer demands and profits are nonnegative.
Each vehicle has capacity \(Q>0\).
Each served customer is assigned to exactly one route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((m^*,\mathcal R^*)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\left\{\sum_{i\in S(\mathcal R)}p_i-\sum_k C(R_k)-fm\right\}.\)

notation.meaning: Union of customers served by the fleet routes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: VRP with profits denotes several distinct variants. No source supports this particular capacitated, variable-fleet, fixed-vehicle-cost formulation as the intended definition.

children.title: Tour-to-Fleet Profit Extensions
children.top_down_role: Structural changes introduced when profitable tours extend to multiple vehicles.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour-to-Fleet Profit Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single profitable tours embed as one-vehicle cases of compatible profit-collecting fleet models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a fleet-profit model whose feasible solution is a collection \(\mathcal R=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\) of depot routes and whose objective is additive across routes and uniquely served customers. If the model permits \(m=1\), gives that vehicle the single-tour resource limits, and uses the same customer profits and route costs, then every feasible profitable tour \(T\) embeds as \((T)\) with identical objective value. Hence the fleet model extends the tour model. The converse reduction holds only when the fleet is restricted to one route; unrestricted multiple routes can enlarge the feasible served subsets and change the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible fleet-profit model contains the profitable-tour model as its one-vehicle restriction, while multiple vehicles generally enlarge the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The fleet formulation permits exactly one used vehicle.
One-vehicle constraints and objective data match the tour formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{tour}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fleet}}\) by \(T\mapsto(T)\), with objective value preserved.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the profitable-tour model.
Feasible set of the fleet-profit model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional one-route embedding is logically sound and fits the relation container, but the claimed tour-to-fleet hierarchy lacks an authoritative source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Coverage Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing to selected service sites, with reward assigned to demand covered within a prescribed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative travel costs, let \(D\) be demand points with rewards \(w_j\ge0\), and let \(N(j)\subseteq V\) be the sites capable of covering demand \(j\). For an admissible route \(R\), define \(S(R)\) as its visited sites and \(y_j(R)=1\) exactly when \(S(R)\cap N(j)\ne\varnothing\). Budgeted coverage routing solves \[\max_R\left\{\sum_{j\in D}w_jy_j(R):C(R)\le B\right\}.\] Each demand reward is counted once even if several visited sites cover it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route through service sites within a travel budget to maximize the total reward of demand points covered by at least one visited site.
assumptions_latex: Travel costs and demand rewards are nonnegative.
Each coverage neighborhood \(N(j)\) is specified.
The admissible route family and budget \(B\ge0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{\sum_{j\in D}w_jy_j(R):C(R)\le B\}.\)

notation.meaning: Sites that cover demand point j.
Indicator that route R covers demand j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coverage objective is coherent, but coverage-routing conventions vary and no citation establishes this neighborhood-coverage formulation for the terminal.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Route Orienteering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-vehicle orienteering under explicitly specified endpoint topology and a single route budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, with nonnegative travel costs \(c_e\), vertex rewards \(p_v\ge0\), budget \(B\ge0\), and prescribed endpoint condition \(\mathcal E\). Single-route orienteering chooses exactly one admissible route \(R\) satisfying \(\mathcal E\) and \(\sum_{e\in R}c_e\le B\), and maximizes \[\sum_{v\in V(R)}p_v,\] counting each visited vertex once. The endpoint condition may specify distinct start and finish vertices or a closed depot tour, but it must be fixed as part of the instance; no reward is pooled across multiple routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one budget-feasible route with the prescribed endpoint topology to maximize the reward of its distinct visited vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(c_e,p_v,B\ge0\).
The endpoint condition \(\mathcal E\) is fixed.
Exactly one route is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{\sum_{v\in V(R)}p_v:R\text{ satisfies }\mathcal E,\ \sum_{e\in R}c_e\le B\}.\)

notation.meaning: Prescribed route endpoint or closure condition.
Distinct vertices visited by route R.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation correctly isolates a single route, but combining point-to-point and closed-depot endpoint topologies under this title requires an authoritative taxonomy source.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with nonnegative arc costs \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\) and vertex prizes \(p:V\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\).
There are \(m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) routes, prescribed endpoint pairs \((s_k,t_k)\), and route budgets \(B_k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal team collects the maximum prize attainable by the fleet under the individual route budgets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fleet version with additive vertex prizes counted once across all routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Team orienteering is the optimization problem
\[
\max_{P_1,\ldots,P_m}\ \sum_{v\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{m}V(P_k)}p(v)
\]
where each \(P_k\) is an \(s_k\)-to-\(t_k\) route satisfying \(c(P_k)=\sum_{a\in P_k}c(a)\le B_k\). A vertex prize is collected at most once, even when the vertex occurs on multiple routes. Repeated vertices or arcs may be forbidden, or removed whenever the cost structure guarantees that a prize-preserving simple route exists; that convention must be fixed for a particular instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible route for each team member to maximize the total prize of vertices visited by at least one route.
knowledge_statements.title: Team Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Team Orienteering leaf and the formulation is internally coherent, including once-only prize collection across routes. However, no citation is supplied, and the admissibility of repeated vertices or arcs is left instance-dependent. An authoritative team-orienteering source with a specific definition, section, or page locator is required before the exact formulation can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Rooted Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Orienteering variants with a prescribed root or depot.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, with nonnegative arc costs and nonnegative vertex prizes.
A root \(r\in V\) and a length budget \(B\ge 0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the greatest prize of any budget-feasible route beginning at \(r\).

notation.meaning: Set of vertices visited by route P

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rooted orienteering with free terminal vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted path version: the start is fixed and the terminal vertex is free.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Rooted orienteering seeks a route \(P=(r=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_q)\) whose initial vertex is the prescribed root \(r\), whose terminal vertex \(v_q\) is unrestricted, and whose cost satisfies
\[
c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^{q}c(v_{i-1},v_i)\le B.
\]
Its objective is
\[
\max_{P}\ \sum_{v\in V(P)}p(v),
\]
with each visited vertex prize counted once. A closed route required to return to \(r\) belongs instead to cycle orienteering under this local convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a route starting at a fixed root, ending anywhere, and collecting maximum vertex prize within a cost budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Rooted Orienteering leaf, and the statement consistently adopts a fixed-start, free-terminal convention. Because rooted orienteering terminology also commonly covers rooted return routes or fixed endpoint variants, a specifically located authoritative source is needed to support this exact local sense.

children.title: Path Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Open-route variants with distinct or unrestricted endpoints.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, with nonnegative arc costs \(c\) and nonnegative vertex prizes \(p\).
Distinct or coincident terminals \(s,t\in V\) and a budget \(B\ge 0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the maximum prize collected by a budget-feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) route.

notation.meaning: A route from s to t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-to-point orienteering with both route endpoints prescribed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Path orienteering is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V(P)}p(v): P\text{ is an }s\text{-to-}t\text{ route and }c(P)\le B\right\},
\]
where \(c(P)\) is the sum of the costs of the traversed arcs and each vertex prize is counted at most once. Feasibility requires the route to begin at \(s\), terminate at \(t\), and respect the single route-cost budget \(B\); vertices other than the two endpoints are optional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible route between fixed endpoints that maximizes the prize of visited vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Path Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Path Orienteering leaf, and the fixed-endpoint formulation is mathematically precise and consistent with the plain statement. No source is cited, however, so a specific definition, section, theorem, or page supporting this point-to-point convention is required.

children.title: Cycle Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Closed-tour variants returning to the initial endpoint.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, with nonnegative arc costs and nonnegative vertex prizes.
A root \(r\in V\) and a budget \(B\ge 0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the maximum prize collected by a budget-feasible closed route through \(r\).

notation.meaning: Prescribed root of the closed route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-route version based at a prescribed root or depot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cycle orienteering seeks a closed route \(C=(r=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_q=r)\) satisfying
\[
c(C)=\sum_{i=1}^{q}c(v_{i-1},v_i)\le B
\]
and maximizing
\[
\sum_{v\in V(C)}p(v).
\]
The route must start and end at the prescribed root \(r\), intermediate vertices are optional, and the prize of a vertex is counted at most once regardless of repeated traversal. If no root is distinguished, the analogous unrooted variant optimizes over all closed routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a closed budget-feasible route through a fixed root that collects maximum vertex prize.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Cycle Orienteering leaf, and the depot-rooted closed-route convention is stated consistently. A specifically located authoritative source is still required because cycle-orienteering terminology and the distinction between rooted and unrooted versions vary across the literature.

children.title: Endpoint-Topology Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural relations among rooted, open-path, plus closed-cycle regimes.

assumptions_latex: All variants use the same graph, costs, prizes, and budget.
Rooted orienteering fixes source \(s\) and permits any terminal vertex; path orienteering fixes both endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The free-terminal rooted optimum is the maximum of the fixed-terminal path optima, while closed rooted routes form a feasible subclass.

notation.meaning: Path optimum from s to t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations use the local convention that rooted orienteering has a free terminal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every source \(s\) and budget \(B\), partitioning rooted feasible routes by their terminal vertex gives
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{R}(s,B)=\max_{t\in V}\operatorname{OPT}_{P}(s,t,B).
\]
Moreover, every cycle feasible for cycle orienteering rooted at \(s\) is a rooted route terminating at \(s\), so
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{C}(s,B)=\operatorname{OPT}_{P}(s,s,B)\le \operatorname{OPT}_{R}(s,B).
\]
These identities presume identical rules for repeated visits and prize counting across the three variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free-terminal rooted orienteering maximizes over all fixed terminals; rooted cycles are exactly paths whose source and terminal coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint-Topology Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind correctly fits the Endpoint-Topology Relations leaf. The displayed identities are valid under the record's stated conventions, provided path instances permit coincident endpoints and all three variants use identical route and prize-counting rules. Because those conventions are terminology-sensitive and none is sourced, a specifically located source or sources are needed to establish that the compared feasible sets have exactly the asserted relationship.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) has nonnegative travel times \(\tau_{ij}\), service times \(s_i\), and prizes \(p_i\ge 0\).
Each optional vertex \(i\) has a service time window \([a_i,b_i]\), and route endpoints are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective maximizes collected prize over routes admitting arrival times that satisfy travel, service, and time-window constraints.

notation.meaning: Arrival or service-start time at vertex i
Travel time from i to j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic hard-window formulation with waiting allowed and prize earned only for serviced vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Orienteering with time windows chooses an endpoint-compatible route \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_q)\) and service-start times \(T_{v_h}\) maximizing \(\sum_{v\in V(P)}p_v\), subject to
\[
a_{v_h}\le T_{v_h}\le b_{v_h}\quad\text{and}\quad T_{v_{h+1}}\ge T_{v_h}+s_{v_h}+\tau_{v_hv_{h+1}}
\]
for every applicable position \(h\). Waiting is represented by strict slack in the second inequality. A vertex contributes its prize only when it is included and serviced within its window; any global duration or endpoint deadline is imposed in addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a prize-maximizing route whose visited vertices can all be serviced inside their time windows, with travel, service, and waiting respected.
knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering with Time Windows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Orienteering with Time Windows leaf, and the statement consistently uses hard service-start windows with waiting allowed. Literature differs on whether windows constrain arrival, service start, or service completion and on endpoint-duration requirements, so an authoritative source with a specific locator is required to support this exact variant.

children.title: Time-Dependent Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants with travel, service, or reward data varying over time.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and each arc \((i,j)\) has a nonnegative departure-time-dependent travel duration \(\tau_{ij}(t)\).
A departure time \(T_0\), endpoint conditions, vertex prizes, and a terminal deadline \(H\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum maximizes collected prize among routes whose recursively determined arrival times meet the deadline and any temporal restrictions.

notation.meaning: Travel duration on arc (i,j) when departed at time t
Arrival time at route position h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic time-dependent arc durations; waiting policy and FIFO assumptions belong to the instance specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Time-dependent orienteering chooses a route \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_q)\) maximizing \(\sum_{v\in V(P)}p_v\). Given departure time \(T_0\), its temporal state obeys
\[
T_{h+1}=T_h+w_h+s_{v_h}+\tau_{v_hv_{h+1}}(T_h+w_h+s_{v_h}),
\]
where \(w_h\ge 0\) is permitted waiting and \(s_{v_h}\ge 0\) is service time. Feasibility requires \(T_q\le H\) and the prescribed endpoint and temporal constraints. If waiting is prohibited, impose \(w_h=0\); if the network is FIFO, every arrival function \(t\mapsto t+\tau_{ij}(t)\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize collected prize when each arc's travel duration depends on its departure time and the resulting route schedule must remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Time-Dependent Orienteering leaf, and the temporal recursion is coherent for deterministic departure-time-dependent arc durations. The admissibility of waiting, treatment of service times, and FIFO assumptions materially distinguish variants, and no citation establishes the selected model. A specifically located authoritative source is required.

children.title: Multi-Period Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants distributing visits or rewards across multiple planning periods.

assumptions_latex: There are periods \(h\in\{1,\ldots,H\}\), each with endpoint conditions and route budget \(B_h\).
Vertices have nonnegative prizes, and cross-period service rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is a collection of period-feasible routes maximizing the prescribed reward of the resulting multi-period visit pattern.

notation.meaning: Indicator that vertex i is serviced in period h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite-horizon formulation; repeat-service rewards and visit-frequency requirements must be specified by the instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multi-period orienteering selects routes \((P_1,\ldots,P_H)\), with each \(P_h\) satisfying its endpoint conditions and \(c(P_h)\le B_h\). Let \(x_{ih}=1\) exactly when \(P_h\) services vertex \(i\). The objective is
\[
\max\ F(x),
\]
where \(F:\{0,1\}^{|V|\times H}\to\mathbb{R}\) is the specified multi-period reward function. Feasibility may additionally impose visit-frequency, spacing, precedence, or exclusivity constraints coupling \(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{iH}\). Thus the model is not determined by independent periodwise routes unless both \(F\) and all side constraints separate by period.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one route per period to maximize a horizon-wide reward while respecting route budgets and any visit-frequency or spacing rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Period Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind is appropriate for the Multi-Period Orienteering leaf, but the record intentionally parameterizes the model by an arbitrary horizon-wide reward function and optional coupling constraints. Whether this constitutes the intended named variant, rather than a generic modeling envelope, depends on the literature definition. A specifically located authoritative source is needed to fix repeat-service rewards and cross-period service rules.

children.title: Temporal-Coupling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where within-period timing interacts with cross-period decisions.

assumptions_latex: A finite set of service decisions is indexed by vertex \(i\) and period or time state \(h\).
Per-period route-feasibility sets \(\mathcal{X}_h\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Temporal coupling is present exactly when the feasible set or objective cannot be expressed as independent periodwise factors and sums.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separability criterion for temporal coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separability criterion distinguishing independent temporal instances from genuinely coupled regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multi-period or time-indexed orienteering model is temporally uncoupled when
\[
\mathcal{X}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{X}_h
\quad\text{and}\quad
F(x^1,\ldots,x^H)=\sum_{h=1}^{H}F_h(x^h).
\]
It is temporally coupled when at least one equality fails. Coupling may arise through time-dependent transitions, repeat-visit rewards, service-frequency bounds, minimum or maximum gaps between visits, inventory carried between periods, or a shared horizon-wide resource. Under the uncoupled condition, optimizing each \(F_h\) over \(\mathcal{X}_h\) independently yields a joint optimum; this decomposition is not justified merely by having distinct route budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is temporally coupled when either feasibility or reward links decisions across times or periods, preventing independent periodwise optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Temporal-Coupling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits a regimes leaf. The factorization criterion gives a useful sufficient-and-necessary definition relative to specified period variables, feasible factors, and additive objective terms, but its claimed exactness is representation-dependent and is not supported by a citation. A specifically located source is needed to establish this as the intended temporal-coupling boundary.

children.title: Capacitated Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Reward-routing variants governed by a primary carrying or service capacity.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) has nonnegative costs and prizes, and each service vertex has demand \(d_i\ge 0\).
A route capacity \(Q\ge 0\), endpoint conditions, and a travel budget \(B\ge 0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum maximizes collected prize subject simultaneously to route-cost and aggregate-demand capacity limits.

notation.meaning: Demand consumed by servicing vertex i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-route additive-consumption model without replenishment, pickup-and-delivery balance, or load-dependent travel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Capacitated orienteering selects an endpoint-compatible route \(P\) solving
\[
\max_{P}\ \sum_{i\in V(P)}p_i
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
c(P)\le B,
\qquad
\sum_{i\in V(P)}d_i\le Q.
\]
Each serviced vertex consumes its nonnegative demand \(d_i\) once, and no capacity is replenished along the route. The capacity constraint is distinct from the travel budget: the former limits serviced demand, whereas the latter limits route cost. Models with evolving vehicle load require additional state equations and constitute a richer capacitated variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a prize-maximizing budget-feasible route whose total serviced demand does not exceed vehicle capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Capacitated Orienteering leaf, and the additive, nonrenewable service-demand formulation is internally precise. Capacitated orienteering can instead involve evolving loads, pickup and delivery, or replenishment, so a specifically located authoritative source is required to support this restricted local convention.

children.title: Multiconstraint Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Reward-routing variants governed by several simultaneous resource limits.

assumptions_latex: Each vertex \(i\) has a nonnegative resource-consumption vector \(d_i\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}\).
A nonnegative capacity vector \(Q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}\), endpoint conditions, and a route-cost budget \(B\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum maximizes collected prize while satisfying every component of the resource-capacity vector and the route budget.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: vector-resource extension of capacitated orienteering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, nonrenewable, vector-valued service resources on a single route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multiconstraint orienteering selects an endpoint-compatible route \(P\) maximizing
\[
\sum_{i\in V(P)}p_i
\]
subject to \(c(P)\le B\) and the componentwise inequalities
\[
\sum_{i\in V(P)}d_{ik}\le Q_k\qquad(k=1,\ldots,K).
\]
All consumptions \(d_{ik}\) and capacities \(Q_k\) are nonnegative, and each visited vertex consumes each resource at most once. Constraints may represent weight, volume, energy, risk, or other additive resources, but resources with replenishment or transition-dependent consumption require an expanded state-space formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize route prize while respecting several additive resource capacities, as well as the travel budget and endpoint requirements.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiconstraint Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the Multiconstraint Orienteering leaf, and the vector of additive nonrenewable resource constraints is mathematically coherent. No cited source establishes that this is the intended named variant or supports the once-only consumption convention. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Resource-Coupling Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits created by interactions among multiple route resources.

assumptions_latex: The capacitated and multiconstraint formulations use additive nonnegative vertex consumptions.
All compared instances retain identical graph, endpoint, prize, and travel-budget data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary, capacitated, and multiconstraint orienteering coincide at the stated parameter boundaries, while multiple active resources generally cannot be represented by one scalar capacity.

notation.meaning: Consumption of resource k at vertex i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parameter-boundary relations among additive resource models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact specialization boundaries for additive, nonrenewable vertex-resource formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multiconstraint orienteering with \(K=1\) is capacitated orienteering after identifying \(d_i=d_{i1}\) and \(Q=Q_1\). Either model reduces to ordinary orienteering when every resource constraint is redundant, for example when
\[
Q_k\ge\sum_{i\in V}d_{ik}\qquad(k=1,\ldots,K).
\]
Conversely, an ordinary instance embeds into either resource model by taking all consumptions to be zero. Several active constraints reduce exactly to one weighted scalar constraint only when that scalar inequality defines the same feasible visited-vertex sets; arbitrary positive weighting generally enlarges or shrinks that family and is not an exact equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One resource gives capacitated orienteering; redundant or zero resource consumption gives ordinary orienteering; several active capacities generally resist exact scalarization.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Coupling Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind correctly fits the Resource-Coupling Boundaries leaf. The one-resource and redundant-capacity specializations are coherent, and the warning that arbitrary scalarization is generally not exact is plausible, but the exact feasible-set equivalence boundary is a nontrivial claim with no citation. A specifically located authoritative source is required.

children.title: Generalized Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Reward-routing variants with group-level visit choices or generalized service alternatives.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge lengths \(c_e\), depot \(r\in V\), and budget \(B\ge 0\).
\(V\setminus\{r\}\) is partitioned into nonempty groups \(\mathcal G\), each having reward \(p_g\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal feasible tour maximizes \(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}p_g z_g\), where \(z_g=1\) exactly when the tour visits at least one vertex of \(g\).

notation.meaning: finite routing graph, edge set, and vertex set
indicator that group g is served

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the group-reward, visit-at-least-one representative convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generalized-orienteering solution is a closed walk \(W\) based at \(r\) whose length satisfies \(c(W)\le B\). For every \(g\in\mathcal G\), define \(z_g=1\) if \(V(W)\cap g\ne\varnothing\), and \(z_g=0\) otherwise. The generalized orienteering problem is
\[
\max_{W:\,c(W)\le B}\ \sum_{g\in\mathcal G}p_g z_g.
\]
A group reward is counted once, irrespective of how many of its vertices are visited.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible depot tour maximizing rewards of groups from which at least one vertex is visited; each group reward is collected at most once.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports identifying the representative-service group-reward convention specifically as generalized orienteering; competing conventions make the exact definition source-dependent.

children.title: Clustered Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants whose vertices are organized into service clusters.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, with nonnegative edge lengths, depot \(r\), and travel budget \(B\).
\(V\setminus\{r\}\) is partitioned into clusters \(\mathcal C\), with reward \(p_C\ge0\) for each cluster.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clustered-orienteering objective is \(\max\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}p_C y_C\) over budget-feasible depot tours satisfying the prescribed cluster-service rule.

notation.meaning: indicator that cluster C is completely served

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses all-vertices cluster service, distinguishing it from representative-based generalized orienteering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the complete-cluster convention, a closed depot walk \(W\) serves cluster \(C\in\mathcal C\) precisely when \(C\subseteq V(W)\). Set \(y_C=1\) in that case and \(y_C=0\) otherwise. Clustered orienteering selects a walk satisfying \(c(W)\le B\) and solves
\[
\max_{W:\,c(W)\le B}\ \sum_{C\in\mathcal C}p_Cy_C.
\]
Partial visitation of a cluster earns no reward under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible depot tour maximizing rewards of clusters whose prescribed service is completed; here completion means visiting every vertex in the cluster.
knowledge_statements.title: Clustered Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The all-vertices cluster-service convention is mathematically coherent, but clustered orienteering has incompatible definitions and no source establishes this local usage.

children.title: Group-Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relations between generalized selection requirements plus cluster-based service.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite routing graph with depot \(r\), nonnegative travel lengths, and budget \(B\).
\(\mathcal G\) is a finite family of vertex subsets with rewards \(p_g\ge0\), and \(q_g\) is a required visit threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Group selection is encoded by \(z_g=1\Rightarrow |V(W)\cap g|\ge q_g\), with objective \(\max\sum_g p_gz_g\).

notation.meaning: indicator that group g is selected and served

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold service unifies representative and complete-group regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed depot walk \(W\) with \(c(W)\le B\), binary group-selection variables obey
\[
z_g=1\ \Longrightarrow\ |V(W)\cap g|\ge q_g,
\qquad g\in\mathcal G,
\]
where \(1\le q_g\le |g|\). The routing-selection problem maximizes \(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}p_gz_g\). The choice \(q_g=1\) gives representative service, while \(q_g=|g|\) gives complete-group service. Overlapping groups remain admissible unless partition structure is separately imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group earns its reward when the tour visits at least its prescribed number of members; thresholds one and group size recover representative and complete service.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Selection Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold representation is coherent, but no source supports it as the intended taxonomy of group-selection regimes, particularly with overlapping groups.

children.title: Set Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants collecting reward through service of designated sets.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, with depot \(r\), nonnegative edge lengths, and budget \(B\).
\(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^V\) is a finite family of service sets, each with reward \(p_S\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set orienteering maximizes \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}p_S z_S\) subject to \(z_S=1\) exactly when \(V(W)\cap S\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: indicator that service set S is hit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the hit-a-set reward convention with overlapping sets allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-orienteering solution is a closed walk \(W\) based at \(r\) with \(c(W)\le B\). For each \(S\in\mathcal S\), let \(z_S=1\) if \(V(W)\cap S\ne\varnothing\), and let \(z_S=0\) otherwise. The problem is
\[
\max_{W:\,c(W)\le B}\ \sum_{S\in\mathcal S}p_Sz_S.
\]
Sets may overlap, and each set reward is collected at most once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a budget-feasible depot tour maximizing the total reward of service sets containing at least one visited vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Set Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation establishes that set orienteering here means rewarding each possibly overlapping set when at least one member is visited.

children.title: Coverage Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants earning reward through direct or indirect coverage.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, with depot \(r\), nonnegative travel lengths, and budget \(B\).
\(U\) is a finite set of demand elements with weights \(w_u\ge0\), and vertex \(v\) covers \(N(v)\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coverage orienteering maximizes \(\sum_{u\in U}w_u y_u\), where \(y_u=1\) exactly when some visited vertex covers \(u\).

notation.meaning: finite universe of coverable demand elements
demand elements covered by vertex v
indicator that demand element u is covered

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indirect service occurs through the union of coverage neighborhoods of visited vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed depot walk \(W\) satisfying \(c(W)\le B\), define
\[
y_u=1\ \Longleftrightarrow\ u\in\bigcup_{v\in V(W)}N(v),
\qquad u\in U.
\]
The coverage-orienteering problem selects \(W\) to maximize
\[
\sum_{u\in U}w_uy_u.
\]
Each demand element contributes its weight once even if several visited vertices cover it; visiting a vertex need not itself carry reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible tour maximizing the weight of demand elements covered by at least one visited vertex, counting each element once.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-coverage formulation is precise and internally consistent, but an inspectable routing-specific source is required to support this definition of coverage orienteering.

children.title: Set-to-Coverage Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences plus boundaries between set service and coverage service.

assumptions_latex: A set-orienteering instance has rewarded sets \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^V\).
A coverage instance has demand universe \(U\) and vertex neighborhoods \(N(v)\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformations \(U=\mathcal S\), \(N(v)=\{S:v\in S\}\) and \(S_u=\{v:u\in N(v)\}\) preserve every tour's reward.

notation.meaning: vertices capable of covering demand u

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for hit-a-set and union-coverage conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Map set orienteering to coverage orienteering by taking \(U=\mathcal S\), assigning \(w_S=p_S\), and defining \(N(v)=\{S\in\mathcal S:v\in S\}\). Then
\[
S\cap V(W)\ne\varnothing\ \Longleftrightarrow\ S\in\bigcup_{v\in V(W)}N(v).
\]
Conversely, map coverage to set orienteering using \(S_u=\{v\in V:u\in N(v)\}\) with reward \(p_{S_u}=w_u\), retaining distinct indexed copies when two elements induce the same vertex set. Both mappings preserve feasibility and tour reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rewarded sets correspond to demand elements, and set membership corresponds to coverage; the two formulations preserve each feasible tour and its reward.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-to-Coverage Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indexed-copy qualification makes the stated reward-preserving correspondence plausible, but the exact equivalence has no cited source.

children.title: Arc-Orienteering Interface
children.top_down_role: Detailed arc-service theory is external.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with depot \(r\), nonnegative traversal costs \(c_a\), budget \(B\), and arc rewards \(p_a\ge0\).
An arc reward is collected at most once, even when the corresponding arc is traversed repeatedly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arc orienteering maximizes \(\sum_{ain A}p_a y_a\) over budget-feasible closed depot walks, with \(y_a\) indicating service of arc \(a\).

notation.meaning: number of traversals of arc a
indicator that arc a is serviced

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface statement only; detailed arc-routing structure is outside this node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed depot walk is represented by traversal counts \(x_a\in\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying flow balance at every vertex and \(\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\le B\), together with connectivity to \(r\). Service indicators satisfy \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\) and \(y_a\le x_a\). The arc-orienteering interface is
\[
\max\ \sum_{a\in A}p_ay_a.
\]
Thus reward attaches to serviced arcs, whereas traversal variables provide the connecting route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc orienteering selects rewarded arcs and a budget-feasible closed depot walk traversing them; traversal may connect service arcs without itself earning reward.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Orienteering Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interface requires an arc-routing source supporting its service and traversal conventions. The conclusion also contains the malformed expression \(\sum_{ain A}\), which should be \(\sum_{a\in A}\).

children.title: Stochastic Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants with probabilistic travel, service, availability, or reward data.

assumptions_latex: Travel times and rewards are random variables with a specified joint distribution, revealed according to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\).
A routing policy must be nonanticipative and must respect budget \(B\) under the stated almost-sure feasibility convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stochastic orienteering chooses \(\pi\in\Pi_{mathrm{NA}}\) maximizing \(\mathbb E[R(\pi,\xi)]\) subject to \(C(\pi,\xi)\le B\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: random scenario containing uncertain routing data
reward and travel cost generated by policy pi in scenario xi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses expected reward with almost-sure budget feasibility and sequential revelation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\) encode uncertain travel times and rewards. A policy \(\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{NA}}\) chooses each next action using only information in the current \(\mathcal F_t\). Under almost-sure budget feasibility, stochastic orienteering is
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{NA}}}\ \mathbb E[R(\pi,\xi)]
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\mathbb P\{C(\pi,\xi)\le B\}=1.
\]
The realized route and collected reward may depend on observations, but decisions cannot depend on unrevealed components of \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a nonanticipative routing policy maximizing expected collected reward while satisfying the travel budget in every scenario except a null set.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Almost-sure budget feasibility, sequential revelation, and expected-reward optimization define only one stochastic-orienteering convention; no source establishes that convention for this leaf.

children.title: Dynamic Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants with requests or data revealed during operations.

assumptions_latex: Requests and routing data arrive over decision epochs \(t=0,1,\ldots,T\).
At epoch \(t\), the decision maker observes state \(s_t\), including current location, remaining budget, and currently known requests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic orienteering selects a causal policy maximizing cumulative served reward while maintaining feasible state transitions and nonnegative remaining budget.

notation.meaning: observable routing state at epoch t
feasible actions available in state s
causal decision rule at epoch t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online finite-horizon formulation with decisions revised after new information arrives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(s_0=(r,B,\mathcal I_0)\). At each epoch \(t<T\), observe newly available information, update \(s_t\), and choose \(a_t=\pi_t(s_t)\in A(s_t)\). Apply the travel and service action to obtain \(s_{t+1}=F_t(s_t,a_t,omega_{t+1})\), requiring the remaining budget component to stay nonnegative. Stop upon returning to the terminal depot or when no feasible action remains. Output the realized route and served requests; optimize \(\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r_t(s_t,a_t)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly update the routing state as information arrives, choose a feasible next action causally, and maximize expected reward before the horizon or budget ends.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a generic policy-control template rather than a specified algorithm, so content_kind algorithm is not justified. The arrival model also lacks a source, and omega_{t+1} should be written \(\omega_{t+1}\).

children.title: Robust Orienteering
children.top_down_role: Variants protecting route quality against specified uncertainty sets.

assumptions_latex: Uncertain routing data \(\xi\) lie in a nonempty uncertainty set \(\mathcal U\).
\(\Pi\) is a prescribed class of static routes or admissible nonanticipative policies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust orienteering solves \(\max_{pi\in\Pi}\min_{xi\in\mathcal U}R(\pi,xi)\) subject to \(C(\pi,xi)\le B\) for every \(\xi\in\mathcal U\).

notation.meaning: reward and cost under decision pi and scenario xi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case reward with budget feasibility throughout the uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given uncertainty set \(\mathcal U\), robust orienteering chooses \(\pi\in\Pi\) by
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \min_{\xi\in\mathcal U}R(\pi,\xi)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
C(\pi,\xi)\le B\quad\text{for every }\xi\in\mathcal U.
\]
If \(\Pi\) contains only routes fixed before uncertainty is revealed, the model is static robust. If \(\Pi\) contains observation-dependent policies, nonanticipativity must additionally be imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a route or policy whose budget is feasible for every allowed scenario and whose worst-case collected reward is as large as possible.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Orienteering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The static-versus-adaptive policy convention and max-min formulation require direct support. In the conclusion, pi and xi are written as literal letter sequences rather than \(\pi\) and \(\xi\).

children.title: Adaptive-Robust Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between policy adaptation plus nonadaptive protection.

assumptions_latex: Uncertainty is revealed sequentially, and policies must be nonanticipative.
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{stat}}\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm{ad}}\) are respectively static-route and adaptive-policy classes under the same uncertainty set \(\mathcal U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adaptive robust value is at least the static robust value, with equality when observations cannot change any feasible continuation or its worst-case reward.

notation.meaning: static and adaptive admissible decision classes
worst-case value over policy class Pi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates static robustness from observation-dependent robust recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
V(\Pi)=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\inf_{xi\in\mathcal U}R(\pi,xi)
\]
over policies robustly satisfying \(C(\pi,xi)\le B\). Since \(\Pi_{\mathrm{stat}}\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm{ad}}\), one has \(V(\Pi_{\mathrm{stat}})\le V(\Pi_{\mathrm{ad}})\). Equality holds whenever every adaptive policy has a static route with no smaller worst-case reward, as when revealed information neither distinguishes feasible continuations nor changes their worst-case payoffs. The boundary fails once informative observations permit scenario-dependent feasible continuations with strictly better worst-case reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive robust policies cannot underperform static routes; they improve strictly only when revealed information enables materially different feasible continuations or rewards.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Robust Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Class inclusion supports the weak value inequality, but the stated equality and strict-improvement boundary is informal and not established as necessary and sufficient. The statement also uses xi instead of \(\xi\) in several formulas.

children.title: Optional-Vertex Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulations centered on explicit service-selection decisions for vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with depot \(r\), arc costs \(c_{ij}\ge0\), vertex prizes \(p_i\ge0\), and budget \(B\).
Binary \(y_i\) selects optional vertex \(i\), and binary \(x_{ij}\) selects routing arc \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree linkages and connectivity constraints yield a single depot tour through exactly the selected optional vertices, maximizing selected prize within budget.

notation.meaning: indicator that optional vertex i is selected
indicator that directed arc (i,j) is used

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed single-tour prize-maximization formulation with optional vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The optional-vertex formulation maximizes \(\sum_{i\in V\setminus\{r\}}p_i y_i\) subject to
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=y_i=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji},
\qquad i\in V,
\]
with \(y_r=1\), \(\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\le B\), and connectivity inequalities
\[
\sum_{i\in S,\,j\notin S}x_{ij}\ge y_k
\quad
(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\},\ k\in S).
\]
Together with \(x_{ij},y_i\in\{0,1\}\), these constraints encode one depot tour containing precisely the selected vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary vertex variables choose profitable optional visits; linked arc variables, a travel budget, and connectivity constraints form one depot tour through those choices.
knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Vertex Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed optional-vertex formulation is plausible and its representation kind fits the leaf, but no routing-specific source supports the exact degree, connectivity, integrality, and single-tour claim.

children.title: Selective-Tour Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulations representing tours over an endogenously selected customer subset.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective-Tour Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-selection formulation for one depot-rooted profitable tour with optional vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\), with depot \(0\), vertex prizes \(p_i\), and arc costs \(c_{ij}\). Binary variables \(y_i\) select vertices and \(x_{ij}\) select tour arcs. A selective tour is represented by
\[\max\ \sum_{i\in V\setminus\{0\}}p_i y_i-\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to \(y_0=1\),
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=y_i=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}\quad(i\in V),\]
and
\[\sum_{i\in S,\,j\notin S}x_{ij}\ge y_k\quad(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{0\},\ k\in S).\]
The degree and connectivity constraints make the selected arcs a depot-rooted tour through exactly the selected vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary vertex and arc variables maximize collected prize minus travel cost, while degree and connectivity constraints enforce one depot-rooted tour through selected vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and contains a distinguished depot \(0\).
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) are given.
A tour visits each selected nondepot vertex at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible integral pairs \((x,y)\) encode depot-rooted selective tours, and the objective equals collected prize minus routing cost.

notation.meaning: binary indicator that arc (i,j) is used
binary indicator that vertex i is selected
vertex prize and arc travel cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Selective-Tour Formulations leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports the routing formulation, its connectivity cuts, or the claimed exact encoding. A routing-specific source with a section, theorem, formulation, or page locator is required.

children.title: Selection–Routing Linkages
children.top_down_role: Structural linkages between service-selection variables plus routing structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Routing Linkages
