knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear link between optional service decisions and tour incidence variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For binary selection variables \(y_i\) and binary arc variables \(x_{ij}\), impose
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=y_i=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}\quad(i\in V\setminus\{0\}).\]
Thus \(y_i=0\) forbids every incident tour arc at \(i\), whereas \(y_i=1\) requires one entering and one leaving arc. Together with \(y_0=1\) and the rooted cuts
\[\sum_{i\in S,\,j\notin S}x_{ij}\ge y_k\quad(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{0\},\ k\in S),\]
every selected vertex belongs to the depot component. Consequently selection cannot create an isolated subtour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree equalities activate routing exactly at selected vertices; rooted cut inequalities connect every activated vertex to the depot.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) has depot \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nondepot vertex is selected exactly when it has one used entering arc and one used leaving arc, and every selected vertex is depot-connected.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering vertex i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the Selection–Routing Linkages leaf, and the degree and rooted-cut implications are plausible. No cited source supports the exact linkage system or depot-connectivity conclusion, so an inspectable routing-specific citation is required.

children.title: Route-Column Formulations
children.top_down_role: Representations using feasible profit routes as decision columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Column Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of profitable routing decisions by complete feasible route columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal R\) be the finite set of feasible depot-rooted routes. For each \(r\in\mathcal R\), let \(a_{ir}=1\) when route \(r\) serves customer \(i\), let \(C_r\) be its routing cost, and define \(w_r=\sum_i p_i a_{ir}-C_r\). A fleet solution is represented by variables \(z_r\in\{0,1\}\), where \(z_r=1\) selects route \(r\). Its profit is
\[\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}w_r z_r.\]
Customer compatibility is expressed through \(\sum_r a_{ir}z_r\le1\), and a fleet bound through \(\sum_r z_r\le K\). Every selected column already satisfies all within-route feasibility restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each column is a complete feasible route; binary column variables choose compatible routes whose total net profit is maximized.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) contains every route permitted by the underlying routing restrictions.
Each customer may be served at most once.
At most \(K\) routes may be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integral column vectors satisfying packing and fleet constraints represent feasible collections of complete routes.

notation.meaning: route net profit and route-selection variable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the Route-Column Formulations leaf. However, the customer index set used in the prize sum and compatibility constraints is not explicitly introduced, and no source supports the claimed correspondence between integral column vectors and feasible route collections.

children.title: Set-Packing Master Formulations
children.top_down_role: Master formulations selecting mutually compatible route columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Packing Master Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-packing master over feasible profitable-route columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given feasible routes \(\mathcal R\), customer incidences \(a_{ir}\), net route profits \(w_r\), and fleet limit \(K\), the integer master problem is
\[\max\ \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}w_rz_r\]
subject to
\[\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}a_{ir}z_r\le1\quad(i\in V\setminus\{0\}),\qquad \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}z_r\le K,\qquad z_r\in\{0,1\}.\]
Replacing integrality by \(0\le z_r\le1\) gives the linear master relaxation. The customer inequalities are packing constraints: no customer occurs in more than one selected route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master chooses profitable feasible routes subject to customer-disjointness and a fleet-size bound; relaxing binary columns yields the LP master.
assumptions_latex: Every column \(r\in\mathcal R\) is an individually feasible depot route.
Route profit \(w_r\) includes all prizes and costs attributable to route \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed binary program is a set-packing formulation of the route-selection problem.

notation.meaning: incidence of customer i in route r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed model is plausibly a set-packing master and the representation kind fits the leaf, but no source is cited for the routing master, its fleet constraint, or its LP relaxation. An inspectable route-based formulation reference is required.

children.title: Column–Master Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural interfaces between route generation plus master-level selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Column–Master Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-profit interface between an LP master and its route-pricing problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the LP relaxation of the set-packing master, let \(\pi_i\ge0\) be the dual multiplier of customer constraint \(i\), and let \(\mu\ge0\) correspond to the fleet constraint. The dual feasibility condition for route \(r\) is
\[\sum_i a_{ir}\pi_i+\mu\ge w_r.\]
Hence its reduced profit is
\[\bar w_r=w_r-\sum_i a_{ir}\pi_i-\mu.\]
The pricing interface searches for a feasible route maximizing \(\bar w_r\). If its maximum is positive, the associated column can improve the restricted master; if every feasible route has \(\bar w_r\le0\), the restricted-master solution is optimal for the full LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Master dual prices modify each route’s profit; pricing finds a positive-reduced-profit route or certifies full LP optimality.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master LP is feasible and has an optimal dual solution.
The pricing oracle optimizes over the complete feasible route set \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No route with positive reduced profit exists if and only if the restricted-master optimum is optimal for the full master LP.

notation.meaning: reduced profit of route column r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the Column–Master Interfaces leaf, but the cited master relaxation explicitly includes upper bounds z_r<=1 while the displayed dual and reduced-profit formula omit their dual multipliers. This is valid only if those bounds are removed or proved redundant under additional column assumptions. A column-generation source and a precise master specification are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Constrained Path Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-expanded path representation for route feasibility and pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each arc \((i,j)\) have cost \(c_{ij}\) and nonnegative resource consumption \(d_{ij}^q\) for resources \(q=1,\ldots,m\), with bounds \(D_q\). A resource-constrained route is an origin-destination path \(P\) satisfying
\[\sum_{(i,j)\in P}d_{ij}^q\le D_q\quad(q=1,\ldots,m).\]
Equivalently, create states \((i,s)\), where \(s\) records accumulated resources, and include transition \((i,s)\to(j,s+d_{ij})\) only when \(s+d_{ij}\le D\) componentwise. An origin-destination path in this expanded network projects to a resource-feasible route; its arc costs may include master-dual adjustments when used for pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulated-resource states convert constrained route generation into a path problem whose feasible state transitions enforce every resource bound.
assumptions_latex: All resource consumptions are nonnegative.
Resource states are discrete or otherwise finitely representable.
The expanded state records every resource needed for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Paths in the state-expanded network correspond to resource-feasible routes under projection to the original graph.

notation.meaning: consumption of resource q on arc (i,j)
expanded state at vertex i with accumulated resource vector s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the topic. The state-expanded construction is plausible for additive, finitely representable resources, but the statement does not fully specify the resource-state domain, origin and destination, or conditions ensuring a finite exact expansion. No resource-constrained path source is cited.

children.title: Budget-to-Quota Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structural conversions between budget-limited plus quota-driven routing.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-to-Quota Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold equivalence between prize maximization under budget and minimum cost under quota.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a common feasible route family \(\mathcal F\), define
\[P(B)=\max\{p(R):R\in\mathcal F,\ c(R)\le B\}\]
and
\[C(Q)=\min\{c(R):R\in\mathcal F,\ p(R)\ge Q\},\]
using \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\) for infeasible maxima and minima. Then for every budget \(B\) and quota \(Q\),
\[P(B)\ge Q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C(Q)\le B.\]
Thus the budget and quota value functions determine one another by threshold inversion, although their complete optimizer sets need not coincide without tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quota is attainable within a budget exactly when the budgeted maximum prize reaches that quota; the two value functions are threshold inverses.
assumptions_latex: Both models use the same feasible route family \(\mathcal F\).
The same functions \(c(R)\) and \(p(R)\) define route cost and collected prize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(B,Q\), the equivalence \(P(B)\ge Q\iff C(Q)\le B\) holds.

notation.meaning: maximum prize attainable within budget B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold equivalence is mathematically plausible and matches the Budget-to-Quota Transformations leaf, but it is an equivalence property rather than a representation in the strict mathematical-role sense. No source supports the value-function conventions or transformation claim.

children.title: Prize-to-Penalty Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structural conversions between collected prizes plus omitted-service penalties.

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-to-Penalty Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constant-shift equivalence between collected prizes and penalties for omitted vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be the optional customer set, let \(S(R)\subseteq U\) be the customers visited by route \(R\), and let \(p_i\) be fixed prizes. For every feasible route,
\[c(R)-\sum_{i\in S(R)}p_i=c(R)+\sum_{i\in U\setminus S(R)}p_i-\sum_{i\in U}p_i.\]
Because the final term is independent of \(R\), minimizing travel cost minus collected prize has exactly the same minimizers as minimizing travel cost plus penalties \(p_i\) for unvisited customers. Equivalently, maximizing collected prize minus travel cost has the same maximizers as the corresponding prize-collecting penalty formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collected-prize rewards can be replaced by equal penalties for omitted vertices because the two objectives differ only by total available prize.
assumptions_latex: The optional customer set \(U\) and prizes \(p_i\) are fixed.
Both formulations use the same feasible route family and travel-cost function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reward and omission-penalty formulations have identical optimizer sets when each omission penalty equals the corresponding prize.

notation.meaning: optional customers visited by route R
prize or equivalent omission penalty of customer i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-shift identity is plausible and locally matches Prize-to-Penalty Transformations, but its mathematical role is an objective-equivalence property rather than a representation. No prize-collecting routing source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Quota-to-Prize Transformations
children.top_down_role: Connections between mandatory reward thresholds plus prize-based objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota-to-Prize Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian conversion of a minimum-cost prize quota into a weighted-prize objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[C(Q)=\min\{c(R):R\in\mathcal F,\ p(R)\ge Q\}.\]
For any multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\), relaxing the quota gives
\[L(\lambda;Q)=\lambda Q+\min_{R\in\mathcal F}\{c(R)-\lambda p(R)\}.\]
Every quota-feasible route satisfies \(L(\lambda;Q)\le C(Q)\). The inner problem is a prize-routing problem with prize weight \(\lambda\). Maximizing \(L(\lambda;Q)\) over \(\lambda\ge0\) yields the Lagrangian dual bound; equality with \(C(Q)\) requires zero Lagrangian duality gap and is not automatic for discrete route families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the prize quota produces a weighted-prize routing problem and a lower bound; exact conversion requires zero Lagrangian gap.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is the common feasible route family.
The quota model is feasible and has finite optimum.
\(\lambda\ge0\) multiplies the constraint \(Q-p(R)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Lagrangian value satisfies \(L(\lambda;Q)\le C(Q)\), and \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0}L(\lambda;Q)=C(Q)\) only under exact duality.

notation.meaning: minimum route cost attaining prize quota Q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the leaf, and the sign of the quota Lagrangian and lower-bound direction are plausible. The exact-duality qualification is appropriately cautious, but no source supports the routing-specific relaxation or its stated validity conditions.

children.title: Transformation Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Restrictions governing preservation of feasibility, objective meaning, or approximation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsupported efficient routes obstruct exact scalarized transformations in discrete routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exact optimizer preservation can fail when a constrained efficient route is unsupported. Consider three feasible routes with cost-prize pairs
\[(c,p)\in\{(0,0),(2,2),(3,4)\}.\]
For quota \(Q=2\), the unique minimum-cost feasible pair is \((2,2)\). A weighted-prize scalarization minimizes \(c-\lambda p\) for \(\lambda\ge0\). Making \((2,2)\) no worse than \((0,0)\) requires \(\lambda\ge1\), while making it no worse than \((3,4)\) requires \(\lambda\le\tfrac12\). No multiplier satisfies both conditions. Hence threshold value relations may remain valid even though no scalar prize weight recovers every constrained optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete quota-optimal route may be unsupported, so no weighted-prize multiplier recovers it even though budget–quota threshold equivalence remains valid.
assumptions_latex: The listed cost-prize pairs are attainable feasible routes.
The scalarized objective is \(c-\lambda p\) with \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quota-optimal pair \((2,2)\) is not optimal for any nonnegative weighted-prize scalarization.

notation.meaning: route cost and collected prize pair

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind exactly fits the leaf, and the numerical unsupported-point calculation is internally consistent. Nevertheless, the record supplies no citation or evidence that situates this counterexample within the claimed profit-routing transformation boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relations among Profit-Routing Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian bound linking budgeted and weighted-profit routing models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[P(B)=\max\{p(R):R\in\mathcal F,\ c(R)\le B\}.\]
For every \(\lambda\ge0\), relaxing the budget constraint yields
\[U(\lambda;B)=\lambda B+\max_{R\in\mathcal F}\{p(R)-\lambda c(R)\}.\]
If \(R\) satisfies \(c(R)\le B\), then \(p(R)\le U(\lambda;B)\); therefore
\[P(B)\le\inf_{\lambda\ge0}U(\lambda;B).\]
The inner maximization is a weighted profit-routing model. Equality holds when some multiplier supports a budget-optimal cost-prize point; otherwise the Lagrangian dual provides only an upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a route budget yields weighted profit routing and an upper bound; exact equivalence holds only at a supported optimum.
assumptions_latex: The budgeted model is feasible with finite value.
\(\lambda\ge0\) multiplies the constraint \(c(R)-B\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weak-duality relation \(P(B)\le\inf_{\lambda\ge0}U(\lambda;B)\) holds, with equality only when the scalarization supports an optimum.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the topic and the weak-duality upper bound has the correct direction. The optimizer-support characterization requires finiteness or suitable attainment assumptions on the route family; these are not stated, and no source supports the routing-specific claim.

children.title: Subset Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State-space approaches indexed by visited or selected customer subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Held–Karp subset recurrence for an exact single selective-tour solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U=V\setminus\{0\}\). Initialize \(D(\{j\},j)=c_{0j}\) for \(j\in U\). For every nonempty \(S\subseteq U\) and \(j\in S\), update
\[D(S,j)=\min_{i\in S\setminus\{j\}}\{D(S\setminus\{j\},i)+c_{ij}\}.\]
Here \(D(S,j)\) is the minimum cost of a depot-starting simple path visiting exactly \(S\) and ending at \(j\). Evaluate each completed tour by
\[\sum_{i\in S}p_i-\min_{j\in S}\{D(S,j)+c_{j0}\},\]
also allowing the empty tour, and return a maximizing subset with predecessor reconstruction. The running time is \(O(n^2 2^n)\) and storage is \(O(n2^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Held–Karp states store the cheapest path through each selected subset and endpoint; closing every state identifies the maximum-profit selective tour.
assumptions_latex: The instance has one depot and \(n\) optional vertices.
Arc costs are defined for every transition allowed in a tour.
A feasible tour visits each selected vertex exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence returns an exact maximum-prize-minus-cost selective tour in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time and \(O(n2^n)\) space.

notation.meaning: minimum depot-to-j path cost visiting exactly subset S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Subset Dynamic Programming, but the recurrence is stated for every nonempty subset, including singletons, where its minimization set is empty and conflicts with the initialization. It must be restricted to |S|>=2. No source supports the recurrence, reconstruction claim, or complexity bound.

children.title: Resource-State Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State-space approaches indexed by route resources plus accumulated reward.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-State Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward labeling for an elementary, resource-constrained profit route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a directed graph have origin \(s\), destination \(t\), vertex profits \(p_i\), arc costs \(c_{ij}\), nonnegative resource consumptions \(a_{ij}\), and capacity \(Q\). A label \(L=(i,S,q,v)\) represents an elementary \(s\)-to-\(i\) path visiting \(S\), consuming \(q\), and attaining profit minus cost \(v\). Initialize \((s,\{s\},0,0)\). For \(j\notin S\), extend to \((j,S\cup\{j\},q+a_{ij},v+p_j-c_{ij})\) whenever \(q+a_{ij}\le Q\). Retain admissible labels, including labels reaching \(t\), and output a terminal label of maximum value; infeasibility is reported if none reaches \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extend elementary path labels while tracking visited vertices, resource use, and net profit; the best feasible label reaching the destination is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(a_{ij}\ge 0\) and \(Q<\infty\).
Each optional vertex may be visited at most once.
Route value is additive over visited vertices and traversed arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum-valued retained label at \(t\) represents an optimal feasible profit route.

notation.meaning: set of vertices already visited by a label

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and terminal content kind fit the resource-state dynamic-programming leaf, but no routing-specific citation with an inspectable locator supports its recurrence and optimality claim.

children.title: Dominance-Based Labeling
children.top_down_role: Labeling frameworks organized around dominance-based state elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance-Based Labeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe label dominance at a common terminal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For labels \(L_1=(i,S_1,q_1,v_1)\) and \(L_2=(i,S_2,q_2,v_2)\) ending at the same vertex, suppose \(S_1\subseteq S_2\), \(q_1\le q_2\), and \(v_1\ge v_2\). If every continuation feasible after \(L_2\) is also feasible after \(L_1\), and continuation value depends only on the current vertex, unavailable vertices, and remaining resources, then \(L_1\) dominates \(L_2\). Consequently, deleting \(L_2\) cannot remove a uniquely optimal complete route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A label can be discarded when another label at the same vertex has no fewer options, no greater resource use, and no smaller value.
assumptions_latex: Both labels terminate at the same vertex \(i\).
Resource feasibility is monotone in remaining capacity.
Future route value is additive and history-independent beyond the recorded state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Label \(L_2\) may be discarded without changing the optimal terminal value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance property is mathematically plausible and appropriately scoped, but its history-independence and safe-deletion claim require a routing-labeling source with a specific locator.

children.title: Bidirectional Labeling
children.top_down_role: Profit-route labeling frameworks using compatible forward plus backward states.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Labeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Meet-in-the-middle labeling for resource-constrained profit routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate forward labels from \(s\) and backward labels from \(t\), each storing its endpoint, visited set, resource consumption, and value. Stop extension on each side at a prescribed resource threshold. Join a forward label \(L^f\) ending at \(i\) to a backward label \(L^b\) beginning at \(j\) across arc \((i,j)\) only if their internal visited sets are disjoint and \(q^f+a_{ij}+q^b\le Q\). The joined value is \(v^f+p_j-c_{ij}+v^b\), with any endpoint contribution counted once. Output the feasible join of maximum value after applying valid dominance independently in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build partial routes from both endpoints and combine compatible label pairs whose visited sets are disjoint and total resource use is feasible.
assumptions_latex: Arc resources are nonnegative.
Forward and backward label values use a consistent endpoint-counting convention.
Every feasible route admits a split covered by the chosen extension thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The best compatible join has the same value as the optimal complete route.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bidirectional-labeling algorithm fits the leaf, but the threshold coverage, joining convention, and exactness conclusion are variant-sensitive and unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Orienteering Bounding Schemes
children.top_down_role: Upper-bound structures used within exact orienteering search.

knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering Bounding Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node upper bounds for maximization branch-and-bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node \(N\), let \(P_N\) be profit already fixed into the partial route and let \(U_N\) be any computable upper bound on additional profit attainable by a feasible completion. Then \(B_N=P_N+U_N\) is a valid node bound provided every feasible completion \(R\) satisfies \(p(R)-P_N\le U_N\). Such an \(U_N\) may come from a relaxation that removes elementarity, connectivity, or integrality constraints while retaining every completion feasible at \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Current profit plus an upper bound on attainable remaining profit certifies an upper bound for every completion of a search node.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a profit-maximization problem.
The relaxation contains every feasible completion consistent with node \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every feasible completion \(R\) at \(N\), \(p(R)\le B_N\).

notation.meaning: profit fixed at search node N
upper bound on additional attainable profit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and upper-bound statement are coherent, but no orienteering or branch-and-bound source is cited for the stated bounding scheme.

children.title: Orienteering Branching Schemes
children.top_down_role: Decision families used to partition orienteering search spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering Branching Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive branching on an undecided visit or arc variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional or unresolved search node, select an unfixed binary decision \(z\), where \(z=y_i\) denotes visiting optional vertex \(i\), or \(z=x_{ij}\) denotes using arc \((i,j)\). Create two children by adding respectively \(z=0\) and \(z=1\), propagate route feasibility restrictions, and solve or bound both children. Continue until every surviving leaf is infeasible, pruned by bound, or has integral route decisions. Because the two child constraints partition the parent feasible set, choosing the best integral leaf preserves global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split on whether an undecided vertex or arc is used; the two children partition the parent solutions and support exact search.
assumptions_latex: The selected decision is binary in every feasible integer route.
Each child inherits all constraints imposed at its parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible integer solutions of the parent equal the disjoint union of those in its two children.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Binary vertex-or-arc branching is a suitable algorithm for this leaf, but its exact-search interpretation lacks an orienteering-specific citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Search-Tree Pruning Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions governing effective or ineffective pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Pruning Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pruning predicates for profit-maximization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be the value of the best feasible incumbent and \(B_N\) a valid upper bound at node \(N\). Node \(N\) may be pruned if its restrictions are infeasible, if \(B_N\le I\), or if its relaxation yields an integral feasible route, after updating \(I\) with that route's value. Dominance pruning is also valid when another active node represents a superset of feasible completions with at least as favorable fixed value and resources. These predicates remove no route capable of improving the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune nodes that are infeasible, cannot beat the incumbent, are already solved integrally, or are safely dominated by another search state.
assumptions_latex: \(B_N\) is a valid upper bound for every completion at \(N\).
The incumbent value \(I\) comes from a feasible route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pruning under any stated predicate cannot eliminate a solution with value greater than \(I\).

notation.meaning: valid upper bound at node N

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard infeasibility, bound, and integrality pruning predicates are coherent, but the additional cross-node dominance predicate is insufficiently formalized and none of the regimes has a cited source.

children.title: Selective-Tour Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Valid-inequality families tailored to optional customer selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective-Tour Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity cuts linking optional selection to tour edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an undirected selective-tour formulation with depot \(r\), edge variables \(x_e\), and optional-vertex variables \(y_i\), every connected tour satisfies \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2y_i\) for every \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\) and every \(i\in S\). Here \(x(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\). Thus, whenever any vertex in \(S\) is selected, at least two tour edges cross the cut separating \(S\) from the depot. Together with degree equations, these inequalities exclude disconnected selected subtours.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a selected vertex lies in a set excluding the depot, at least two used tour edges must cross that set's boundary.
assumptions_latex: The route is an undirected closed tour containing depot \(r\).
Each selected nondepot vertex has tour degree two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible selective tour satisfies \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2y_i\) for all eligible \(S\) and \(i\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selective-tour connectivity inequality is precise and the condition content kind fits, but no selective-tour polyhedral source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Prize-Tour Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Valid-inequality families tailored to prize or penalty tour objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Tour Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-cover inequalities for prize-collecting tour selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be the travel budget and let \(\ell(C)\) be a valid lower bound on the length of any depot tour visiting every vertex in \(C\). If \(\ell(C)>B\), then the selection variables of every budget-feasible prize tour satisfy the cover inequality \(
\sum_{i\in C}y_i\le |C|-1.
\) Any lifting coefficients added to vertices outside \(C\) must preserve validity for every feasible selection. The inequality excludes a set of prizes that cannot all be collected within the route budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When no budget-feasible tour can visit every vertex of a set, at least one vertex in that set must remain unselected.
assumptions_latex:
\(
\ell(C)
\) lower-bounds every depot tour visiting all vertices of \(C\).
Route length may not exceed \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
If \(
\ell(C)>B
\), then \(
\sum_{i\in C}y_i\le |C|-1
\) is valid.

notation.meaning: lower bound on a tour visiting C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The budget-cover implication is mathematically coherent, but its placement as a prize-tour cut family and the lifting statement require a specific supporting source.

children.title: Profit-Tour Separation Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Separation structures shared across selective plus prize-tour formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit-Tour Separation Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of violated connectivity and budget-cover inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a fractional solution \((x^*,y^*)\), first separate selective connectivity cuts: for each optional vertex \(i\), compute a minimum \(r\)-to-\(i\) cut under edge capacities \(x_e^*\); add \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2y_i\) when its capacity is below \(2y_i^*\). Next search for a vertex set \(C\) with \(
\ell(C)>B
\) and \(
\sum_{i\in C}y_i^*>|C|-1
\); any such set yields a violated budget-cover cut. Stop when neither oracle finds a violation, or pass the added cuts to the relaxation solver and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use minimum cuts for connectivity violations and an infeasible-cover oracle for budget violations, repeatedly adding any violated inequalities found.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) and \(y^*\) satisfy the current linear relaxation.

The cover oracle's value \(
\ell(C)
\) is a valid tour-length lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every returned inequality is valid and violated by \((x^*,y^*)\).

notation.meaning: lower bound for visiting cover C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation framework correctly matches the two prerequisite cut forms, but the cover oracle and repeated separation procedure lack a profit-tour-specific citation.

children.title: Team-Orienteering Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing subproblems for multiple cooperating orienteering routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Team-Orienteering Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-profit route subproblem for a team-orienteering set-packing master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_o\) be the optional customers, \(\mathcal R\) the resource-feasible elementary routes, and \(m\) the fleet limit. Consider the maximization master with variables \(\lambda_r\ge 0\), customer constraints \(\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\alpha_{ir}\lambda_r\le 1\) for \(i\in V_o\), and fleet constraint \(\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\lambda_r\le m\). Let their dual variables be \(\pi_i\ge 0\) and \(\sigma\ge 0\). If route \(r\) has original profit \(g_r=\sum_{i\in V_o}p_i\alpha_{ir}-c_r\), its reduced profit is \(\bar p_r=g_r-\sum_{i\in V_o}\pi_i\alpha_{ir}-\sigma=\sum_{i\in V_o}(p_i-\pi_i)\alpha_{ir}-c_r-\sigma\). Pricing maximizes \(\bar p_r\) over \(r\in\mathcal R\); a route is an improving column exactly when \(\bar p_r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximization set-packing master, pricing finds a feasible elementary route maximizing collected profits adjusted by customer dual prices, travel cost, and the fleet dual price; a positive reduced profit identifies an improving column.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master is a maximization set-packing formulation with customer constraints of type \(\le\).
The fleet-cardinality constraint is of type \(\le\).
Pricing is solved over the complete route set \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No improving route column exists exactly when \(\max_{r\in\mathcal R}\bar p_r\le 0\).

notation.meaning: indicator that route r visits optional customer i
dual value of optional customer i's packing constraint
dual value of the fleet-cardinality constraint

children.title: Fleet Profit-Route Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing subproblems for heterogeneous or capacitated profit-routing fleets.

knowledge_statements.title: Fleet Profit-Route Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vehicle-type-specific reduced-profit pricing for heterogeneous fleets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be the set of vehicle types and, for each \(k\in K\), let \(\mathcal R_k\) be the feasible routes of type \(k\). Let \(\pi_i\) be the dual value of customer packing constraint \(i\), and let \(\sigma_k\) be the dual value of the type-\(k\) fleet constraint. For \(r\in\mathcal R_k\), let \(\alpha_{ir}=1\) exactly when route \(r\) serves customer \(i\), let \(p_{ik}\) be the profit from serving \(i\) with type \(k\), and let \(c_{rk}\) be the route cost. The reduced profit is \(\bar z_{rk}=\sum_i(p_{ik}-\pi_i)\alpha_{ir}-c_{rk}-\sigma_k\). Pricing decomposes by vehicle type into problems maximizing \(\bar z_{rk}\) over \(r\in\mathcal R_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each vehicle type, pricing maximizes collected profit adjusted by customer dual prices, route cost, and the dual price of using that vehicle type.
assumptions_latex: The master is a maximization formulation using the displayed reduced-profit sign convention.
Each route belongs to exactly one vehicle type \(k\in K\).
Route feasibility, service profits, and costs may depend on vehicle type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No improving fleet column exists exactly when \(\max_{r\in\mathcal R_k}\bar z_{rk}\le 0\) for every \(k\in K\).

notation.meaning: feasible routes for vehicle type k
dual value of customer i's packing constraint
dual value of the type-k fleet constraint
reduced profit of type-k route r

children.title: Profit-Routing Master Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Master-level stabilization structures for route-column optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit-Routing Master Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal dual stabilization for profit-route column generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(\pi)\) be the restricted-master dual objective on its dual-feasible set \(\Pi\), let \(\bar\pi\in\Pi\) be a stabilization center, and choose \(\mu>0\). At an iteration, compute a stabilized trial vector \(\pi^+\) by maximizing \(D(\pi)-\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert\pi-\bar\pi\rVert_2^2\) over \(\pi\in\Pi\), and price profit routes using \(\pi^+\). Add every selected improving column, update \(\bar\pi\) when the prescribed serious-step test is satisfied, and otherwise retain the center while updating \(\mu\). Terminate only after solving the ordinary restricted master and exact pricing certifies that its resulting dual vector has no improving column in the full route set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal penalty limits movement of the pricing dual vector around a center, while final optimality is certified only by exact pricing at an ordinary restricted-master dual solution.
assumptions_latex: The restricted-master dual objective \(D\) is concave under the adopted maximization convention.
The stabilization center satisfies \(\bar\pi\in\Pi\), and \(\mu>0\).
Final certification uses exact pricing over the full route set at an unstabilized restricted-master optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal term changes the dual search trajectory, while termination retains the ordinary column-generation certificate of no positive-reduced-profit route.

children.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures preserving tractable profit-route pricing.

assumptions_latex: The branch-and-price master has binary route variables \(x_r\) for feasible routes \(r\in\mathcal R\).
Pricing minimizes reduced cost over a route family represented by a resource-constrained path model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The child-node pricing problems remain in the same resource-constrained path class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for branching rules in route-based branch-and-price.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A branching disjunction is pricing-compatible if each child can be enforced by deleting arcs, fixing finitely many arc or service decisions, or augmenting the pricing state by polynomially many resources, while preserving exact reduced-cost minimization. Formally, if the parent pricing domain is \(\mathcal R\), each child domain \(\mathcal R_k\subseteq\mathcal R\) must admit the same resource-constrained path representation with only polynomial growth in encoding size. Ryan–Foster branching on a customer pair is compatible when together/apart requirements can be represented by finite-state resources or equivalent arc restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching rule is pricing-compatible when every child restriction can be imposed in the pricing model with only polynomial growth and without changing its fundamental path-problem structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but no citation supports the asserted polynomial-size pricing representation or the stated compatibility of Ryan–Foster branching. These claims depend on the precise route-pricing formulation.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, edge lengths and prizes are nonnegative integers, and the budget is integral.
A route starts at \(s\), ends at \(t\), and collects each visited vertex prize at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision version of orienteering is NP-complete, and the optimization version is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical discrete orienteering with an explicit length budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\), terminals \(s,t\), edge lengths \(c_e\), vertex prizes \(p_v\), a budget \(B\), and a target \(Q\), decide whether an \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk of length at most \(B\) collects prize at least \(Q\). This problem lies in NP and is NP-hard even when every prize equals one: an instance of Hamiltonian \(s\)-to-\(t\) path reduces by assigning unit edge lengths, setting \(B=|V|-1\), and requiring \(Q=|V|\). Hence its decision form is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orienteering is NP-hard, already with unit prizes and unit edge lengths, because collecting every vertex within n−1 edges encodes a Hamiltonian terminal-to-terminal path.
knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction is mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits the hardness leaf, but NP-completeness and the exact terminal-path variant require an authoritative, inspectable citation.

children.title: Quota-Routing Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness arising from mandatory reward or service thresholds.

assumptions_latex: The quota-routing objective is the minimum length of a depot tour collecting total prize at least \(Q\).
Edge lengths form a finite metric and vertex prizes are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric quota routing is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric single-depot quota routing with additive vertex prizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a metric traveling-salesperson instance on \(V\), assign every vertex prize \(p_v=1\) and set the quota \(Q=|V|\). Every quota-feasible depot tour must then visit every vertex, and every traveling-salesperson tour is quota-feasible with the same length. Thus this transformation preserves feasible solutions and objective values. Since metric traveling salesperson is NP-hard, computing a minimum-length tour whose collected prize is at least \(Q\) is NP-hard, even for unit prizes and quota equal to the number of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quota routing is NP-hard because setting unit prizes and requiring the full prize forces a tour through every vertex, exactly recovering metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.title: Quota-Routing Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-prize, full-quota embedding of metric TSP is plausible and appropriately classified as a complexity bound, but the hardness claim has no supporting source or reduction locator.

children.title: Prize-Collecting Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness arising from prize collection plus omission penalties.

assumptions_latex: The prize-collecting TSP objective is tour length plus penalties for unvisited vertices.
Edge lengths form a finite metric and penalties are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric prize-collecting TSP is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric prize-collecting TSP with additive omission penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\sum_{e}c_e\), and transform a metric traveling-salesperson instance by assigning each nondepot vertex penalty \(\pi_v=C+1\). A tour visiting all vertices has objective at most \(C\), whereas any tour omitting a vertex has objective at least \(C+1\). Consequently every optimal prize-collecting tour visits all vertices, and among such tours it minimizes traveling-salesperson length. The transformation has polynomial encoding length, so exact optimization for metric prize-collecting TSP is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prize-collecting TSP is NP-hard because sufficiently large omission penalties force every optimal solution to visit all vertices, leaving the metric TSP objective unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominating-penalty reduction is plausible and fits the hardness leaf, but the source support required for the metric prize-collecting-TSP formulation and polynomial penalty encoding is absent.

children.title: Quota–Prize Hardness Transfers
children.top_down_role: Complexity transfers between quota-driven plus prize-collecting models.

assumptions_latex: All edge lengths and prizes or penalties are nonnegative integers with polynomial encoding length.
Reductions preserve the same metric and depot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hardness of metric TSP transfers to both quota TSP and prize-collecting TSP through polynomial special-case embeddings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-complexity transfers through full-service parameter choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two polynomial embeddings transfer exact hardness from metric traveling salesperson. For quota TSP, choose positive prizes and set \(Q=P=\sum_{v\in V}p_v\), which forces every positive-prize vertex to be visited. For prize-collecting TSP, choose each omission penalty larger than an explicitly computable upper bound on the cost of a full tour, which forces every vertex to be visited by an optimum. In either embedding, feasible optimal solutions correspond to traveling-salesperson tours and retain their travel cost ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full quota or dominating omission penalties force complete service, embedding metric TSP into quota and prize-collecting routing and transferring exact NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.title: Quota–Prize Hardness Transfers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle matches the transfer leaf and carefully limits itself to exact hardness, but neither special-case embedding is cited. A source must also specify the quota and prize-collecting formulations to which the transfers apply.

children.title: Time-Window Profit-Routing Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness introduced by customer-specific service intervals.

assumptions_latex: Service times and travel times are nonnegative integers.
Each vertex has a time window, and collected prizes are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time-window profit routing is NP-hard, even when all windows are identical and nonbinding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-maximizing routing with service time windows and a route-duration bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take any orienteering instance with route budget \(B\), retain its graph, travel times, terminals, and prizes, set every service time to zero, and assign every vertex the common time window \([0,B]\). A route is time-window feasible exactly when its travel length is at most \(B\), and it collects the same prize as in the original instance. This polynomial, value-preserving embedding shows that maximizing collected profit subject to time windows is NP-hard even when the windows impose no restriction beyond the global route budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time-window profit routing remains NP-hard with identical nonbinding windows, since ordinary orienteering is then recovered exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Window Profit-Routing Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inherited-hardness argument is plausible only for a formulation retaining the global route-duration bound and constraining terminal completion consistently. No source identifies and supports that exact time-window variant.

children.title: Multi-Route Profit-Routing Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness introduced by coordinating several reward-collecting routes.

assumptions_latex: The number of available routes satisfies \(m\ge 1\).
Each route obeys the same feasibility rules, and each customer prize is collected at most once across the fleet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multi-route profit routing is NP-hard for every model class that permits the special case \(m=1\).

notation.meaning: number of available routes or vehicles

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fleet profit routing whose input domain includes a one-vehicle instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Map an orienteering instance to the fleet problem by setting \(m=1\) and retaining all travel data, prizes, terminals, and route budget. The feasible fleet solutions are then precisely the feasible orienteering routes, with identical objective values. Therefore any exact polynomial-time algorithm for the multi-route model would solve orienteering in polynomial time. The multi-route profit-routing optimization problem is consequently NP-hard whenever its admissible parameter domain includes \(m=1\); this argument alone does not classify variants requiring a fixed \(m>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fleet profit-routing model is NP-hard whenever it allows one vehicle, because its one-route restriction is exactly orienteering.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Route Profit-Routing Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-vehicle restriction is a valid-looking hardness inheritance and the record correctly excludes fixed-m variants, but an authoritative source is needed to establish that the target model admits m=1 and coincides with orienteering there.

children.title: Temporal–Fleet Hardness Coupling
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects caused by combining service timing with route multiplicity.

assumptions_latex: The combined model permits identical nonbinding time windows.
Its fleet-size domain includes \(m=1\), or unused vehicles are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding both temporal and fleet structure does not remove the inherited NP-hardness of single-route orienteering.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inheritance of hardness in models combining time windows and multiple vehicles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an orienteering instance with budget \(B\), assign every customer the window \([0,B]\) and set \(m=1\); equivalently, when unused vehicles are permitted, set any allowed \(m\) and leave \(m-1\) routes empty. The resulting temporal-fleet instance has a feasible solution of profit at least \(Q\) exactly when the original instance does. Hence the combined model inherits NP-hardness through simultaneous parameter restriction. This embedding does not establish stronger hardness caused specifically by interacting tight windows and multiple mandatory routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal fleet model inherits orienteering hardness when common wide windows and one used vehicle are allowed; this does not prove interaction-specific hardness.
knowledge_statements.title: Temporal–Fleet Hardness Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement appropriately disclaims interaction-specific hardness, but its inheritance claim depends on the combined model allowing one used vehicle, empty routes, and nonbinding windows. No cited source fixes those conventions.

assumptions_latex: An instance \(I\) is a finite metric orienteering instance with nonnegative prizes.
The algorithm returns a route satisfying the prescribed terminals and length budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(\alpha\)-approximation returns profit at least \(\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance, in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: optimal collectible prize for instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee convention for metric orienteering variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a specified orienteering variant, a polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximation, under the maximization convention, if for every admissible instance \(I\), the route \(A(I)\) is feasible for the same terminals and budget and satisfies \(p(A(I))\ge \alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Approximation results belong to different regimes according to whether the metric is general, directed, Euclidean, or induced by a tree, and whether endpoints, time windows, or multiple routes are prescribed; guarantees cannot be transferred between these regimes without an explicit reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orienteering approximation must return a budget-feasible route earning a fixed fraction of optimum; guarantees are variant-specific and require explicit reductions between regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Orienteering Approximation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a standard maximization-approximation definition, but condition is not the best role for this definitional statement, and the approximation-family leaf is not populated with any sourced regime-specific result or landmark.

assumptions_latex: The instance is a finite metric with nonnegative omission penalties.
The objective is tour length plus penalties of unvisited vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(\rho\)-approximation has objective at most \(\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every admissible instance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation convention for metric prize-collecting TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an instance \(I\), define \(F_I(T)=c(T)+\sum_{v
otin V(T)}\pi_v\), where \(T\) is a depot tour and \(\pi_v\) is the penalty for omitting \(v\). A polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) is a \(ho\)-approximation if \(F_I(A(I))\le ho\min_T F_I(T)\) for every admissible \(I\). This guarantee is multiplicative for the combined travel-and-penalty objective; it does not separately bound tour length or omitted penalty, and it does not automatically yield the same factor for quota orienteering formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prize-collecting-TSP approximation bounds the combined travel cost and omitted penalties multiplicatively; it need not separately approximate either component.
knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting-TSP Approximation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The combined-objective ratio convention is coherent, but it is a definition rather than a condition and supplies no sourced prize-collecting-TSP approximation result for this family leaf.

children.title: Quota-TSP Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation landmarks for tours subject to reward quotas.

assumptions_latex: The instance is a finite metric with nonnegative prizes and quota \(Q\).
A feasible tour must collect total prize at least \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(\rho\)-approximation returns a quota-feasible tour of length at most \(\rho\operatorname{OPT}_Q(I)\).

notation.meaning: minimum length of a tour meeting quota Q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation convention for metric quota TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible quota-TSP instance \(I\), a polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) is a \(\rho\)-approximation if its output tour satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V(A(I))}p_v\ge Q\) and \(c(A(I))\le ho\operatorname{OPT}_Q(I)\). The approximation factor concerns travel length while quota feasibility is exact. Separate regimes arise for unit versus weighted prizes, rooted versus unrooted tours, and general versus structured metrics. A bicriteria algorithm that collects less than \(Q\) is not a \(\rho\)-approximation under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quota-TSP approximation must meet the quota exactly and bound travel length relative to the shortest quota-feasible tour; quota violation is bicriteria, not ordinary approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Quota-TSP Approximation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordinary quota-TSP approximation convention is precise, but it is definitional rather than a condition and does not identify any authoritative approximation ratio or specifically sourced regime.

children.title: Selective-TSP Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation landmarks for tours over optional vertex subsets.

assumptions_latex: The instance is a finite metric with nonnegative vertex prizes.
A feasible solution is a tour satisfying the variant’s budget, cardinality, or service constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approximation ratios are defined against the optimum of the same selective-tour formulation and constraint regime.

notation.meaning: objective value of a selective tour T
optimal value under the same constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variant-sensitive approximation convention for selective traveling-salesperson problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a selective-TSP formulation before assigning an approximation factor. For a maximization formulation, a polynomial-time algorithm is an \(\alpha\)-approximation if its feasible tour \(T\) satisfies \(f_I(T)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), where \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). For a length-minimization formulation with a mandatory selection requirement, it is a \(ho\)-approximation if the requirement is met and \(c(T)\leho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), where \(ho\ge1\). These conventions are not interchangeable; the selection constraint and objective direction must remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selective-TSP approximation depends on the precise variant: profit maximization and length minimization use different ratio directions and must preserve the same selection constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Selective-TSP Approximation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly warns that maximization and minimization conventions differ, but it blends multiple unnamed selective-TSP formulations. The exact variant, mathematical role, and regime-specific approximation claims require sources before a reliable replacement can be formed.

children.title: Quota–Selection Approximation Transfers
children.top_down_role: Approximation-preserving relations between quota plus selective formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota–Selection Approximation Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bicriteria transfer from quota-TSP approximation to budgeted prize selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let rewards be nonnegative integers and define \(\operatorname{OPT}_Q=\min\{c(T):p(T)\ge Q\}\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_B=\max\{p(T):c(T)\le B\}\), where \(T\) ranges over depot-rooted tours. Suppose an algorithm returns \(T_Q\) satisfying \(p(T_Q)\ge Q\) and \(c(T_Q)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_Q\). For a budget \(B\), run it for every attainable integer quota and choose the largest \(Q\) with \(c(T_Q)\le\alpha B\). Because \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\operatorname{OPT}_B}\le B\), the selected tour has reward at least \(\operatorname{OPT}_B\) and cost at most \(\alpha B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-approximation for quota TSP yields a tour attaining optimal budgeted reward while violating the travel budget by at most alpha.
assumptions_latex: Rewards are nonnegative integers with polynomially enumerable total reward.
Tours use the same depot, cost function, and reward convention in both formulations.
The quota algorithm is an \(\alpha\)-approximation for every attainable quota.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction is a \((1,\alpha)\)-bicriteria approximation for budgeted prize selection.

notation.meaning: total reward collected by tour T

review_flags: The polynomial enumeration assumption excludes unrestricted binary-encoded rewards.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bicriteria transfer is mathematically plausible under polynomial enumeration of integer quotas, but no inspectable citation supports the exact transfer or its encoding assumptions.

children.title: Geometric Profit-Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation behavior under Euclidean, planar, or bounded-dimensional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Profit-Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean optional-service routing in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric profit-routing instance consists of a depot \(r\in\mathbb{R}^d\), finitely many customer points \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\), rewards \(p_v\ge0\), and optionally a length budget \(B\ge0\). Travel cost is Euclidean distance \(c(u,v)=\lVert u-v\rVert_2\). A feasible solution is a closed polygonal tour beginning and ending at \(r\), and its collected reward is the sum of rewards of distinct visited customers. The budgeted regime maximizes collected reward subject to tour length at most \(B\); the quota regime minimizes tour length subject to collected reward at least a prescribed \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Customers are Euclidean points, and a depot tour either maximizes reward under a length budget or minimizes length while meeting a quota.
assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\) is fixed when a fixed-dimensional geometric regime is claimed.
Customer rewards are nonnegative.
A customer reward is counted at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is a Euclidean specialization of budgeted or quota prize routing.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard Euclidean budgeted-orienteering and quota-routing formulation.
Source locator needed for terminology alignment.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the geometric profit-routing container and is internally consistent, but it has no citation or specific locator establishing the terminology and formulation.

children.title: Time-Window Profit-Routing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation behavior under service-window restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Window Profit-Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optional-service routing with customer availability intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-window profit-routing instance has a depot \(r\), customers \(V\), nonnegative rewards \(p_v\), service durations \(s_v\), time windows \([a_v,b_v]\), and nonnegative travel times \(\tau(u,v)\). For a served sequence \(r,v_1,\ldots,v_k,r\), let \(t_i\) be the service-start time at \(v_i\). Temporal feasibility requires \(a_{v_i}\le t_i\le b_{v_i}\) and \(t_{i+1}\ge t_i+s_{v_i}+\tau(v_i,v_{i+1})\) for every consecutive pair; the inequality permits waiting after an early arrival. If a horizon \(H\) is imposed, the return must satisfy \(t_k+s_{v_k}+\tau(v_k,r)\le H\). The objective is to maximize \(\sum_{i=1}^k p_{v_i}\), with each served customer appearing at most once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A route selects customers, starts each service within its time window, respects travel and service times, returns by any imposed horizon, and maximizes collected reward.
assumptions_latex: Travel times \(\tau(u,v)\) are nonnegative.
Waiting is permitted.
Each customer is served at most once and contributes its reward once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility depends jointly on the selected customers, their order, and their service-start schedule.

notation.meaning: service-start time at the ith served customer
travel time from u to v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Service-start variables avoid conflating early arrival with service-window compliance.
An authoritative formulation with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Geometric–Temporal Interaction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits arising when geometric structure is combined with service timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric–Temporal Interaction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why geometric insertion cost alone cannot characterize time-window feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In Euclidean profit routing with time windows, the geometric insertion increment \(\Delta(u,v,w)=\lVert u-v\rVert_2+\lVert v-w\rVert_2-\lVert u-w\rVert_2\) does not determine whether inserting \(v\) between consecutive visits \(u,w\) is temporally feasible. Feasibility also requires an arrival time \(t_v\in[a_v,b_v]\) and sufficient downstream slack so that every later visit remains within its window. Consequently, two insertions having the same value of \(\Delta\) can differ in feasibility because their release times, deadlines, service durations, or downstream slack differ. A purely geometric approximation argument therefore does not automatically transfer to the time-window regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal geometric insertion costs can have different time-window feasibility, so spatial approximation guarantees do not transfer without temporal slack control.
assumptions_latex: Travel time equals Euclidean distance.
Waiting is allowed but deadlines cannot be violated.
The route contains at least one temporally constrained downstream visit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Geometric insertion cost alone is not a certificate of temporal feasibility.

notation.meaning: extra Euclidean length caused by inserting v between u and w
time window of inserted customer v

children.title: Nearest-Neighbor Tour Construction

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Neighbor Tour Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The classical nearest-unvisited-vertex TSP construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a complete weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), a start vertex \(r\in V\), and edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). Initialize \(v_0=r\), \(U=V\setminus\{r\}\), and the walk \(T=(r)\). While \(U\ne\varnothing\), choose \(v_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in U}c(v_k,u)\), append \(v_{k+1}\) to \(T\), remove it from \(U\), and increment \(k\). After all vertices have been selected, append \(r\). The output is the Hamiltonian cycle \((v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|-1},v_0)\); a fixed rule resolves ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at a chosen vertex, repeatedly visit the nearest unvisited vertex and finally return to the start.
assumptions_latex: The input graph is complete.
All edge costs are finite and nonnegative.
A deterministic tie-breaking rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a Hamiltonian cycle through every vertex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the conventional nearest-neighbor TSP heuristic.
Source locator needed for final certification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-neighbor TSP construction and its worst-case bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the construction rule, its metric upper and lower bounds, and failure without metric assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from any vertex, repeatedly visit a nearest unvisited vertex and return to the starting vertex after all other vertices have been visited. For an \(n\)-vertex TSP with nonnegative costs satisfying \(c_{uv}+c_{vw}\ge c_{uw}\) for all \(u,v,w\in V\), the resulting tour has cost at most \(\left(\tfrac12\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+\tfrac12\right)\operatorname{OPT}\). There are such metric instances with arbitrarily many vertices on which the algorithm can return a tour costing \(\tfrac13\left\lceil\log_2(n+1)+\tfrac49\right\rceil\operatorname{OPT}\). Without these metric assumptions, even four-vertex instances can yield an arbitrarily large approximation ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearest neighbor repeatedly visits a nearest unvisited vertex and finally returns to its start. Under nonnegative metric costs it has the stated logarithmic upper bound, and metric families give the stated logarithmic lower bound. Without the metric assumptions, its ratio can be arbitrarily large even on four vertices.
assumptions_latex: |V|=n
c_{uv}\ge 0\quad\text{for all edges}
c_{uv}+c_{vw}\ge c_{uw}\quad\text{for all }u,v,w\in V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\mathrm{NN})\le\left(\frac12\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+\frac12\right)\operatorname{OPT}

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Edge Tour Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cheapest-link or multifragment greedy TSP construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a complete weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative edge costs. Sort edges by nondecreasing cost and initialize \(F=\varnothing\). Scan edges in that order. Add an edge \(e\) to \(F\) exactly when every endpoint would retain degree at most two and, unless the addition would produce the final Hamiltonian cycle, \(F\cup\{e\}\) contains no cycle. Stop when \(|F|=|V|\). The degree and premature-cycle tests then make \(F\) a single spanning cycle. Ties in the edge ordering are resolved by a fixed deterministic rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add the cheapest admissible edge while forbidding degree above two and every cycle except the final spanning cycle.
assumptions_latex: The graph is complete.
Edge costs are finite and nonnegative.
A deterministic ordering resolves equal-cost edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected edge set \(F\) is a Hamiltonian cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Construction Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case limitations of locally cheapest TSP constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Metricity alone does not give nearest-neighbor construction a constant approximation factor. There exists a sequence of finite metric TSP instances with \(n\) vertices and designated starting vertices for which the nearest-neighbor tour \(T_{NN}\) satisfies \(c(T_{NN})/c(T^*)=\Omega(\log n)\), where \(T^*\) is an optimal tour. Thus choosing the locally shortest available continuation can accumulate globally expensive connections despite the triangle inequality. Analogous local edge-selection heuristics require separate analysis: admissibility by degree and subtour tests does not imply either an MST lower-bound comparison or a matching-based constant-factor certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triangle inequality does not prevent greedy local choices from accumulating logarithmically worse cost, and local admissibility alone supplies no constant-factor certificate.
assumptions_latex: Instances are finite metric complete graphs.
Nearest-neighbor uses a designated start and fixed tie-breaking.
Approximation ratio is measured against an optimal Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nearest-neighbor metric TSP has worst-case approximation ratio at least \(\Omega(\log n)\).
review_flags: A precise lower-bound construction and theorem locator are required.
The final sentence distinguishes absence of a certificate from an impossibility result.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic nearest-neighbor lower bound is a nontrivial theorem requiring a precise construction or theorem locator. The statement properly avoids claiming an analogous impossibility result for cheapest-link construction.

knowledge_statements.title: TSP Insertion Heuristics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parameterized family of tour constructions that repeatedly inserts an unvisited vertex into a current cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a complete weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|\ge3\), finite nonnegative costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and a simple seed cycle \(C\) whose vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies \(|S|\ge3\). At each iteration choose an unvisited vertex \(v\in V\setminus S\) according to the specified insertion variant, choose an edge \((i,j)\) of \(C\), and replace \((i,j)\) by \((i,v)\) and \((v,j)\). Cheapest insertion jointly chooses \((v,(i,j))\) minimizing \(\Delta(v;i,j)=c(i,v)+c(v,j)-c(i,j)\); nearest-, farthest-, and regret-insertion use different vertex-selection criteria while choosing a feasible insertion position. Add \(v\) to \(S\) and repeat until \(S=V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertion heuristics start from a valid seed cycle and repeatedly insert an unvisited vertex; cheapest insertion minimizes the added cost over all vertex-position pairs.
assumptions_latex: The graph is complete and has at least three vertices.
The seed is a simple cycle on at least three vertices.
Ties are resolved by a fixed rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration preserves a simple cycle, and the final cycle visits every vertex exactly once.

notation.meaning: vertices currently contained in the cycle
cost increment from inserting v between i and j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: A simple seed cycle requires at least three vertices in the ordinary undirected TSP convention.
A source with a specific algorithm locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subset\mathbb{R}^2 contain n points. For every order in which the points are processed, inserting each point at a current-tour edge of minimum cost increase produces a tour C satisfying |C|\leq(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+1)|\operatorname{TSP}(S)|.

|S|=n
\text{each processed point is inserted at a minimum-increase tour edge}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\text{ insertion orders},\quad |C|\leq(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+1)|\operatorname{TSP}(S)|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TSP insertion heuristics and metric approximation bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the insertion framework and the farthest, nearest, and cheapest selection rules together with the stated worst-case guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An insertion heuristic begins with a tour through two vertices and inserts each remaining vertex at a position that minimizes the resulting increase in tour cost. Farthest insertion next selects an uninserted vertex maximizing its minimum cost to a vertex of the current tour; nearest insertion minimizes that quantity; cheapest insertion selects the vertex whose best insertion causes the least tour-cost increase. For an \(n\)-vertex TSP with nonnegative costs satisfying the triangle inequality, any such insertion heuristic has cost at most \((\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+1)\operatorname{OPT}\). Nearest insertion and cheapest insertion each have cost at most \(2\operatorname{OPT}\), and this factor is essentially tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertion heuristics maintain a tour and insert remaining vertices at minimum-cost positions. Farthest, nearest, and cheapest insertion use different rules to select the next vertex. On nonnegative metric TSP instances, the family has the stated logarithmic bound; nearest and cheapest insertion have an essentially tight factor-two bound.
assumptions_latex: |V|=n
c_e\ge 0\quad\text{for all edges }e
c_{uv}+c_{vw}\ge c_{uw}\quad\text{for all }u,v,w\in V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\mathrm{insertion})\le(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+1)\operatorname{OPT},\qquad c(\mathrm{nearest}),c(\mathrm{cheapest})\le2\operatorname{OPT}

children.title: Savings-Based Tour Construction
children.top_down_role: Tour construction organized by route-merging savings.

knowledge_statements.title: Savings-Based Tour Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unconstrained parallel savings construction of a single depot-rooted TSP tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a depot \(r\), a finite customer set \(V\), and finite symmetric nonnegative costs \(c\), initialize one route \((r,i,r)\) for each \(i\in V\). For every unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\subseteq V\), compute \(s_{ij}=c(r,i)+c(r,j)-c(i,j)\), and process the pairs in nonincreasing order of \(s_{ij}\). When \(i\) and \(j\) belong to distinct routes and are both nondepot endpoints, orient those routes and merge them using edge \((i,j)\). Continue until one route contains every customer, processing remaining endpoint pairs if necessary. The resulting depot-rooted route is a Hamiltonian cycle on \(V\cup\{r\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with one depot trip per customer and merge distinct routes at their customer endpoints in decreasing order of savings until one tour remains.
assumptions_latex: Costs are finite, symmetric, and nonnegative.
Each customer initially belongs to exactly one route.
Equal savings are resolved by a fixed ordering, and no capacity or duration constraint is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction outputs one depot-rooted Hamiltonian cycle containing every customer.

notation.meaning: saving associated with joining customer endpoints i and j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The unconstrained TSP specialization continues endpoint merges until one tour remains.
A specific source locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Tour Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The doubled-MST construction and its guarantee for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a complete undirected metric graph \(G=(V,E,c)\), compute a minimum spanning tree \(M\), duplicate every edge of \(M\), compute an Euler tour of the resulting connected Eulerian multigraph, and shortcut repeated vertices in first-visit order. The output is a Hamiltonian cycle \(T\), and the triangle inequality gives \(c(T)\le 2c(M)\le 2c(T^*)\), where \(T^*\) is an optimal Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double an MST, traverse the Eulerian multigraph, and shortcut repeated vertices to obtain a tour costing at most twice optimum.
assumptions_latex: The graph is complete and undirected.
Costs are nonnegative and satisfy the triangle inequality.
A minimum spanning tree and an Euler tour are computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output tour \(T\) satisfies \(c(T)\le2c(T^*)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The doubled-MST construction and factor-two guarantee are classical.
An authoritative theorem or algorithm locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree construction and approximation guarantee for metric TSP.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a minimum spanning tree, double its edges, traverse the resulting Eulerian multigraph, and shortcut repeated cities. The triangle inequality ensures that shortcutting does not increase cost, yielding a tour costing at most twice optimum.
assumptions_latex: The instance is a metric traveling-salesman instance.
$\operatorname{OPT}$ is the cost of an optimal tour.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\text{output tour})\le 2\operatorname{OPT}.
