knowledge_statements.statement_title: Christofides's Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree, parity-correction, Euler-tour, and shortcutting construction for an undirected metric traveling-salesperson instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a complete undirected graph \(G\) with metric edge weights: (1) find a minimum-weight spanning tree \(S\); (2) let \(T=\{v\in V(G):|\delta_G(v)\cap S|\text{ is odd}\}\); (3) find a minimum-weight perfect matching \(F\) on the vertices in \(T\); (4) form the Eulerian multigraph with multiset of edges \(S\uplus F\) and find an Eulerian tour; (5) shortcut repeated vertices to obtain a Hamiltonian tour of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Christofides's heuristic finds a minimum spanning tree, adds a minimum-weight perfect matching on its odd-degree vertices, takes an Eulerian tour of the resulting multigraph, and shortcuts repeated vertices to produce a Hamiltonian tour.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a complete undirected graph with metric edge weights}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a Hamiltonian tour of }G

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Augmented Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Christofides' MST-plus-matching construction for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a complete undirected metric graph \(G=(V,E,c)\), compute a minimum spanning tree \(M\), let \(O\subseteq V\) be the set of odd-degree vertices of \(M\), and compute a minimum-cost perfect matching \(J\) on \(O\). Compute an Euler tour of the connected Eulerian multigraph \(M\cup J\), then shortcut repeated vertices to obtain a Hamiltonian cycle \(T\). For an optimal Hamiltonian cycle \(T^*\), the construction satisfies \(c(T)\le\tfrac{3}{2}c(T^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment an MST's odd-degree vertices with a minimum-cost perfect matching, take an Euler tour, and shortcut it to obtain a three-halves approximation.
assumptions_latex: The graph is complete and undirected.
Costs are nonnegative and satisfy the triangle inequality.
A minimum-cost perfect matching on \(O\) is computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed tour satisfies \(c(T)\le\tfrac{3}{2}c(T^*)\).

notation.meaning: set of odd-degree vertices of the tree

children.title: Spanning-Structure Quality Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Structure Quality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The distinction between doubled-tree accounting and matching-augmented guarantees for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric metric TSP, the standard doubled-tree certificate combines \(c(M)\le c(T^*)\) with \(c(T)\le2c(M)\), yielding \(c(T)\le2c(T^*)\). These two inequalities alone cannot certify a factor below two. In the unit-cost complete metric on \(n\) vertices, \(c(M)=n-1\), the duplicated-tree Eulerian walk has cost \(2n-2\), and an optimal tour has cost \(n\); thus the walk-level accounting ratio approaches two, even though shortcutting can produce an optimal tour on that instance. Augmenting the odd-degree vertices of \(M\) with a minimum-cost perfect matching yields the stronger Christofides certificate \(c(T)\le\tfrac{3}{2}c(T^*)\) under symmetry and the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree doubling certifies factor two, and the unit metric makes that walk-level accounting approach two without proving a tight output ratio; odd-vertex matching gives the stronger three-halves certificate in symmetric metric TSP.
assumptions_latex: The TSP instance is complete, undirected, and metric.
The spanning tree \(M\) is minimum.
The matching augmentation uses a minimum-cost perfect matching on the odd-degree vertices of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The doubled-tree accounting certifies factor \(2\), whereas matching augmentation certifies factor \(\tfrac{3}{2}\) in the symmetric metric setting.

notation.meaning: number of vertices in the unit-metric example

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The unit metric demonstrates the limitation of the doubled-walk accounting, not tightness of the shortcut tour's approximation ratio.
Authoritative source locators for both approximation certificates are required.

children.title: 2-Opt Neighborhoods

knowledge_statements.title: 2-Opt Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric TSP edge-exchange neighborhood on Hamiltonian cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be an undirected Hamiltonian cycle on vertex set \(V\). For two nonadjacent tour edges \(\{a,b\}\) and \(\{c,d\}\), deleting them produces two paths. The unique alternative reconnection forming a Hamiltonian cycle inserts \(\{a,c\}\) and \(\{b,d\}\), up to relabeling, and reverses one path. The 2-opt neighborhood is
\[
N_2(T)=\{T-\{\{a,b\},\{c,d\}\}+\{\{a,c\},\{b,d\}\}:\text{the result is a Hamiltonian cycle distinct from }T\}.
\]
For edge costs \(c_e\), the move is improving exactly when \(c_{ab}+c_{cd}>c_{ac}+c_{bd}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-opt move deletes two nonadjacent tour edges and reconnects the resulting paths in the other feasible way. It improves the tour precisely when the inserted edges cost less.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is an undirected Hamiltonian cycle.
Edge costs \(c_e\) are additive over tour edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_2(T)\) consists exactly of feasible two-edge reconnections distinct from \(T\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the 2-opt definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and additive-cost improvement test are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the stated 2-opt convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: 2-Opt Tour Improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-edge-exchange local improvement for an existing TSP tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from any tour C on S, repeatedly remove two tour edges and reconnect their endpoints using the alternative pairing that remains a single tour and has strictly smaller total length. Each accepted move reverses a contiguous subsequence of C. Halt when no admissible improving exchange exists; the output is then 2-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The 2-Opt heuristic repeatedly replaces two tour edges by a shorter reconnection that still forms one tour. Each move reverses a contiguous tour segment, and the method stops when no improving two-edge exchange exists.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a tour on }S
\text{only reconnections forming one tour are admissible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{on termination, no admissible two-edge exchange strictly decreases }|C|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: 2-opt tour improvement and its k-opt extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the 2-opt procedure and 2-optimality, distinguishes quadratic verification from potentially exponential convergence, and records the k-opt extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a tour \(T\), 2-opt considers each pair of nonadjacent tour edges, deletes them, and reconnects the resulting two paths in the other way to form a tour \(T'\). If \(c(T')<c(T)\), replace \(T\) by \(T'\) and repeat. Terminate when no pair yields an improvement; the resulting tour is 2-optimal. Checking all pairs, with each cost change evaluated in constant time, tests 2-optimality in \(O(|V|^2)\) time. This does not imply polynomial-time convergence: some choices of improving interchanges can produce an exponential-length sequence. More generally, \(k\)-opt removes \(k\), or at most \(k\), tour edges and tests reconnections of the resulting paths; the number of edge subsets grows exponentially with \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: 2-opt repeatedly replaces two nonadjacent tour edges when the alternative reconnection lowers cost and stops when no improving two-edge exchange exists. Verifying 2-optimality takes quadratic time, but reaching it can require exponentially many exchanges under unfortunate choices. The k-opt extension examines removals of k, or at most k, edges.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a tour on vertex set }V
\text{the cost change of a fixed 2-interchange is evaluable in }O(1)\text{ time}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}(\text{check 2-optimality})=O(|V|^2),\qquad \text{an improving sequence may contain exponentially many interchanges}

knowledge_statements.title: 3-Opt Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact three-edge exchange neighborhood for a symmetric TSP tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be an undirected Hamiltonian cycle. Choose three distinct tour edges whose deletion yields three vertex-disjoint paths. An exact 3-opt move reconnects the six path endpoints with three edges so that the result \(T'\) is a Hamiltonian cycle and none of the deleted edges is reinserted. Define
\[
N_3(T)=\{T':|T\setminus T'|=|T'\setminus T|=3\}.
\]
If \(D=T\setminus T'\) and \(A=T'\setminus T\), then the move is improving for additive edge costs precisely when \(\sum_{e\in D}c_e>\sum_{e\in A}c_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact 3-opt move replaces three tour edges by three different edges that reconnect the resulting paths into one tour. Improvement is determined by deleted cost minus inserted cost.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is an undirected Hamiltonian cycle.
The objective is the sum of edge costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_3(T)=\{T':|T\setminus T'|=|T'\setminus T|=3\}\).
review_flags: Exact versus inclusive 3-opt conventions require an authoritative routing source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative source is required to establish the exact rather than inclusive 3-opt convention. The prose also assumes six path endpoints, whereas adjacent deleted tour edges can produce coincident endpoints unless pairwise nonadjacency is required.

children.title: Exchange-Size Quality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Search-quality plus computational distinctions across exchange sizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Size Quality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical distinction between bounded-exchange local optimality and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a tour \(T\), let \(N_{\le k}(T)=\bigcup_{r=2}^{k}N_r(T)\), where \(N_r(T)\) contains tours obtained by replacing exactly \(r\) tour edges. If \(k\leq \ell\), then \(N_{\le k}(T)\subseteq N_{\le \ell}(T)\); hence local optimality for \(N_{\le \ell}(T)\) implies local optimality for \(N_{\le k}(T)\). Moreover,
\[
f(T)\leq f(T')\quad\text{for every tour }T'
\]
holds exactly when no improving exchange of any feasible size exists. Thus optimality under a fixed bounded exchange size excludes only the moves represented in that neighborhood and is not, by itself, a global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger exchange neighborhoods impose stronger local-optimality conditions. Only the neighborhood covering every alternative tour characterizes global optimality; fixed-size local optimality alone does not.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set consists of Hamiltonian cycles on a fixed finite vertex set.
\(N_r(T)\) uses exact edge-set difference size \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\le k}(T)\subseteq N_{\le \ell}(T)\) for \(k\leq\ell\), while bounded-size local optimality need not certify global optimality.

notation.meaning: union of exchange neighborhoods through size k

review_flags: No supplied locator supports exchange-neighborhood quality boundaries.
Quantitative approximation claims intentionally omitted pending a source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood-inclusion argument fits this property leaf, but the global-optimality inequality implicitly assumes minimization and no cited locator supports the exchange-size boundary claim.

children.title: Or-Opt Segment Relocation
children.top_down_role: Neighborhoods relocating short contiguous tour segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Or-Opt Segment Relocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation-preserving relocation of a contiguous tour segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write a directed cyclic tour as \(T=(v_1,\ldots,v_n,v_1)\). Choose a contiguous segment \(P=(v_i,\ldots,v_{i+\ell-1})\) with \(1\leq\ell\leq n-2\), delete the arcs entering and leaving \(P\), and join its former predecessor directly to its former successor. An Or-opt move inserts the intact, orientation-preserved segment \(P\) between two consecutive vertices of the residual tour. Its neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{Or},L}(T)\) contains every feasible resulting tour with \(1\leq\ell\leq L\); the insertion position must not reproduce \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Or-opt removes a contiguous block of at most L vertices and reinserts that block elsewhere without changing its internal order.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a cyclic directed ordering of \(n\) distinct vertices.
The relocated segment remains contiguous and preserves orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{Or},L}(T)\) is the set of distinct feasible tours obtained by relocating one orientation-preserved segment of length at most \(L\).

notation.meaning: number of vertices in the segment
Or-opt neighborhood with maximum segment length L

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the Or-opt convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The segment-relocation definition fits the leaf, but Or-opt is often defined with a particular permitted set of short segment lengths. No source establishes the record's generalized maximum-length convention.

children.title: Single-Node Relocation
children.top_down_role: Neighborhoods moving one vertex to another tour position.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Node Relocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relocation neighborhood obtained by moving exactly one tour vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) contain consecutive arcs \((a,v)\), \((v,b)\), and \((p,q)\), with \(v\notin\{p,q\}\) and the chosen insertion not reproducing \(T\). A single-node relocation deletes \((a,v),(v,b),(p,q)\) and inserts \((a,b),(p,v),(v,q)\), provided the result is a Hamiltonian cycle. Its cost change is
\[
\Delta=c_{ab}+c_{pv}+c_{vq}-c_{av}-c_{vb}-c_{pq}.
\]
The relocation is improving for minimization exactly when \(\Delta<0\), and its neighborhood equals the length-one Or-opt neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-node relocation removes one vertex, closes its former gap, and inserts it into another tour edge. The move improves the tour when its explicit cost change is negative.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a directed Hamiltonian cycle.
Tour cost is additive over arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{reloc},1}(T)=N_{\mathrm{Or},1}(T)\), and improvement is equivalent to \(\Delta<0\).

notation.meaning: new tour cost minus old tour cost
cost of arc from i to j

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the relocation formula.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The move and cost expression are standard in the nonoverlapping case, but the stated endpoint restrictions do not explicitly exclude every overlap between the removed gap and insertion arc. A sourced convention is needed.

children.title: Relocation-Length Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search breadth plus computational effects of permitted relocation length.

knowledge_statements.title: Relocation-Length Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested relocation neighborhoods indexed by maximum segment length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(1\leq L	extless n-1\), define \(R_L(T)\) as the tours obtained by relocating one contiguous, orientation-preserved segment of length at most \(L\). Then
\[
R_1(T)\subseteq R_2(T)\subseteq\cdots\subseteq R_{n-2}(T).
\]
Consequently, if \(T\) is locally optimal for \(R_{L+1}(T)\), it is locally optimal for \(R_L(T)\). The exact-length layer is \(R_L(T)\setminus R_{L-1}(T)\), subject to coincidences caused by cyclic symmetry. Restricting \(L\) reduces the move family but can exclude improving relocations requiring longer contiguous segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing longer relocated segments produces nested neighborhoods and stronger local-optimality tests. A length cap may omit improvements that move a longer block.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a Hamiltonian cycle on \(n\) vertices.
Relocations preserve the segment's internal orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_L(T)\subseteq R_{L+1}(T)\) for every \(1\leq L<n-2\).

notation.meaning: relocation neighborhood with segment length at most L

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports relocation-length regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nested at-most-length neighborhoods are plausible, but the set difference need not equal all outcomes generated by exact-length moves because the same tour can admit representations at different lengths. The boundary convention needs sourcing and clarification.

children.title: Variable-Depth Exchange
children.top_down_role: Exchange neighborhoods whose move depth varies during search.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Depth Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential tour exchange whose number of exchanged edges is selected during search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a Hamiltonian cycle \(T\), a variable-depth exchange constructs ordered edge sequences \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\subseteq T\) and \(Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_r)\), with \(Y\cap T=\varnothing\), sequentially. Partial choices may form paths rather than tours, but the terminal edge set
\[
T'=(T\setminus X)\cup Y
\]
must be a Hamiltonian cycle. The depth \(r\) is not fixed before the search; extension, backtracking, and closure rules determine it. For additive edge costs, a completed exchange improves \(T\) exactly when \(G_r=\sum_{i=1}^{r}(c(x_i)-c(y_i))>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-depth exchange builds alternating deleted and inserted edges, choosing the exchange depth adaptively. Intermediate structures may be paths, but a completed result must be a tour, and it is improving exactly when its total gain is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a Hamiltonian cycle.
Deleted and inserted edges are selected sequentially.
The objective is additive over edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A completed exchange forms a Hamiltonian cycle, and it improves \(T\) exactly when \(G_r>0\).

notation.meaning: ordered sequences of deleted and inserted edges
total cost reduction of the exchange

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses variable-depth TSP exchange.

children.title: Lin–Kernighan Search
children.top_down_role: Adaptive sequential-exchange search in the Lin–Kernighan family.

knowledge_statements.title: Lin–Kernighan Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sequential-exchange form of the Lin–Kernighan improvement heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a Hamiltonian cycle \(T\). Choose a tour edge \(x_1\) to delete and alternately choose an admissible inserted edge \(y_i\) and a tour edge \(x_{i+1}\) incident to the newly reached vertex. Maintain partial gain \(G_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i}(c(x_j)-c(y_j))\), feasibility of eventual closure, and a best closing edge that converts the alternating sequence into a Hamiltonian cycle. Extend or backtrack according to the fixed candidate and gain rules. If a closure yields gain \(G>0\), replace \(T\) by the improved tour and restart. Terminate when every permitted starting edge and continuation has been exhausted without an improving closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lin–Kernighan search adaptively builds and backtracks through alternating edge exchanges, accepts a feasible positive-gain closure, and stops when its permitted search finds none.
assumptions_latex: The input \(T\) is a Hamiltonian cycle with additive edge costs.
Candidate, feasibility, closure, and backtracking rules are fixed for the implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a tour having no improving exchange discoverable under the algorithm's permitted starts, continuations, and closures.

notation.meaning: deleted and inserted edges at exchange step i

review_flags: Lin–Kernighan variants differ in admissibility, closure, and backtracking rules.
No supplied locator identifies a canonical variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lin–Kernighan completeness and 3-opt parameter guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantees for exhaustive and bounded parameter regimes of Lin–Kernighan search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Lin--Kernighan algorithm: (a) if $G=K_n$ and $p_1=p_2=\infty$, then, if there exists a proper closed alternating walk $P$ such that $(V(T),E(T)\mathbin{\triangle}E(P))$ is a tour, the algorithm finds a proper closed alternating walk having this property; (b) if $G=K_n$, $p_1=5$, and $p_2=2$, then the algorithm returns a $3$-opt tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the complete candidate graph and unlimited depths, Lin–Kernighan finds a proper closed alternating exchange producing a tour whenever one exists. With complete candidates, backtracking depth five, and infeasibility depth two, it returns a 3-opt tour.
assumptions_latex: \text{The Lin--Kernighan algorithm is applied to a TSP instance}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&G=K_n,\ p_1=p_2=\infty\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\text{ a feasible proper closed alternating walk}\bigr)\Rightarrow\bigl(\text{the algorithm finds one}\bigr),\\&G=K_n,\ p_1=5,\ p_2=2\ \Longrightarrow\ T_{\mathrm{out}}\text{ is }3\text{-opt}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-gain alternating-walk cost identity and proper reordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural exchange lemma for Lin–Kernighan search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(K_n,c)$ be a TSP instance, let $T$ be a tour, and let $P$ be a closed alternating walk relative to $T$ with $g(P)>0$. Then
\[
c\bigl(E(T)\mathbin{\triangle}E(P)\bigr)=c(E(T))-g(P).
\]
Moreover, there exists a proper closed alternating walk $Q$ relative to $T$ such that $E(Q)=E(P)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-gain closed alternating walk changes the edge-set cost by exactly minus its gain. Its exchange edges can also be ordered as a proper closed alternating walk.
assumptions_latex: (K_n,c)\text{ is a TSP instance}
T\text{ is a tour}
P\text{ is a closed alternating walk relative to }T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c\bigl(E(T)\mathbin{\triangle}E(P)\bigr)=c(E(T))-g(P),\qquad \exists Q\text{ proper and closed relative to }T\text{ with }E(Q)=E(P).

children.title: Sequential-Exchange Gain Criteria
children.top_down_role: Gain-based structures controlling admissible sequential exchanges.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential-Exchange Gain Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain tests used to extend and accept sequential edge exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For alternating deleted edges \(x_1,\ldots,x_i\) and inserted edges \(y_1,\ldots,y_i\), define
\[
G_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\bigl(c(x_j)-c(y_j)\bigr).
\]
Under the positive-prefix extension rule, a partial exchange is extended only if \(G_i>0\). A proposed terminal closure at depth \(r\) is improving exactly if it produces a Hamiltonian cycle and \(G_r>0\). Positive-prefix extension is a pruning rule, not a necessary condition for every improving completed exchange; it can exclude an improvement for which every admissible construction ordering has a nonpositive prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a positive-prefix rule, sequential search extends only partial exchanges with positive accumulated gain and accepts only positive-gain tour closures. This pruning rule can discard improving completed exchanges.
assumptions_latex: Tour cost is additive over edges.
The exchange alternates deleted and inserted edges.
The implementation uses the positive-prefix extension rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extension requires \(G_i>0\), while acceptance requires both Hamiltonian closure and \(G_r>0\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports the positive-prefix criterion.

children.title: Variable-Depth Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance or candidate restrictions limiting variable-depth search quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Depth Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which restricted variable-depth search may miss an improving exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{S}(T)\) be the exchange outcomes actually explored from \(T\), and let \(\mathcal{N}(T)\) be the intended variable-depth exchange neighborhood. For a minimization objective, termination certifies only
\[
f(T)\leq f(T')\quad\text{for every }T'\in\mathcal{S}(T).
\]
If \(\mathcal{S}(T)\subsetneq\mathcal{N}(T)\) because of a depth cap, candidate-edge restriction, positive-prefix pruning, or incomplete backtracking, this condition does not imply local optimality over \(\mathcal{N}(T)\). Search fails to find an existing improvement whenever every improving exchange outcome lies outside \(\mathcal{S}(T)\), including when all admissible constructions of such an exchange require a nonpositive intermediate gain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted variable-depth search certifies optimality only over explored moves. Depth limits, candidate sets, prefix pruning, or incomplete backtracking can hide improving exchanges.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{S}(T)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(T)\).
The objective \(f\) is minimized.
The algorithm exhausts \(\mathcal{S}(T)\), not necessarily \(\mathcal{N}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local optimality over \(\mathcal{S}(T)\) does not imply local optimality over \(\mathcal{N}(T)\) when \(\mathcal{S}(T)\subsetneq\mathcal{N}(T)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports Lin–Kernighan failure regimes.
Statement gives a logical search-coverage boundary; concrete TSP examples remain unsourced.

children.title: Candidate-Set Construction
children.top_down_role: Structures selecting promising edges or vertices for local search.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Set Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-cost construction of bounded edge-candidate sets used to restrict tour exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite complete weighted graph \(G=(V,E,c)\) and an integer \(q\geq 1\). For each vertex \(v\in V\), order \(V\setminus\{v\}\) by nondecreasing \(c_{vu}\), breaking ties by a fixed rule, and retain the first \(\min\{q,|V|-1\}\) vertices as \(C_q(v)\). Define the symmetrized undirected candidate edge set by
\[
E_q=\bigl\{\{u,v\}\in E:u\in C_q(v)\text{ or }v\in C_q(u)\bigr\}.
\]
A candidate-restricted exchange under this construction may insert only edges in \(E_q\). The output is the family \((C_q(v))_{v\in V}\) together with \(E_q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each vertex, retain its q cheapest incident neighbors, resolve ties deterministically, and symmetrize the retained pairs. Exchange search under this construction inserts only candidate edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,c)\) is a finite complete weighted graph.
\(q\geq 1\), and ties are resolved by a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction outputs candidate lists \(C_q(v)\) and their symmetrized candidate edge set \(E_q\).

notation.meaning: q-nearest-cost candidate list of vertex v

review_flags: This is one precise nearest-cost candidate construction, but no supplied locator supports it.

children.title: Geometric Neighborhood Restriction
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood restriction using spatial proximity or geometric sparsification.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Neighborhood Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of inserted exchange edges by a prescribed geometric graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let points \(p_v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) define a geometric TSP instance, and let \(H=(V,E_H)\) be a fixed geometric proximity graph constructed from them. For an exchange \(T'=(T\setminus X)\cup Y\), the geometric neighborhood restriction holds exactly when
\[
Y\subseteq E_H.
\]
Thus the restricted neighborhood is
\[
\mathcal{N}_H(T)=\{T'\in\mathcal{N}(T):T'\setminus T\subseteq E_H\},
\]
and \(\mathcal{N}_H(T)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(T)\). Equality holds exactly when every edge inserted by every move in \(\mathcal{N}(T)\) belongs to \(E_H\); otherwise at least one exchange outcome is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric restriction allows an exchange only when every inserted edge belongs to a chosen proximity graph. It preserves the full neighborhood exactly when that graph covers all edges inserted by its moves.
assumptions_latex: Each vertex \(v\in V\) has a point \(p_v\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
\(H=(V,E_H)\) is a fixed geometric proximity graph.
\(\mathcal{N}(T)\) is the unrestricted exchange neighborhood of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{N}_H(T)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(T)\), with equality exactly when \(T'\setminus T\subseteq E_H\) for every \(T'\in\mathcal{N}(T)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports geometric TSP candidate restrictions.
Specific proximity graphs and coverage guarantees require separate sourcing.

children.title: Candidate-Set Coverage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which restricted candidate sets omit improving moves.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a Hamiltonian tour on a finite complete graph \(G=(V,E)\) with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\).
\(\mathcal M(T)\) is an unrestricted move set and \(C(T)\subseteq E\) is a candidate-edge set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is locally optimal for the restricted neighborhood exactly when \(\Delta(T,m)\ge 0\) for every \(m\in\mathcal M_C(T)\); this implies unrestricted local optimality if and only if \(\mathcal M_C(T)\) contains every move \(m\in\mathcal M(T)\) with \(\Delta(T,m)<0\).

notation.meaning: moves whose inserted edges all belong to the candidate set
cost change produced by applying a move

review_flags: Relevant routing-heuristics source locator is absent; the boundary is stated from the neighborhood definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coverage criterion for candidate-restricted TSP exchange search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal M_C(T)=\{m\in\mathcal M(T):E^+(m)\subseteq C(T)\}\), where \(E^+(m)\) denotes the edges inserted by \(m\), and define \(\Delta(T,m)=c(m(T))-c(T)\). Candidate restriction preserves all improving opportunities at \(T\) precisely when \[\{m\in\mathcal M(T):\Delta(T,m)<0\}\subseteq\mathcal M_C(T).\] If this inclusion fails, restricted local optimality need not imply unrestricted local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate set preserves local-search coverage exactly when it admits every improving unrestricted move; otherwise restricted local optimality can be spurious.
knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Set Coverage Boundaries

children.title: Restriction–Search Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Navigation across computational savings plus lost neighborhood coverage.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1(T)\subseteq C_2(T)\subseteq E\) are two candidate-edge sets for every tour \(T\).
The search evaluates every admissible move in the corresponding restricted neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{C_1}(T)\le I_{C_2}(T)\) and \(L_{C_2}\subseteq L_{C_1}\); enlarging candidate sets weakly increases per-iteration move coverage while weakly decreasing the set of terminal tours.

notation.meaning: number of restricted moves inspected at a tour
tours locally optimal under candidate set C

review_flags: Relevant routing-heuristics source locator is absent; the monotonic tradeoff requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion tradeoff between search effort and restricted local-optimum quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(j\in\{1,2\}\), let \(\mathcal M_{C_j}(T)\) contain moves whose inserted edges lie in \(C_j(T)\). Then \(C_1(T)\subseteq C_2(T)\) gives \(\mathcal M_{C_1}(T)\subseteq\mathcal M_{C_2}(T)\), hence \(I_{C_1}(T)\le I_{C_2}(T)\). Moreover, with \(L_C=\{T:\Delta(T,m)\ge0\text{ for all }m\in\mathcal M_C(T)\}\), one has \[L_{C_2}\subseteq L_{C_1}.\] Thus stronger restriction reduces move evaluations but can enlarge the terminal set.

children.title: Local Optimality Criteria
children.top_down_role: Local-solution status relative to a specified TSP move class.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a finite feasible-solution set with objective \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\).
\(N(x)\subseteq\mathcal F\) is the neighborhood of each \(x\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is an \(N\)-local minimum if and only if \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\); it is strict when every such inequality is strict for \(y\ne x\).

notation.meaning: set of local minima under N

review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses local-search optimality; authoritative source confirmation is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-form local optimality for a fixed TSP move neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set of local minima induced by \(N\) is \[L_N=\{x\in\mathcal F:f(x)\le f(y)\text{ for every }y\in N(x)\}.\] Thus \(x\) is locally optimal exactly when no admissible neighborhood move has negative objective change. If \(N(x)\) includes \(x\), strict local optimality requires \(f(x)<f(y)\) only for distinct \(y\in N(x)\setminus\{x\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution is locally optimal when no solution reachable by one allowed move has smaller objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Optimality Criteria

children.title: Neighborhood Strength
children.top_down_role: Quality distinctions induced by increasingly expressive neighborhoods.

assumptions_latex: \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\) for every feasible solution \(x\in\mathcal F\).
Both neighborhoods use the same minimization objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(N_2\)-local minimum is an \(N_1\)-local minimum, so \(L_{N_2}\subseteq L_{N_1}\); the reverse inclusion need not hold.

notation.meaning: set of local minima under neighborhood N_i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood strength ordered by pointwise inclusion of reachable solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call \(N_2\) at least as strong as \(N_1\) when \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathcal F\). Since local optimality under \(N_2\) tests every comparison made under \(N_1\), \[L_{N_2}=\{x:f(x)\le f(y)\ \forall y\in N_2(x)\}\subseteq L_{N_1}.\] Equality occurs exactly when every \(N_1\)-local minimum also has no improving \(N_2\)-move.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger neighborhood tests more moves and therefore can only reduce, never enlarge, the set of local minima.

children.title: Move-Class Dependence

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a specified class of feasible tour transformations.
\(N_M(T)=\{m(T):m\in M,\ m(T)\text{ is feasible}\}\).

tours locally optimal for move class M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local optimality parameterized by the chosen class of feasible exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tour \(T\), define \(N_M(T)=\{m(T):m\in M,\ m(T)\text{ is feasible}\}\) and \[L_M=\{T:c(T)\le c(T')\text{ for every }T'\in N_M(T)\}.\] Consequently, the assertion that \(T\) is locally optimal is incomplete unless \(M\) is specified. intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly makes local optimality relative to a specified feasible move class and fits the terminal container, but no supporting TSP local-search source is cited.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) ranges over instances possessing an optimal value \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
\(L_N(I)\) is the nonempty set of solutions locally optimal under neighborhood \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case locality gap is \(\sup_I\sup_{x\in L_N(I)} f_I(x)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\); an infinite value means no finite approximation factor follows from \(N\)-local optimality alone.

notation.meaning: optimal objective value of instance I

review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats locality gaps for routing; authoritative source confirmation is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative worst-case gap for minimization and a fixed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem and neighborhood rule \(N\), define the instance-wise locality gap by \[\rho_N(I)=\sup_{x\in L_N(I)}\frac{f_I(x)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}.\] The worst-case locality gap over an instance class \(\mathcal I\) is \[\rho_N(\mathcal I)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\rho_N(I).\] Thus \(\rho_N(\mathcal I)\le\alpha\) exactly when every \(N\)-local minimum on every instance in \(\mathcal I\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locality gap is the largest ratio between a neighborhood-local optimum and the global optimum over the chosen instance class.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Locality Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicative minimization locality-gap definition is coherent under the stated positivity assumptions and fits the topic, but it has no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Smoothed Instance Behavior
children.top_down_role: Local-search behavior under small random perturbations of routing instances.

assumptions_latex: An adversary chooses a base instance \(I\), after which a random perturbation \(\xi\sim D_{I,\sigma}\) produces \(I_\xi\).
Algorithm \(A\) has runtime \(T_A(I_\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The smoothed runtime at noise scale \(\sigma\) is the worst-base-instance expectation \(\sup_I\mathbb E_{\xi\sim D_{I,\sigma}}[T_A(I_\xi)]\).

notation.meaning: perturbation distribution around base instance I

review_flags: The perturbation model and routing-specific theorem are unspecified; only the standard smoothed-runtime quantity is defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard smoothed-analysis quantity for a specified perturbation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a perturbation family \(\{D_{I,\sigma}\}\), where \(\sigma>0\) controls noise magnitude. For algorithm \(A\), its smoothed runtime is \[\operatorname{SmoothedTime}_A(n,\sigma)=\sup_{I:\,|I|=n}\mathbb E_{\xi\sim D_{I,\sigma}}\bigl[T_A(I_\xi)\bigr].\] Any claim of polynomial smoothed behavior must specify \(D_{I,\sigma}\), the encoding size \(n\), and the range of \(\sigma\) for which this quantity is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothed runtime is the worst, over base instances, expected runtime after a specified random perturbation of controlled magnitude.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Instance Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a standard abstract smoothed-runtime quantity, but the perturbation family is not concretely specified and no authoritative source supports this formulation or its intended routing-local-search sense.

children.title: Probabilistic Runtime Profiles
children.top_down_role: Runtime behavior over specified random-instance distributions.

assumptions_latex: For fixed input size \(n\) and perturbation level \(\sigma\), runtime \(T\) is a nonnegative random variable.
Probabilities and expectations are taken over perturbations and any algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The runtime profile is equivalently described by \(F(t)=\Pr(T\le t)\) or \(S(t)=\Pr(T>t)\), with \(\mathbb E[T]=\int_0^\infty S(t)\,dt\) when the expectation is finite.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses probabilistic local-search runtime profiles; source confirmation is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional runtime profile beyond a single expected-value summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For runtime random variable \(T\ge0\), define \(F(t)=\Pr(T\le t)\) and \(S(t)=1-F(t)=\Pr(T>t)\) for \(t\ge0\). Quantiles are \(q_p=\inf\{t:F(t)\ge p\}\). When \(\mathbb E[T]<\infty\), the tail-integral representation is \[\mathbb E[T]=\int_0^\infty S(t)\,dt.\] Hence equal expected runtimes do not imply equal runtime profiles, because their tails or quantiles may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probabilistic runtime profile records the full runtime distribution, including tails and quantiles, rather than only its mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Runtime Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The CDF, survival-function, quantile, and tail-integral representation are internally consistent and the representation content kind fits, but the record lacks a specific source locator.

children.title: Perturbation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of search outcomes on perturbation scale or distribution.

assumptions_latex: Instances lie in a metric space \((\mathcal I,d)\).
A deterministic local-search procedure maps each instance \(I\) to an output \(A(I)\) in a metric solution space \((\mathcal X,d_X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output stability radius at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is \(r_\varepsilon(I)=\sup\{r\ge0:d(I,J)\le r\Rightarrow d_X(A(I),A(J))\le\varepsilon\}\); radius zero identifies arbitrarily close output-instability.

notation.meaning: stability radius at output tolerance epsilon

review_flags: The node does not specify a perturbation metric or sensitivity observable; this record selects output stability and needs source validation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output sensitivity under metric perturbations of routing-instance data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \[r_\varepsilon(I)=\sup\{r\ge0:\ d(I,J)\le r\Longrightarrow d_X(A(I),A(J))\le\varepsilon\text{ for every }J\in\mathcal I\}.\] A positive \(r_\varepsilon(I)\) certifies local output stability at tolerance \(\varepsilon\). If \(r_\varepsilon(I)=0\), then for every \(r>0\) there exists \(J\) with \(d(I,J)\le r\) but \(d_X(A(I),A(J))>\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbation sensitivity measures how far instance data may move before the local-search output changes beyond a chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed stability radius is mathematically coherent, but Perturbation Sensitivity does not uniquely select output-metric stability. A source is needed to validate this observable and its relevance to routing local search.

assumptions_latex: A capacitated VRP has depot \(0\), customers \(V\), demands \(q_i\ge0\), vehicle capacity \(Q\), and symmetric costs \(c_{ij}\).
Each customer initially forms route \((0,i,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Processing savings \(s_{ij}=c_{i0}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}\) in nonincreasing order and merging feasible route ends yields a capacity-feasible route collection when no admissible merge remains.

notation.meaning: saving from directly joining customers i and j

review_flags: The supplied locators do not cover Clarke–Wright savings; an authoritative routing source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel Clarke–Wright construction for the symmetric capacitated VRP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize one route \((0,i,0)\) for each \(i\in V\). Compute \(s_{ij}=c_{i0}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}\) for distinct customers and scan pairs in nonincreasing \(s_{ij}\). Merge the routes containing \(i\) and \(j\) only if they are distinct, \(i\) and \(j\) are depot-adjacent route ends, and their combined demand is at most \(Q\); orient the routes so that deleting \((i,0)\) and \((0,j)\) and inserting \((i,j)\) is valid. Output the routes after the scan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with one route per customer, then greedily join compatible route ends in decreasing order of depot-bypass savings.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke–Wright Savings Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record resembles the parallel Clarke–Wright algorithm and the algorithm content kind is appropriate. However, no routing source identifies the exact variant, and the treatment of nonpositive savings under merely symmetric, nonmetric costs remains unsupported.

children.title: Sweep-Based Route Construction
children.top_down_role: Angular or radial customer ordering used to form preliminary routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sweep-Based Route Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-first planar sweep heuristic followed by intracluster routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a starting ray and sort customers cyclically so that \(\theta_{i_1}\le\cdots\le\theta_{i_n}\). Scan this order, adding customer \(i_k\) to the current block while its total demand remains at most \(Q\); otherwise close the block and start a new one with \(i_k\). For every resulting block \(B\), construct a depot tour through exactly \(B\). Output the collection of these tours; each customer occurs once and every route has demand at most \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sweep heuristic orders customers around the depot, forms consecutive capacity-feasible angular blocks, and builds one route per block.
assumptions_latex: Customers have planar coordinates, demands \(q_i\ge0\), depot \(o\), and vehicle capacity \(Q\).
Every customer satisfies \(q_i\le Q\).
A deterministic rule resolves equal polar angles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sorting customers by polar angle and partitioning the cyclic order into capacity-feasible consecutive blocks, then routing each block, produces a capacity-feasible VRP solution.

notation.meaning: polar angle of customer i around the depot

review_flags: An authoritative vehicle-routing source with a specific locator is required for the sweep heuristic.

children.title: Geometric Cluster Formation
children.top_down_role: Spatial grouping mechanisms for constructing route-compatible customer clusters.

assumptions_latex: Customers form a finite set \(V\) with positions \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\), demands \(q_i\ge0\), and capacity \(Q\).
Every customer satisfies \(q_i\le Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy nearest-centroid assignment with a capacity check terminates with a partition \(V=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_k\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in B_h}q_i\le Q\) for every cluster.
review_flags: The title does not identify a canonical clustering rule; this precise capacity-constrained geometric construction requires source and scope review.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit capacity-constrained geometric clustering rule for route-first conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U=V\). While \(U\ne\varnothing\), choose a deterministic seed \(i\in U\), set \(B=\{i\}\), and remove \(i\) from \(U\). Repeatedly compute the centroid \(\mu_B=|B|^{-1}\sum_{j\in B}p_j\) and add a customer \(h\in U\) minimizing \(\|p_h-\mu_B\|_2\) among those satisfying \(q_h+\sum_{j\in B}q_j\le Q\). Close \(B\) when no such customer exists, and output all closed clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Seed a cluster, repeatedly add its nearest capacity-feasible customer, close it when no addition fits, and continue until all customers are assigned.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Cluster Formation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The procedure terminates and yields capacity-feasible clusters under the stated individual-demand bound, but the broad title does not identify this nearest-centroid rule as canonical. Its selection and exact scope require a supporting source.

children.title: Cluster-to-Route Conversion
children.top_down_role: Interfaces that turn geometric clusters into feasible routed solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-to-Route Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts a feasible customer cluster into one depot-rooted route by solving or approximating its induced traveling-salesperson problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given depot \(0\), customer cluster \(C\), and arc costs \(c_{ij}\), construct a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{|C|})\) of \(C\). Return the route \(R=(0,\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{|C|},0)\), choosing \(\pi\) to minimize, exactly or heuristically, \[c_{0\pi_1}+\sum_{t=1}^{|C|-1}c_{\pi_t\pi_{t+1}}+c_{\pi_{|C|}0}.\] If the cluster satisfies all route-level resource constraints and the chosen ordering preserves them, output \(R\); otherwise declare the cluster infeasible for direct conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order every customer in a cluster into a depot-to-depot tour of minimum or heuristically small cost, rejecting the conversion if route constraints fail.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is finite and every customer must be visited exactly once.
\(c_{ij}\) is defined for every permitted directed arc.
\(C\) satisfies the applicable cluster-level capacity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=(0,\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{|C|},0)\) is a route visiting exactly the customers in \(C\).

notation.meaning: cost of traversing arc from i to j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cluster-first VRP conversion by routing each cluster

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically coherent and fits the terminal container, but no citation supports the cluster-to-route conversion rule or its infeasibility convention.

children.title: Route-First Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Partitioning a preliminary giant tour into feasible vehicle routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Route-First Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical route-first, cluster-second construction for capacitated depot routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given depot \(0\), customers \(V\), demands \(q_i\), capacity \(Q\), and travel costs, first construct a giant-tour permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\) of \(V\). Partition \(\pi\) into consecutive nonempty segments \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in S_r}q_i\le Q\). Select the partition minimizing the sum of depot-rooted segment-route costs, commonly by a shortest-path dynamic program on positions \(0,\ldots,n\). Return one route \((0,S_r,0)\) for every segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build one ordering of all customers, then split that ordering into capacity-feasible consecutive depot routes, preferably using an optimal split dynamic program.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and each customer appears once in the giant tour.
\(0\le q_i\le Q\) for every \(i\in V\).
Each consecutive segment has a well-defined depot-rooted route cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}\) partitions \(V\), preserves the giant-tour order, and satisfies \(\sum_{i\in S_r}q_i\le Q\) for every \(r\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard route-first, cluster-second VRP construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The route-first algorithm and split formulation fit the container, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the classical construction or shortest-path split claim.

children.title: Cluster-First Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing performed after customers have been assigned to vehicle clusters.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-First Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical cluster-first, route-second construction for capacitated depot routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given depot \(0\), customers \(V\), demands \(q_i\), and capacity \(Q\), first construct a partition \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) of \(V\) such that \(\sum_{i\in C_r}q_i\le Q\) for every \(r\). For each cluster independently, choose a permutation \(\pi^r\) of \(C_r\) by an exact or heuristic traveling-salesperson procedure and output \(R_r=(0,\pi^r_1,\ldots,\pi^r_{|C_r|},0)\). Stop when every cluster has been converted or report any cluster violating a route-level constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition customers into capacity-feasible clusters first, then independently order each cluster into a depot-rooted route.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(0\le q_i\le Q\) for every customer.
\(\mathcal C\) is a pairwise-disjoint cover of \(V\).
Each cluster can be checked against all applicable route constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{R_1,\ldots,R_m\}\) serves every customer exactly once whenever every cluster-to-route conversion succeeds.

notation.meaning: customer cluster assigned to route r

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cluster-first, route-second VRP construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cluster-first algorithm is internally consistent and appropriately classified, but it has no citation with a specific locator supporting the construction and route-level failure convention.

children.title: Ordering Choice Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of choosing routing before clustering or clustering before routing.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Choice Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the irreversible decisions made by route-first and cluster-first constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For route-first partitioning, every produced route must be a consecutive segment of the fixed giant-tour order \(\pi\); hence a feasible solution requiring an interleaving of customers from distinct segments is unreachable without changing \(\pi\). For cluster-first routing, every produced route must contain exactly one preselected cluster \(C_r\); hence a solution moving customers between clusters is unreachable without changing the partition. Neither restriction contains the other in general, so minimizing only the first-stage ordering or clustering objective need not minimize the final routing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route-first methods restrict route boundaries along one ordering; cluster-first methods restrict route membership. Either first-stage choice can exclude a better final solution.
assumptions_latex: The construction does not revise its first-stage giant tour or cluster partition.
Final routes must respect the corresponding first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{RF}}(\pi)\) and \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{CF}}(\mathcal C)\) are generally incomparable strict subsets of the full feasible-solution set.

notation.meaning: solutions obtainable by splitting giant tour pi
solutions respecting fixed cluster partition C

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of fixing the first-stage representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the tradeoff container, but the general incomparability and strict-subset claims require a source or a precisely scoped counterexample-based formulation.

children.title: Cheapest-Insertion Construction
children.top_down_role: Route construction driven by immediate insertion-cost criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Cheapest-Insertion Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential VRP construction using the least feasible marginal insertion cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a collection of depot-rooted seed routes and let \(U\) contain all unserved customers. For every \(u\in U\), route \(R\), and consecutive vertices \((i,j)\) of \(R\), compute \(\Delta(u;i,j)=c_{iu}+c_{uj}-c_{ij}\) whenever inserting \(u\) between \(i\) and \(j\) preserves feasibility. Choose a feasible triple minimizing \(\Delta\), perform the insertion, and remove \(u\) from \(U\). Repeat until \(U=\varnothing\); if no feasible triple exists while \(U\ne\varnothing\), open an allowed new route or report failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly make the feasible customer insertion having the smallest increase in route cost until all customers are served or construction fails.
assumptions_latex: Initial seed routes are feasible.
Feasibility can be tested after each candidate insertion.
Arc costs \(c_{ij}\) are defined for all permitted arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the procedure terminates with \(U=\varnothing\), its routes form a feasible complete solution.

notation.meaning: marginal cost of inserting u between i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cheapest-insertion algorithm is standard, precise, and suited to the container, but no inspectable citation supports the construction rule and new-route convention.

children.title: Regret-Based Construction
children.top_down_role: Customer selection based on the opportunity cost of delayed insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Regret-Based Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential construction prioritizing customers whose delayed insertion has high opportunity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each unserved customer \(u\), list its feasible insertion costs in nondecreasing order \(\Delta_1(u)\le\cdots\le\Delta_k(u)\), padding a missing alternative by \(+\infty\) if that convention is adopted. Define the \(k\)-regret score \[\rho_k(u)=\sum_{h=2}^{k}\bigl(\Delta_h(u)-\Delta_1(u)\bigr).\] Select a customer maximizing \(\rho_k(u)\), insert it at the position attaining \(\Delta_1(u)\), update all affected insertion costs, and repeat until every customer is served. If no customer has a feasible insertion, open an allowed route or report failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert the customer whose best option is most valuable relative to its next-best options, using that customer’s cheapest feasible position.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge2\) is fixed.
Current routes are feasible and candidate insertions are feasibility-tested.
At least one feasible insertion or permitted new-route action exists at each successful iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful termination yields feasible routes serving every customer exactly once.

notation.meaning: h-th smallest feasible insertion cost for customer u
number of ranked insertion alternatives considered

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common sum-based k-regret insertion convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the container, but regret definitions vary; a source is required to validate the stated sum-based k-regret formula and infinity-padding convention.

children.title: Seed Selection Effects
children.top_down_role: Influence of initial routes or customers on insertion-based solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Seed Selection Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of sequential insertion constructions on their initial routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(S)\) denote a deterministic insertion heuristic initialized with feasible seed set \(S\), including fixed tie-breaking. Candidate insertions at every later iteration are computed from the current routes, so changing \(S\) can change feasibility, marginal insertion costs, the selected insertion sequence, the number of routes, and final cost. Consequently, seed invariance is not guaranteed: there may exist feasible seeds \(S\) and \(S'\) for the same instance such that \(H(S)\ne H(S')\), even when both runs successfully serve all customers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different feasible seeds can alter every later insertion decision and produce different route counts, costs, or even construction success.
assumptions_latex: The insertion rule and tie-breaking are fixed.
At least two admissible seed sets are available for the same instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(S)=H(S')\) need not hold for distinct feasible seeds \(S\) and \(S'\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: state-dependent sequential insertion implies seed sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the seed-effects container, but the existential seed-sensitivity claim and listed possible consequences have no cited example or authoritative locator.

children.title: Relocate Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves that transfer a customer or customer segment to another position.

knowledge_statements.title: Relocate Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-customer or contiguous-string relocation within or between VRP routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible routing solution \(x\) and integer \(p\ge1\), a \(p\)-relocate move removes a contiguous string \((v_1,\ldots,v_p)\) from one route and inserts that string, with its internal order preserved, between two consecutive vertices of the same or another route. All vacated and inserted boundary arcs are reconnected. The relocate neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{reloc}}^{p}(x)\) is the set of distinct solutions obtainable by one such move that preserves every route-feasibility constraint; empty routes may be deleted if the model permits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relocate neighbor moves one customer or a consecutive customer string to another position, possibly on another route, while retaining feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible collection of depot-rooted routes.
The relocated string excludes depot occurrences.
Every resulting route is checked against the model constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{reloc}}^{p}(x)=\{x':x'\text{ is obtained from }x\text{ by one feasible }p\text{-relocate move}\}\).

notation.meaning: length of the relocated customer string

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard VRP relocate and Or-opt-style neighborhood definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits relocate neighborhoods and is internally consistent, but the extension from single-customer relocate to arbitrary order-preserving strings requires a cited convention.

children.title: Exchange Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves that swap customers or customer segments between positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise exchange of customers or customer strings within or between routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible routing solution \(x\) and positive integers \(p,q\), a \((p,q)\)-exchange move selects two disjoint contiguous customer strings of lengths \(p\) and \(q\), removes them, and inserts each string at the position vacated by the other, using a specified orientation convention. The exchange neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{ex}}^{p,q}(x)\) contains every distinct solution obtainable by one such move whose reconnections preserve all route constraints. The two strings may lie on the same route or on different routes when the selected scope permits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exchange neighbor swaps two disjoint customers or customer strings, within one route or across two routes, subject to feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible collection of depot-rooted routes.
The selected customer strings are disjoint and exclude depots.
The resulting routes satisfy every model constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ex}}^{p,q}(x)=\{x':x'\text{ results from one feasible }(p,q)\text{-exchange}\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard VRP string-exchange neighborhood definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exchange-neighborhood definition fits the container, but string orientation and same-route versus interroute scope vary and are unsupported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Cross-Exchange Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves that exchange route segments across distinct routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Exchange Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interroute exchange of two contiguous route segments with boundary reconnection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_a\ne R_b\) be two routes of a feasible solution \(x\). A cross-exchange selects a nonempty contiguous customer segment \(P_a\) of \(R_a\) and a nonempty contiguous customer segment \(P_b\) of \(R_b\), removes both segments, and inserts \(P_a\) at the location vacated by \(P_b\) and \(P_b\) at the location vacated by \(P_a\), with chosen segment orientations. The neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{cross}}(x)\) consists of all distinct feasible solutions produced by one such exchange and the necessary boundary-arc reconnections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-exchange swaps two nonempty consecutive customer segments belonging to different routes and reconnects both routes feasibly.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) contains two distinct feasible depot-rooted routes.
Each selected segment is contiguous, nonempty, and contains no depot.
Both reconstructed routes satisfy all model constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{cross}}(x)=\{x':x'\text{ is obtained by one feasible interroute segment swap}\}\).

notation.meaning: customer segments selected from distinct routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is appropriate for cross-exchange neighborhoods, but nonempty-segment and orientation conventions vary and require a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Route-Scope Variants
children.top_down_role: Intra-route versus inter-route realizations of relocation or exchange moves.

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Scope Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions relocate and exchange neighborhoods by whether modified positions share a route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any move family \(M\) and feasible solution \(x\), define \(N_M^{\mathrm{intra}}(x)\) using moves whose selected positions or strings all belong to one route, and define \(N_M^{\mathrm{inter}}(x)\) using moves involving two distinct routes. Then \[N_M(x)=N_M^{\mathrm{intra}}(x)\cup N_M^{\mathrm{inter}}(x),\qquad N_M^{\mathrm{intra}}(x)\cap N_M^{\mathrm{inter}}(x)=\varnothing,\] when moves are classified by their pre-move route incidence. Interroute variants can change customer allocation and route loads; intraroute variants preserve each route's customer set and load.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood moves split into intraroute and interroute variants; only interroute moves change customer allocation and route loads.
assumptions_latex: Each move is classified from the routes containing its selected elements before the move.
The move family involves at most two routes.
Only feasible resulting solutions enter the neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_M(x)=N_M^{\mathrm{intra}}(x)\mathbin{\dot\cup}N_M^{\mathrm{inter}}(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: route-incidence partition of standard VRP neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits route-scope variants and is coherent under the stated at-most-two-route assumption, but the partition and load-change assertions lack an inspectable source.

children.title: 2-Opt* Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Two-route edge reconnection structures in vehicle-routing search.

knowledge_statements.title: 2-Opt* Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-route tail exchange obtained by deleting and reconnecting one arc from each route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_a\ne R_b\) be directed depot-rooted routes in a feasible solution \(x\), and select arcs \((i,i^+)\in R_a\) and \((j,j^+)\in R_b\). A \(2\)-Opt* move deletes these arcs and reconnects the two route prefixes to the opposite route suffixes by adding \((i,j^+)\) and \((j,i^+)\). The neighborhood \(N_{2\text{-Opt}^*}(x)\) contains every distinct solution obtained from one such reconnection for which both resulting depot-rooted routes satisfy all model constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-Opt* neighbor cuts one arc in each of two routes and exchanges the route tails through crosswise reconnection.
assumptions_latex: \(R_a\) and \(R_b\) are distinct directed depot-rooted routes.
The selected cuts and reconnections produce well-defined routes.
Both resulting routes satisfy all capacity and side constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{2\text{-Opt}^*}(x)=\{x':x'\text{ results from one feasible crosswise two-route reconnection}\}\).

children.title: Route-Reconnection Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Broader route-tail or route-segment reconnection structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Reconnection Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-cut-and-reconnect neighborhoods for feasible vehicle routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible collection of depot-rooted routes with edge set \(E(x)\). A route-reconnection move selects distinct routes, removes a set \(F\subseteq E(x)\), and inserts edges \(A\) between endpoints exposed by those removals. Its neighbor is \(x'\) with \(E(x')=(E(x)\setminus F)\cup A\), provided every customer has route degree two, every resulting component is a permitted depot-rooted route, and all routing constraints remain satisfied. The route-reconnection neighborhood is \[\mathcal N_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\{x':x'\text{ is obtained by such a feasible reconnection}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The neighborhood contains feasible solutions obtained by cutting edges in distinct routes and reconnecting the exposed endpoints into valid depot-rooted routes.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible vehicle-routing solution.
Every customer must belong to exactly one permitted depot-rooted route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)\) is precisely the set of feasible route systems obtainable by the specified cut-and-reconnect operation.

notation.meaning: edge set of routing solution x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard edge-reconnection neighborhood definition for vehicle routing

children.title: Endpoint Pairing Variants
children.top_down_role: Alternative endpoint pairings available after route edges are removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Pairing Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration of reconnections through perfect matchings of exposed endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose cuts expose four endpoint occurrences \(U=\{a,b,c,d\}\), with the deleted edges inducing the original pairing \(M_0\). Every endpoint-pairing variant is represented by a perfect matching \(M\) of \(U\). Replacing the deleted edges by \(M\) gives \(E_M=(E(x)\setminus F)\cup M\). The admissible variant set is \[\mathcal M_{m adm}(x,F)=\{M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }U,\ M\ne M_0,\ E_M\text{ induces feasible permitted routes}\}.\] Distinct admissible matchings encode the possible endpoint reconnections, including orientation changes when routes are represented as directed sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After two edges are cut, each reconnection variant is a perfect matching of the four exposed endpoints that produces feasible routes and differs from the deleted pairing.
assumptions_latex: Exactly two route edges are removed, exposing four endpoint occurrences.
A candidate pairing is accepted only if it induces permitted feasible routes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M_{m adm}(x,F)\) represents exactly the admissible endpoint-pairing variants for the selected cuts.

notation.meaning: multiset of four exposed endpoint occurrences
pairing defined by the deleted edges

children.title: Ejection-Chain Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Linked displacement structures initiated by an infeasible or costly insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Ejection-Chain Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential displacement neighborhoods spanning one or more routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0=x\). An ejection chain of length \(k\ge 1\) is a sequence of states \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k\) and displaced customers \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\) such that step \(i\) inserts \(u_i\) at a selected position and, if necessary, ejects \(u_{i+1}\) from the affected route; the final step leaves no displaced customer. Intermediate states may violate only constraints explicitly permitted by the chain scheme, while \(x_k\) must be feasible. For an allowed depth set \(K\), \[\mathcal N_{m EC}^{K}(x)=\{x_k:k\in K\text{ and an admissible terminating ejection chain connects }x\text{ to }x_k\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ejection-chain neighbor results from successive insertions that displace further customers until the chain terminates at a feasible routing solution.
assumptions_latex: The chain scheme specifies permitted elementary insertions and temporary violations.
Every returned terminal state is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{m EC}^{K}(x)\) contains exactly the feasible terminal solutions reachable by admissible ejection chains of allowed lengths.

notation.meaning: customer displaced or inserted at chain step i
