The candidate-move condition only requires adding a missing guide attribute or removing a conflict; it does not require monotone reduction of attribute distance and therefore does not by itself ensure guide reachability or prevent cycling. A source with a precise algorithmic locator is needed to establish the intended move rule.

children.title: Solution-Pool Diversity
children.top_down_role: Structural diversity criteria for retained routing solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Pool Diversity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise dispersion of a finite routing-solution pool under a declared dissimilarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subseteq S\) be a finite pool with \(n\ge2\), and let \(d:S\times S\to\mathbb R_+\) be a symmetric routing-solution dissimilarity satisfying \(d(x,x)=0\). The mean pairwise diversity of \(P\) is \[D_{\mathrm{avg}}(P)=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}d(x_i,x_j).\] The minimum pairwise diversity is \[D_{\min}(P)=\min_{1\le i<j\le n}d(x_i,x_j).\] The first measures average dispersion; the second detects the closest duplicate pair. Comparisons between pools require the same dissimilarity and normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pool diversity is quantified by average or minimum pairwise dissimilarity among feasible routing solutions, using one fixed distance convention.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq S\) is finite with \(|P|=n\ge2\).
\(d\) is nonnegative, symmetric, and zero on identical solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{avg}}(P)\ge0\) and \(D_{\min}(P)\ge0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Solution-Pool Diversity, and both displayed formulas are internally correct for a finite pool of at least two solutions. These are reasonable dispersion measures but are not uniquely canonical for routing pools, and no source or inspectable locator supports their selection or interpretation in this container.

children.title: Pool-to-Trajectory Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Use of stored solutions as endpoints or guides for trajectory search.

knowledge_statements.title: Pool-to-Trajectory Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface selecting elite solution pairs and initializing a path-relinking trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite elite pool \(P\) of feasible routing solutions, a distance \(d\), and objective value \(f\), select distinct endpoints \(x^{s},x^{g}\in P\) by a prescribed rule, such as maximizing \(d(x^{s},x^{g})\) subject to an elite-quality threshold. Initialize \(x_0=x^{s}\). At iteration \(t\), form the admissible neighborhood \(N_t\) of solutions obtained by moves that introduce at least one attribute of \(x^{g}\) absent from \(x_t\). Select \(x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in N_t} f(y)\), breaking ties deterministically. Stop when \(x_t=x^{g}\) or \(N_t=\varnothing\), and return the best feasible solution encountered, optionally inserting it into \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select two sufficiently diverse elite routes, move from one toward the other by introducing target attributes, and return the best feasible intermediate solution.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite and contains at least two feasible routing solutions.
\(d\) and the endpoint-selection rule are fixed.
Each trajectory move has a specified feasibility convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{out}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{f(x_t):x_t\text{ is feasible and visited}\}\).

notation.meaning: elite pool of feasible routing solutions
admissible target-directed neighborhood at iteration t

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the pool-to-trajectory interface or its endpoint-selection convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the interface leaf, but no cited source supports the endpoint rule or trajectory convention. Introducing a guiding attribute without requiring retained progress does not exclude cycling or justify termination.

children.title: Customer Insertion Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves that add profitable unserved customers to routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Customer Insertion Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-customer insertion in a selective or profit-routing solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be the customer set and let \(S=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\) be a feasible routed solution serving customer set \(U(S)\subseteq V\). A customer-insertion move chooses \(v\in V\setminus U(S)\), a route \(R_k=(0,i_1,\ldots,i_q,0)\), and a position between consecutive vertices \((i_j,i_{j+1})\), where depot occurrences are allowed. It replaces that arc by \((i_j,v)\) and \((v,i_{j+1})\), leaving every other route unchanged. The move is feasible exactly when the resulting solution satisfies all routing constraints. Its cardinality effect is \(|U(S')|=|U(S)|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert one currently unserved customer between consecutive vertices of a route, provided all routing constraints remain satisfied.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is feasible before the move.
\(v\notin U(S)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses selective-routing insertion neighborhoods.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and single-customer insertion statement fit the leaf and are internally coherent, but no inspectable citation supports this selective-routing neighborhood convention.

children.title: Customer Removal Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves that remove served customers from routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Customer Removal Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-customer removal in a selective or profit-routing solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\) be a feasible routed solution serving \(U(S)\), and suppose route \(R_k\) contains consecutive vertices \((i,v,j)\) with customer \(v\). A customer-removal move deletes \(v\) and replaces arcs \((i,v)\) and \((v,j)\) by \((i,j)\), leaving every other route unchanged. If empty routes are permitted, removal of the sole customer produces the depot-only route; otherwise that route is deleted according to the fleet convention. The resulting solution \(S'\) serves \(U(S')=U(S)\setminus\{v\}\), so its served-customer cardinality decreases by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete one served customer, reconnect its predecessor to its successor, and apply the model’s convention for a route that becomes empty.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is feasible before the move.
\(v\in U(S)\) occurs on exactly one route.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses selective-routing removal neighborhoods.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and removal statement fit the leaf, including the empty-route convention, but no inspectable citation supports the stated neighborhood.

children.title: Customer Replacement Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves that substitute unserved customers for currently served customers.

knowledge_statements.title: Customer Replacement Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-for-one exchange of a served and an unserved customer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a feasible routed solution serving \(U(S)\subseteq V\). A customer-replacement move chooses a served customer \(u\in U(S)\) and an unserved customer \(v\in V\setminus U(S)\). It removes \(u\) from its route and inserts \(v\) at any allowed position, possibly the position vacated by \(u\) or a position on another route. All other customer occurrences remain unchanged. The move is admissible when the resulting routed solution \(S'\) satisfies the model’s fleet, capacity, duration, time-window, and visit constraints. It changes membership but preserves the number of served customers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace one served customer with one unserved customer, possibly on another route, while retaining feasibility and served-set size.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is feasible before the move.
\(u\in U(S)\) and \(v\in V\setminus U(S)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator fixes the intended replacement-neighborhood convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes that replacement may reinsert on another route or fixes the intended admissibility convention.

children.title: Cardinality-Changing Effects
children.top_down_role: Effects of neighborhood moves on the number of served customers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Changing Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of elementary selective-routing moves on the served set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a routed solution \(S\), let \(n(S)=|U(S)|\) denote the number of distinct served customers. If \(S'\) is obtained by one elementary insertion, removal, or one-for-one replacement, with no duplicated customer visits, then respectively \(n(S')-n(S)=1\), \(n(S')-n(S)=-1\), or \(n(S')-n(S)=0\). Thus insertion and removal connect different served-cardinality layers of the solution space, whereas replacement remains within one layer. These identities concern served-set cardinality only; route count, travel cost, collected reward, and feasibility slack may change independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertion raises served cardinality by one, removal lowers it by one, and one-for-one replacement preserves it; other route statistics may still change.
assumptions_latex: Every customer is visited at most once.
Each move affects exactly the customers specified by its elementary definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta n\in\{1,-1,0\}\), with values determined by insertion, removal, and replacement respectively.
review_flags: The property follows from the local move definitions, but no supplied source documents this neighborhood decomposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the effects leaf, and the cardinality identities follow from the stated elementary moves. However, those prerequisite move definitions and this decomposition lack cited evidence.

children.title: Route Exchange Moves
children.top_down_role: Transfer or exchange of customers, segments, or assignments across routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Route Exchange Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange of customer blocks between two team routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\) be a routed team solution. A route-exchange move selects distinct routes \(R_a,R_b\), a nonempty consecutive customer block \(A\) of \(R_a\), and a nonempty consecutive customer block \(B\) of \(R_b\). It deletes both blocks and inserts \(B\) at the position formerly occupied by \(A\), and \(A\) at the position formerly occupied by \(B\), reconnecting the exposed route endpoints. Internal block order is preserved unless reversal is explicitly allowed. The move is feasible when both modified routes and all team-level constraints remain satisfied; the global served-customer set is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swap customer blocks between two routes, reconnecting both routes and preserving the global customer set when the resulting team solution is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(R_a\) and \(R_b\) are distinct routes.
Selected blocks contain customers and are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U(S')=U(S)\), while the assignments of customers in \(A\cup B\) to routes are exchanged.
review_flags: No supplied source fixes whether route exchanges permit unequal blocks, empty blocks, or reversal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but route-exchange conventions vary concerning unequal or empty blocks, reversal, and reinsertion positions; no source fixes the asserted variant.

children.title: Team Rebalancing Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves that redistribute service assignments across the available routing team.

knowledge_statements.title: Team Rebalancing Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inter-route relocation intended to rebalance assigned workload.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(R_1,ldots,R_m)\) be a feasible team-routing solution, and let \(w(R_k)\ge 0\) measure route workload. A team rebalancing move selects distinct routes \(R_a,R_b\), removes a nonempty consecutive customer block \(A\) from \(R_a\), and inserts it into an allowed position of \(R_b\), preserving customer uniqueness. The move is accepted as rebalancing when the resulting feasible solution \(S'\) satisfies \(\Phi(S')<\Phi(S)\), where \(\Phi\) is a specified imbalance measure, such as the workload range \(\max_k w(R_k)-\min_k w(R_k)\). The served-customer set is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relocate a customer block between routes and call the move rebalancing when a specified workload-imbalance measure strictly decreases.
assumptions_latex: \(w\) and the imbalance measure \(\Phi\) are fixed.
The relocation preserves feasibility and unique customer assignment.
review_flags: No supplied source specifies the workload metric or admissible team-rebalancing neighborhood.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but no source supports defining a rebalancing move by strict decrease of a chosen imbalance measure. The route tuple also contains the malformed text \(R_1,ldots,R_m\) instead of \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\).

children.title: Workload Redistribution Effects
children.top_down_role: Changes in route workload, reward, or utilization caused by cross-route moves.

knowledge_statements.title: Workload Redistribution Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation and imbalance effects of inter-route customer transfers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose route workload is additive, \(w(R_k)=\sum_{i\in R_k}q_i\), for nonnegative customer loads \(q_i\). If a block \(A\) is transferred from route \(R_a\) to route \(R_b\) without changing customer service, and \(Q(A)=\sum_{i\in A}q_i\), then \(w(R_a')=w(R_a)-Q(A)\), \(w(R_b')=w(R_b)+Q(A)\), and every other route workload is unchanged. Consequently total workload is conserved. For squared deviation from the mean, the transfer improves balance exactly when \(0<Q(A)<w(R_a)-w(R_b)\), assuming \(R_a\) is initially heavier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transferring load conserves total workload; under squared imbalance, moving a positive amount from a heavier route helps exactly before the load ordering is over-reversed.
assumptions_latex: Customer workload is nonnegative and additive by route.
The transfer preserves the served-customer set.
Initially \(w(R_a)>w(R_b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k w(R_k')=\sum_k w(R_k)\), and squared imbalance decreases exactly when \(0<Q(A)<w(R_a)-w(R_b)\).

notation.meaning: total workload of the transferred block

review_flags: The additive-load calculation is standard, but no supplied source supports its routing-neighborhood interpretation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits and the additive workload updates are algebraically coherent. However, the exact squared-deviation measure is not explicitly defined, and no routing-neighborhood source supports the interpretation.

children.title: Reward-Aware Destroy Operators
children.top_down_role: Removal mechanisms sensitive to customer reward or route profitability.

knowledge_statements.title: Reward-Aware Destroy Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial-solution destruction using marginal reward and removal-cost information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible selective-routing solution \(S\), removal count \(k\), rewards \(p_i\), and travel-cost weight \(\lambda\ge 0\), initialize \(S_0=S\). For \(t=0,\ldots,k-1\), compute for each currently served customer \(i\) its travel-cost saving \(s_i(S_t)\) upon removal and score \(\rho_i=p_i-\lambda s_i(S_t)\). Select a customer of minimum \(\rho_i\), using a fixed tie-breaking or randomized rank rule, remove it, and update affected scores. Stop after \(k\) removals or when no removable customer remains. Return the partial solution and the removed set for subsequent repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly remove customers whose retained reward is least attractive relative to their removal cost saving, then pass the partial solution to repair.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is initially feasible.
Rewards and the removal count are specified.
Removal savings are evaluated under a fixed cost convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_k,D_k)\) is returned with \(D_k=U(S)\setminus U(S_k)\) and \(|D_k|\le k\).
review_flags: Reward-aware destroy scores have multiple conventions; no relevant heuristic source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the destroy-operator leaf, but the reward-minus-weighted-saving score and selection convention are source-dependent and have no citation.

children.title: Reward-Aware Repair Operators
children.top_down_role: Reinsertion mechanisms balancing reward contribution against routing cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Reward-Aware Repair Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy feasible reinsertion using reward-adjusted incremental travel cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a partial feasible solution \(S_0\), candidate set \(D\) of unserved customers, rewards \(p_i\), and weight \(\lambda\ge 0\), compute every feasible insertion \((i,k,j)\), where customer \(i\in D\) is inserted at position \(j\) of route \(k\). Let \(\Delta c_{ikj}\) be its incremental travel cost and define gain \(g_{ikj}=p_i-\lambda\Delta c_{ikj}\). Repeatedly choose a feasible insertion of maximum gain, apply it, remove that customer from \(D\), and recompute affected gains. Stop when no feasible insertion with positive gain remains, or when the prescribed repair rule requires full reinsertion. Return the repaired solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedily insert the feasible customer-position pair with greatest reward-adjusted gain until no profitable insertion remains or full repair is required.
assumptions_latex: \(S_0\) is a feasible partial solution.
Insertion feasibility and incremental cost are computable.
A stopping convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^{\mathrm{out}}\) is feasible and contains no unperformed feasible insertion with positive computed gain at termination.
review_flags: Reward-aware repair and stopping rules vary across profit-routing heuristics; no relevant source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the repair-operator leaf, but no source supports the gain rule. The alternative full-reinsertion stopping convention is also insufficiently specified when some remaining customers have no feasible insertion.

children.title: Profit–Feasibility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interaction between collected reward plus restored route feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit–Feasibility Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized evaluation of reward, travel cost, and constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a possibly infeasible routed solution \(S\), let \(P(S)=\sum_{i\in U(S)}p_i-c(S)\) be net profit and let \(v_r(S)\ge 0\) quantify violation of constraint family \(r\), with \(v_r(S)=0\) exactly when that family is satisfied. A penalty evaluation is \(F_{\mu}(S)=P(S)-\sum_r\mu_r v_r(S)\), where \(\mu_r\ge 0\). For two solutions \(S,T\), the penalized rule prefers \(S\) precisely when its profit advantage exceeds its weighted excess violation. Feasibility is recovered when all violation terms vanish; finite penalties do not generally guarantee that a maximizer is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalized search accepts extra violation only when its profit advantage exceeds the weighted violation increase; finite penalties alone need not enforce feasibility.
assumptions_latex: Each violation measure is nonnegative and vanishes exactly for its constraint family.
Penalty weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mu}(S)\ge F_{\mu}(T)\iff P(S)-P(T)\ge\sum_r\mu_r\bigl(v_r(S)-v_r(T)\bigr)\).
review_flags: No supplied source addresses penalty evaluation in profit-routing removal–reinsertion search.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the tradeoff leaf, and the comparison identity is internally correct. No inspectable source supports this penalty formulation in the stated profit-routing search context.

children.title: Route-Pool Generation
children.top_down_role: Creation or enrichment of candidate-route collections for later recombination.

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Pool Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation of feasible route columns for later set-partitioning recombination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given customer set \(V\), routing constraints, and a generation budget \(B\), initialize a route pool \(\mathcal R=\varnothing\) and a collection of seed solutions. For each seed, apply a prescribed constructive or neighborhood search. Whenever a feasible depot-to-depot route \(r\) is encountered, canonicalize it and insert it into \(\mathcal R\) unless already present, recording its cost \(c_r\), reward \(p_r\), and incidence values \(a_{ir}=1\) exactly for customers visited by \(r\). Continue until \(B\) route evaluations, a time limit, or pool capacity is reached. Return \(\mathcal R\) and its column data for the recombination master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collect distinct feasible routes encountered by constructive or local search, record their costs, rewards, and customer incidences, and return them as master-problem columns.
assumptions_latex: Route feasibility is decidable under the routing model.
A finite generation budget or stopping limit is supplied.
Duplicate routes have a fixed canonical representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is finite, and every \(r\in\mathcal R\) is feasible with recorded column \((c_r,p_r,(a_{ir})_{i\in V})\).
review_flags: The supplied locators do not cover route-pool generation for set-partitioning routing matheuristics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the route-pool generation leaf, but the inventory contains no source for this routing matheuristic procedure, its canonicalization convention, or its recorded column data.

children.title: Set-Partitioning Recombination
children.top_down_role: Selection of compatible routes from a pool through a restricted master model.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Partitioning Recombination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recombines feasible routes from a fixed pool into a minimum-cost fleet solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given customers \(V\), a pool \(\mathcal R\) of individually feasible routes, route costs \(c_r\), incidences \(a_{ir}\in\{0,1\}\), and an optional fleet limit \(m\), solve \[\min_{y}\ \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}c_r y_r\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}a_{ir}y_r=1\ \ (i\in V),\qquad \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}y_r\le m,\qquad y_r\in\{0,1\}.\] Omit the fleet constraint when fleet size is unrestricted. Return the selected routes \(\{r\in\mathcal R:y_r=1\}\); declare pool infeasibility if the restricted model has no feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a set-partitioning model over pooled feasible routes, selecting minimum-cost routes that cover every customer exactly once and respect any fleet limit.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(\mathcal R\) are finite.
Every \(r\in\mathcal R\) satisfies the original route-level constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an optimal feasible recombination within \(\mathcal R\), or a certificate that no such recombination exists.

notation.meaning: Indicator that route r serves customer i.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports route-pool set-partitioning recombination.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and set-partitioning formulation fit the leaf and are mathematically coherent, but no inspectable citation supports the route-pool recombination model or its infeasibility conclusion.

children.title: Pool-Coverage Limits
children.top_down_role: Improvement limits caused by missing customers, structures, or high-quality routes in the pool.

knowledge_statements.title: Pool-Coverage Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when restriction to a generated route pool loses feasibility or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible solutions of the full routing model and let \(\mathcal F(\mathcal R)\subseteq\mathcal F\) be those expressible using routes from pool \(\mathcal R\). If some customer \(i\) satisfies \(a_{ir}=0\) for every \(r\in\mathcal R\), then \(\mathcal F(\mathcal R)=\varnothing\). More generally, if \(z^*=\min_{x\in\mathcal F}c(x)\) and \(z_{\mathcal R}=\min_{x\in\mathcal F(\mathcal R)}c(x)\), with \(z_{\mathcal R}=+\infty\) when empty, then \(z_{\mathcal R}\ge z^*\). Equality is guaranteed only when \(\mathcal R\) contains all routes of at least one globally optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A route pool can destroy feasibility or exclude every optimum; its restricted optimum cannot improve upon the full-model optimum.
assumptions_latex: The full routing problem has finite feasible set \(\mathcal F\).
Route costs in the restricted and full models agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricted recombination is globally exact precisely when \(\mathcal F(\mathcal R)\) contains a global optimum; otherwise it may have a positive or infinite gap.

notation.meaning: Full-model solutions representable using only pooled routes.
Optimal objective value restricted to the route pool.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports route-pool coverage and optimality limits.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and restricted-feasible-set comparison fit the leaf, but the route-pool feasibility and global-exactness claims have no cited source.

children.title: Local-Branching Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Exact subproblems restricted by distance from an incumbent routing solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Branching Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary local branching around an incumbent routing solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary mixed-integer routing formulation with binary index set \(B\) and incumbent \(\bar x\in\{0,1\}^{B}\), define \(B_1=\{j\in B:\bar x_j=1\}\) and \(B_0=B\setminus B_1\). The radius-\(k\) local-branching neighborhood is the original feasible region intersected with \[\sum_{j\in B_1}(1-x_j)+\sum_{j\in B_0}x_j\le k.\] The left side is the Hamming distance between the binary vectors \(x_B\) and \(\bar x_B\). Exact optimization over this restricted formulation returns the best feasible solution differing from the incumbent in at most \(k\) binary decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-branching neighborhood contains feasible solutions whose binary decision vector lies within a prescribed Hamming distance of the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a nonnegative integer.
\(\bar x\) is feasible for the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible point of the restricted model has binary Hamming distance at most \(k\) from \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Binary indices active in the incumbent.

review_flags: A direct source for the local-branching inequality was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly states the binary local-branching Hamming inequality and fits the terminal container, but the defining formula lacks a source locator.

children.title: Fix-to-Optimize Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Exact subproblems formed by fixing selected routing decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fix-to-Optimize Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reoptimization after fixing decisions outside a selected routing neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a mixed-integer routing model \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\), an incumbent \(\bar x\in X\), and a selected set \(F\) of integer-variable indices, form the subproblem \[\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ x_j=\bar x_j\text{ for every integer index }j\notin F\}.\] Solve it to proven optimality or a prescribed exact-solver limit. Replace \(\bar x\) by the returned feasible solution only if its objective is smaller; otherwise retain \(\bar x\). Repeating with different sets \(F\) defines a fix-to-optimize search, while each solved subproblem explores exactly the feasible completions of the released variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix incumbent integer decisions outside a chosen subset, optimize the resulting exact subproblem, and accept an improving feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in X\) is feasible.
The subproblem retains the original objective and constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted update is feasible for the original model and has objective value no greater than \(f(\bar x)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports routing fix-to-optimize subproblems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm accurately describes incumbent-based fixing and reoptimization, but no source supports this routing matheuristic formulation.

children.title: Variable-Fixing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing which routing decisions remain fixed or free.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Fixing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions defining valid static or adaptive variable fixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) index the integer variables of a routing formulation and let \(\bar x\) be a feasible incumbent. A fixing regime is specified by a released set \(F_t\subseteq I\) at iteration \(t\), with constraints \(x_j=\bar x_j\) for \(j\in I\setminus F_t\). It is incumbent-preserving when every fixed value equals its incumbent value, because then \(\bar x\) remains feasible. It is exhaustive over a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^I\) when every \(S\in\mathcal S\) occurs as some \(F_t\). Static regimes choose \(F_t\) independently of solver feedback; adaptive regimes may condition \(F_t\) on earlier solutions or bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixing regime chooses released variables; incumbent-value fixing preserves feasibility, while static and adaptive regimes differ in their dependence on search feedback.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
\(\bar x\) satisfies the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixing all indices outside \(F_t\) to incumbent values yields a nonempty restricted feasible region containing \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Integer-variable indices released at iteration t.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports variable-fixing regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition record clearly distinguishes incumbent-preserving, static, adaptive, and exhaustive regimes, but these classifications lack cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Very-Large-Scale Neighborhoods via Exact Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood search whose implicitly defined neighborhood is optimized by an exact solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible incumbent \(\bar x\in X\), construct a restricted feasible set \(N(\bar x)\subseteq X\) by fixing variables, limiting changed components, selecting a route pool, or imposing another neighborhood predicate, with \(\bar x\in N(\bar x)\). Solve \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in N(\bar x)} f(x)\] exactly, or retain a valid lower bound and best feasible point if terminated early. If \(f(x^*)<f(\bar x)\), set \(\bar x\leftarrow x^*\); otherwise the exact solution certifies that no improving point exists in the current neighborhood. Iterate with a newly constructed neighborhood until the prescribed stopping rule holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Define a large neighborhood implicitly, optimize it as an exact subproblem, accept improvement, and use exact optimality to certify neighborhood-local optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the original feasible set.
Each neighborhood contains its incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact nonimprovement certifies \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)\) for every \(x\in N(\bar x)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports very-large-scale neighborhoods solved as exact subproblems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the topic and correctly limits an exact nonimprovement certificate to the current neighborhood, but no citation supports the very-large-scale-neighborhood characterization.

children.top_down_role: Routing-specific preprocessing, solver coordination, validation, and scalability boundaries; generic solver engineering and experimental methodology remain external.

children.title: Metric Closure Construction
children.top_down_role: Shortest-path completion of routing costs over an underlying network.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Closure Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs an all-pairs shortest-path metric from nonnegative network lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative arc lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb R_+\), define \[d(u,v)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in P}\ell(e):P\text{ is a directed }u\text{-to-}v\text{ path in }G\right\},\] taking \(d(u,v)=+\infty\) when no such path exists. Compute these values by an all-pairs shortest-path algorithm and return the complete directed distance representation on all finite pairs. Then \(d(u,u)=0\) and \(d(u,w)\le d(u,v)+d(v,w)\). Store a predecessor or next-hop witness when original-network path reconstruction is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace network arcs by all-pairs shortest-path distances, obtaining a directed metric on reachable pairs and retaining witnesses when paths must be reconstructed.

children.title: Distance-Oracle Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal query contract connecting closure distances to reconstructible network paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distance oracle for a finite network \(G=(V,E)\) is an interface that, for each ordered pair \((u,v)\), returns either \((d(u,v),P_{uv})\) or an unreachable symbol. Its contract requires that every returned \(P_{uv}\) be a valid \(u\)-to-\(v\) path and \[d(u,v)=\sum_{e\in P_{uv}}\ell(e)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}\ell(e).\] If only distances are exposed, downstream routing remains cost-faithful but cannot certify realizability without separate witnesses. For asymmetric networks the interface must preserve ordered pairs: generally \(d(u,v)\ne d(v,u)\).

children.title: Closure Fidelity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where closure distances omit routing-relevant path details or constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Fidelity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies which original routing constraints survive metric-closure replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing each closure arc \((u,v)\) by a shortest path \(P_{uv}\) preserves additive travel cost and endpoint order. It preserves feasibility only for constraints determined entirely by visited endpoints and additive quantities correctly accumulated along \(P_{uv}\). Fidelity can fail when internal vertices or arcs affect feasibility, including forbidden transit, turn restrictions, path-dependent resources, time-dependent travel, or requirements that customers not be traversed implicitly. Thus a closure solution is valid for the original instance only if every selected closure arc has a witness path and the concatenation of those witnesses satisfies every original path-level constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric closure preserves shortest-path cost, but not constraints depending on internal arcs, vertices, turns, timing, or other path-dependent state.
assumptions_latex: Each closure arc is assigned an original-network path witness.
Original route cost is additive over traversed arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Endpoint-level closure feasibility implies original-network feasibility only after all expanded witness paths satisfy the original path-level constraints.

notation.meaning: Original-network witness path for closure arc (u,v).

children.title: Candidate-Edge Selection

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Edge Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects a sparse routing edge set using admissible scores and mandatory edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a routing graph \(G=(V,E)\), an edge score \(s:E\to\mathbb R\), an integer budget \(k_v\ge1\) for each vertex, and mandatory set \(M\subseteq E\), initialize \(E'=M\). For each vertex \(v\), add the \(k_v\) incident edges of smallest score, or all incident edges when fewer exist. Optionally add edges required by a separately checked connectivity condition. Return \(G'=(V,E')\). The score may encode distance, reduced cost, geometric proximity, or search history, but the selection rule must state its tie-breaking convention and must never remove mandatory edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain mandatory edges and a bounded number of best-scoring incident edges per vertex, then add any edges required by connectivity checks.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
Every edge receives a comparable score with deterministic tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned graph contains \(M\) and each vertex's selected top-ranked incident candidates.

children.title: Graph Sparsification Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural or geometric criteria used to remove edges from routing graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Sparsification Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable admissibility conditions for a routing candidate-edge graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected routing graph \(G=(V,E)\), a candidate subgraph \(G'=(V,E')\) with \(E'\subseteq E\) satisfies the basic sparsification criterion when \(|E'|<|E|\), every required edge lies in \(E'\), and every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) obeys \[|\delta_{E'}(S)|\ge \lambda,\] where \(\lambda=1\) preserves connectivity and \(\lambda=2\) prevents bridges. A stronger objective-fidelity criterion requires that \(E'\) contain all edges of at least one optimal solution. Cut conditions are directly checkable; objective fidelity generally is not known without solving or valid edge-elimination certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse candidate graph should retain mandatory edges and required cut connectivity; exact objective fidelity additionally requires retaining an optimal solution's edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed cut inequalities certify the prescribed connectivity level, but alone do not certify preservation of an optimal routing solution.

children.title: Connectivity Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of sufficient graph structure for feasible or competitive routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut or spanning-tree certificates for connectivity after candidate-edge deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G'=(V,E')\) be a finite undirected candidate-edge graph. A spanning tree \(T\subseteq E'\) is a polynomially verifiable certificate that \(G'\) is connected: verify that \(T\) contains \(|V|-1\) edges, is acyclic, and spans \(V\). Equivalently, connectivity holds exactly when \(\delta_{E'}(S)\ne\varnothing\) for every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\). For preservation of \(\lambda\)-edge-connectivity, the corresponding certificate condition is \(|\delta_{E'}(S)|\ge\lambda\) for every such \(S\), which may be checked by a global minimum-cut computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retained spanning tree certifies connectivity; minimum-cut value at least lambda certifies lambda-edge-connectivity after sparsification.
assumptions_latex: \(G'=(V,E')\) is finite and undirected.
\(\lambda\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid spanning tree certifies connectedness, while minimum cut at least \(\lambda\) certifies \(\lambda\)-edge-connectivity.

children.title: Route-Feasibility Screening

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Feasibility Screening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary screening for capacitated routes with time windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a candidate route \(r=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k,v_{k+1})\), initialize \(T_0=a_{v_0}\) and compute \(T_{j+1}=\max\{a_{v_{j+1}},T_j+s_{v_j}+t_{v_jv_{j+1}}\}\). Reject \(r\) immediately if \(T_j>b_{v_j}\) for some \(j\), if \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}q_{v_j}>Q\), or if a required arc or precedence relation is violated. Otherwise return “not rejected”; this output does not certify feasibility when the routing model contains additional resources or side constraints not included in the screen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagate earliest arrival times and test capacity, arcs, and precedence. Any violation proves infeasibility; passing only means that further feasibility checks are required.
assumptions_latex: Travel times satisfy the deterministic FIFO convention used by the propagation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A rejected route is infeasible for every model containing the screened constraints.

children.title: Incompatibility Detection

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatibility Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pairwise route incompatibility and sound sufficient detection tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For customers \(i\ne j\), declare \(i\perp j\) exactly when no feasible route contains both customers. A sound preprocessing detector may certify \(i\perp j\) if \(q_i+q_j>Q\), or if both possible service orders are time-window impossible: \(a_i+s_i+t_{ij}>b_j\) and \(a_j+s_j+t_{ji}>b_i\). Any detected pair yields the valid same-route exclusion \(y_{ir}+y_{jr}\le1\) for every route \(r\). Failure of these sufficient tests does not imply compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two customers are incompatible when no feasible route serves both. Capacity or impossibility of both service orders provides a verifiable sufficient certificate.

children.title: Preprocessing Interaction Effects
children.top_down_role: Interactions between feasibility reductions plus incompatibility-based exclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Interaction Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safety criterion for sequentially composed routing reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_0\) be a routing instance and let \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) be preprocessing transformations, with \(I_j=R_j(I_{j-1})\). Suppose that, for every \(j\), every optimal solution of \(I_j\) can be lifted to a feasible solution of \(I_{j-1}\) having the same objective value, and \(\operatorname{opt}(I_j)=\operatorname{opt}(I_{j-1})\). Then the composite reduction preserves the optimal value, and successive lifting recovers an optimal solution of \(I_0\). Safety established only relative to \(I_0\), rather than each current instance \(I_{j-1}\), is insufficient for this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential preprocessing is safe when every reduction is safe for the instance produced immediately before it and its solutions can be lifted without cost change.
assumptions_latex: The sequence \(I_j=R_j(I_{j-1})\) is finite.
Each reduction supplies a same-value lifting map on optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{opt}(I_m)=\operatorname{opt}(I_0)\), and an optimum of \(I_m\) lifts to an optimum of \(I_0\).

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Preprocessing
children.top_down_role: Removal of equivalent routing representations before or during model construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical-orbit reduction for finite routing symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on the feasible routing solutions \(X\), preserving feasibility and objective value. Fix a total order \(\preceq\) on an encoding of \(X\). For every orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\), retain only its canonical representative \(\kappa(x)=\min_{\preceq}Gx\), equivalently impose constraints selecting exactly these representatives. Solve the restricted instance and return its solution. Because every discarded solution has a retained orbit-equivalent solution with equal objective value, the restricted and original instances have the same optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a finite symmetry group preserves feasibility and cost, retain one canonical solution from each orbit; optimization over representatives preserves the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and acts on the feasible set \(X\).
For every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\), \(gx\in X\) and \(c(gx)=c(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}c(x)=\min_{x\in\kappa(X)}c(x)\).

children.title: Dominance-Based Elimination

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance-Based Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension-preserving dominance certificate for partial routes or labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For partial-route labels \(L_1,L_2\) at the same state, let \(c(L)\) be accumulated cost and \(E(L)\) the set of feasible completions. Label \(L_1\) dominates \(L_2\) if \(c(L_1)\le c(L_2)\), \(E(L_2)\subseteq E(L_1)\), and every \(e\in E(L_2)\) satisfies \(\Delta c(L_1,e)\le\Delta c(L_2,e)\). The displayed inequalities and inclusion certify that \(L_2\) may be deleted: every complete route extending \(L_2\) has a feasible extension of \(L_1\) with no larger cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial route may be removed when another same-state label admits every one of its completions and realizes each at no greater total cost.
assumptions_latex: Labels \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) represent the same terminal state required for comparable extensions.

children.title: Reduction Safety Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which preprocessing reductions may remove valid or valuable solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Safety Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective invariance and extension preservation delimit safe reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Feasibility symmetry alone does not justify symmetry deletion. Let \(X=\{a,b\}\), let the permutation \(g\) exchange \(a\) and \(b\), and set \(c(a)=0\), \(c(b)=1\). Both points are feasible and form one orbit, but preprocessing that retains only \(b\) changes the optimum from \(0\) to \(1\). Likewise, dominance deletion is unsafe when the proposed dominator lacks a feasible completion available to the deleted label. Thus objective invariance for symmetry reduction and extension containment for dominance reduction are essential safety boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility-preserving permutation can still destroy the optimum when costs differ; dominance is likewise unsafe without containment of feasible completions.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem over the finite feasible set \(X=\{a,b\}\).
The preprocessing rule retains one arbitrary representative of each feasibility orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(c(gx)=c(x)\), orbit reduction need not preserve \(\min_{x\in X}c(x)\).

children.title: Separation-Oracle Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interface for separating a routing relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational point \(x^*\) and a polyhedron \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), a separation oracle returns either a row \((\alpha,\beta)\) satisfying \(\alpha^Tx\le\beta\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(\alpha^Tx^*>\beta\), or the certificate \(x^*\in P\). In a cutting-plane interface, every returned inequality is added to the current relaxation, which is then reoptimized. A declaration of membership is valid only when the oracle is complete for the designated inequality family or polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle either returns a valid inequality violated by the current point or certifies membership in the designated polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
The oracle uses exact arithmetic or certified tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle output is either \(\alpha^Tx^*>\beta\ge\sup_{x\in P}\alpha^Tx\) or \(x^*\in P\).

children.title: Pricing-Oracle Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost interface for route-column generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a restricted master problem with dual vector \(\pi\), each admissible route column \(r\) has reduced cost \(\bar c_r=c_r-\pi^Ta_r\), including any fixed dual contributions in this expression. A minimization pricing oracle returns a feasible route \(r^*\) minimizing \(\bar c_r\), or certifies \(\bar c_r\ge0\) for every admissible route. If \(\bar c_{r^*}<0\), add its column and reoptimize. Otherwise the current restricted-master solution is optimal for the full linear master problem, provided the master dual is feasible and pricing is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing finds a feasible route of negative reduced cost or certifies none exists; exact nonnegative pricing establishes full-master LP optimality.

The restricted master is solved to primal-dual optimality and pricing is exact.

children.title: Oracle Coordination
children.top_down_role: Scheduling, information exchange, or priority choices across routing oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exact coordination of separation and pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a feasible restricted master. At each iteration, solve it to primal-dual optimality, invoke separation at its primal solution, and add every selected violated valid inequality. After reoptimization, invoke pricing using the resulting dual vector and add a negative-reduced-cost route when one exists. Repeat because new cuts alter dual prices and new columns alter primal solutions. Stop only when separation certifies no designated violation and pricing certifies no negative reduced-cost admissible route. With finite cut and column pools and no duplicate additions, this procedure terminates at an optimum of the full designated LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate reoptimization, cut separation, and route pricing until neither oracle finds an improvement; exact finite pools then yield the designated full LP optimum.
assumptions_latex: The designated cut and route-column pools are finite.
Both oracles and every restricted-master solve are exact.
Every added cut is valid and every added column is admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the current solution is optimal for the LP containing all designated cuts and columns.

children.title: Branching Management

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive branching compatible with route pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional node solution \(x^*\), choose disjoint child regions \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\) satisfying \(X\cap D=\bigcup_{h=1}^k(X\cap D_h)\), where \(D\) is the parent region and \(X\) is the integer-feasible routing set. Create one child for each nonempty region, propagate its restrictions to the master and pricing problem, and prune a child only by infeasibility, bound dominance, or an incumbent cutoff. If every pricing oracle generates exactly the routes admissible under its child restrictions, exhaustive node processing preserves global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch into regions covering every parent integer solution, enforce each branch inside pricing, and prune only with valid infeasibility or bound certificates.
assumptions_latex: The child regions cover all integer-feasible solutions of the parent and may overlap only harmlessly.
Node bounds and pricing results are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive processing returns a globally optimal solution or certifies \(X=\varnothing\).

children.title: Cut Management
children.top_down_role: Selection, activation, aging, or removal of routing cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-preserving insertion and retirement of routing cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an active cut set \(C\). After solving the current relaxation at \(x^*\), accept a candidate inequality \(\alpha^Tx\le\beta\) only after certifying validity for every integer-feasible routing solution and violation \(\alpha^Tx^*>\beta+\varepsilon\). Add selected cuts, reoptimize, and optionally deactivate cuts after a stated inactivity rule. Deactivation removes only a relaxation constraint and therefore cannot exclude a feasible integer solution; any bound derived before deactivation remains usable only with its original node certificate. Terminate cut separation when no designated inequality exceeds the violation tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add only certified valid and sufficiently violated cuts. Retiring cuts preserves integer feasibility, but bounds must remain tied to the relaxation that produced them.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is the declared separation tolerance.
Every accepted inequality is valid for the integer-feasible routing set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut insertion never removes an integer-feasible solution, and cut deactivation cannot invalidate feasibility of any retained solution.

children.title: Column Management

knowledge_statements.title: Column Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact route-column insertion, retirement, and regeneration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an active route set \(R_A\). Solve the restricted master, call exact pricing, and add any admissible route \(r\notin R_A\) with reduced cost \(\bar c_r< -\varepsilon\). A nonbasic inactive column may be deleted from storage only if pricing can regenerate it whenever it again has improving reduced cost; basic columns are retained until a valid basis replacement is made. Stop when pricing certifies \(\bar c_r\ge-\varepsilon\) for all admissible routes. With \(\varepsilon=0\) and exact master solves, the resulting objective equals the full master LP optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add improving route columns, retire only regenerable nonbasic columns, and stop after exact pricing certifies that no admissible route has negative reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master remains feasible after every retirement operation.
Pricing ranges over the complete admissible route set.
For exact optimality, \(\varepsilon=0\) and arithmetic is exact.
