children.title: Cross-Component Coordination
children.top_down_role: Compatibility among branching decisions, active cuts, plus generated columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination invariant for branch-cut-column routing solvers at one search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a node relaxation with branching restrictions \(B\), active cuts \(C\), and generated columns \(J\), solve the restricted master over \(B\cap C\) using \(J\). Repeatedly: separate a violated valid inequality and add it to \(C\); price an admissible column of negative reduced cost and add it to \(J\); and re-solve. If the solution is integral, validate it before updating the incumbent. Fathom the node by its relaxation bound only after separation finds no violated required cut, pricing proves no improving admissible column exists, and every restriction in \(B\) is enforced. Otherwise branch using disjunctions compatible with both separation and pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate cut separation, column pricing, and reoptimization; accept validated integer incumbents and use node bounds only after all three components certify consistency.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master is solved to the accuracy required by its bound certificate.
Separation and pricing preserve the node's branching restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting incumbent and node-bound decisions are coordinated across branching, cutting, and column generation.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports branch-cut-column coordination semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the coordination leaf, but no cited source supports its branch-cut-price termination conditions. The phrase “master over B intersect C” is also ill-typed unless B and C denote feasible regions rather than collections of restrictions.

children.title: Warm-Start Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of prior routing solutions or solver state into a new solve.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe transfer of solver state between related routing formulations or reoptimization episodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the solved model and \(P'\) the modified model. Map each retained variable and constraint by a stable identifier. Transfer a primal vector \(x\) only after projecting it to the variables of \(P'\) and checking feasibility in \(P'\). Transfer a basis or factorization only when the mapped matrix rows, columns, bounds, and senses remain compatible; otherwise use it solely as a repair seed. Transfer dual multipliers only as search hints unless dual feasibility for \(P'\) is rechecked. Initialize the new solve with the accepted state, and derive no bound or optimality claim from unchecked transferred data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map reusable state into the modified model, revalidate every transferred certificate, and treat incompatible primal, basis, or dual information only as a heuristic seed.
assumptions_latex: Models \(P\) and \(P'\) have stable identifiers for retained objects.
The solver exposes the relevant primal, basis, or dual state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every state item used certifiably for \(P'\) is feasible or compatible under \(P'\); all other items are noncertifying hints.
review_flags: Solver-state transfer rules require a direct implementation or optimization-solver source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits warm-start transfer, but the certificate-preserving conditions for primal, basis, factorization, and dual transfer require a solver or optimization reference. Projection alone also does not specify values for newly introduced variables.

children.title: Incumbent Exchange
children.top_down_role: Movement of feasible routing solutions across solver components.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange protocol for feasible routing incumbents among cooperating solver components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a global incumbent \((x^*,z^*)\), initially absent. When a component publishes a candidate \(x\), reconstruct its complete routing representation and independently validate integrality, tour or route structure, service coverage, and all active resource, schedule, and precedence constraints. Recompute \(z=c^\top x\) from the authoritative objective data. For minimization, replace \((x^*,z^*)\) by \((x,z)\) exactly when validation succeeds and either no incumbent exists or \(z<z^*-\varepsilon\). Broadcast only the validated pair and its model-version identifier; recipients must reject it if their feasible region or objective version differs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Share an incumbent only after independent feasibility and objective checks, accepting genuine improvements solely between components using the same model version.
assumptions_latex: The routing problem is a minimization problem.
The comparison tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every broadcast incumbent is feasible for its identified model version and has an authoritatively recomputed objective value.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not document a solver-level incumbent exchange protocol.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches incumbent exchange and is internally coherent for minimization, but no inspectable source supports the proposed validation, versioning, and broadcast protocol.

children.title: Reoptimization Triggers
children.top_down_role: Events that initiate renewed optimization after model or solution changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Reoptimization Triggers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate deciding when accumulated routing-model changes require another optimization solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_k\) be the model state at the last certified solve and \(M\) the current state. Reoptimization is required when \(M\ne M_k\) and at least one change can alter feasibility, the objective ordering, or a certified bound. Concretely, trigger when a variable, constraint, coefficient, bound, objective coefficient, branching restriction, cut, or priced column has been added, removed, or changed and its effect has not been certified redundant. Also trigger when an incumbent improves enough to change pruning decisions or when accumulated numerical residuals exceed their prescribed tolerances. Mere metadata or logging changes do not trigger reoptimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reoptimize after any uncertified change that can affect feasibility, objective ordering, bounds, pruning, or numerical validity; ignore purely descriptive changes.
assumptions_latex: Model states carry versioned mathematical data.
Numerical feasibility and optimality tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trigger predicate holds exactly for an uncertified change capable of invalidating the current solve state or its search decisions.

notation.meaning: Model at the last certified solve

review_flags: A direct source is needed for the intended solver-state trigger policy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the claimed exact trigger predicate is implementation-dependent and unsupported. In particular, an improved incumbent can alter pruning without necessarily requiring reoptimization of every relaxation.

children.title: State-Reuse Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where retained solver state becomes invalid, stale, or counterproductive.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Reuse Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Changes beyond which reused routing-solver state ceases to be a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solver state is certifying only relative to the model for which its defining predicates were checked. Adding a constraint can make a stored incumbent infeasible; deleting a constraint can invalidate a previously optimal dual bound; changing \(c\) can invalidate reduced costs and objective comparisons; and changing the row or column set can invalidate a basis or factorization. Thus, for a modified model \(P'\), an old state item may be reused as a certificate only after rechecking its primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, dimensional-compatibility, and objective-consistency predicates that are affected by the modification. Without those checks, reuse is bounded to heuristic initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model changes can invalidate incumbents, bounds, reduced costs, and bases; unchecked old state may initialize search but cannot certify feasibility or optimality.
assumptions_latex: The original and modified models are \(P\) and \(P'\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unchecked state from \(P\) supplies no feasibility, bound, or optimality certificate for \(P'\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly establishes solver-state certificate boundaries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and local meaning are appropriate, but no cited source establishes the stated certificate boundaries for incumbents, dual bounds, reduced costs, bases, and factorizations.

children.title: Tour Validation
children.top_down_role: Structural checks for claimed TSP tours.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for a directed Hamiltonian tour in a routing graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\), a sequence \(T=(v_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_{\pi(n)},v_{\pi(1)})\) validates a tour exactly when \(\pi\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \((v_{\pi(i)},v_{\pi(i+1)})\in A\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), where \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). The certificate is checked by marking vertices during one scan and testing each consecutive arc. It certifies one closed walk visiting every vertex exactly once, independently of any claimed objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tour certificate is a cyclic permutation of all vertices whose consecutive directed arcs, including the closing arc, belong to the graph.
assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
The claimed tour explicitly includes or implies its closing arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated sequence is a directed Hamiltonian circuit of \(G\).

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Hamiltonian circuits and the traveling salesman problem p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Hamiltonian circuits and the traveling salesman problem p. 5

children.title: Route Validation
children.top_down_role: Structural checks for individual vehicle routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Route Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural certificate for depot-based vehicle routes before resource and scheduling checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have depot set \(D\). A claimed route \(R=(d,v_1,\ldots,v_m,d')\) is structurally valid when \(d,d'\in D\), every consecutive pair in \(R\) belongs to \(A\), every internal vertex belongs to \(V\setminus D\), and any vertex declared nonrepeatable occurs at most once. If closed single-depot routes are required, additionally \(d=d'\). A route collection is structurally valid when every member satisfies these conditions and its number of routes does not exceed the available fleet size. Resource, timing, precedence, and global coverage remain separate validation obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each route must connect permitted depots through available arcs, obey vertex-repeat rules, and fit the fleet count; other constraints require separate checks.
assumptions_latex: The routing graph and depot set are finite.
The instance specifies whether routes are closed and which vertices may repeat.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The claimed sequences constitute structurally admissible depot routes, subject to separate cross-constraint validation.
review_flags: The supplied TSP locator does not directly support depot-route and fleet validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate fits structural route validation and properly separates resource and scheduling obligations, but it has no source supporting the depot, repeatability, and fleet-size criteria.

children.title: Service-Coverage Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks for required, optional, duplicated, or omitted customer service.

knowledge_statements.title: Service-Coverage Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multiplicity check for customer service across a route collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) index routes, let \(C\) be the customer set, and let \(y_{ik}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) count validated service occurrences of customer \(i\) on route \(k\). Given required multiplicities \(r_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), exact service coverage is certified by \(\sum_{k\in K}y_{ik}=r_i\) for every \(i\in C\). For optional service with acceptance variable \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\), replace the right-hand side by \(r_i a_i\). Counts must be derived from the authoritative route sequences rather than accepted from a separate unverified assignment array.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count each customer's service occurrences directly from validated routes and compare the total with its required multiplicity or accepted optional demand.
assumptions_latex: All routes in \(K\) have been structurally validated.
Each service occurrence has an unambiguous customer identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every customer receives exactly its required number of services under the selected service policy.

notation.meaning: Service count for customer i on route k

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports fleet-routing service multiplicity validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicity certificate is mathematically coherent and fits service-coverage validation, but no inspectable routing source is cited for the required and optional-service formulations.

children.title: Representation Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency across arc, sequence, assignment, or route-pool representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency certificate between route sequences, arc variables, and service variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given validated route sequences \(\mathcal R\), define \(m_{ij}(\mathcal R)\) as the number of traversals of arc \((i,j)\) and \(s_i(\mathcal R)\) as the number of services of customer \(i\). An arc-service representation \((x,y)\) is consistent with \(\mathcal R\) exactly when \(x_{ij}=m_{ij}(\mathcal R)\) for every modeled arc and \(y_i=s_i(\mathcal R)\) for every modeled customer. If vehicle-indexed variables are used, the equalities hold route by route. Zero must be checked for modeled arcs and customers absent from the sequences; otherwise omitted entries can conceal inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reconstruct arc traversals and service counts from route sequences, then require exact equality with every corresponding model variable, including zeros.
assumptions_latex: The route-to-vehicle correspondence is known when variables are vehicle-indexed.
All modeled arcs and customers can be enumerated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence, arc, and service representations encode the same routing solution.
review_flags: No supplied source directly treats consistency among fleet-routing representations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate matches representation consistency, but exact equality depends on whether arc and service variables encode binary use or traversal multiplicity. No source fixes those representation semantics.

children.title: Resource Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks for capacity, energy, loading, or other route resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cumulative-resource feasibility certificate along each vehicle route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each route \(R_k=(v_{k0},\ldots,v_{km_k})\), resource \(q\), initial level \(u_{kq0}\), transition function \(F_q\), and permitted interval \([L_{vq},U_{vq}]\), validate levels recursively by \(u_{kq,r+1}=F_q(u_{kqr},v_{kr},v_{k,r+1})\). The route is resource-feasible exactly when \(L_{v_{kr},q}\le u_{kqr}\le U_{v_{kr},q}\) at every position and every resource-specific terminal condition holds. For additive consumption, the transition is \(F_q(u,i,j)=u+g_{ijq}\). Reported levels certify feasibility only when they satisfy both the transitions and all bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagate every resource along each route and check all position bounds and terminal conditions; reported levels alone are insufficient.
assumptions_latex: Resource transitions are deterministic for the claimed route.
Every resource has specified initial, positional, and terminal conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each validated route respects every modeled cumulative-resource constraint.

notation.meaning: Level of resource q at route-k position r
Permitted resource interval at vertex v

review_flags: A vehicle-routing source covering cumulative-resource feasibility is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive certificate fits cumulative-resource validation, but its general transition model, positional bounds, and terminal conditions lack an inspectable vehicle-routing source.

children.title: Schedule Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks for service times, travel times, waiting, or route duration.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-window and travel-propagation certificate for a fixed route collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For route \(R_k=(v_{k0},\ldots,v_{km_k})\), let \(t_{kr}\) be service-start time, \([a_v,b_v]\) the time window, \(s_v\) service duration, and \(\tau_{ij}\) travel time. The schedule is valid exactly when \(a_{v_{kr}}\le t_{kr}\le b_{v_{kr}}\) for every position and \(t_{k,r+1}\ge t_{kr}+s_{v_{kr}}+\tau_{v_{kr},v_{k,r+1}}\) for every consecutive pair. Any route-duration, shift, synchronization, or depot-return deadline specified by the instance must also hold. Waiting is represented by strict slack in the propagation inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check every service time against its window, propagate service and travel durations along routes, and enforce all route-level deadlines and synchronization constraints.
assumptions_latex: Travel and service durations are expressed in a common time scale.
The claimed route order is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The claimed service-start times form a temporally feasible schedule for the route collection.

notation.meaning: Service-start time at route-k position r
Travel time from i to j

review_flags: The supplied locators do not directly cover vehicle-routing schedule validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-window propagation certificate fits schedule validation and is internally consistent, but no cited source supports the routing-specific schedule and synchronization obligations.

children.title: Precedence Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks for required ordering among pickups, deliveries, or services.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Route-membership and ordering certificate for pickup-delivery or general precedence pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq V\times V\) be required precedence pairs, where \((i,j)\in P\) means service at \(i\) must precede service at \(j\). For each serviced vertex \(v\), record its route index \(k(v)\) and position \(p(v)\). If a pair requires common carriage, validate \(k(i)=k(j)\); in every case validate the applicable order predicate, ordinarily \(p(i)<p(j)\). For time-based precedence, additionally require \(t_j\ge t_i+s_i+\delta_{ij}\), where \(\delta_{ij}\) is the prescribed minimum lag. All predicates must be checked for every active pair, including conditionally activated pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every active precedence pair, verify required route sharing, visit order, and any minimum time lag between the two services.
assumptions_latex: Each serviced vertex has an unambiguous route and position.
The instance identifies common-route and time-lag requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every active precedence relation is respected by the claimed routes and schedule.

notation.meaning: Position of serviced vertex v on its route

review_flags: A direct pickup-delivery or precedence-constrained routing source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate fits precedence validation, but no source supports the pickup-delivery and conditional-pair rules. Position comparisons are meaningful only on a common route; cross-route precedence requires a separately specified time-based predicate.

children.title: Cross-Constraint Consistency
children.top_down_role: Checks for interactions among resources, schedules, plus precedence restrictions.

assumptions_latex: A candidate fleet solution specifies finite routes, service start times, vehicle loads, and resource states.
All travel, service, precedence, time-window, capacity, and resource data use common units and indexing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is cross-constraint consistent if and only if every route transition and customer assignment satisfies the combined validation predicate \(C(S)=1\).

notation.meaning: indicator that all coupled constraints hold

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint validation of routing, resources, timing, and precedence for one reported fleet solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each served customer \(i\), let \(r(i)\) be its unique assigned route. A candidate solution \(S\) is cross-constraint consistent when every customer is assigned exactly once, every route is depot-compatible, and all state recursions use the same route order: arrival and service times respect travel, service, and time-window constraints; loads and other resources respect transition equations and bounds; and every precedence pair \((i,j)\) requires compatible assignment and \(t_i+s_i+\tau_{ij}\le t_j\) whenever direct or prescribed precedence applies. The finite collection of these checks is a certificate \(C(S)\), with \(C(S)=1\) precisely when no constraint is validated using assignments, arcs, or states inconsistent with another check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is certified only when assignment, route, time, resource, and precedence checks all refer to the same decisions and satisfy every coupled constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Constraint Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the validation leaf, but no source supports the combined predicate or the stated precedence-time condition, whose applicability depends on the routing model.

children.title: Objective Recomputation
children.top_down_role: Independent recomputation of routing cost, reward, penalties, or composite objectives.

assumptions_latex: The instance and reported solution determine every objective component without solver-internal state.
All objective coefficients and numerical conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified primal value is \(z(S)=\sum_{k}\sum_{(i,j)}c_{ij}^{k}x_{ij}^{k}+\sum_k f_k y_k+P(S)\), independently recomputed from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent recomputation for an additive minimization objective, including fixed and penalty terms.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Problem Formulation and Applications p. 52
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a reported solution \(S\), first reconstruct each indicator \(x_{ij}^{k}\) from consecutive visits of vehicle \(k\), and set \(y_k=1\) exactly when vehicle \(k\) is used. Evaluate every distance, duration, fixed-cost, service, and penalty term directly from the instance data and reconstructed decisions. For an additive minimization objective, output \[z(S)=\sum_k\sum_{(i,j)}c_{ij}^{k}x_{ij}^{k}+\sum_k f_k y_k+P(S).\] Accumulate terms under the declared exact or tolerance-controlled arithmetic convention. The recomputed value, rather than a solver log or rounded display value, is the objective used for primal-bound and gap certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reconstruct objective terms from the submitted routes and instance data, sum them under declared arithmetic rules, and use that independent total for certification.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Recomputation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Problem Formulation and Applications p. 52
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the cited shortest-path formulation does not establish this fleet-objective reconstruction with vehicle fixed costs and the unspecified term P(S). A routing-specific objective and validation source is required.

children.title: Primal-Bound Status
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of incumbent objective values as primal bounds.

assumptions_latex: The routing problem is a minimization problem with optimum \(z^*\).
The candidate solution \(S\) has passed all feasibility checks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(U=z(S)\) is a certified primal upper bound satisfying \(z^*\le U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound status for a feasible solution to a minimization routing problem.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the primal-bound status of a reported solution \(S\) by \(\operatorname{PB}(S)=\mathrm{certified}\) exactly when feasibility validation accepts \(S\) and independent objective recomputation returns a finite value \(U=z(S)\). Since \(S\) then belongs to the feasible set of the minimization problem, \[z^*\le z(S)=U.\] If feasibility is rejected, an objective component cannot be reproduced, or the reported value differs from the recomputed value beyond the declared numerical tolerance, the reported primal bound is not certified. The certificate consists of the validated solution, the recomputed objective decomposition, and the arithmetic convention used to obtain \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution with a reproducible objective value certifies an upper bound for minimization; failed feasibility or objective checks leave the bound uncertified.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Bound Status

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

children.title: Dual-Bound Status
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of relaxation or search bounds as dual bounds.

assumptions_latex: The routing problem is a minimization problem with optimum \(z^*\).
A stated relaxation, dual problem, or valid bounding procedure is mathematically specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A verified value \(L\) is a certified dual lower bound only when \(L\le z^*\) follows from weak duality or another valid bound argument.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certification by a feasible dual witness or another explicitly valid relaxation bound.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Interpretation of CS and the Dual Problem p. 162
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A claimed value \(L\) has certified dual-bound status when it is accompanied by a verifiable witness \(\lambda\) feasible for the explicitly stated dual or bounding relaxation, all reduced-cost or dual-feasibility inequalities are satisfied under the declared tolerance, and evaluation of the dual objective at \(\lambda\) yields \(L\). Weak duality then gives \[L\le z_R^*\le z^*,\] where \(z_R^*\) is the relaxation optimum. A solver-reported best bound without a reproducible witness or independently checkable valid-bound derivation has reported status only; it is not a mathematical certificate. Any tolerance adjustment must preserve a rigorously valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound is certified when an independently checkable dual or relaxation witness proves it no larger than the true minimization optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Status

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.1 Interpretation of CS and the Dual Problem p. 162
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

children.title: Gap Certification
children.top_down_role: Validation of claimed absolute or relative optimality gaps.

assumptions_latex: The certified bounds satisfy \(L\le z^*\le U\).
The problem is a minimization problem and \(U\) and \(L\) use the same objective convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The absolute gap \(G=U-L\) certifies \(0\le U-z^*\le G\); if \(U=L\), the incumbent is optimal.

notation.meaning: relative gap under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative optimality-gap certificates for minimization with separately certified bounds.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given independently certified bounds \(L\le z^*\le U\), define the absolute gap by \(G=U-L\). Then \[0\le U-z^*\le U-L=G.\] Thus \(G\) certifies the incumbent's maximum absolute suboptimality, and \(G=0\) certifies optimality. When a relative gap is requested and \(\max\{|U|,|L|,\epsilon\}>0\), a declared convention may use \[g_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{U-L}{\max\{|U|,|L|,\epsilon\}},\] with fixed \(\epsilon>0\). The certificate must state this denominator convention; a percentage without it is ambiguous near zero or when bounds have different signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified lower and upper bounds give an absolute optimality gap; equality proves optimality, while relative gaps require an explicit denominator convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap Certification

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

children.title: Relaxation Weakness
children.top_down_role: Routing formulations whose continuous relaxations poorly constrain feasible integer solutions.

assumptions_latex: A minimization formulation has integer feasible set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and relaxation \(P\supseteq X\).
Both integer and relaxation optima are finite for the objective considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation is weak for objective \(c\) when \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\) is large relative to the chosen normalization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-dependent weakness of a linear relaxation for a minimization routing formulation.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.1. Problem Formulation p. 215

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For objective vector \(c\), define \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X\}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)=\min\{c^\top x:x\in P\}\). Since \(X\subseteq P\), \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)\). The relaxation is weak on a family of routing instances when there exist objectives for which the additive gap \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\), or a stated scale-invariant ratio when its denominator is positive, becomes large. The failure mechanism is the presence of fractional points in \(P\) that combine incompatible route, connectivity, or resource decisions and attain costs substantially below every integral fleet solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation is weak when fractional routing solutions satisfy its constraints yet achieve objective values substantially better than every feasible integer solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Weakness

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.1. Problem Formulation p. 215

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and objective-dependent definition are reasonable, but the cited minimum-cost-flow formulation section does not support the routing integrality-gap claim or its asserted failure mechanism.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Growth
children.top_down_role: Instance or formulation regimes associated with widening primal–dual separation.

assumptions_latex: For each instance size \(n\), the integer and relaxed minimization optima are finite.
The denominator used for any multiplicative gap is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gap growth occurs when \(g_n=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(n)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\) or \(\rho_n=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(n)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\) is unbounded along an instance subsequence.

notation.meaning: integer and relaxation optima at size n

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic additive or multiplicative gap growth along a specified routing-instance family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a sequence of routing instances \((I_n)\) with integer optima \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(n)\) and relaxation optima \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\). The formulation exhibits additive integrality-gap growth if \[g_n=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(n)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\] is unbounded along some subsequence. When \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)>0\), it exhibits multiplicative gap growth if \[\rho_n=\frac{z_{\mathrm{IP}}(n)}{z_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)}\] is unbounded, or exceeds a claimed uniform approximation factor. The family, objective scaling, and choice of additive or multiplicative normalization must be fixed; otherwise gap growth can be created or removed merely by rescaling or translating objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrality-gap growth means a fixed formulation's integer and relaxation optima separate without bound along a clearly normalized family of routing instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the normalization qualifications are important, but no source supports the asserted asymptotic routing-family gap criterion.

children.title: Formulation-Strengthening Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits of practical strengthening through additional variables or inequalities.

assumptions_latex: A base relaxation is \(P\), and \(\mathcal C\) is a specified class of valid inequalities.
The strengthened region is \(P_{\mathcal C}=P\cap\bigcap_{a^\top x\le b\in\mathcal C}\{x:a^\top x\le b\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strengthening by \(\mathcal C\) is insufficient whenever \(P_{\mathcal C}\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(X)\), equivalently when a fractional point survives every inequality in \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of a specified inequality family, without claiming a universal lower bound on all formulations.

source_refs.locator: 5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the integral routing solutions and let \(P\) be a relaxation. For a specified inequality class \(\mathcal C\), form \[P_{\mathcal C}=P\cap\bigcap_{a^\top x\le b\in\mathcal C}\{x:a^\top x\le b\}.\] The strengthening reaches its structural limit if there exists \(\bar x\in P_{\mathcal C}\setminus\operatorname{conv}(X)\). Such a fractional point satisfies every inequality allowed by \(\mathcal C\), so no additional inequality from that same class can remove it. For any objective separating \(\bar x\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\), a relaxation gap remains. This statement concerns the declared class \(\mathcal C\); it does not imply that extended formulations or inequalities outside \(\mathcal C\) are ineffective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality class reaches its limit when a fractional routing point survives every inequality in the class, leaving the strengthened region larger than the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Formulation-Strengthening Limits

source_witnesses.locator: 5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the statement is properly limited to a specified inequality class. The cited total-dual-integrality section does not specifically support the surviving-fractional-point or separation claims.

children.title: Pricing-Subproblem Explosion
children.top_down_role: Growth in the size or difficulty of routing pricing subproblems.

assumptions_latex: Pricing seeks a minimum-reduced-cost feasible route over a customer set.
Routes may be required to be elementary and satisfy side constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explicit route search space can contain exponentially many routes, and elementary constrained pricing contains NP-hard route-selection problems as special cases.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case combinatorial growth of elementary resource-constrained route pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pricing oracle must compute \(\min\{\bar c_r:r\in\mathcal R\}\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the set of feasible routes. Even before resource restrictions, the number of elementary customer sequences may be \[\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!},\] which is exponential in \(n\). With elementarity and route-length or resource constraints, the oracle contains prize-collecting, constrained shortest-path, or traveling-salesperson-type selection as special cases, so polynomial enumeration of all routes is unavailable in general unless additional structure is imposed. The scaling boundary is reached when exact pricing requires exploring exponentially many combinatorial route choices or solving an NP-hard embedded selection problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing can face exponentially many elementary routes and NP-hard constrained route selection, so exact column generation may spend most computation inside its pricing oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Subproblem Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is suitable for this leaf, but the embedded NP-hard special-case claim requires an authoritative pricing or elementary resource-constrained shortest-path source. The route count grows as 2^{Theta(n log n)}, so calling it merely exponential is imprecise.

children.title: Label-Set Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Rapid growth of nondominated or temporarily retained pricing labels.

assumptions_latex: A label-setting pricing algorithm stores nondominated partial paths at each vertex.
Dominance compares reduced cost and all resource coordinates componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vertex may retain \(\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}=2^{\Theta(d)}/\Theta(\sqrt d)\) mutually nondominated labels.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case antichain size under componentwise resource dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a vertex \(v\), construct one label \(\ell_S\) for every subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) of size \(\lfloor d/2\rfloor\), with equal reduced costs and binary resource vector \(q(\ell_S)=\mathbf 1_S\). For distinct \(S\) and \(T\) of equal size, neither \(q(\ell_S)\le q(\ell_T)\) nor \(q(\ell_T)\le q(\ell_S)\) holds componentwise. Hence no label dominates another, and \[|\mathcal L(v)|\ge\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}=\frac{2^{\Theta(d)}}{\Theta(\sqrt d)}.\] Thus a correct label-setting algorithm may retain exponentially many labels at one vertex, even before accounting for different visited-customer memories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise dominance can leave an exponentially large antichain of resource vectors, forcing a label-setting algorithm to retain exponentially many partial routes at one vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Label-Set Proliferation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The antichain argument is plausible, but the record does not establish that all constructed labels are reachable and feasible in one pricing instance. Also, the central binomial coefficient should be stated as Theta(2^d/sqrt(d)), not 2^{Theta(d)}/Theta(sqrt(d)).

children.title: Dominance Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Regimes where dominance tests remove too few pricing labels.

assumptions_latex: Labels at one vertex are compared by reduced cost and componentwise resource use.
Every constructed label remains extendable under the same continuation conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The labels \(\ell_S\) indexed by equal-cardinality subsets are pairwise incomparable, so ordinary componentwise dominance removes none of them.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of componentwise label dominance with many independent resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\ge2\) and create, at the same vertex, labels \(\ell_S\) for all subsets \(S\subseteq\{1,ldots,d\}\) with \(|S|=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\). Give every label the same reduced cost and resource vector \(q(\ell_S)=\mathbf 1_S\), and arrange identical feasible continuations. Under ordinary dominance, \(\ell_S\) dominates \(\ell_T\) only if its cost is no larger and \(\mathbf 1_S\le\mathbf 1_T\) componentwise. Equal cardinality makes this possible only when \(S=T\). Consequently all \(\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\) labels survive. The breakdown is caused by mutually conflicting resource advantages: each partial route is better in some coordinates and worse in others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-cost labels using different equal-sized subsets of resources are pairwise incomparable, so standard componentwise dominance cannot discard any of them.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits, but the set is malformed as {1,ldots,d}, and no construction or source establishes that the labels have realizable identical continuations in a resource-constrained pricing instance.

children.title: Resource-Dimension Scaling
children.top_down_role: Label-growth effects caused by additional or finer-grained resource dimensions.

assumptions_latex: There are \(d\) integer resources with bounds \(0\le q_j\le B_j\).
A dynamic program distinguishes exact resource-state vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource-state space has at most \(\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\) vectors and can require that order in the absence of effective dominance.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial state scaling for integer-resource label dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integer resources \(q_j\in\{0,1,\ldots,B_j\}\), the Cartesian resource-state space contains \[N_q=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\] vectors. A vertex-indexed dynamic program that distinguishes exact resource vectors therefore has a pseudo-polynomial state bound proportional to \(|V|N_q\), before path-memory states are included. When dominance or reachability does not eliminate a constant fraction of these vectors, time and memory can scale on this order. If every \(B_j\ge1\), then \(N_q\ge2^d\); hence the state representation is exponential in the number of independently tracked resources, although it is polynomial in the numerical bounds when \(d\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact integer-resource states scale as a product of resource bounds, becoming exponential in the number of resource dimensions even when each bound is small.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Dimension Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product is a correct upper count for bounded integer resource vectors, but the claim that this order can be required needs a sourced construction showing reachability and nondominance of that many states.

children.title: Degenerate Master Solutions
children.top_down_role: Restricted-master regimes with many equivalent or weakly distinguished basic solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Master Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a basic feasible solution in a route-based restricted master linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the route-based restricted master problem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(r\). Let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a basis with \(|B|=r\), and let \(x^*\) be its basic feasible solution. The master solution is degenerate with respect to \(B\) exactly when \(x_i^*=0\) for some \(i\in B\); equivalently, fewer than \(r\) basic variables are strictly positive. Degeneracy is a boundary at which distinct bases may represent the same primal solution, but the existence of an alternative basis requires additional pivot structure and is not implied by degeneracy alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted-master basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic route variable is zero. Distinct bases may then represent the same solution, but degeneracy alone does not guarantee an alternative basis.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=r\).
The index set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a basis with \(|B|=r\), and \(x^*\) is its basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution \(x^*\) is degenerate with respect to \(B\) if and only if \(x_i^*=0\) for at least one \(i\in B\).

notation.meaning: Restricted-master matrix, right-hand side, and cost vector.
Rank of the restricted-master constraint matrix.

children.title: Bound-Improvement Tail-Off
children.top_down_role: Late-stage regimes with diminishing improvement in routing bounds.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), the valid restricted-master bound is \(L_k\), with \(L_{k+1}\ge L_k\).
A tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) and a window length \(w\in\mathbb N\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tail-off over the window ending at \(k\) is certified by \(0\le L_k-L_{k-w}\le\varepsilon\) while the chosen termination condition remains false.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound after iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational tail-off predicate for monotone bounds in routing column generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L_k)_{k\ge0}\) be the nondecreasing sequence of valid lower bounds produced by a minimization-oriented restricted-master procedure. For fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(w\in\mathbb N\), bound-improvement tail-off is present at iteration \(k\ge w\) when \[0\le L_k-L_{k-w}\le\varepsilon\] and the algorithm's exact stopping condition is still false. A relative variant replaces the right-hand inequality by \(L_k-L_{k-w}\le\varepsilon\max\{1,|L_{k-w}|\}\). The predicate diagnoses slow progress; it does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail-off occurs when a monotone valid bound improves by at most a chosen tolerance over a fixed window although exact termination has not occurred.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Improvement Tail-Off

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predicate is mathematically coherent and fits a condition leaf, but the tolerance, window, bound convention, and stopping test are algorithm-dependent and have no cited routing column-generation source.

children.title: Dual Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Unstable dual-price behavior across successive master problem solutions.

assumptions_latex: The restricted master has a nonempty dual-optimal set \(D^*\).
The algorithm produces dual iterates \(\pi^k\) in a normed finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual oscillation occurs when \(\operatorname{dist}(\pi^k,D^*)\to0\) but \((\pi^k)\) does not converge.

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic dual nonconvergence despite approach to the optimal dual face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\pi^k)_{k\ge0}\) be dual multipliers generated by successive restricted masters, and let \(D^*\) be the dual-optimal set of the full master problem. Dual oscillation means that \[\operatorname{dist}(\pi^k,D^*)\longrightarrow0\] while \((\pi^k)\) itself does not converge. Equivalently in finite dimensions, it has at least two distinct accumulation points in \(D^*\). A finite-window diagnostic may detect repeated large displacements, but only the accumulation-point condition defines the asymptotic failure; changing multipliers alone is insufficient if all iterates converge to one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual oscillation means dual iterates approach the optimal dual set but fail to converge, having at least two distinct optimal accumulation points.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Oscillation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed equivalence with two accumulation points requires boundedness or relative compactness of the dual sequence. Distance to an unbounded optimal set can tend to zero while the iterates diverge and have no accumulation point. A source is also required for the chosen notion of dual oscillation.

children.title: Stabilization Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where stabilization provides insufficient control or impedes useful pricing signals.

assumptions_latex: The unstabilized pricing problem uses reduced cost \(\bar c_r(\pi)=c_r-a_r^{\mathsf T}\pi\).
A stabilization rule replaces \(\pi^k\) by a pricing center \(s^k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure is witnessed if stabilization either permanently excludes a negative-reduced-cost route or fails to control nonconvergent dual displacement.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of route r under dual vector pi.
Column vector and cost of route r.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic boundary separating ineffective stabilization from stabilization that preserves exact pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stabilization scheme is in a failure regime if at least one of two properties is violated. Exactness fails when there exist an iteration \(K\) and a route \(r\) such that \(\bar c_r(\pi^k)<0\) for some \(k\ge K\), yet the stabilized pricing rule permanently prevents \(r\) and every equivalent improving column from entering. Control fails when the stabilized centers satisfy \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|s^{k+1}-s^k\|>0\) along a bounded sequence while bound improvement tends to zero. The first mechanism can invalidate convergence; the second makes stabilization ineffective against oscillation or tail-off.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stabilization fails if it permanently suppresses genuinely improving routes or does not control persistent dual movement while bound progress vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Stabilization Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exactness and control criteria are not established generic stabilization boundaries. A route having negative reduced cost at one iteration does not alone make its permanent exclusion convergence-invalid, and persistent center displacement with vanishing bound improvement need not prove stabilization failure. Scheme-specific hypotheses and evidence are required.

assumptions_latex: At a branch-and-price node, feasible columns belong to \(\mathcal R\), and branching imposes predicate \(B(r)\).
The pricing oracle searches a representable family \(\mathcal R_P\subseteq\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching and pricing are incompatible when \(\mathcal R_P\ne\{r\in\mathcal R:B(r)\}\), unless omitted feasible routes are provably irrelevant.

notation.meaning: Route family representable by the pricing oracle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability boundary for branching constraints in a route-pricing oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the branching decision retain exactly the route family \(\mathcal R_B=\{r\in\mathcal R:B(r)\}\), and let \(\mathcal R_P\) be the family actually representable by the pricing oracle after branching. Branching and pricing are compatible when \(\mathcal R_P=\mathcal R_B\) and reduced costs are evaluated with the branched master dual. They are incompatible when the oracle admits a route outside \(\mathcal R_B\), or excludes a route in \(\mathcal R_B\) that can have negative reduced cost. Incompatibility respectively yields invalid columns or an incomplete optimality test at the branch-and-price node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching rule is pricing-incompatible when the modified pricing oracle generates forbidden routes or cannot represent an allowed route that may have negative reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching–Pricing Incompatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the container, but equality of represented and branched route families is stronger than necessary unless representation, feasibility filtering, and reduced-cost completeness are defined precisely. A branch-and-price source is required.

children.title: Disconnected Neighborhood Graphs
children.top_down_role: Structural barriers that prevent local search from reaching relevant regions of the routing solution space.

assumptions_latex: The feasible routing-solution set \(S\) is finite.
A symmetric move relation \(N\subseteq S\times S\) defines allowable local-search transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The neighborhood graph is disconnected if and only if \(S\) has a nonempty proper subset \(C\) with no neighborhood edge from \(C\) to \(S\setminus C\).

notation.meaning: Finite set of feasible routing solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity of the undirected graph induced by feasible local-search moves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite feasible set \(S\) and symmetric neighborhood relation \(N\), define the neighborhood graph \(G_N=(S,E_N)\) by \(\{x,y\}\in E_N\) exactly when \(x\ne y\) and \((x,y)\in N\). The graph is disconnected precisely when there exists a nonempty proper subset \(C\subset S\) such that no edge joins \(C\) to \(S\setminus C\). Consequently, a local search initialized in \(C\) and restricted to moves from \(N\) cannot reach any feasible solution outside \(C\), irrespective of its acceptance or selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A routing neighborhood graph is disconnected when feasible solutions split into components with no allowed move between them, making cross-component search impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Neighborhood Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-theoretic statement is precise and the definition fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports its application to routing neighborhoods.

children.title: Search-State Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated revisitation of routing states or move patterns without durable progress.

assumptions_latex: The deterministic local-search update is a map \(T:S\to S\) on a finite state space \(S\).
The trajectory satisfies \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cycling occurs exactly when \(x^{k+p}=x^k\) for some \(k\ge0\) and minimal period \(p\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic cycling for deterministic finite-state local search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and let \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) for a deterministic update map \(T:S\to S\). Search-state cycling occurs when there exist \(k\ge0\) and a least integer \(p\ge2\) such that \(x^{k+p}=x^k\). Determinism then implies \(x^{t+p}=x^t\) for every \(t\ge k\), so the trajectory repeats the same \(p\) states indefinitely. The restriction \(p\ge2\) distinguishes cycling from stagnation at a fixed point, for which \(T(x^k)=x^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic local search cycles when it enters a periodic orbit of at least two states; a one-state orbit is stagnation instead.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-State Cycling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended finite-state cycling definition is standard, but the least period must be the least positive integer satisfying the recurrence. As written, taking the least integer only among those at least two can misclassify a fixed point, since it also satisfies a two-step equality. A source and corrected quantifier are required.

children.title: Local-Search Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Prolonged failure to improve routing quality despite continued neighborhood exploration.

assumptions_latex: The routing objective is \(f:S\to\mathbb R\), to be minimized.
The neighborhood of \(x\) is \(N(x)\subseteq S\), and only strict improvements are accepted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Search stagnates at \(x^k\) when \(f(y)\ge f(x^k)\) for every \(y\in N(x^k)\), although a better feasible solution may exist outside that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagnation under strict-improvement acceptance in a fixed routing neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization over \(S\), a strict-improvement local search stagnates at state \(x^k\) when \[f(y)\ge f(x^k)\quad\text{for every }y\in N(x^k).\] Its update therefore returns \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). This condition certifies only local optimality relative to \(N\). Global suboptimal stagnation occurs when, in addition, there exists \(z\in S\) with \(f(z)<f(x^k)\). Thus stagnation can result from a restrictive neighborhood even when the neighborhood graph itself is connected through nonimproving intermediate states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict-improvement search stagnates at a neighborhood-local optimum; stagnation is globally suboptimal when a better feasible routing solution exists elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Search Stagnation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-optimality condition is sound, but strict-improvement acceptance alone does not imply that the update returns the same state unless the algorithm's no-improvement behavior is specified. No local-search source is cited.

children.title: Pathology Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operating regimes in which neighborhood separation or repeated motion develops into persistent stagnation.

assumptions_latex: A parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\) determines feasible set \(S_\theta\), neighborhood relation \(N_\theta\), and update map \(T_\theta\).
Each \(S_\theta\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pathology transition occurs at \(\theta_0\) when every neighborhood of \(\theta_0\) contains parameters with different pathology predicates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary points where a parameterized search changes its qualitative pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\theta\in\Theta\), let \(P(\theta)\) encode one specified pathology: disconnection of \(G_{N_\theta}\), existence of a periodic orbit of \(T_\theta\) with period at least two, or existence of a globally suboptimal neighborhood-local optimum. A point \(\theta_0\) is a pathology transition when every neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta_0\) contains \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in U\) such that \(P(\theta_1)\ne P(\theta_2)\). A transition regime is any subset of \(\Theta\) formed by such boundary points for the chosen predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pathology transition is a parameter boundary arbitrarily close to which the search alternates between having and not having a specified pathology.
knowledge_statements.title: Pathology Transition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition uses neighborhoods and boundary points without specifying a topology on the parameter space. The selected pathology predicate must also be fixed rather than blended across disconnection, cycling, and stagnation. Supporting evidence is absent.

children.title: Uncertainty-Model Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between represented uncertainty and the demand, travel, service, or disruption conditions encountered in routing.

assumptions_latex: The nominal uncertainty law is \(P_0\), while the data-generating law is \(P\).
A discrepancy \(d\) is defined on the admissible probability laws \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The uncertainty model is \(\delta\)-misspecified when \(d(P,P_0)>\delta\).

notation.meaning: Nominal uncertainty law used for routing decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional misspecification relative to a chosen probability-law discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\in\mathcal P\) be the uncertainty law used to construct a routing policy, let \(P\in\mathcal P\) be the data-generating law, and let \(d:\mathcal P\times\mathcal P\to[0,\infty]\) be a stated discrepancy. For tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), the uncertainty model is \(\delta\)-misspecified exactly when \[d(P,P_0)>\delta.\] The declaration is meaningful only after specifying both the modeled random quantities and \(d\); matching finitely many moments does not imply absence of misspecification unless those moments determine the law within \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncertainty model is misspecified beyond tolerance delta when the actual and nominal probability laws differ by more than delta under a stated discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Model Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold condition is internally consistent and fits a condition leaf, but it is a chosen operational definition whose meaning depends on the modeled random quantities, admissible law class, discrepancy, and tolerance. No stochastic-routing source is supplied.

children.title: Routing-Policy Fragility
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of routing decisions or performance to deviations from the conditions used for policy design.

assumptions_latex: A routing policy \(\pi\) has expected loss \(J(\pi,P)\) under uncertainty law \(P\).
The nominal law is \(P_0\), with discrepancy \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy is locally fragile at \(P_0\) when its worst-case loss slope \(\operatorname{Frag}(\pi;P_0)\) is infinite.

notation.meaning: Expected routing loss under law P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local worst-case sensitivity of a fixed routing policy to distributional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed policy \(\pi\), define its local worst-case sensitivity at \(P_0\) by \[\operatorname{Frag}(\pi;P_0)=\limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P\\0<d(P,P_0)\le\delta}}\frac{[J(\pi,P)-J(\pi,P_0)]_+}{d(P,P_0)},\] where \([u]_+=\max\{u,0\}\). The policy is locally fragile when \(\operatorname{Frag}(\pi;P_0)=+\infty\). It is locally robust with modulus \(L<\infty\) when the same quantity is at most \(L\), yielding first-order loss growth bounded by the distributional perturbation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A routing policy is locally fragile when arbitrarily small distributional changes can cause loss increases whose ratio to perturbation size is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Policy Fragility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed sensitivity is a plausible custom definition, but no source establishes it as routing-policy fragility. A finite limsup gives an asymptotic slope bound, not the unqualified local modulus statement asserted without additional regularity or slack.

children.title: Misspecification Propagation
children.top_down_role: Pathways through which uncertainty-model errors affect route selection, recourse behavior, or service outcomes.

assumptions_latex: For every fixed policy \(\pi\), \(|J(\pi,P)-J(\pi,Q)|\le Ld(P,Q)\).
The nominal optimizer \(\pi_Q\) minimizes \(J(\pi,Q)\), and \(\pi_P\) minimizes \(J(\pi,P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le J(\pi_Q,P)-J(\pi_P,P)\le2L d(P,Q)\).

notation.meaning: Expected loss of policy pi under law P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of distributional error into out-of-model policy regret under uniform Lipschitz loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the expected loss is uniformly \(L\)-Lipschitz in the uncertainty law: \(|J(\pi,P)-J(\pi,Q)|\le Ld(P,Q)\) for every admissible policy \(\pi\) and laws \(P,Q\). If \(\pi_Q\in\arg\min_\pi J(\pi,Q)\) and \(\pi_P\in\arg\min_\pi J(\pi,P)\), then the regret caused by optimizing the misspecified law \(Q\) satisfies \[0\le J(\pi_Q,P)-J(\pi_P,P)\le2L d(P,Q).\] Thus a law error of size \(\delta\) propagates into at most \(2L\delta\) excess expected routing loss under these assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform Lipschitz sensitivity implies that optimizing a misspecified law incurs at most twice the Lipschitz constant times the law discrepancy in actual expected loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Misspecification Propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-Lipschitz regret bound is mathematically valid under the stated uniform Lipschitz and optimizer-existence assumptions, but it is a derived theorem-like bound rather than merely descriptive propagation. No inspectable stochastic-optimization source is cited.

children.title: Policy Robustness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits beyond which a routing policy no longer maintains acceptable operational behavior under uncertainty shifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Policy Robustness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an instance-space radius beyond which a routing policy loses feasibility or exceeds an accepted regret tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta\) be a routing-instance space with metric \(d\), let \(\theta_0\in\Theta\) be nominal, and let \(\pi\) be a fixed routing policy. For loss \(L(\pi,\theta)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), optimal value \(L^*(\theta)=\inf_{\pi'\in\Pi}L(\pi',\theta)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), define
\[
 r_\varepsilon(\pi,\theta_0)=\sup\left\{r\ge0:\ \pi\text{ is feasible for every }\theta\text{ with }d(\theta,\theta_0)\le r,\ \sup_{d(\theta,\theta_0)\le r}\bigl(L(\pi,\theta)-L^*(\theta)\bigr)\le\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
This radius is the policy robustness boundary. If \(r>r_\varepsilon(\pi,\theta_0)\), then the radius-\(r\) uncertainty set contains an instance on which \(\pi\) is infeasible or has regret exceeding \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robustness boundary is the largest uncertainty radius on which a fixed routing policy remains universally feasible and within the accepted regret tolerance; every larger radius admits a violating instance.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is a metric on the routing-instance space \(\Theta\).
\(L^*(\theta)\) is well-defined in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
